title: Nonprofit Pass
pitch: Nonprofit Pass helps youth-led organizations outlive graduation by enabling founders, successors, and AI agents to discover opportunities, prepare applications, and complete handoffs together.
about_excerpt: Nonprofit Pass helps youth-led organizations outlive graduation by enabling founders, successors, and AI agents to discover opportunities, prepare applications, and complete handoffs together. Like Comment Story Updates Home Page Throughout high school, I led a nonprofit that impacted more than 20,000 people. Building the organization was one of the most meaningful experiences of my life, but when I moved to college, I could no longer give it the time and attention it deserved. I began trying to transition the organization to a new leader, only to discover how difficult nonprofit succession can be. The organization’s knowledge, relationships, documents, and responsibilities were spread across different places, and there was no simple way to prepare another student to take over. In college, I was selected to attend one of America’s premier youth service summits. At the conference, I met other young nonprofit founders who were experiencing the same problem. They had created organizations that were making a real difference, but graduation, college, and new responsibilities made it difficult for them to continue leading. Their nonprofits were not ending because their missions were no longer important. They were at risk because they did not have an effective way to find, prepare, and support their next leaders. That experience inspired me to build Nonprofit Pass, a WebMCP-powered platform that helps student-led nonprofits survive leadership transitions. The platform gives founders, potential successors, and AI agents a shared space in which they can plan and complete a responsible handoff. A student interested in becoming a successor can use Nonprofit Pass to discover leadership opportunities, search and filter organizations, save nonprofits to a shortlist, compare opportunities, and prepare an application. A founder can evaluate whether an organization is ready for succession, identify missing documents or institutional knowledge, create a structured 30-day transition plan, and leave important notes for the next leader. Both people can see the same transition progress, creating continuity between the person who built the organization and the person who will lead it next. I built the project using HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, with browser-based storage to preserve user progress. I integrated WebMCP through the document.modelContext API, allowing AI agents to understand and interact with the application through structured tools. The project includes 11 WebMCP tools that can search for nonprofits, retrieve organization details, maintain a shortlist, compare opportunities, prepare and review applications, assess handoff readiness, update transition tasks, add shared notes, and summarize transition progress. My goal was not simply to let an agent click buttons. I wanted the agent to become a useful collaborator. An AI agent can organize information, identify gaps, prepare drafts, and recommend next steps, while people remain responsible for consequential decisions. Submitting an application and approving a final leadership handoff are intentionally human-only actions. This makes the agent helpful without allowing it to make irreversible decisions on someone’s behalf. One of the greatest challenges was determining how much authority an agent should have. Leadership succession affects real organizations and the communities they serve, so completely automating the process would be irresponsible. I addressed this challenge by separating assistance from approval. Agents can help people understand their options and prepare their work, but final decisions stay with the founder and successor. Another challenge was designing the application for two users with very different needs. Successors need a simple way to discover and evaluate opportunities, while founders need tools for documentation, readiness assessment, and transition planning. I created role-specific experiences for each person while connecting them through a shared transition workspace. I also added visible activity tracking so users can understand which actions were completed by a human and which were assisted by an agent. Building Nonprofit Pass taught me that an agent-native application requires much more than exposing existing interface controls to AI. It requires carefully deciding what context agents receive, which actions they may perform, how their contributions are communicated, and where human judgment must remain mandatory. I also learned that succession is not a single moment when one leader replaces another. It is an ongoing process involving trust, documentation, training, shared memory, and accountability. In the future, I hope to connect Nonprofit Pass with real nonprofit opportunities and verified organizational accounts. The platform could eventually include document integrations, mentor verification, founder-successor introductions, transition health monitoring, and long-term impact tracking. My goal is to ensure that a student’s graduation does not have to mean the end of an organization. Young founders create projects that address meaningful needs, and those projects deserve the opportunity to continue. By helping founders, successors, and AI agents work together, Nonprofit Pass creates a path for a nonprofit’s mission and impact to outlive its original founder. title: Action Check
pitch: Deterministic validation for WebMCP agent actions. Stop trusting AI agent replies. Action Check independently verifies WebMCP tool execution.
about_excerpt: Deterministic validation for WebMCP agent actions. Stop trusting AI agent replies. Action Check independently verifies WebMCP tool execution. Like Comment Story Updates Native WebMCP ready: three registered tools and the agent instruction (Chrome 152, 3 Sep) Human checkpoint: approve the exact payment, amount and request ID; the button is not a tool Checker validated: known-bad 2 calls -> 2 effects, protected 2 calls -> 1, read from the ledger Browser without WebMCP: the same four steps run by a labelled simulated agent Inspiration I started this hackathon building the same kind of thing most entries are: a site that exposes tools to an agent. The first commit in my working history, was an OAuth recovery workbench with six registered tools. A day into it I threw that out, because of something in Chrome's WebMCP evals guidance. In the troubleshooting table, for the case where a tool's output is wrong, it asks: was the UI state correctly updated, and did the agent receive the right information about the side effect? I went looking for anything that answered that question by actually calling a tool and then checking the site, and the readiness scanners I found only check whether a site exposes tools at all. When an agent calls issue_refund or add_to_cart , the reply is the only information it gets. If the reply says "done" when nothing happened, or when it happened twice, the agent cannot tell, and neither can the person who asked it. So I built the test. What it does Action Check calls a page's registered WebMCP tool the way an agent would, through document.modelContext.executeTool in real Chrome, and does not take the reply at face value. Before and after the call it runs an observe() function that reads the site's own state, whatever fits that site: a cart in localStorage, rendered rows, a read-only endpoint. The verdict comes from comparing what the tool claimed with what actually changed. observe() is never given the tool's result. It gets the live page, the phase (before or after), the tool name, the input and the page origin, and nothing else. I did it that way because the obvious shortcut, when you are writing an observer late at night, is to read the reply and return whatever it says, and I did not want that to be possible even for me. This is what WebMCP makes possible that scripted clicks did not. Before, checking a site's action from outside meant driving its UI, and what you ended up testing was the UI. Now the tool is an addressable thing with a name and a schema, so the check a developer runs from the command line is the same call the agent makes. The person's part gets smaller: approve the exact values once, on the page, and step back. The agent does the calls and the retries. The proof step reads a record neither of them wrote, so nobody has to take anybody's word for it. How I built it The live page registers three tools, stage_refund_comparison , issue_refund and prove_refund_comparison , and answers one question a payments team would ask before exposing a refund tool: can a retry refund twice? The state lives in a small Cloudflare Worker with a SQLite Durable Object per lane and run. /v1/invoke returns only a claim; /v1/observe returns the durable state, effect IDs and an evidence digest. Every trial starts with /v1/reset , which has to prove a zero-effect baseline, and the Worker caps each trial at two invocations per lane on its own, whatever the browser does. To make the retry path run, the harness commits the first refund and drops the provider's acknowledgement on purpose. The agent gets a bounded error and retries with the same request ID. On the known-bad lane that is two refunds from two calls; on the protected lane the request ID is honoured and there is one. The person approves the exact payment, amount, currency and request ID first, with a button that is an ordinary page control, so an agent cannot press it. The three tools register one after another under a single AbortController , with an abort check between each, and the page shows the count going up; it only says the tools are ready once all three are in. Taking the view down aborts that controller. The signal that execute receives is passed through to the fetch that posts to /v1/invoke , so cancelling a tool call cancels the request, and because a cancelled request is not proof of a cancelled refund the session treats it as uncertain and re-reads the ledger. Inputs are checked twice: each tool advertises a frozen JSON schema, and execute parses the same arguments again with a strict Zod schema before anything moves. A failed parse comes back as INPUT_MISMATCH naming the fields. Every error carries a code, a message and a nextAction , and the hints depend on state, so an agent that calls things in the wrong order is told what to do next. The tools carry readOnlyHint and untrustedContentHint . The CLI came on 2 September. It launches the installed Chrome with --enable-features=WebMCP (Playwright's bundled Chromium does not have WebMCP), reads the page's tools through document.modelContext.getTools() , and invokes the target once or twice with identical input. The target's own description, schema and annotations from that getTools() response go into the run's proof JSON, so each run records the contract it was checking in the site's words. Chrome 152 wants the input as JSON text, which the native test had already shown on 1 September, so the CLI sends text first and falls back to an object. On 3 September I added the external-target mode, so the same check can be pointed at a page I have nothing to do with. Challenges I ran into My own checker being wrong. Against Google's public WebMCP demos I recorded eighteen runs and set six aside because I could not stand behind the verdict. Three were on the observer side: a count-based observe() cannot see a retry that mints a second confirmation ID under the same banner, or a cart count hard-coded to 1. Three were my claim heuristic: it read a playful success reply ("You can't see me") as a refusal, and it had no answer for a tool that aborts its own registration mid-call. Those six are documented in the repository and not published. A fourth heuristic gap turned up on one of the published runs and I did fix that the same afternoon: a reply shaped {"status":"error"} now counts as a refusal, with two unit tests. A claim I had written in three places that turned out to be false. I had said the verdict "never comes from the tool's reply". In retry mode that is true, the verdict depends only on the observed delta. In once mode the verdict compares the reply's claim against the delta, which is how it tells a false success from an honest refusal. I corrected the page, the README and this text. What I can say accurately is that the observer never sees the reply. A page can only see tools registered on its own document.modelContext , not another origin's, so there is no way to build "paste a URL and check it" into the web page. The check has to drive a real Chrome from outside, which is why the CLI is the real product and the page is the front door to it. I added a builder to the page that takes a target URL, tool name, JSON input and mode, and writes out a starter observe() module and the exact command, so the first run is not a blank editor. Accomplishments that I'm proud of The results on pages I do not own. On 3 September, in Chrome 152, I ran twelve recorded checks against seven of Google's own WebMCP demos, and five found a bug. The ticket-booking demo's select_showtime replied "You can now proceed to checkout" while the checkout section stayed hidden, because the tool re-renders the page after opening it. The sports storefront's add_search_result_to_cart , retried once with identical input, put two of the same ball in the cart. Luxe Leather's add_to_cart doubled the quantity and the subtotal on retry while the header badge still said 1. Smart Home's rearrangeDOMComponents replied "Dashboard successfully updated with requested components" and rendered nothing. zaMaker's add_topping duplicated the topping on retry. The other seven runs passed and I published those too: three honest refusals, three that were idempotent, one positive control. The proof JSON for every run is in docs/evidence/ . The verdict names ended up more useful than I expected when I wrote them. Retry mode gives DUPLICATE_EFFECT , NO_EFFECT or IDEMPOTENT . Once mode gives FALSE_SUCCESS , SILENT_EFFECT , EFFECT_CONFIRMED or HONEST_REFUSAL . "Your tool claimed success and nothing appeared" is a bug report someone can act on. What I learned An agent cannot verify its own work by asking the tool, and no amount of prompting fixes that; the check has to sit outside. A verdict is only as good as what the observer reads, and I should say so. Chrome's implementation has quirks the docs do not cover yet (the JSON-text input, tools that navigate mid-call and leave nothing to observe), and a harness has to report those as harness errors, not dress them

title: Release Airlock
pitch: The agent investigates. You retain production authority.
about_excerpt: The agent investigates. You retain production authority. Like Comment Story Updates ChatGPT in its in-app browser resolved the incident on the live URL: checkout restored, 2 of 2 approved by you, 0 writes went round you The plan opens onto why the order matters, a read opens onto the exact bytes the agent got, and every lever states its cost on hover Mid-incident: the service strip shows where the failure enters the chain, and the dock says how to attach an agent and what to ask What this page lets the agent do in Triage: 13 tools now, 14 more as the response stage moves on The command palette: every lever on the console, with what it costs At a glance. A deploy console where an agent reaches 27 WebMCP tools and cannot execute any of them; every write is a proposal a person decides on the same page, beside the evidence. Stage-gated surface (13 tools in Triage, 27 in Recovery), a plan tool for order-dependent fixes, provenance grading for writes justified by untrusted content, a live storefront that breaks and recovers. Verified: 229 unit tests, 144 hit-tested Playwright gates, 91 machine-checked scenario variants, Chrome webmcp-evals 24/24 live, Lighthouse agentic 4/4, 488 real-model runs. Found and filed against the spec: a host that both calls tools and drives the DOM can complete the page's human step itself (webmachinelearning/webmcp#288, with a one-file repro and a page-side mitigation verified against the host). Live: https://release-airlock.vercel.app · Repo: https://github.com/Sidharth1999/webmcp-airlock Inspiration An on-call engineer, mid-incident, probably awakened at like 4am by their PagerDuty, wants an agent's speed without handing it authority over production -- speed literally means less revenue lost to the business and less users impacted by outages. But we can't be careless about what agents are allowed to do with our systems. This is not a hypothetical based on some research. In the last fourteen months there have been nine documented cases of a coding agent destroying data, most of them with a permission system switched on that the agent talked its way past. Examples: https://adversa.ai/blog/ai-coding-agent-incidents/ https://mondoo.com/blog/5-lessons-from-9-seconds-ai-agent-deleted-production-database Every one of those permission systems lived either inside the model, which can be argued out of anything, or in a generic host confirmation, which knows the verb and the target and nothing about where the idea came from or what the operator is looking at. Three more facts shaped the design. The cost of an incident is deciding, not clicking ( Rootly ). Mitigation happens in a console, and the kill switch beats the rollback ( LaunchDarkly ). Stage-gated access is an established pattern, just-in-time and break-glass ( IBM ). And Chrome's own WebMCP security guide asks for exactly this shape: "it's impossible to guarantee safety inside of a large language model" ( secure tools ). WebMCP puts the tool server in the page. For this problem, that location is the whole point. The page is where the operator, the evidence, and the levers already are, so the page can be the authority on what the agent may do. What it does Release Airlock is a deploy and incident console where an agent can reach every lever, and not one of them moves without you. Live: https://release-airlock.vercel.app (opens inside a running incident; works in ChatGPT's in-app browser and in Chrome with WebMCP enabled) Source, MIT: https://github.com/Sidharth1999/webmcp-airlock Video: https://youtu.be/gqN-fXtGodk It exposes 27 WebMCP tools on document.modelContext: six reads, a notebook the agent writes its findings into, nineteen propose_* writes, and propose_plan. A write tool's entire effect is to put a card in front of the operator. The world moves when a person decides, and not before. The tool surface is a function of console state. Move the response stage from Triage to Diagnosis to Recovery and tools are registered and unregistered underneath the live session (AbortController, so a real host fires toolchange). Triage grants 13 tools. Nothing that touches production exists in Triage; it is absent, not gated. A withdrawn tool leaves a tombstone, and explain_surface tells the agent why its capabilities changed. The gate is re-checked when the human decides, against the stage the operator has set by then. The page grades the evidence it served. Every read is audited into the same event log the page renders from. When an agent proposes rolling back a deploy id that appeared nowhere in the console's state and reached the agent only inside a customer-supplied log line, the card quotes the line, names the read that served it, and promotes the write to a two-key approval. For the operator, an incident is a stitching problem. The hard incidents are the ones where the order you do things in decides the outcome, and no single screen says "shed load first." The agent is good at exactly that stitching, and the console lets you audit the stitching before you let it act: One ledger. Every beat is a row on one spine: connect, each tool call, each finding, the plan, each step, what that step did. A tool call opens onto the exact bytes the agent got back, with the log position they reflect and a link to the console surface they came from. A citation is a place. "Contention cleared (#42)" is a button that lands you on log line 42. The agent objects before your click. Reach for a control it has ruled out and its reasoning appears beside that control. It counsels; it never blocks. A plan numbers the console rows it will touch and prices every step. Every executed write says what it did. When nothing moved, it says why: "No effect: scale to 9 has no effect, the autoscaler ceiling for api is 6." The customer is on screen. A storefront breaks when the incident starts, shows the status post you approved at step 4 word for word, and takes payments again when the fix lands. The receipt reads 7 of 7 approved by you, 0 writes went round you. While an agent host is attached, approval is a held gesture, not a click. The console stands on its own without an agent. Every lever is clickable by hand, states its cost, and is worth having on a bad day. How we built it One event log is the truth. The world is a pure fold over it; the UI, the tool results, and the metrics all derive from (events, world). There is no second source of state to drift. A Web Worker owns the log ; the main thread renders and forwards. The tests and the unattended driver invoke tools through the same execute path real WebMCP uses. 27 tools, documented from the registration path itself. The surface reference in the repo is generated by walking the real registration code through every stage, so it cannot disagree with the bundle. Reads return pages under 1.2 KB with a log position on every answer. Writes return only a proposal id. The gate is checked on both sides. One table decides what the agent can see; a separate table decides what the engine will execute; a test asserts they agree, because the engine must never trust that a tool was unregistered. Determinism is enforced. No wall clock and no randomness anywhere in the simulator; a linter fails the build. Same seed, byte-identical replay. Scenarios are compiled and verified, not asserted. 91 variants across four families are machine-generated and accepted only if a scripted correct run beats doing nothing and every declared trap costs more than doing nothing, probed to the same horizon. 229 unit and property tests, 142 hit-tested Playwright gates against the real page, CI on every push. No backend, no API keys; it runs in the browser. Challenges we ran into UX. Vibe-coding the UX for the project was a huge uphill battle and required hours of ruthlessness and discipline on teaching AI how to effectively present information on a page. Release Airlock deals with so much system state information and computation over with with an AI agent and that density needed to be presented really well in juxtaposition with the actual layout of an incident console. There were at least 20 iterations that were roughly functional before we landed on the most satisfactory one. AI frustration. Prompting is extremely taxing and simply aligning your vision with your AI is an uphill battle. It makes strange assumptions, gaslights you about completed work, and will sometimes even reject your judgment when it's the right call. It's important here to always have a bearing on the state of the project so you can actually assume authority on direction without the project getting derailed by your AI. A paginated tool whose contract lived only in prose the model skims. The first paid model run opened every read with cursor 0, and three tools answered with a silently empty page. The model reasoned about an incident having seen no deploys, no logs, and no traffic. The fix was one sentence in the description: "Omit it for the newest page; there is no page 0." title: FullCalendar WebMCP
pitch: WebMCP tooling for FullCalendar React applications without replacing the UI or the backend.
about_excerpt:
WebMCP tooling for FullCalendar React applications without replacing the UI or the backend.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 


 



 
 Inspiration 

 I mainly got inspired because two of the projects I developed for a couple of small businesses use FullCalendar (React), so I was hoping to add agent functionality for scheduling. This was the perfect opportunity and the perfect tool. 

 What it does 

 Exposes six tools for reading calendar context, finding events, and reading individual events, and interact with them to create, update, and delete. 

 How we built it 

 I used AI agents like Codex and Cursor. I did have experience with the FullCalendar implementation, what I did not have experience with was Chrome-specific or Chromium-specific developer tooling. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 The hardest challenge was to contain the boundary between the adapter and the host application because it could really easily outgrow and become opinionated about the implementation, which is contradictory to the ergonomics I'm looking for. 

 Coding agents have this tendency that makes us overbuild, so I actually created three implementations before actually trimming about 60% of features I'd say, before freezing. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 I think is easy to understand, and it can be very developer-agent-friendly. 

 What we learned 

 I learned that less is more and clarity is the best way to communicate a tool description for agents. I mean, AI has come so far that it can pretty much understand intent even if you mess up your prompts. 

 What's next for FullCalendar WebMCP 

 I think this implementation can grow as an open-source project, especially since FullCalendar is used in production by many devs (9M+ monthly npm downloads). And not only FullCalendar, I actually bought a domain called protocoltooling.com that I probably would like to convert to a webmcp-focused tool creation organization for widely-used web-integrations like FC.

title: Fieldset - AI-native form platform using WebMCP
pitch: Forms you and your AI agent build, fill, and analyze together — same page, same controls, with everything the agent touches highlighted.
about_excerpt: Forms you and your AI agent build, fill, and analyze together — same page, same controls, with everything the agent touches highlighted. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Every team form carries the same hidden tax. Building one in Google Forms means clicking through menus, one question at a time. Filling one means retyping details you've given a hundred times. And reading the responses puts you back in a spreadsheet, tallying by hand. WebMCP made us realize all three chores could collapse into one. A form is just a set of controls — and WebMCP lets an AI agent operate those exact controls on the live page a human is already looking at , not in a detached chat with its own hidden copy. So we built forms that you and your agent work on together . What it does Fieldset is an agent-native form platform. Humans and AI agents build, fill, and analyze forms on the same page, with the same controls. Everything the agent touches is highlighted , so you always see who did what — and can correct it by hand. Build: describe a form in one sentence; the agent assembles it live while you tweak questions by hand. Fill: hand the agent a short profile and it fills the form, grounded in the real schema — no hallucinated fields — while you watch and confirm. Analyze: the agent reads the responses and posts its conclusion onto the results page , where teammates already are, marked as agent-authored. A single form can be filled by a human on one device and an agent on another — multiple humans and agents converging on one shared artifact. 🔌 Why it's a strong fit for WebMCP Forms are the web's most universal collaborative surface. Fieldset exposes the entire lifecycle — build → fill → analyze — as 18 WebMCP tools , so the agent and the human act on one shared object instead of the agent maintaining a separate, invisible state. Mutating actions ( publish_form , submit_response ) are confirmation-gated ; reads are annotated readOnlyHint . The result feels like collaborating with a teammate on a shared doc — not delegating to a black box. How we built it Next.js (App Router) + React + TypeScript. Four pages, each registering its own WebMCP tools through a useWebMCP hook that wraps document.modelContext.registerTool() . Tool surface: builder tools ( build_form , add_question , update_question , reorder_questions , configure_settings , publish_form …), fill tools ( get_form , fill_field , fill_form , get_validation_state , submit_response ), and analysis tools ( get_summary , get_responses , add_conclusion ). Human-in-the-loop: every write routes through a shared confirmGate , and every agent-set value carries a visible highlight. Conditional logic: dependent questions (e.g. cuisine → mains) resolve their options live from another answer. Persistence: Upstash Redis (with an in-memory fallback for local dev). Deployed on Vercel; works in ChatGPT's in-app browser and Chrome with WebMCP enabled. Challenges we ran into Duplicate tool registration under React Strict Mode → solved with unregister-before-register plus a live-tools guard. Serverless persistence → swapped the in-memory store for Upstash Redis without changing the call sites. "Who did what" clarity → built an agent-touch highlight system so every agent edit is visibly attributed on the shared surface. Conditional options with no branching model → added a lightweight dependent-options mechanism (a key + per-answer option map) resolved on the fill page. Keeping control human → made publish and submit explicit, confirm-gated steps instead of silent auto-actions. Accomplishments that we're proud of The whole form lifecycle is agent-operable — build, fill, and analyze, exposed as 18 WebMCP tools . Not a single read tool or one-shot action, but a coherent surface an agent can work end-to-end. A genuinely shared human + agent canvas. Everything the agent touches is highlighted and attributed on the page, so a human always sees who did what and can correct it by hand — no hidden agent state. Human-in-the-loop by design. Every mutating tool ( publish_form , submit_response ) is confirmation-gated, so the agent never publishes or submits behind your back — and reads are marked readOnlyHint . Grounded filling, no hallucinated fields. Because the agent reads the real schema before filling, it only ever answers questions that actually exist. Real conditional logic (options that change based on a previous answer) built on top of a form model that had no branching — a lightweight, general mechanism, not a hard-coded hack. A complete, deployed product — not a proof of concept. Redis-backed persistence, a polished light/dark theme, four ready-to-try example forms, and it runs end-to-end in ChatGPT's in-app browser and Chrome + WebMCP. What we learned WebMCP's tool-registration lifecycle matters: React Strict Mode's double-mount caused InvalidStateError: Duplicate tool name , which taught us to unregister before re-registering and guard live tools. Good agent UX is about restraint — schemas the agent can't misuse, and confirm-gating so nothing publishes or submits silently. Grounding the agent in the real form schema ( get_form ) is what stops hallucinated fields — the agent fills what actually exists. Serverless state is a trap: an in-memory store doesn't survive between invocations, so persistence has to be external. title: Agent Market: agents negotiate, you confirm
pitch: A marketplace where your browser's agent haggles a full deal (price, quantity, free add-ons, shipping, coupons) with the store's agent through WebMCP page tools. You confirm every order.
about_excerpt: A marketplace where your browser's agent haggles a full deal (price, quantity, free add-ons, shipping, coupons) with the store's agent through WebMCP page tools. You confirm every order. Like Comment Story Updates negotiation between seller and buyer interface Inspiration People delegate the boring parts of shopping, but the boring part that a plain API integration can never capture is the haggle . A price is one number; a real deal is price times quantity, which freebie the seller throws in, whether shipping is waived, and which coupon stacks on top. We wanted the shopper's browser agent to work that whole space on the site the user is already looking at, and still leave the final yes/no to a human. What it does Agent Market is a multi-vendor storefront with 95k+ real products. Every page registers storefront tools on document.modelContext (WebMCP): search, product details, cart, add-ons, coupons, and a full negotiation set. A buyer's agent opens a negotiation and haggles a multi-dimensional deal against the store's agent over several rounds. When they settle, the page shows a Confirm dialog and nothing is bought until the human confirms the price . The same tools work in a WebMCP browser (ChatGPT's in-app browser, Chrome with the flag) or drive an in-page agent loop that needs no API key from the user. How we built it Frontend: Next.js 15 / React 19 / TypeScript on Vercel. StorefrontTools registers every tool on document.modelContext ; lib/agent-loop.ts is a tool-agnostic agent harness that discovers tools from the registry and runs a hand-rolled chat-completions loop. Backend: Spring Boot (Java) on Render, Azure SQL, Flyway, Hibernate. One mutation path: every state change (buyer, seller, or the server-side auto-negotiator) goes through OffersService.applyTurn , a pure function that is the only code allowed to decide a negotiation transition. It enforces the two hard economic limits (buyer total <= budget, seller net >= floor); which freebie and how much to concede is agent judgment. Human gate: accepting mints an HMAC confirm token; the order is placed only when the human clicks Confirm. Model: Google Gemini through the OpenAI-compatible endpoint, key server-side only. Challenges we ran into Gemini "thinking" models and tool history. Gemini 3.x rejects a multi-turn tool conversation unless each function call's thought_signature is echoed back. The OpenAI-compat shim dropped it, so turn 2 always 400'd. We now capture tool_calls[].extra_content on the way in and replay it on the way out. Small models stall on long tool loops. Asking a fast model to drive search then offer then counter then counter then accept meant it derailed a turn later every time. We collapsed the buyer's negotiation into a single deterministic negotiate tool: the server plays both sides of the haggle, persists every round so the transcript is real, and returns a confirm token. The agent's job is now two calls, and reaching the confirm step no longer depends on the model finishing a loop. Optimistic concurrency vs agent reliability. A strict round guard made the agent stall forever when its round number drifted. We made the guard opt-in for proposals and mandatory only for the binding accept. What we learned WebMCP's value is not "expose an API"; it is that the agent operates the same surface the human sees, so the human can step in on any turn. And the moment a flow depends on an unreliable model completing N steps, move the deterministic part What we learned WebMCP's value is not "expose an API"; it is that the agent operates the same surface the human sees, so the human can step in on any turn. And the moment a flow depends on an unreliable model completing N steps, move the deterministic part to the server and leave the model the judgment call. What's next Seller-side takeover controls, agent-negotiated bundles across multiple sellers, and a browser-vs-browser two-agent mode for a fully agentic negotiation. title: Canvasflow
pitch: A financial analysis canvas built for humans and AI agents.
about_excerpt:
A financial analysis canvas built for humans and AI agents.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 1 
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 


 



 
 We wanted to explore a simple question: 

 What would it look like if web applications were designed to be used by both humans and AI agents from the beginning? 

 For the OpenAI Hackathon, we wanted to build something genuinely useful with WebMCP rather than creating a demo that only showcased an agent clicking around a website. 

 We chose financial analysis because analysts constantly work with structured data, explore relationships between variables, generate visualizations, and iterate on insights. These workflows are highly interactive, but much of the existing web experience is still designed exclusively around human interaction. 

 That led to CanvasFlow — an agent-native financial analysis workspace designed to make data exploration and visualization accessible to both humans and AI agents. 

 What it does: 

 CanvasFlow provides an interactive workspace for financial data analysis and visualization. 

 Users can bring data into the canvas, explore it, analyze relationships within the dataset, and generate visual representations of their findings. 

 The key difference is that CanvasFlow is not only designed around the traditional human UI. 

 We exposed core application capabilities through WebMCP, allowing an AI agent to interact with CanvasFlow through structured tools rather than having to interpret the interface and figure out where to click. 

 This creates two complementary interaction layers: 

 Humans get the visual canvas.
Agents get structured tools. 

 Instead of an agent simply reading a financial dashboard, it can actually operate the application's capabilities to perform analysis and manipulate the workspace. 

 The goal is to demonstrate what becomes possible when web applications are designed to be agent-operable, rather than merely agent-readable. 

 How we built it: 

 CanvasFlow was built as a WebMCP-enabled web application with the goal of keeping the architecture simple and focused on the core interaction between the application and an AI agent. 

 We designed the application around a set of useful financial analysis and visualization capabilities and exposed those capabilities as WebMCP tools. 

 This allows an agent to discover and invoke functionality directly through structured tool calls. 

 The application was prototyped extremely quickly using Google Antigravity, allowing us to go from the initial idea to a functional WebMCP-enabled prototype in less than 20 minutes. 

 Rather than spending the majority of the hackathon building a complex interface, we focused on validating the underlying idea: 

 Can a web application expose meaningful functionality to an agent while remaining intuitive for a human? 

 CanvasFlow is our answer to that question. 

 Challenges we ran into: 

 The biggest challenge was not getting an agent to interact with a webpage. 

 It was deciding what the agent should actually be able to do. 

 There is a significant difference between exposing UI actions as tools and exposing meaningful application capabilities. 

 We had to think carefully about the right level of abstraction for each WebMCP tool: tools needed to be understandable to an agent while still mapping cleanly to useful actions inside the application. 

 We also had to balance two different users. 

 A financial analyst needs an intuitive visual workspace, while an AI agent needs structured, deterministic capabilities. 

 Designing for both without allowing one interaction model to compromise the other became one of the most interesting parts of the project. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of: 

 We're proud that CanvasFlow demonstrates a practical use case for WebMCP rather than treating it as a novelty. 

 We built a working agent-native financial analysis environment in less than 20 minutes, while still demonstrating a meaningful interaction between an AI agent and a web application. 

 We're particularly proud of the fact that the application doesn't require the agent to simply “look at the screen” and imitate a human. 

 The agent can interact with actual application capabilities through structured WebMCP tools. 

 More importantly, CanvasFlow gave us a practical way to explore what we believe is a much larger shift: 

 The next generation of web applications may need two interfaces — one for humans and one for agents. 

 What we learned: 

 Our biggest lesson was that agent accessibility is fundamentally different from traditional web accessibility. 

 Humans are exceptionally good at interpreting interfaces. We can look at a chart, understand what a button probably does, navigate unfamiliar layouts, and adapt when something isn't obvious. 

 Agents need something different: clear capabilities, structured inputs, predictable outputs, and explicit actions. 

 WebMCP provides an interesting bridge between those worlds. 

 We also learned that building for agents changes how you think about application architecture. Instead of asking only: 

 «“What should the user be able to click?”» 

 you start asking: 

 «“What should an agent be able to accomplish?”» 

 That shift in perspective influenced almost every design decision we made in CanvasFlow. 

 What's next for CanvasFlow: 

 CanvasFlow is currently a prototype, but we see several directions for taking it much further. 

 We want to expand its financial analysis capabilities, support more sophisticated datasets and visualizations, and make the agent capable of performing longer multi-step analytical workflows. 

 We also want to explore collaboration between human analysts and agents — where an analyst can direct an agent to investigate a question, review its analysis, modify the direction of the investigation, and ultimately turn the results into a polished financial insight. 

 Longer term, CanvasFlow is less about being another financial dashboard and more about exploring a broader idea: 

 What happens when every useful capability inside a web application is designed to be accessible to both humans and agents? 

 CanvasFlow is our first experiment in building toward that future.

StudyFlow - An adaptive study planner that helps students build realistic schedules, explore better study plans, and adapt when their workload changes.

 Story

 Overview of upcoming work, workload, and study capacity, with the same planning context available to the agent through WebMCP. 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 Visualizes deadlines and scheduled study sessions, while WebMCP lets the agent simulate, draft, and apply schedule changes.

 Overview of upcoming work, workload, and study capacity, with the same planning context available to the agent through WebMCP. 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 Visualizes deadlines and scheduled study sessions, while WebMCP lets the agent simulate, draft, and apply schedule changes. 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Lets students manage recurring study hours and blocked periods, which the agent can also update through WebMCP. 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Overview of upcoming work, workload, and study capacity, with the same planning context available to the agent through WebMCP. 
 
 1 2 3 4 



 
 Inspiration 

 Students often know what work they need to finish, but they don't know if it will fit into the time they have. We did a survey with 16 students and found that the majority 31.3% of the students say that the actual time taken to complete their task is usually longer than they estimated. 50% of the students said they experience increased stress due to planning difficulties. So, as fellow students, we understand that, so we are inspired to build StudyFlow. 

 What it does 

 StudyFlow compares academic tasks and deadlines with a student’s available study time. It helps students manage tasks, review their workload, and create realistic study schedules. 

 WebMCP fits StudyFlow because we think planning is an iterative process. Students usually need to ask questions, explore alternatives, and make changes based on their current workload. WebMCP lets the agent interact with StudyFlow’s tasks, availability, and scheduling engine. 

 For this hackathon, we added WebMCP with 9 tools: 

 
 Read Study Plan State 
 Add Academic Task 
 Update Study Time 
 Manage Academic Task 
 Simulate Study Plan 
 Draft Study Plan 
 Accept Study Plan 
 Reject Study Plan 
 Record Missed Study Session 
 

 These tools let a student work with an agent through the full planning process. The agent can understand the situation, test changes, prepare a plan, and help the student recover after a missed session. 

 How we built it 

 We started building StudyFlow by brainstorming the features we want and turning them into concrete specifications. We then used agentic coding tools to build the specification part by part. And then we would do manual verification and code review of the AI generated code. 

 After starting this hackathon, we connected the frontend to WebMCP. and then add tools where they each have an input schema, purpose, and result. We also added a backend simulation endpoint where the agent can simulate schedules with hypothetical availability, blocked periods, or deadlines without saving them. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 
 We had to think of how we design the WebMCP tools while making sure we keep the user in the loop. The user should be able to approve or reject actions that would make changes to their persisted schedule. 
 Since the WebMCP tool calls are outside of our React flow, we had to make an event system so that we can refresh our UI when the tool call is done. 
 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 Our main accomplishment that we are proud of is that StudyFlow is agent compatible. With this new interface, we will be able to reach more users and allow them to have a natural interaction with our web app. 

 What we learned 

 We learned how to add WebMCP agent tools to an app in way where we had to think about the quality of human-agent interaction. Meaning, we had to come up with a tool where the user can discuss and iterate on their schedule with hypothetical conditions while leveraging our scheduling engine. We believe that it is similar to how we normally use AI agents, so it should feel familiar for our users and hope they find this WebMCP addition useful. 

 Of course, we learned how to add WebMCP into our website and add tools that allow AI agents to perform actions in our web app. It is going to be a very valuable technical experience for us as we're going deeper into the AI era. 

 What's next for StudyFlow 

 Next, we want StudyFlow to learn from actual study time and be able to estimate task duration using AI. We also want to offer more ways to compare possible schedules.

title: Stratum
pitch: The agent can do your job. WebMCP just makes sure it can't do the one part that's actually yours.
about_excerpt: The agent can do your job. WebMCP just makes sure it can't do the one part that's actually yours. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration The starting point was a question we could not answer cleanly: when an agent holding a valid session asks to move 40,000 dollars, what should the page say? Our first answer was to say nothing and return an error. We built that, watched it, and found the failure mode immediately. A bare refusal tells the agent it failed but not that it should stop, so the sensible next move for a capable agent is to try again differently. The refusal was correct and the outcome was still wrong. Reading the WebMCP specification changed the shape of the answer. Once a page can describe its capabilities in a channel the agent reads, a boundary stops having to be an error at all. It can be a documented part of the contract, with a stated reason and a route forward. That is a thing we wanted to exist, so we built it. What it does STRATUM is a treasury desk that an agent and a person operate together. The agent reads the ledger, prices a payment, checks it against the agreement, and stages it. It then calls release_funds and is refused, in a structured reply that explains why and names request_human_confirmation as the thing to call instead. It calls that, the gate opens in the same tab carrying the agent's own note, and the person confirms at a depth set by what is at stake: one confirmation for a 12 dollar renewal, a live challenge for a new payee, and full presence, authenticity and binding checks for a 41,800 dollar wire. The agent polls, reads the sealed receipt, and verifies the record is intact. How we built it React and Vite on Vercel for the desk, with the whole tool surface in one module that registers on mount and unregisters on unmount. A FastAPI service on Render holds the state machine and an append only hash chain, one block per event, so refusals are evidence rather than log lines. The tiering is derived from the action in about fifteen lines, kept deliberately plain so a reader can check the rule against the demo in seconds rather than running the code to predict it. The boundary is enforced in three independent places: component state no tool can reach, an isTrusted check on every settlement, and the server state machine behind both. Testing was done against the deployed URL rather than a local build, because the thing that has to work is the thing a judge will open. Challenges we ran into Making the refusal useful. Returning a clean error was easy and it was not enough. The work was in deciding what a refusal owes its caller, and the answer turned out to be three things: an unambiguous statement that retrying will not help, a plain reason, and the next tool with its input. Writing next_tool into the payload was a one line change that altered the behaviour on the other side completely. Not overclaiming the defence. isTrusted is a real property that page script cannot forge, and it is not protection against a browser extension or a driver attached at the CDP layer. It would have been easy to describe it as tamper proof. Instead the README states precisely what it does and does not cover, and the receipt records the depth that was actually performed rather than the one that was requested. A backend that sleeps. The audit service runs on a free instance with a cold start of up to a minute, which would have been fatal for a judge opening the page cold. Every call to it is now best effort with a timeout, and the boundary is enforced locally as well as remotely, so a cold backend degrades the evidence trail and never the refusal itself. Accomplishments that we're proud of The refusal carries its own remedy. release_funds does not throw. It returns a readable explanation plus the name and input shape of the tool to call instead, so the agent recovers on its next call rather than retrying into a wall. The tiering is the part that would survive real users. Proportionate friction is what keeps a control switched on, and a control that has been switched off protects nothing. Deriving the tier from the action rather than accepting it from the caller is what makes the tiering meaningful rather than decorative. The honesty holds up under inspection. The faces in the presence gate are synthetic, the numbers measure the matcher rather than real skin, and that caveat is printed on the certificate the system issues. A system built to state what it could not establish should be held to that same standard itself. What we learned A boundary is an interface, and it has an audience of two. Most security design assumes the only reader is a person, which is why it produces modals and codes. An agent reads too, and it reads differently. It needs to know not only that it was refused but what to do next, or it will invent something. Registering a capability is a promise you have to keep. Once release_funds is in the list, it has to refuse every time, from every caller, whether or not the backend is awake. That constraint pushed the enforcement down into three independent layers and made the architecture simpler rather than harder. What's next for STRATUM The tiering rules belong to whoever operates the desk, not to us, so the next step is a declarative policy the operator writes and the page enforces, rather than thresholds living in a module. After that, cryptographic binding of the receipt to the session that produced it, using a WebAuthn assertion, so the record proves which device and which present human settled it rather than asserting it. The longer aim is that none of this stays a product. It is a small, plain, well described pattern that any page can register, so an agent meeting a limit anywhere on the web learns the same thing in the same shape. title: AquaEye
pitch: Agentic water safety system that connects live industrial sensors, PLC control, and WebMCP tools for intelligent monitoring and safe pump decisions.
about_excerpt: Agentic water safety system that connects live industrial sensors, PLC control, and WebMCP tools for intelligent monitoring and safe pump decisions. Like Comment Story Updates WebMCP tools Siemens_TIA_Portal_PLC_Program AquaEye dashboard Sensors + PLC + Raspberry Pi Inspiration## Inspiration Water safety systems often generate large amounts of sensor data, but operators still need to interpret those signals and interact with industrial control systems manually. We wanted to explore how an AI agent could work with a real physical system while keeping industrial safety logic in control. This led to AquaEye — an intelligent water safety system combining real-time water sensing, Siemens PLC control, Raspberry Pi edge computing, and WebMCP-based AI-agent interaction. What AquaEye Does AquaEye monitors water conditions using pH, turbidity, and flow sensors connected to a Siemens PLC. The system architecture consists of: Industrial sensors for real-time water monitoring Siemens PLC for industrial control and safety logic Raspberry Pi as the edge-computing layer Python backend communicating with the PLC using Snap7 Web dashboard for human monitoring WebMCP tools that allow AI agents to interact with AquaEye through the browser The backend converts the physical sensor signals into structured information and evaluates the water condition against configured safety limits. WebMCP Integration WebMCP is the key interface between AquaEye and AI agents. AquaEye exposes five tools: get_water_status — retrieves the current water measurements and system condition. analyze_water_safety — analyzes the current water parameters and returns a safety decision. get_system_status — provides the overall system state. start_pump — provides controlled pump-start interaction. stop_pump — provides controlled pump-stop interaction. This allows an AI agent to discover AquaEye's capabilities and interact with live system information through the browser instead of relying only on a traditional dashboard. Human + Agent Collaboration The dashboard is designed for the human operator, while WebMCP provides an interface for AI-agent interaction. The human can visually monitor the physical system and dashboard, while an AI agent can request structured system information and analyze the current water-safety condition. Importantly, the AI interaction does not replace the industrial safety layer. The PLC and programmed safety logic remain responsible for the physical control system. How It Was Built The physical sensors are connected to the Siemens PLC. The Raspberry Pi communicates with the PLC using Snap7 and runs the AquaEye backend. The Flask backend exposes the system data through APIs. The web frontend presents the live information to the operator. WebMCP is implemented directly in the frontend using document.modelContext.registerTool(...) . Each registered tool connects an agent request to the corresponding AquaEye backend capability. Challenges One of the main challenges was connecting the browser-based WebMCP layer to a real industrial PLC system. We had to integrate PLC communication, Raspberry Pi networking, the Python backend, the web dashboard, and WebMCP while maintaining a clear separation between AI interaction and physical safety control. Another challenge was making the system work with live industrial data rather than a simulated software-only environment. What I Learned This project demonstrated how WebMCP can become an interface between AI agents and real-world systems. I learned how to combine industrial automation, PLC communication, edge computing, web technologies, and agent-facing tools into one architecture. The project also showed that AI-agent interaction can be added on top of an existing industrial control architecture without removing the deterministic safety logic that protects the physical system. What's Next The next stage for AquaEye is to expand the system with additional water-quality parameters, richer historical analysis, predictive monitoring, and more intelligent agent workflows. The long-term goal is to develop AquaEye into a platform where AI agents can assist operators in monitoring, diagnosing, and managing industrial water systems while maintaining appropriate industrial safety boundaries. title: spool
pitch: Turns messy CSV migration into a deterministic, agent-driven workflow with phase-aware WebMCP tools, validation, recovery, and verified export
about_excerpt: Turns messy CSV migration into a deterministic, agent-driven workflow with phase-aware WebMCP tools, validation, recovery, and verified export Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration What it doesSPOOL SPOOL is a local-first, agent-assisted data migration system designed to turn messy CSV files into validated, structured, database-ready outputs without forcing the user to manually supervise every transformation. The user provides a source file and selects the desired outcome. SPOOL then runs a deterministic workflow that profiles the data, infers field types and mappings, creates a transformation plan, dry-runs it, identifies unsafe ambiguities, executes the migration, verifies the result, and produces an export. Its key WebMCP innovation is Temporal WebMCP. Instead of exposing every tool to an AI agent permanently, SPOOL dynamically exposes only the capabilities that are valid for the current workflow state. For example, planning tools are available only after profiling is complete, execution tools appear only when the migration is ready, and stale capabilities disappear when mappings or source state change. This means the website—not the model—owns workflow correctness. SPOOL uses constrained deterministic transformations rather than arbitrary AI-generated code. It includes typed schema inference, data validation, revision-aware mappings, dry runs, Worker-based execution, recovery after refresh, violation reporting, and spreadsheet formula-injection protection. The product is designed around a simple experience: Add data → choose outcome → run Autopilot → resolve only genuine ambiguities → receive verified output. The broader idea behind SPOOL is that complex web workflows should expose agent capabilities contextually rather than giving agents a permanent toolbox and expecting them to manage application state correctly themselves. title: ForgeMCP-Multi-Agent Research & Game Studio
pitch: Humans and AI agents use real WebMCP tools to observe Earth, test Cube Chess 512 AI, create 3D systems, verify evidence, and keep final decisions human-controlled.
about_excerpt: Humans and AI agents use real WebMCP tools to observe Earth, test Cube Chess 512 AI, create 3D systems, verify evidence, and keep final decisions human-controlled. Like 1 Comment Story Updates ForgeMCP — Multi-Agent Research & Game Studio ForgeMCP is an agent-native web platform where people and AI agents use real browser-native WebMCP tools to observe Earth, test a deterministic 8×8×8 chess engine, create verifiable 3D systems, and keep consequential decisions under human control. Core workflow HUMAN → COORDINATOR → SPECIALIST AGENTS → WEBMCP TOOLS → REAL DATA / ENGINE → VERIFICATION → HUMAN DECISION What it does ForgeMCP brings three working systems into one visible, auditable workflow: OBSERVE — Terra Observation System A user can select or search for an area of interest and investigate environmental change using public Earth-observation sources. Terra can retrieve location context, bounded research areas, representative satellite imagery, terrain/elevation context, hydrology signals and public hazard observations. Results return structured provenance, timestamps, confidence, uncertainty and a verification state. Terra never presents an AI-generated picture as satellite evidence. Missing or failed provider responses remain INSUFFICIENT_DATA or NOT_CONNECTED . Observations, anomalies, hypotheses, preliminary risk alerts and verified findings are kept separate. A hypothesis is not promoted to a fact without supporting evidence and, where required, field or in-situ verification. LEARN & COMPETE — Cube Chess 512 AI Cube Chess 512 is a deterministic three-dimensional chess laboratory with an 8×8×8 board and 512 addressable fields. ForgeMCP uses a pinned rules engine to execute a small candidate-versus-baseline benchmark with paired seeds and side swaps. The records contain replayable legal moves, results, termination state, legality checks, a deterministic material proxy and engine provenance. The application does not invent Elo ratings, game counts or training results. A candidate cannot be promoted merely because an agent recommends it: legality and regression gates must pass, a recorded result must exist, and literal human approval is required. CREATE — Game and 3D Creation Studio The Game Studio lets a person and agents configure procedural station concepts, generate deterministic low-poly glTF assets and PNG textures, inspect the exact generated geometry, compare visible results, run QA and export a manifest. It also includes a deterministic basic Capture Chess blueprint and a separate link to the playable Cube Chess 512 deployment. Concept artwork is labelled as concept artwork. A generated prototype is not described as manufactured hardware, an original satellite product or a production-ready model. How we built it The public application is built with React, TypeScript, Vite and browser-based 3D rendering. Real tools are registered through: document.modelContext.registerTool(...) Each tool has a focused responsibility, a validated input schema, structured output, explicit error states and a traceable source or engine boundary. The coordinator is deterministic and does not claim that an LLM ran when it did not. The live tool inventory covers system status, place and AOI handling, Terra observation and verification workflows, the pinned Cube benchmark and promotion gates, visual QA, reversible actions and guarded commerce drafts. Chrome 149+ smoke tests discover and execute the native WebMCP tools in a real browser session instead of mocking document.modelContext . The dashboard exposes the human request, coordinator decision, active specialist, WebMCP tool, validated input, real source or engine, structured output, provenance, confidence, uncertainty, verification result, proposed action and human approval state. The hardest challenges The hardest problem was not adding more AI. It was defining where AI must stop. For Terra, the authority must be the original observation, provider metadata, measurement method and verification record. For Cube, the authority must be the deterministic rules engine, legal execution and saved game result. For mutations, the authority remains the human. A second challenge was integrating two projects that existed before the competition without presenting older work as new. The public repository therefore separates: PRE-CHALLENGE WORK: earlier Terra data integrations, Earth-observation research, Cube rules engine, self-play experiments, 3D models and game UI. NEW WEBMCP CHALLENGE WORK: ForgeMCP coordinator, browser-native tool registration, integrated Terra/Cube/Create workflows, structured provenance, verification timeline, approval gates, public dashboard, judge path and demo. A third challenge was making failures honest and visible. A provider timeout, missing image, unconnected service or unsupported browser must not quietly become a fabricated answer. Accomplishments we are proud of A public working web application with real document.modelContext.registerTool(...) handlers. Fifty registered central tools discoverable through the live capability inventory. Terra workflows grounded in public providers with provenance, uncertainty and strict evidence classes. A pinned deterministic Cube engine that executes the current-run benchmark and rejects illegal promotion paths. Real-browser Chrome 149+ WebMCP smoke testing. Visible PASS / WARNING / FAIL states, audit history, human approval and rollback boundaries. A free judge path with public source code, an open-source license, run instructions and a short demonstration video. What we learned WebMCP is most valuable when it lets a person and an agent operate a real application together, not when it merely adds another chat box. Small, single-purpose tools are easier to validate and audit than one oversized agent action. Structured results are safer than persuasive prose. Provenance and uncertainty must be visible at the same time as the result. Most importantly, an agent can coordinate and propose, but evidence, deterministic engines and human judgment must remain the final authorities. Why it matters My long-term goal is to use technology to help people and protect the environment. Terra approaches that goal through earlier investigation of water loss, rivers, lakes, terrain and environmental hazards. Cube Chess 512 approaches it through logic, spatial reasoning, competition and learning. The Creation Studio provides a practical space for turning ideas into testable visual systems. ForgeMCP connects those directions around one principle: AI should help humans observe, learn, create and verify — while real evidence and human decisions stay in control. What is next The next steps are to expand the audited Terra tool coverage, strengthen browser and regression testing, connect additional verified data adapters, run larger reproducible Cube candidate evaluations, improve accessibility and mobile performance, and keep every new mutation behind explicit approval, audit logging and rollback. The project will continue separating observations from hypotheses and challenge-period work from earlier research. The aim is not to claim certainty where it does not exist, but to help people reach better, faster and more transparent decisions with real tools. title: Itta Recovery DNA
pitch: WebMCP turns a registration photo into Recovery DNA, helping people and agents identify a changed bicycle and prepare a safe, human-reviewed recovery report.
about_excerpt: WebMCP turns a registration photo into Recovery DNA, helping people and agents identify a changed bicycle and prepare a safe, human-reviewed recovery report. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Inspiration Itta is an existing QR-based recovery service for bicycles and personal mobility devices. While working on its registration flow, I noticed two connected problems. First, registration is harder than it looks. Owners of older bicycles often cannot remember the exact manufacturer, model, official color, or size. Second, even a correctly identified model is not enough for recovery. Replaceable parts can change, logos can be covered, and two bicycles from the same product line can look almost identical. That led to Recovery DNA: a visual passport made from the small details that belong to one specific bicycle. What it does The experience begins with registration. The owner selects a vehicle type and adds a representative photo. A browser agent examines the photo already visible on the page and uses WebMCP tools to present likely manufacturer, model, color, and size candidates. The suggestions are never applied automatically. The owner reviews the evidence, chooses the best candidate, edits anything necessary, and remains responsible for the final registration. The agent can then propose a Recovery DNA made from distributed visual anchors: decal placement, frame geometry, distinctive marks, damage, accessories, and personal signs of wear. It also distinguishes durable evidence from parts that can easily be replaced. The owner reviews and confirms these anchors before they can be reused. Later, when a bicycle is found, the agent compares the new photo with the owner-confirmed Recovery DNA. It explains which details remain, which parts changed, what is missing, and how likely it is to be the same bicycle. Finally, it prepares a recovery report for human review. Nothing is sent automatically, and the result is presented as a visual probability assessment—not forensic proof of ownership. Why WebMCP This workflow needs more than a chatbot response. The agent must understand the page’s current state, inspect the photo already shared with the user, request additional evidence when necessary, and return structured results to the correct interface. WebMCP provides that bridge between the agent’s reasoning and Itta’s product UI. The tools do not receive raw image files, private owner data, contact information, or location. The agent visually inspects what is already rendered in the shared browser, while WebMCP carries only limited context and validated structured results. This creates a continuous human-agent journey across registration, identification, comparison, and recovery—while keeping every consequential decision with a person. How I built it The demo is built with React, TypeScript, and Vite and deployed on Vercel. I implemented eight WebMCP tools using document.modelContext.registerTool() : Registration tools read the current draft, request focused evidence, and render up to three specification candidates. Recovery DNA tools expose limited owner or finder context, render visual anchors, display an identity comparison, and prepare a recovery-report draft. Tools are registered only after the user explicitly opens the relevant assistant. They are removed with an AbortController when the scene changes, the component unmounts, or the photo is replaced. This prevents stale tools from modifying the wrong stage of the experience. The public challenge route is isolated from Itta’s production authentication, database, analytics, and reporting systems. All demo state stays in browser memory. Challenges The biggest design challenge was making WebMCP essential rather than decorative. Simple specification autofill was useful, but it did not fully demonstrate what becomes possible when a person and an agent share the same web experience. Recovery DNA made the collaboration more meaningful: the agent contributes visual reasoning across two moments in time, while the product contributes structured state, validation, lifecycle control, and human confirmation. Another challenge was judge accessibility. A reviewer may not have a bicycle photo available, so the demo includes a fictional before-and-after sample. The bicycle changes its saddle, front wheel, and visible branding to demonstrate why a model name or basic photo match is insufficient. Unsupported browsers also receive a clearly labeled simulation preview. It demonstrates the interface without pretending that a WebMCP call occurred. What I learned WebMCP is most valuable as a trusted interaction boundary—not as a replacement for the interface or the user. Agents are good at interpreting ambiguous evidence. Websites are good at holding state, validating structured actions, protecting private data, and asking for confirmation. Combining those strengths creates experiences that would be difficult to achieve with either side alone. What's next The next step is to connect owner-confirmed Recovery DNA to Itta’s real registration and QR recovery flows. The same approach could later support scooters, pets, luggage, and other registered objects whose identity depends on more than a serial number or product name. title: Unfolded
pitch: Convert 3D shapes into buildable clay templates. Agent handles complexity, human decide, they collaborate and the template is always exported with precise, deterministic geometry by the app itself
about_excerpt: Convert 3D shapes into buildable clay templates. Agent handles complexity, human decide, they collaborate and the template is always exported with precise, deterministic geometry by the app itself Like 1 Comment Story Updates Mobile screens ( Dark mode ) Light mode ( Desktop ) Dark mode (Desktop) The problem we are solving Design initiated by Chat-GPT Design initiated by Chrome tab more mobile screens ( light mode ) mobile screens ( light mode ) Light / Dark mode From a printed template back to a design The exported printable PDF template ( multi page ) webMCP tools available ( 1 of 3 ) webMCP tools available ( 2 of 3 ) webMCP tools available ( 3 of 3 ) Design system ( Dark mode ) Inspiration I've been cutting pottery templates out of cereal boxes for years now. AI chats are great at generating shapes and make complex changes with unusual requirements, but their non deterministic output produce unexpected and misaligned PDFs, especially during the discovery phase of a new piece where the requirements constantly changes. The problem is, the potter notice the failure only after hours of building in the studio. Try for yourself to generate with any AI agent a multipage template for a simple mug, same prompt in 3 separate sessions. The result is always different, most of the time fail silently where it matters the most. I have created Unfolded to move the template generation part of the workflow away from the AI chat into a more deterministic output I can control. The output is a multi page PDF template that always work is always true to the 3D shape you have built. The idea is to retain AI for complexity, difficult math calculations and things that are practically impossible to do in a deterministic UI. When is connected to unfolded, you can ask AI things like: Keep the same vessel style but change the volume to 500ml Prepare a template inspired by this photo, for a porcelain vase with thin walls This container should hold a large americano comfortably 10 bowls like this should be stackable and only 1cm of each one should be visible when stacked What Unfolded does Unfolded is a parametric 3D builder that helps with both the template generation and the decision of what to make. It's a shared 3D workspace where a potter and an AI agent shape a vessel together: the potter keeps the creative decisions, the agent inspects and revises the live design through WebMCP, and Unfolded guarantees the geometry: clay shrinkage, clay type wall thickness, mid-surface-developed. It was thought from the ground up with the potter workflow in mind and its strenght is how flexibly it is and can adapt to many unexpected use case and workflow without letting you down. Most problems related to pottery known how, PDF generations and cross browsers workflow are automagically prevented under the hood without anyone noticing. My favourite features ( try them in the app, especially on mobile ) I've worked a lot at the UX flow for the cross-device handshake . The potter can also design and work with agents on non webMCP capable browsers. One tap on Open in ChatGPT hands off into the ChatGPT app with a prompt that already carries a single-use pairing code; Chat-GPT hidden browser joins the potter's live session over WebSockets. From then on every agent edit appears in the browser within about a second, every browser edit is visible to the agent on its next tool call, and every change ( human or agent ) is a shared undo step. Undo/redo work for both humand and AI changes, no matter what device pushed them. The handover works both ways ( or even 3 ways! ): The agent reads the current design, changes the form, sees the same 3D preview the potter sees — and solves problems that are genuinely hard at the workbench. "Make it hold exactly 350 ml but keep the proportions" --> one sentence for an agent, an afternoon of guesswork by hand. The generated PDF is really well thought ( if I say so myself! ): True-scale printable templates and a calibration ruler on every sheet, QR code to reproduce the design in the browser even after it was printed, seam allowance to glue the template together. This is fully designed around the potter's workflow. The app registers 13 typed WebMCP tools on document.modelContext the moment it loads. The reasons there are so many tools is that I got a little carried away about performance measurament of webMCP. I even made a npm package called MCP-profiler to measure everything from the tools speed to the agent harness time. Most of the slowness in my app ( 30seconds to connect the tools at times ) is unsurprisely caused by my 3D model and the whole context I am passing over with each tool. Something I will definitely look into after the hackathon. How I built it React, TypeScript, Three.js, React Three Fiber, Zustand, Zod, Tailwind CSS, and shadcn/ui, with jsPDF generating the true-scale multi-page templates. Live cross-device sync runs on a Cloudflare Worker with a per-session Durable Object; pairing invitations are single-use and short-lived, so no URL ever carries a durable capability. The interface and the WebMCP tools share the same Zustand store and Zod schemas, so human and agent edits stay synchronized by construction . Everything sits behind a test gate (geometry, schemas, sync protocol), end-to-end suites running real Chromium against the production bundle and two deeper suites that spin up a local Worker to exercise the pairing protocol with two real browsers. Along the way I published webmcp-profiler , also sitting in this repo, an npm package that benchmarks every tool's execution time and payload size. Profiling my own app with it caught a ~20% trim in tool-definition metadata that every conversation was paying for. Challenges and lessons The geometric challenge: complex curved surfaces cannot be flattened without distortion, so for the demo I focused on symmetrical, faceted forms built from planar slabs, where the unroll is exact , not approximate. But my ambitions are higher for this tool and I already have a full plan for complex shapes and things that were not really possible until now. The UX challenge was one I haven't seen discussed anywhere: when ChatGPT drives a WebMCP page, it does so in a built in, hidden browser. Solving the two-way conversation between that invisible tab and the browser the user actually looks at — live sessions, one-tap pairing prompts, agent share links carrying single-use join tokens — became the heart of the project. Here is a page with a nice breakdown of the different user flow the user can face (I have done this for myself, but could be helpful for someone judging the project): User Flows mapped out I am not satisfied with the solution I have found for the pairing, In the future my goal is to merge the link with token, pairing, webMCP concept into a single binary flag. The user does not need to know about webMCP at all, it should simply copy a prompt on his agent to start building from anywhere. The bigger lesson is that WebMCP shines with a clear division of labour: the agent is brilliant at intent and connected constraints, the app owns the deterministic math, and the human keeps the creative decisions. The agent chooses the parameters; the geometry is always right. What's next Better UX. Curved profiles, more construction types and layers, performance optimisation of webMCP and assembly guidance. Maybe a login, and reusable studio presets and lids and matching sets, where the shrinkage math matters most.
