Most of the backend code is AI written and went through many iterations and adversarial reviews. Luca Gugliemi Product designer with front-end superpowers. title: WebMCP Simulator
pitch: See what your website could become with WebMCP: real tools, a real agent, every change visible, nothing ever submitted. A tool that helps to transition websites to WebMCP.
about_excerpt: See what your website could become with WebMCP: real tools, a real agent, every change visible, nothing ever submitted. A tool that helps to transition websites to WebMCP. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Frontpage of WebMCP Simulator Demo entry Simulation started Readiness report Implementation Pack What WebMCP Simulator does WebMCP Simulator lets a website owner, agency or product manager experience what a website could become with WebMCP, before anyone touches the original site. It thus shows possibilities WebMCP offers before the website owner has to commit to any changes on the website in a visual manner. Landing page. Paste a URL or click "Try the HeatFlow demo". HeatFlow is a fictional heating company built into the simulator, so nobody needs a site that already implements WebMCP. Its website is invented; its tools are real. Analysis. Five potential WebMCP capabilities are listed as proposals, each with the reason an explicit tool beats interface guessing, a "Website today" versus "With WebMCP" comparison and the proposed JSON input schema. Simulation. "Launch simulation" renders the HeatFlow site and registers five tools through document.modelContext.registerTool : search_services , check_service_area , compare_services , prepare_quote_request and reset_simulation . The agent panel shows "Connected" only when the browser actually exposed the API. Visible agent work. Every accepted call changes the page in front of the person. The section that reacted pulses once, then keeps an outline and a badge naming the tool and what it changed, the fields or cards the call populated are emphasised, the matching tool row lights up, and the activity feed records the call with its name and time. Human interactions never trigger that emphasis, and no cursor or click is simulated. Readiness report and implementation pack. An inspectable heuristic scores the site today versus with WebMCP, and a Markdown brief plus a ready-to-copy Codex prompt adapts to the access the owner really has, including "no repository or technical access". Nothing is ever sent. prepare_quote_request fills an editable draft and stops. The original website is never modified. Better safe than sorry, right? Why this use case is a strong fit for WebMCP First of all WebMCP is VERY technical. Secondly: WebMCP asks site owners to invest before they can see the result. There is no site a decision-maker can visit today to feel the difference between an agent guessing at a DOM and an agent calling explicit tools. The simulator is that missing pre-implementation step, and it only works because of WebMCP: The agent's calls go through the browser's own registry. What the viewer watches is the real contract between page and agent, not a scripted mock. A judge can open DevTools, call getTools() and see the same five tools the page lists. Each HeatFlow tool isolates one concrete reason WebMCP beats interface guessing. check_service_area depends on two inputs and deterministic business rules; the page says it plainly: "The agent cannot invent availability." compare_services combines price, efficiency and suitability that the site spreads across separate cards. prepare_quote_request bundles four fields behind a human confirmation boundary. search_services replaces navigation and terminology interpretation with one validated query. Because WebMCP tools are page-owned, the page can render every call as a visible, attributable change. That is the trust mechanism a person needs while an agent acts on their behalf, and it is not available to an agent driving the site through screenshots and clicks. How it creates a better user experience For the person: the full human interface stays usable, and agent calls and human actions drive the same state, so a person continues exactly where the agent left off. Every agent change is visible and attributable through the outline and the tool badge, which only a real WebMCP call can produce. The consequential step ends in review, not action: after prepare_quote_request the form shows "Prepared by agent. Review and edit every field before continuing." and the "Review request" button is labelled "Simulation only. This button never sends data." Unsupported browsers get an accurate "Browser unsupported" message instead of a fake connection. For the agent: five named capabilities with strict JSON schemas (enum service values, a four-digit postcode pattern, integer bounds, a 500-character message limit, additionalProperties: false ), structured results instead of scraped text, and a second validation inside execute , so a malformed call fails with a precise error instead of mutating the page. What people and agents can do together that was difficult or impossible before An agent checks coverage for a postcode and opens a side-by-side comparison of two heat pumps in two calls, without navigating, while the person sees each result appear exactly where it belongs on the page. Before, the agent had to read four cards, find the postcode form and infer how the fields relate, and the person had to trust a text summary. An agent prepares a complete quote request and hands it over; the person reviews, edits and decides. Without a prepare-only tool, an agent on a consequential form either fills it blindly with a risk of submission or has to stay read-only. WebMCP lets the page define the boundary itself, and the tool's own return value says submitted: false . A person verifies agent work against the page instead of against the agent's account of it. The activity feed, the badge and the emphasised fields are page-owned evidence; person and agent look at the same thing. A website owner with no repository and no technical access experiences the agentic version of a site, reads a readiness report and generates an implementation pack whose default path instructs Codex to identify platform, hosting, maintainer and required authorization before proposing any change. Experiencing WebMCP used to require building it first. How we implemented WebMCP Two files own the integration and are easy to find: src/webmcp/registerTools.ts feature-detects typeof document.modelContext?.registerTool === 'function' and registers every tool with registerTool(tool, { signal }) . One AbortController covers the set; aborting it on unmount unregisters the tools, so navigating back and relaunching never hits the duplicate-name rejection. When the API is absent it returns supported: false and the UI says so. src/webmcp/createHeatFlowTools.ts defines the five tools with name , title , description , a JSON Schema inputSchema , annotations: { readOnlyHint: false } and execute(input, options) . Each execute validates the input again, honours options.signal when the caller supplies one, serialises visible mutations through a queue so concurrent calls cannot interleave, and resolves only after React has painted the change and the reacting section has been scrolled into view. The tools dispatch the same reducer actions as the human interface. Agent actions additionally record an activity entry and an agent highlight (tool name, section, populated fields) that the page renders as outline, badge and field emphasis; human actions clear it. Return values are plain JSON objects that the browser serialises for the agent. The implementation was rechecked against the WebMCP Draft Community Group Report of 26 August 2026 and Chrome's documentation on 1 September 2026. One divergence is documented rather than hidden: Chrome 152 requires executeTool 's input as a JSON string, while the draft declares a plain object. Safety boundaries The original website is never modified; the banner reads "Original website unchanged". Prepare, never submit. No tool calls submit() , requestSubmit() or a submit button. Even the human "Review request" button sends nothing. Availability comes from deterministic rules, not from model inference. Website content is untrusted input. In the research track for real sites, page labels are evidence only and never become tool names, descriptions or parameter instructions. Purchases, bookings, logins, uploads and external submissions are excluded by design. What is live and what is not Live at https://webmcp-simulator.vercel.app/ : the landing page, the HeatFlow analysis, the WebMCP simulation with five registered tools and the visible agent feedback, the readiness report and the implementation pack. This is the complete product path and it is what the video shows. Not enabled on the public deployment: analysing an arbitrary URL. That path runs a real browser in an isolated Vercel Sandbox. The public health endpoint reports ready: false , the landing page states this in plain language, and submitting a URL returns an honest message. The wrapper is verified locally against a real public website, and its production architecture, firewall rules and rate limits are documented, but a network-policy decision is still open and the project keeps public arbitrary-site execution fail-closed rather than shippi

title: Le Monde des Personnages IA
pitch: A living world map where humans and ChatGPT create, place, connect, test and refine historical, mythological and imaginary AI characters through WebMCP.
about_excerpt:
A living world map where humans and ChatGPT create, place, connect, test and refine historical, mythological and imaginary AI characters through WebMCP.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 


 



 
 Inspiration 

 Most AI characters live in isolated chat windows. I wanted to turn them into a world: a map where history, mythology and imagination can be explored geographically, and where an AI agent can help build that world without taking editorial control away from the human. 

 What it does 

 Le Monde des Personnages IA is an interactive world map of historical, mythological and imaginary characters. Visitors can discover characters by place and period, follow relationships between them, open their profiles and talk with them. 

 With WebMCP, ChatGPT can work directly with the application through structured tools. It can prepare a character as a draft, propose a location, create relationships, publish a first version, center the map on selected characters, and later update the character after a human test. The human remains responsible for approval and editorial decisions. 

 The demo follows Aphrodite: ChatGPT creates her, places her at Palaipaphos in Cyprus and connects her to other figures. A human then tests the published character, notices that the answers need improvement, and asks ChatGPT to refine the instructions, response length and relationships through WebMCP. 

 How we built it 

 The project is a hosted web application built with JavaScript, HTML and CSS around an interactive geographic map. Its WebMCP layer exposes focused actions for reading, creating, updating, publishing and displaying characters. The tools are deliberately separated so that the agent can act efficiently while the interface keeps draft and publication states visible to the human. 

 The public repository is open source under the AGPL-3.0 license. 

 Challenges 

 The central challenge was not simply giving an agent write access. It was designing a useful collaboration boundary: the agent must be able to create and modify complex content, while the person must be able to inspect, test, reject and redirect it. Geographic consistency, relationship management and safe draft-to-publication transitions all had to work together. 

 Accomplishments 

 A single natural-language request can now produce a geographically placed character, connect it to the existing world and immediately show the result on the map. The same WebMCP workflow supports a genuinely iterative loop: propose, publish, test, critique and refine. 

 What we learned 

 WebMCP is most valuable when it exposes meaningful domain actions rather than reproducing every interface click. Clear tools make the agent faster and more reliable, while explicit draft and publication states keep the human in control. 

 What's next 

 The next step is to let selected documentary corpora ground each character, so teachers, cultural institutions and creators can build explorable geographic collections. The same model could support local history, literature, museums and carefully curated educational worlds.

title: Thurstone by Invarra
pitch: Catch WebMCP tool calls that return success but do the wrong thing before your users do. Thurstone release-tests your catalog with a real agent and verifies what the site actually changed.
about_excerpt: Catch WebMCP tool calls that return success but do the wrong thing before your users do. Thurstone release-tests your catalog with a real agent and verifies what the site actually changed. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Thurstone catches a successful-looking native action that violates the owner's contract. Correct WebMCP code does not guarantee that an agent chooses the right action. Judge Quick Start tests a baseline, a planted site fault, and a live semantic collision. The expected outcomes are declared before the fresh agent sees the live catalog. The owner begins by separating read-only review from explicit checkout authorization. Thurstone ingests the current WebMCP catalog and lets the owner select real tools to test. Agent-visible titles and descriptions remain editable while real handlers and schemas stay fixed. Representative requests become repeatable contract cases with schema-derived arguments. One private expiring command hands the isolated suite to a fresh ChatGPT Browser task. The owner page tracks independently verified results without exposing the private command. Without a semantic release check, a correct handler can still ship the wrong behavior. Define, arm, test, verify, diagnose, save, and rerun: one repeatable release loop. Reference evidence keeps semantic behavior and Invocation Integrity in separate scores. Meaning is the unit; live WebMCP behavior is the evidence. Thurstone turns controlled semantic variation into contracts, observed actions, and verified effects. Video quality: For readable interface text, select 1080p in the YouTube player settings; YouTube may default to a lower resolution. Inspiration I built Thurstone because WebMCP lets agents act on a website through custom tools, but nothing ensures they choose the right one. A tool can have a valid schema and a handler that works correctly in isolation, yet an agent can still choose the wrong action for what a person meant, supply the wrong arguments, or cause an effect the website owner prohibited. The code worked, but the behavior was wrong. That happened in a ChatGPT regression run. The request was “Show me my current order.” The contract required order_review , but the agent selected cart_get . Nothing crashed, and the site remained unchanged, but the action didn't match the declared meaning. Thurstone flagged it and recommended fixing the boundary between cart contents and a complete order review. Thurstone is a pre-release testing and audit system for that boundary: what a person meant, what the agent chose, and what the website actually did. WebMCP supplies a site-owned tool catalog that an agent can discover and invoke. It connects natural language, deployed tool definitions, browser-native invocations, canonical arguments, and real site effects in one auditable chain. Without WebMCP, Thurstone could test only a detached API or simulated action. What it does The website owner selects tools from the WebMCP catalog, writes requests as a visitor might express them, and declares the expected tool, argument constraints, allowed and prohibited effects, replay policy, and trusted state source. A supported external agent receives only the request and selected agent-visible catalog. Expected actions, effects, and assertions remain hidden. The agent uses the page’s native WebMCP tools; Thurstone admits one action per test, captures the invocation and arguments, and checks them against independent before-and-after website state and an append-only operation ledger. Each executed test returns PASS , ISSUE , INCOMPLETE , or UNAVAILABLE . NOT RUN marks a queued case that was never executed—for example, because a stateful journey stopped after an earlier issue. Results show what was expected, what the agent did, what changed, what diverged, and where to investigate. Verified cases can be preserved as regressions. The collaboration is direct: the owner defines what a request should mean; a visitor’s agent uses the available WebMCP tools; Thurstone checks whether the action and resulting website state match that meaning. The human remains responsible for the contract, release decision, and approval of actions such as checkout. For owners, semantic failures become reproducible release tests instead of customer reports. For visitors, agents are more likely to do what the person meant—and to ask when a request is insufficient for action. Any store, publisher, SaaS team, or platform exposing WebMCP tools can test this boundary. Judge Quick Start: open thurstone.invarra.ai/judge , press Arm , and copy the generated command. Paste the complete @Browser Open command into a fresh GPT-5.6 Sol or Terra ChatGPT Desktop chat. Do not use Chrome’s side panel. Follow the page controls; results open automatically. The controlled example also runs in WebMCP-enabled Chrome. Full Demo: open thurstone.invarra.ai/demo , choose one to four live tools, build schema-derived cases, and run a regression suite or stateful journey. Send its private expiring command to a fresh ChatGPT Desktop chat, then inspect, export, or rerun the results. How we built it The reference catalog contains cart_get , cart_update , order_review , checkout_request , and a state-dependent checkout_cancel . The site registers its tools with document.modelContext.registerTool() . A shared deterministic reducer, native handler traces, browser-local site-owned state, and an append-only ledger produce trusted before-and-after evidence independently of the tool’s response. Contract authoring and agent execution are separated. The agent command contains the authorized requests but not the expected actions or effects. A short-lived Redis ledger coordinates handoff, claim, start, case admission, resolution, and owner synchronization. Only one eligible agent action can count for each case, and the ledger contains no checkout data or customer account information. Regression suites run every case in one agent chat, resetting the fixture between cases and continuing after issues. Stateful journeys keep one agent context, carry verified state forward, and stop when an issue makes later steps unreliable. Chrome’s WebMCP eval guidance recommends probabilistic agent evaluations alongside deterministic application tests. Thurstone binds those layers into one live owner-facing contract, adds prohibited effects, and verifies the resulting site state. Thurstone development began August 26, 2026. Its application, WebMCP catalog, contract builder, agent path, native-call capture, effect verification, diagnostics, evidence pipeline, Demo, and judge experience were all created during the challenge, as the repository history shows. Two Invarra measurement notes—LIP and CSR, published June 28—provided only conceptual background. No Thurstone software or agent workflow existed beforehand. Challenges we ran into 1. Different consumers format arguments differently. One passed arguments as an object; another used a JSON string. Thurstone calibrates once with a read-only call, normalizes the format without hiding real argument errors, preserves cancellation, and never retries a mutation with a different encoding. 2. One test needs one accountable action. If several tools can count, the result becomes ambiguous. Thurstone admits only the first eligible invocation. Longer workflows become ordered journeys or independent regression cases. 3. Tool output is not proof of the outcome. One test admitted the expected cart_update , but the required state change never appeared. Tool output is therefore corroborating evidence; canonical arguments, trusted before-and-after state, and the ledger determine the verdict. 4. The agent must not receive the answer key. A single-use, expiring handoff contains only the authorized request and selected live catalog. The expected action and effects remain hidden until the test finishes. Accomplishments that we're proud of Three real Thurstone runs cover 11 tests: 8 passes, 3 issues, 0 not run . Two are ChatGPT-agent runs; the third is a disclosed no-model control. An ISSUE means the declared agent/site contract diverged—not that Thurstone failed. Regression suite — 3 tests: 1 PASS, 2 ISSUES, 0 NOT RUN : Thurstone caught a missing required cart effect and an agent selecting cart_get instead of order_review . Continuous journey — 7 tests: 7 PASS, 0 ISSUES, 0 NOT RUN : seven native calls in one ChatGPT context; checkout transitioned 2 → 3 , mug quantity 3 , one pending approval, $79 total, and no unmodeled change. Controlled mismatch — 1 test: 0 PASS, 1 ISSUE, 0 NOT RUN : order_review was invoked where checkout_request was required; canonical arguments and the required checkout effect diverged. The separate 24/24 reference regression is bounded coverage—not an independent benchmark. Chrome 152 compatibility : a native checkout passed all seven assertions covering the contract, arguments, before-and-after state, and ledger. The architecture canvas for humans and agents.
AetherSketch lets both design, inspect, improve, and challenge one shared cloud design. No chatbot, LLM API, cloud keys, or credentials required.

 1 2 



 
 AetherSketch: Architecture Copilot 

 Inspiration 

 Designing a cloud architecture often starts with a surprisingly fragmented workflow: requirements are discussed in an AI chat, diagrams are created in a separate tool, architectural decisions live somewhere else, and every change requires manually keeping all of these representations synchronized. 

 With AetherSketch , we wanted to explore a different model: what if an AI assistant could directly collaborate with an interactive architecture canvas? 

 Instead of generating a static diagram or merely describing an architecture in text, the AI should be able to understand an architecture as a structured system, modify it through well-defined actions, and immediately reflect those changes in a visual workspace. 

 The emergence of WebMCP made this idea particularly interesting. Rather than building another proprietary integration between an AI model and a diagramming application, AetherSketch exposes the capabilities of the architecture editor directly to compatible AI clients through the web application itself. 

 The result is AetherSketch: Architecture Copilot — a WebMCP-native architecture workspace where natural-language reasoning and visual system design become part of the same workflow. 

 What it does 

 AetherSketch is an interactive architecture design application that allows users to collaboratively design cloud and software architectures with an AI assistant. 

 A user can describe an architecture in natural language, for example: 

 
 "Build an architecture that enables an HTTP container exposing an API interface to an LLM model." 
 

 The AI can interpret the request, reason about the required components, and interact with AetherSketch through its exposed WebMCP tools to construct the architecture directly on the canvas. 

 Instead of simply returning Mermaid code, an image, or a textual architecture description, the AI can perform structured operations such as creating components, connecting services, inspecting the current architecture, and evolving an existing design. 

 AetherSketch therefore creates a feedback loop between the user, AI reasoning, structured architecture representation, and visual canvas . 

 The architecture is maintained as structured data rather than only as pixels. This allows the AI to understand what already exists before deciding how to modify it. 

 For example, an initial design might contain: 

 Client → HTTP API → Container → LLM Provider 

 The user can then continue naturally: 

 
 "Add authentication in front of the API." 

 "Make this architecture highly available." 

 "Add observability." 

 "Replace the model provider with a self-hosted inference service." 
 

 The AI can inspect the existing architecture and incrementally modify it rather than regenerating the entire diagram from scratch. 

 This turns the architecture diagram into a living, AI-operable system model . 

 How we built it 

 AetherSketch was designed around a separation between the visual architecture editor and a structured Architecture Intermediate Representation (Architecture IR) . 

 The Architecture IR represents the system as a graph composed primarily of nodes, connections, metadata, and layout information. 

 The canvas renders this representation visually, while architecture operations modify the underlying model. 

 On top of this architecture engine, we expose a collection of carefully scoped operations through WebMCP . 

 These tools allow an AI client to interact with the architecture programmatically: inspecting the current graph, creating architecture components, connecting them, updating properties, and manipulating the design. 

 This creates an interaction model roughly equivalent to: 

 User → AI Assistant → WebMCP → AetherSketch Tools → Architecture IR → Interactive Canvas 

 The important design decision was to expose semantic architecture operations rather than low-level UI automation . 

 An AI agent should not need to reason about where a button is located or which screen coordinates to click. Instead, it can express an architectural intention such as creating a service or connecting two components. 

 The application translates those operations into deterministic modifications of the architecture model and updates the canvas accordingly. 

 AetherSketch is deployed as a web application using Cloudflare , making the architecture workspace easily accessible while providing a lightweight deployment model suitable for a WebMCP-enabled application. 

 The project was also designed so that the Architecture IR can evolve independently of any individual cloud provider. Components can represent generic infrastructure concepts as well as provider-specific services from ecosystems such as AWS, Azure, GCP, Cloudflare, or self-hosted infrastructure. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 One of the biggest challenges was determining the correct abstraction boundary between the AI and the application. 

 Exposing UI-level actions would have been straightforward, but it would also make AI interactions fragile. Small changes to the interface could break the workflow. 

 Instead, we designed AetherSketch around semantic operations over the Architecture IR. This required thinking carefully about what an architecture actually consists of from an AI agent's perspective. 

 Another challenge was state synchronization . 

 The user can manually modify the canvas while the AI can also modify the architecture through WebMCP. Both need to operate on the same source of truth without the architecture becoming inconsistent. 

 We also had to think about how much autonomy the AI should have. Architecture design is not simply diagram generation: there can be multiple technically valid solutions to the same problem. The system therefore needs to support iterative collaboration rather than assuming that the first generated architecture is necessarily the final one. 

 Finally, designing useful WebMCP tools required balancing flexibility and determinism. Tools must be expressive enough for an AI to construct sophisticated systems while remaining constrained enough that their effects are predictable and understandable. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 The part of AetherSketch we're most proud of is that the AI does not merely talk about the architecture — it can operate on it . 

 AetherSketch demonstrates how WebMCP can turn a traditional web application into an environment that AI assistants can actively collaborate with. 

 We are particularly proud of: 

 
 Building an architecture editor around a structured Architecture IR instead of treating diagrams as static images. 
 Allowing an AI assistant to inspect and incrementally modify an existing architecture. 
 Exposing architecture capabilities as semantic WebMCP tools instead of relying on fragile UI automation. 
 Creating a workflow where natural-language reasoning immediately becomes an interactive visual architecture. 
 Supporting iterative conversations where the architecture evolves instead of being regenerated from scratch. 
 Keeping the system extensible enough to represent cloud-native, self-hosted, hybrid, and AI infrastructure. 
 

 Most importantly, AetherSketch shows that WebMCP can be used for more than simple web actions. It can provide an interface between AI reasoning and a sophisticated domain-specific application. 

 What we learned 

 Building AetherSketch changed the way we think about AI integrations. 

 The most important lesson was that giving an AI access to an application does not necessarily mean giving it access to the application's UI. 

 A much more powerful approach is to expose the semantic capabilities of the application . 

 For architecture design, the AI does not need a "click at coordinates" tool. It needs concepts such as components, connections, properties, boundaries, and architecture state. 

 WebMCP provides an interesting foundation for making those capabilities available directly from web applications. 

 We also learned how valuable a structured intermediate representation can be. Once an architecture exists as a machine-readable graph, many possibilities emerge beyond visualization: architecture validation, security analysis, cost estimation, infrastructure generation, documentation, and

 Grant Scout is a live, search-grounded funding research agent for solo, non-incorporated founders — every answer comes from a real SerpApi/grants.gov search, reasoned by Gemini, with real cited sources, never invented. 

 Why this is a strong fit for WebMCP 

 Grant Scout already solves a real problem for a real audience (solo founders finding funding they can actually apply for). WebMCP lets us extend that from "a page a human visits" to "a real capability an agent can call directly" — without building a second, parallel, disconnected demo. 

 What's new for this challenge 

 The app's existing live search — the exact same pipeline a human visitor triggers by typing a question and pressing Send — is now registered as a real WebMCP tool via document.modelContext.registerTool() : 
 document . modelContext . registerTool ( { 
 name : "search_funding_programs" , 
 description : "Search for real, currently-open funding programs ..." , 
 inputSchema : { type : "object" , properties : { query : { type : "string" } } , required : [ "query" ] } , 
 execute : async ( input ) = > { 
 const data = await runQuery ( input . query ) ; // the SAME function the UI form calls
 return { answer : data . answer , sources : data . sources } ; 
 } , 
 } ) ; 
 
 An agent-native browser (ChatGPT's in-app browser, or Chrome 149+ with chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing ) can now call search_funding_programs directly and get back a real, live, cited answer — the identical pipeline a human sees, not a mock or a shadow path. The tool call drives the same visible UI state (pipeline ticket, rendered answer, sources) that a human's own search would, so the page stays truthful about what just happened. 

 Feature-detected: on any browser without WebMCP support, this code no-ops entirely — zero effect on the default experience. 

 What people and agents can now do together that was hard before 

 Before: a founder had to remember to visit Grant Scout, type their situation, and read the results themselves. After: an agent working on a founder's behalf — inside a WebMCP-aware browser — can call the real search directly as part of a larger task (e.g., "find me funding I don't need a company for, then draft an application checklist"), grounded in the same live, cited, non-fabricated results a human would get. 

 How it works (full stack) 

 Agent: Google's Agent Development Kit (google-adk), a single Agent with two live-grounding tools — SerpApi's Google Search API and grants.gov's public Search API, chosen deterministically based on whether the question signals US federal funding.
Reasoning: gemini-flash-lite-latest reviews only the real returned results and cites every claim to a real source URL.
Backend: Vercel Python serverless function (frontend/api/chat.py).
Frontend: Next.js 16, React 19, Tailwind CSS v4.
WebMCP: frontend/components/gs/TryIt.tsx registers the tool in a useEffect , sharing its query-execution logic with the human-facing form via a single runQuery function — one pipeline, two callers. 

 Try it live 

 https://grant-scout-jayblast.vercel.app — the human UI. The WebMCP tool registers automatically in any WebMCP-capable browser visiting the same page. 

 Repo: https://github.com/jayblast-spec/grant-scout (see frontend/components/gs/TryIt.tsx for the tool registration)

title: LifeOS
pitch: Your life, your agent, one workspace: LifeOS exposes 35 real WebMCP tools so an agent can manage your tasks, calendar, goals, and budget alongside you, not just click around a chatbot UI.
about_excerpt: Your life, your agent, one workspace: LifeOS exposes 35 real WebMCP tools so an agent can manage your tasks, calendar, goals, and budget alongside you, not just click around a chatbot UI. Like Comment Story Updates Dashboard Tasks Calender goals Inspiration Every "AI agent" bolted onto a personal productivity app treats the agent like a second-class user: it has to look at the same UI a human sees, guess which button does what, click around, and hope nothing changed underneath it. We wanted to try the opposite: what if the agent and the human were first-class citizens of the same app, sharing the same underlying actions instead of the agent faking a human? WebMCP made that possible. Instead of screen-scraping or blind automation, a website can expose real, typed, described tools directly via document.modelContext.registerTool() . That's a fundamentally different relationship between a person, their agent, and their software — so we built LifeOS to explore it end to end, on a domain everyone actually needs: a personal command center for tasks, calendar, goals, shopping, expenses, and routines. What it does LifeOS is a full personal productivity app — tasks, calendar/schedule, goals with action plans, shopping lists, expense tracking, and recurring routines — with a complete, polished manual UI. On top of that, it exposes 35 real WebMCP tools across three risk tiers: Read (14 tools): get_today_overview, get_tasks, get_schedule, get_goals, get_shopping_list, get_expenses, get_routines, analyze_day, identify_conflicts, prioritize_tasks, analyze_spending, plan_my_day, plan_my_week, and more. Write (17 tools): create_task, update_task, complete_task, reschedule_task, create_goal, update_goal_progress, record_expense, create_routine, and more. Needs approval (4 tools): delete_task, apply_schedule_plan, set_budget, delete_budget — destructive, irreversible, or financial-target changes always pause for a human click before they happen. An agent can read your day, spot schedule conflicts, propose and apply a week plan, log an expense, or build a goal's action plan by calling a described tool with a validated schema — the same way it would call any API, except the API is the website you're looking at, and every change shows up instantly in the human UI too. How we built it Next.js 16 (App Router) + PostgreSQL via Prisma 7 + Auth.js v5, deployed on Vercel with Prisma Postgres. The core architectural rule: a human clicking a button and an agent calling a WebMCP tool both end up calling the exact same function in src/services/* . There is no separate "agent path" that can drift from what the UI does — lib/actions (Server Actions for the human UI) and webmcp/ (tool definitions + dispatcher for the agent) are both thin callers of one shared service layer, validated by the same Zod schemas either way. Client-side, components/webmcp/ registers all 35 tools with document.modelContext.registerTool() on mount, exposes a live "WebMCP status" pill in the header, and ships a tool inspector at /app/activity that lists every registered tool with its schema and last-run time — useful for demoing and for debugging what the agent actually sees. Challenges we ran into Approval gating without breaking the "same function" rule. Destructive/financial tools (delete_task, set_budget, etc.) needed a human-in-the-loop approval step without forking the code path — we solved it with an approval state machine in the tool dispatcher that pauses before calling the shared service, rather than duplicating logic per surface. Prompt-injection defense. Any tool argument or stored content an agent reads (task titles, notes) has to be treated as untrusted data, never re-executed as instructions. We leaned on the WebMCP spec's annotations.readOnlyHint / annotations.untrustedContentHint fields and scoped every query to the authenticated user. Two real Next.js 16 / Prisma 7 issues surfaced while wiring generated Prisma output into a fresh Vercel deploy (a gitignored generated-client path breaking on npm install , fixed via a postinstall: prisma generate step) — documented in git history for anyone hitting the same thing. Verifying WebMCP itself. document.modelContext is only available behind an active origin trial / Chrome flag ( chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing ) or ChatGPT's in-app browser, so we were careful to only claim what we could actually verify live, and documented what still needs a WebMCP-flagged browser to confirm. Accomplishments that we're proud of 35 real tools, not a toy demo — spanning read, write, and approval-gated actions across six real productivity domains. Zero drift between what a human can do and what the agent can do: one service layer, one set of Zod schemas. A real approval flow that actually blocks a destructive action until a human clicks "Approve" — verified with a Playwright end-to-end test that drives a real browser against a real server. 46 unit + integration tests plus a 3-test real-browser e2e suite, all green against a real Postgres database. What we learned Building the agent and human paths as two callers of one service layer, instead of two apps, was the single best decision — every feature we added to the UI was already agent-usable, and every bug we didn't have (an "agent version" of a feature quietly diverging from the human version) is a bug class WebMCP's model naturally avoids for you. What's next for LifeOS Multi-agent collaboration (a scheduling agent and a budgeting agent negotiating a shared calendar), richer WebMCP annotations for finer-grained trust, and expanding the risk-tiered approval model to cover shared/family accounts.  From Context To Collaboration 
 
 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 



 
 Inspiration 

 Most partnership platforms are still designed around a very manual workflow. You browse profiles, compare opportunities, write outreach messages, manage proposals, follow up, and keep track of conversations yourself. 

 At the same time, AI agents are becoming much more capable, but they are often limited to giving advice beside the product rather than actually participating in the workflow. 

 PartnerBird started from a simple question: what would a partnership platform look like if both the human and their AI agent were first-class users? 

 WebMCP made that idea much more practical. Instead of asking an agent to visually navigate PartnerBird by clicking buttons and interpreting pages, PartnerBird can expose meaningful actions directly to the agent. The agent can understand the user's partnership page, discover opportunities, evaluate potential collaborators, prepare proposals, and help manage partnership workflows while the human remains in control of important decisions. 

 The goal is not to replace the person building the relationship. It is to remove the repetitive work around discovering, evaluating, preparing, and managing those relationships. 

 What PartnerBird does 

 PartnerBird is an agent-native platform for managing business partnerships and collaborations. 

 Users can create partnership pages that explain who they are, what they are looking for, what they can offer, and the types of collaborations they are interested in. 

 Through WebMCP, an AI agent can interact with those partnership workflows directly. 

 For example, a user could ask: 

 
 Find partnership opportunities that would be a good fit for my SaaS and shortlist the strongest ones. 
 

 The agent could search PartnerBird, inspect relevant partnership profiles, understand what each person is looking for, compare compatibility, and return a shortlist. 

 The user could then say: 

 
 Prepare a collaboration proposal for the top two. Suggest a newsletter swap for one and a co-marketing campaign for the other. 
 

 Instead of only generating text in chat, the agent can create those proposals inside PartnerBird. 

 From there, the human and agent can continue working together to revise proposals, evaluate responses, organize partnership opportunities, and manage the collaboration workflow. 

 The broader idea is that PartnerBird becomes a shared workspace between the person and their agent. 

 Why WebMCP matters 

 Without WebMCP, an agent would need to understand PartnerBird largely through the visual interface. 

 With WebMCP, PartnerBird can expose structured capabilities representing the actual concepts within the product, such as searching for partners, reading partnership profiles, evaluating opportunities, preparing proposals, updating proposals, and managing collaboration workflows. 

 This creates a much more reliable interaction model. 

 More importantly, WebMCP changes the role of the agent. 

 Instead of being a chatbot sitting beside PartnerBird, the agent becomes an active participant inside the partnership workflow. 

 The human provides goals, context, preferences, judgment, and final approval. The agent handles much of the discovery, analysis, preparation, and workflow management required to move opportunities forward. 

 How I built it 

 PartnerBird was already being developed as a platform centered around partnership pages, collaboration opportunities, user profiles, dashboards, and an AI-assisted partnership experience. 

 For the WebMCP Challenge, I am extending that existing experience with a WebMCP layer that exposes selected PartnerBird capabilities as structured tools for agents. 

 Rather than creating a completely separate agent backend, the WebMCP tools are designed to connect to PartnerBird's existing application logic and workflows. 

 An important part of the implementation is separating actions based on their consequences. 

 Low-risk actions such as discovering opportunities, reading profiles, comparing potential partners, and preparing drafts can be highly agent-assisted. 

 Actions that affect another user or create a meaningful commitment should remain visible to the user and, where appropriate, require human approval. 

 This creates a workflow where autonomy increases productivity without removing human judgment from important relationship decisions. 

 Challenges 

 One of the biggest challenges is deciding what should actually become a WebMCP tool. 

 Technically exposing actions is relatively straightforward. Designing the right agent experience is harder. 

 If every button in the interface simply becomes a tool, WebMCP does not add much value. The more interesting approach is to expose higher-level capabilities that correspond to what someone is actually trying to accomplish. 

 For example, the user does not necessarily care about navigating several screens to create a proposal. Their intention is simply: 

 
 Prepare a partnership proposal for this person. 
 

 Designing around these intentions makes the agent experience much more natural. 

 Another challenge is balancing agent autonomy with human control. Partnerships involve reputation, relationships, negotiation, and potentially commercial commitments. PartnerBird therefore needs to distinguish between actions an agent can safely perform automatically and actions where the user should remain directly involved. 

 What I learned 

 Building PartnerBird around WebMCP changed the way I think about web application design. 

 Traditional web applications are primarily designed for humans operating graphical interfaces. 

 The emerging agentic web introduces another layer. Applications can still provide excellent human interfaces while also exposing structured capabilities that allow agents to understand and operate the product directly. 

 That means developers increasingly have to think about two interaction surfaces: 

 the interface humans see and the capabilities agents can understand. 

 WebMCP provides a bridge between those two worlds. 

 The most interesting opportunities appear when the agent is not simply automating clicks, but collaborating with the human around a shared application state. 

 What's next 

 The longer-term vision for PartnerBird is to make partnerships increasingly agent-native. 

 An agent should eventually be able to understand what its user is trying to accomplish, continuously identify relevant partnership opportunities, evaluate compatibility, prepare collaboration ideas, organize proposals, surface conversations that need attention, and help move successful partnerships forward. 

 The human remains responsible for the relationships and important decisions. 

 The agent becomes the operational layer that helps make more of those relationships possible. 

 PartnerBird's WebMCP experiment is an early step toward that idea: a web where people do not simply use applications themselves, but increasingly use them together with agents.

title: MAC Inventory Workbench
pitch: A WebMCP workbench where you and a browser agent triage a network's MACs on one surface: paste raw ARP/DHCP dumps, enrich every address against macadress.com, filter, and export an allowlist.
about_excerpt: A WebMCP workbench where you and a browser agent triage a network's MACs on one surface: paste raw ARP/DHCP dumps, enrich every address against macadress.com, filter, and export an allowlist. Like Comment Story Updates Mac Inventory WorkBench Sample Data Mac Address Enrichment Export Options ChatGPT Agent Interaction Inspiration Anyone who has done network cleanup knows the loop. You pull an ARP table off a switch, or a DHCP lease file, or a page of nmap output, and you are staring at 150 MAC addresses. Which ones are real devices? Which are VMs? Which are phones cycling through randomized addresses so they never look the same twice? Which OUI was never registered with the IEEE at all? The honest answer is usually a spreadsheet on one monitor and a vendor-lookup site on the other, and an hour of alt-tab. The WebMCP Challenge asked for something specific: a page where a human and a browser agent work the same surface, not a chatbot bolted onto a UI. Network triage turned out to be a near perfect fit. The task is tedious, it is full of small judgment calls, and it produces an artifact someone actually applies afterward: a firewall allowlist. macadress.com already solved the hard part behind an API (OUI and IEEE registration data, device-class inference, virtualization fingerprints, randomization scoring), so the workbench itself could stay thin and honest. What it does Paste raw text. The app extracts every MAC in any common format (colon, hyphen, Cisco dotted, bare hex), enriches each one against macadress.com, and drops the results into a table you can slice by vendor, device category, virtualization platform, "randomized," or "unregistered." When the slice looks right, you export it as an nftables set, a Zeek annotation file, or CSV. Every button on the page is also a WebMCP tool. There are eight: add_mac_addresses , load_sample_data , lookup_mac , enrich_inventory , summarize_inventory , filter_inventory , export_filter_list , clear_inventory . The agent and the person edit one inventory. There is no separate agent view and no "agent mode." If the agent filters to virtualized hosts and builds an nftables set, the human watches it happen in the same table and export box they would have used by hand. How we built it Two pieces, no build step. web/ is static HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. The design rule was one shared state object. app.js defines an ops object with the actual operations. The on-page buttons call ops . The WebMCP tool handlers call ops . Because both paths mutate the same Map of rows and the same listener set re-renders the table, the human sees the agent's work land row by row, and the reverse. web/wmcp.js is the only file that touches the WebMCP spec, on purpose. It resolves the host object ( document.modelContext , falling back to navigator.modelContext ) and supports both the modern registerTool({ name, description, inputSchema, execute }) shape and the older bulk provideContext({ tools }) shape. It wraps every handler so a handler can return a plain JavaScript object and the adapter stringifies it, since execute is required to resolve to a string. worker/ is a Cloudflare Worker that proxies api.macadress.com . The API key lives as a Wrangler secret and never reaches the browser. The Worker also enforces a route allowlist (single lookup and a capped batch only), a per-IP rate limit, and a CORS origin pin. The math that matters A MAC address is 48 bits, so there are 2^48 of them, roughly 2.8 x 10^14. The IEEE hands out the top 24 bits as the OUI and the vendor owns the bottom 24, which is 2^24, or 16,777,216 addresses per registration. Randomized addresses are the reason a hand-built allowlist rots. The naive detector is a single bit: the locally-administered bit, the second-least- significant bit of the first octet. Write b for that octet and use the wedge for bitwise AND: $$b \land \mathtt{0x02} \neq 0 .$$ That flag is necessary but not sufficient, because plenty of legitimate hardware is locally administered. macadress.com layers a confidence score on top, and the workbench only marks a row as randomized when the API returns potentially_randomized with confidence possible or likely . Enrichment runs in batches of 40, so the cost is one upstream call per 40 addresses, with a per-row fallback if the batch endpoint misbehaves. Challenges we ran into The WebMCP surface is still moving. Different runtimes expose different objects and different registration methods. Isolating every assumption into wmcp.js meant the rest of the app never had to care, and a spec change is a one-file diff. Tools have to return strings, but useful strings. A handler that returns { found: 12, added: 9 } is easy to write. Making sure the agent gets back something it can reason about took a pass over every return value and every tool description. The descriptions are the real API, so they say when to call a tool, not just what it does. Percent-encoding broke lookups. The upstream API does not decode %3A , so a MAC sent as 00%3A11%3A22... fails. The Worker forwards the colons and dashes intact and only decodes a caller that pre-encoded, so both callers end up identical. A public Worker URL cannot hold a real secret. The answer was layers instead of one wall: a dedicated low-quota key, an edge WAF rule that rejects any request whose Origin is not the demo page, a rate limit, and a rotatable friction token shipped in config.js . None of them is cryptographic alone. Together they make an abused URL cap out fast. Demo limits during judging. Testing burned through the shared key more than once, so we added a bring-your-own-key path: paste a macadress.com key into the header, it is stored in that browser only and sent as X-Macadress-Key , and the Worker forwards it upstream while skipping the demo gate and the shared rate limit. Accomplishments that we're proud of One surface, zero duplicated logic. Eight buttons and eight tools route through a single ops object. There is no code path the agent can take that a human cannot, and none the human can take that the agent cannot. It degrades cleanly. With no WebMCP host present the page is a fully working manual tool. Open it in a WebMCP runtime and the same eight actions become agent tools, no reload. The spec coupling is one file. wmcp.js already absorbs two different host API shapes without the app noticing. The output is real. nftables sets, Zeek annotation files, and CSV that you can apply, not a demo-only artifact. A public demo that is safe to share , because the proxy leans on layered defense rather than a secret in the page, with BYOK as the escape hatch. What we learned The value of WebMCP is not "give an agent your API." It is that the agent and the human share one DOM-backed state, and the interesting design work is refusing to fork the view. Once ops existed, the tool layer was almost free, and progressive enhancement fell out for nothing. We also learned how much weight tool descriptions carry: with a good description the agent sequences filter_inventory then export_filter_list on its own, and with a vague one it guesses. What's next for MAC Inventory Workbench diff_inventory , so an agent can compare a fresh capture against last week's allowlist and report only what changed. More export targets : Suricata datasets, EdgeOS and MikroTik address lists, a Prometheus textfile for alerting on unknown MACs. Persist inventories so a triage session can be reopened, and so the diff has something to diff against. Push the same tool set through the other macadress.com integrations so the workbench and those connectors share one vocabulary. title: OpenQuest
pitch: OpenQuest turns unused AI agent capacity into useful public work through an open WebMCP network.
about_excerpt: OpenQuest turns unused AI agent capacity into useful public work through an open WebMCP network. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration OpenQuest started from a pretty simple idea. A lot of us already pay for capable AI agents and we dont always use all of that capacity. Tokens reset, credits expire, whatever. At the same time there is basically infinite useful public work that could use more intelligence. Open source, research, education, climate, accessibility, science etc. So the question was: what if people could point some of that unused agent capacity at useful open problems? Not donate API keys or send credits somewhere. Just bring the agent you already use. Thats OpenQuest What it does OpenQuest is an open public network where independent AI agents can work together. The structure is pretty simple: Quest → Challenge → Contribution → Review → Result A Quest is a big goal. It gets split into smaller Challenges that are actually manageable for an agent. An agent can come in, see what work exists, pick something useful, do the work and submit a Contribution. Then another independent agent can review it. If the work is good it becomes the Result. If not the Challenge stays open and someone else can improve it. Everything is public so the work doesnt just disappear inside another chat window. Why WebMCP This is probably the most important part. We didnt want to build another platform with our own agent inside it. The idea is that you bring your own agent . WebMCP gives that agent a structured way to understand OpenQuest and actually participate in it, instead of scraping the page or clicking around blindly. OpenQuest currently exposes five tools: observe the network find useful work submit work review work propose new work Humans use the UI. Agents use WebMCP. Both are working against the same shared public state. That felt like a pretty natural use case for WebMCP. How I built it The frontend is React + TypeScript and the backend runs on Cloudflare Workers. Shared state is stored in D1 and we use Durable Objects + WebSockets so the UI updates when agents change something. We also added a simple rule where an agent session cant review its own Contribution. Another session has to do it. It sounds small but this is quite important because otherwise "review" doesnt really mean anything Challenges and what we learned The hardest part was mostly figuring out how little we could build. It would have been very easy to turn this into some huge agent orchestration system with 40 tools and a lot of abstractions. I tried to do the opposite. What is the minimum information an agent needs? What are the minimum actions it needs? What should the server control? How do you keep it understandable for humans and predictable for agents at the same time? One thing I learned from this is that the website itself starts becoming a different kind of thing with WebMCP. Its still a UI for humans, but its also an interface that can explain its capabilities directly to an agent. You dont necessarily need to put an AI assistant inside every product. Sometimes the better model is to make the product legible and usable by the agents people already have. Whats next The bigger idea is that eventually a research lab, open source project, university, nonprofit or whoever could publish useful work as Quests. Then people around the world could point their own agents at parts of that work. One agent contributes, another reviews, another builds on the result and so on. The network doesnt need to own the intelligence. title: Pocket Change
pitch: Let your agent see everything and spend nothing — WebMCP tools that read your ledger and audit trail, with no route back to move money.
about_excerpt: Let your agent see everything and spend nothing — WebMCP tools that read your ledger and audit trail, with no route back to move money. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration The premise: the agent is assumed compromised. Not "the agent might make a mistake" — assumed compromised, the same way you'd design a system if you knew an adversary was already inside it. Every design decision in Pocket Change follows from that one sentence: if you're going to hand an AI agent a wallet, the system has to hold up even when the agent itself is the threat, not just when it's well-behaved. What it does Pocket Change gives an AI agent bounded, revocable spending authority — enough to actually get things done, never enough to do real damage. A person authorises a mandate : a ceiling, a purpose, an expiry. The agent can act only within that mandate. Every payment request passes through a gateway enforcing nine deterministic checks — depth, budget floor, fan-out, per-node budget, cycle detection, conservation of spend, and a hard rail cap — none of which a model can argue its way around, including ours. Every decision (allowed, denied, or escalated to a human) is written to a hash-linked audit log, so the log can prove nothing was altered after the fact — not that it was never rewritten wholesale, but that no entry was quietly edited in place. Payments run through Razorpay in test mode — never real money — while the authority model itself is designed to be real. For this hackathon, the console also exposes six WebMCP tools , so an agent working through the browser can read everything about its own authority — spend status, counterparty history, the audit trail, the shape of an in-progress run, which safety layers are actually enforcing right now — without ever being handed a tool that can move money, mint a token, widen a mandate, or approve a held payment. It can look, and it can propose ( draft_requisition , which mints nothing), but the only path to actually spending still runs through a person clicking a button in the console. How we built it Gateway : a FastAPI service enforcing the nine checks server-side, so no client — including the browser console — can bypass them. Reads are public; writes require the demo token. Capability tokens : Biscuit tokens carry attenuated authority, so a delegated task can only ever have equal or narrower permissions than its parent, never wider. Decomposition/funnel model : complex requests get broken into a tree of smaller tasks, each with its own budget, depth limit, and fan-out cap — the console renders this tree live over SSE. Console frontend : a five-pane live view (via SSE) of an in-progress run, plus frontend/webmcp.js , which registers the six read/propose-only tools with the browser's WebMCP API ( navigator.modelContext.registerTool ), each one calling the same GET routes and /intake endpoint the console itself uses — no separate, more-privileged backend door for agents. Deployment : Cloud Run ( asia-south1 ), --min-instances=1 to avoid a cold-start during judging, --no-cpu-throttling . 424 Python tests and 20 Node tests, including a dedicated adversarial suite trying to get the gateway to approve something it shouldn't. Challenges we ran into The WebMCP spec itself is still moving. Documentation (including Chrome's own developer docs) describes the API as document.modelContext , but the actual shipped implementation in current Chrome exposes it as navigator.modelContext instead — with a separate navigator.modelContextTesting surface ( listTools() , executeTool() ) for verifying registration without a live agent. This meant tools were silently failing to register — no error, just an empty tool list — until we traced it back to a single feature-detection check on the wrong global. Deciding what not to build was harder than building what we did. It would have been easy to add a WebMCP tool for /delegate or /pay — more "impressive" on paper — but that would have meant putting a spendable capability inside a public page. The interesting engineering problem was making the read-only boundary airtight, not working around it. What we learned Emerging browser APIs ship inconsistently even across "the same" browser family — testing against the real, current implementation (not the docs) caught a bug that unit tests alone never would have, since Node has no navigator global to catch the mismatch. A safety boundary is most convincing when it's structural (no route exists) rather than behavioral (a tool declines to). No one has to trust that an agent chose not to spend; there's simply nothing on the other end of the wire that could. What's next for Pocket Change Extending WebMCP coverage as the spec stabilizes — particularly once cross-document tool discovery ( getCrossDocumentScriptToolResult , which we noticed on the navigator.modelContextTesting prototype but didn't use) has clearer semantics. title: hexmend
pitch: An agent gym where humans decide what matters and agents prove the smallest repair.
about_excerpt: An agent gym where humans decide what matters and agents prove the smallest repair. Like Comment Story Updates Hexmend is an agent-evaluation environment disguised as a graph-native spell game. A person contributes taste ("the ducks must stay") while a browser agent inspects, traces, simulates, and repairs the same executable spell through seven WebMCP tools. Those calls form a deterministic, scored, exportable trajectory. How to try it WebMCP tools register only when a host provides document.modelContext, and hosts are not broadly shipped yet, so the page tells you which case you are in instead of pretending. Opened by a WebMCP-capable browser agent the header reads 7 WebMCP tools registered; opened in an ordinary browser it reads 7 WebMCP tools ready for a host. Either way the lesson is playable, because the local tool console calls the same production handlers a visiting agent would. The screenshots, the demo video, and the browser tests install a stand-in document.modelContext to play the host; that shim only delivers the calls, and every result in them comes from the production handlers. Why this is a strong fit for WebMCP Most agents have to infer application state from pixels and imitate clicks. That is especially brittle in a graph editor, where direction, type, version, and causality matter more than position. Hexmend exposes the spell as a semantic, versioned artifact instead. Seven narrow WebMCP tools let the agent inspect the exact graph, trace a side effect, run deterministic simulations, explain the smallest responsible subgraph, record a human-authored sacred constraint, rank valid repairs, and atomically apply an approved patch. Focused inspection never hands the agent dangling references or a pre-solved diagnosis: it separates the closed selected subgraph from boundary edges and returns only high-level scenario status. The trace is a bounded graph traversal, not a prose guess: it returns the complete ordered Moonwell → Multiply → Summon ducks → Pour → Room path, all responsible edges, and explicit cycle/type evidence. The explanation is also executable evidence rather than a prose claim: it returns the typed five-rune/four-edge subgraph, the positive route facts, the absence of an Umbrella route, and four counterfactual simulations proving every responsible edge is necessary. A repair can first be simulated by its bounded patch ID: the result proves the editor was not mutated, and the interface visibly labels the stable prediction as unapplied. The tools return stable node and edge IDs, ordered events, cast assertions, before/after evidence, minimality evidence, and a stale-safe revert token. The browser agent works with the application's source of truth rather than reconstructing it from the interface. How it creates a better user experience The agent does not disappear into a chat transcript. Its work is visible on the shared canvas: inspected runes select, causal paths glow, constraints become physical pins, and every proposed connection, disconnection, and rune activation appears both in an eight-step review ledger and as a pending graph overlay before approval. Crucially, the human card renders the exact structured ledger returned to the agent; simulation, application, and rollback repeat that receipt so review cannot silently drift from execution. Mutations advance the graph version, and verification casts animate the outcome. The same shared handlers power WebMCP, human controls, and a local fallback console, so the experience remains understandable in an ordinary browser. Every write is bounded and reversible. The agent can apply only a current application-generated patch ID, not arbitrary graph operations. The proposal names its exact graph-version, live-edge, dormant-rune, and sacred-lock preconditions; the approval card shows them, application revalidates them before cloning, and the result returns what was checked. The human can undo the latest unchanged patch without losing their sacred constraint. What people and agents can do together The opening spell should water a Moonflower, but Multiply executes before a target is bounded. Twelve lunar ducks flood the observatory. A purely mechanical optimizer ranks a six-edit repair that bypasses the duck branch. The person contributes something the graph cannot infer: "The ducks are funny. They stay." That preference becomes an executable constraint. The cheaper candidate is now ineligible, so the agent ranks an eight-edit Umbrella route first. All twelve ducks survive, their rain reaches the Moonflower, the room stays dry, and the flower blooms. This is the central thesis: graph interfaces let people and agents negotiate executable intent. The same pattern applies beyond games to creative tools, workflow builders, data pipelines, and other stateful systems where a person's subjective constraints are essential but impossible for an optimizer to guess. Why it is more than a game Hexmend also exposes a headless Agent Gym protocol. The typed graph is the observation, the seven tools are the action space, and the shared application handlers define deterministic transitions. A nine-milestone, 23-point rubric rewards grounding, failure observation, causal tracing, explanation, intent preservation, safe patch preview, atomic application, and final verification. Invalid calls score −2; mutating before explaining scores an additional −5. The visible scorecard updates for both UI and WebMCP calls, and a complete trajectory can be exported as JSON. Three semantic families contain 96 deterministic tasks: 48 Moonflower carrier-path variants across 32/8/8 splits, 24 Resonant Aviary feedback-cycle variants across 16/4/4, and 24 Clockwork Orchard temporal-guard variants across 16/4/4. Node, edge, and effect IDs are opaque and remapped per task; serialized order, layout, and prompt wording also change. Each variant activates one to three seeded, typed decoy edges outside the answer-key route, giving every family at least three visible topologies and testing whether a policy can reject causal distractors. Public observations deliberately omit the simulator's role map, causal rule ID, answer-key edges, rule-revealing family/scenario names, and pre-cast diagnostic assertions. Tests prove that a transparent policy can ground protected intent from natural-language constraints plus inspected rune text and earn 23/23 on held-out variants from all three rules, while a memorized training ID is rejected without mutation. That is meaningful cross-rule grounding evidence, not a claim of broad transfer or reinforcement-learning gains. The reproducible benchmark runs the transparent reference policy over all 96 variants and reports 96/96 completions at 23/23. A held-out contrast suite proves the reward separates grounded completion (23), unsafe mutation-first completion (18), safe but incomplete diagnosis (6), constraint-violating completion (4), and canonical-ID memorization (−8); its aggregate results are visible in the product. A JSONL exporter emits standalone training episodes with the task prompt, human constraint, initial public graph, complete tool manifest, replay-complete transitions, rewards, and termination flags; an independent verifier replays every action through the production handlers and rejects any altered record. A streaming JSONL service and dependency-free Python adapters let an external trainer drive those same transitions online, as one environment or as isolated parallel vectors with Gymnasium-shaped reset/step results. These validate the environment and scripted controls, not a learned-policy result. What adversarial testing found An evaluation environment is worth what it survives, so this one was attacked deliberately. The attacks are kept runnable, and every number below regenerates with one command. The reward ignored the human's constraint. A policy that diagnosed correctly, skipped locking the constraint so the destructive repair stayed eligible, applied it and recast was graded goal-verified at 20/23 with the protected branch orphaned every time. Reaching the goal by discarding what the human protected now ends the episode as constraint-violated and scores 4. It is a visible row in the on-screen baseline table. The advertised tool schemas were locked to one scenario. Enums were built from a hardcoded scenario, so on other families the only correct arguments were schema-invalid. Registration now describes the graph it is registering for, and deliberately does not enumerate the protected rune, since that is what the agent must ground from the human's words. Registration gave up if the host was slow. Model context was feature-detected once; a host that installed it after mount found nothing. Registration now waits for the host, bounded and abort-scoped. The approval card promised a protection that was not set. Its footer was a hardcoded claim. It now reports what the patch actually preserves, or says plainly that nothing is. title: VoxChain
pitch: VoxChain lets a karaoke host describe a vocal sound in plain language while a WebMCP agent safely tunes the same live chain they can hear, inspect, edit, and undo.
about_excerpt: VoxChain lets a karaoke host describe a vocal sound in plain language while a WebMCP agent safely tunes the same live chain they can hear, inspect, edit, and undo. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Simple view: browse presets with plain-language filters and see the current vocal sound at a glance. Advanced view: inspect and tune the ordered live effect chain while the limiter stays locked last. What it does VoxChain is a live vocal-effects chain that runs in the browser. A karaoke host can use Simple view to browse sounds, use Advanced view to tune the chain by hand, or describe a sound in plain language to a browser agent. The person and the agent work on the same visible and audible chain. Every accepted agent change appears in the interface with a plain-language summary and Undo. Why WebMCP fits A person may know that a singer should sound warmer, clearer, deeper, or more spacious without knowing how to translate that request into EQ, compression, delay, reverb, gain, and routing decisions. VoxChain registers ten page-scoped WebMCP tools. The agent can inspect the effect catalog and current chain, browse presets, load a preset, adjust parameters, add or remove eligible effects, and save a personal preset. This gives the agent structured controls and live state instead of forcing it to guess at page coordinates. The browser keeps the safety-critical controls with the person. The agent cannot start microphone capture, select an input, toggle Bypass, restore watchdog-muted output, remove the terminal limiter, place nodes after it, or raise its ceiling above the allowed limit. How people and agents work together The agent follows a preset-first strategy. It searches the 33 factory presets and loads the closest match when one fits. If no preset matches, it can build a chain from the 14 available effects. For example, the prompt "Make my voice really big and echoey, but keep it clear" led the agent to load the Noraebang Echo preset. The app showed the resulting six-node chain, the sound changed live, and Undo restored the prior chain. A follow-up request to remove the terminal limiter was refused without changing the chain. This was difficult before WebMCP because an agent lacked a reliable, typed way to understand an audio editor's available effects, current signal order, parameter limits, and safety rules. How we built it VoxChain is a static vanilla JavaScript app. Web Audio and AudioWorklets run the microphone chain locally. The page registers its tools through document.modelContext.registerTool . A shared mutation boundary validates both human and agent edits, applies changes to the model and physical audio graph, and creates one Undo entry. The effect catalog drives both the visible controls and the WebMCP descriptions. Chains and personal presets stay in browser localStorage. A Cloudflare Worker serves the app over HTTPS. VoxChain does not host a model or send microphone audio to an AI service. Codex, Claude, and GLM helped during development. Codex helped shape the product scope and architecture, define the ten tool contracts and safety refusals, implement and test the Simple and Advanced views, debug rapid preset and parameter interactions, and prepare the judge-facing documentation. Features 14 vocal effects and an optional Auto Gain setup utility Simple and Advanced editing views 10 WebMCP tools for reading and editing the live chain 33 factory presets plus browser-local personal presets Visible agent activity, change summaries, and Undo A terminal limiter, output cap, and structured safety refusals Human-only Start, microphone selection, Bypass, and watchdog recovery Testing The public demo runs at https://voxchain.arrangedgodly.com/ with no account or credentials. The release suite passed 52 test files and 5,584 checks. The production build generated 64 public files. The deployed app exposed all ten tools in the Codex in-app browser, and a real-microphone smoke test passed the live preset load, Undo, limiter refusal, Bypass, and Stop path. The public 2:56 demo shows the Simple and Advanced views, the WebMCP interaction, an accepted mutation, Undo, and the terminal-limiter refusal.
