video_transcript_excerpt: Hi there, my name's Grady. I'm part of Code Bros, and today I'm super excited to demonstrate Vox Chain for you all. So, let's get straight into it. Vox Chain is a home audio utility application that allows users to create sound effects for their microphone on the fly. One of the coolest parts, of course, is leveraging Web MCP protocols. This is a pretty new technology where you can prompt your AI agent to build an audio effect for you. So, here's a basic example. I want my voice to be really big and echoey, but I still want it to be clear. And then, we wait for our agent to respond. Oh, and then you see that once the AI decides a preset, we get this nice little undo pop-up if we'd like to revert our changes. One of my favorite parts is plain language prompting. I love that users don't have to have technical knowledge to be able to get the results they're looking for from their agent. Now, there are some guardrails built in. Every chain has a protection limiter on the back end to prevent clipping. And let's just show, if we attempt to prompt remove the terminal limiter. We do get an error message from the agent saying that it's a requirement to have that limiter restriction on each chain. Now, there are two different views. We start in simple view by default. That's if you're just looking to browse presets and have a general overview of the devices utilized. Let's try Rock Night. >> Deep narrier. >> Jazz seller. Then, we also have the advanced view for more technical users where we can come in and adjust parameters directly. We can drag and drop plugins to reorder and click to add new devices it will. Now Web MCP protocols aren't just limited to the simple view. We can use this in the advanced mode as well. Let's demonstrate that. I'd like you to build me a chain from scratch that focuses on cutting all of the high end out of my voice and keeping power in the low end. I want ample distortion and a tiny bit of chorus. Now as you can see, it was able to build a chain from scratch and mimic the exact requests I was looking for. The project ships with 14 effects as well as the auto gain utility. It was really fun developing this project for the DevPost hackathon and I look forward [clears throat] to developing it further after the competition.

title: Synapse Studio
pitch: Build, stress-test, and optimize cloud architectures with AI agents. Synapse lets humans and agents collaborate on a live system canvas through WebMCP
about_excerpt: Build, stress-test, and optimize cloud architectures with AI agents. Synapse lets humans and agents collaborate on a live system canvas through WebMCP Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Cloud architecture is usually designed as a static diagram, while testing, optimization, security review, and infrastructure generation happen in separate tools. We wanted to explore what happens when that architecture becomes a living, interactive system that both humans and AI agents can work with directly . WebMCP inspired us to build Synapse Studio around this idea: instead of an agent guessing how to operate a complex interface, the application can expose structured tools for inspecting, simulating, optimizing, and modifying the architecture. What it does Synapse Studio is an agent-native cloud architecture and simulation studio where humans and AI agents collaborate on the same live architecture canvas. Users can visually design systems, connect services, adjust configurations, and define goals. AI agents can then use WebMCP tools to: Inspect the current architecture and live metrics Simulate traffic spikes and infrastructure failures Detect bottlenecks and security risks Optimize cost, latency, and resilience Propose architectural changes Highlight affected components on the canvas Apply approved changes directly to the architecture Generate infrastructure-as-code from the approved design The result is a workflow that goes from design → simulation → diagnosis → recommendation → human approval → implementation → verification . How we built it We built Synapse Studio as a web application with a centralized architecture state shared across the canvas, simulation engine, agent interface, and WebMCP tools. The application exposes structured WebMCP tools through document.modelContext.registerTool , including architecture inspection, node creation, service connections, chaos simulation, optimization, security auditing, visual highlighting, and IaC generation. A deterministic simulation engine models system behavior such as throughput, latency, resource utilization, failures, and estimated cloud cost. This allows agents to test architectural decisions and compare results before and after changes. We also built a WebMCP activity inspector so users can see which tools the agent is calling, what the agent is doing, and how the architecture changes in response. Challenges we ran into One of the biggest challenges was balancing technical ambition with a reliable product experience . It is easy to build many individual tools, but much harder to make them work together as one coherent human-agent workflow. We also had to design a simulation model that feels realistic enough to demonstrate meaningful engineering trade-offs without depending on real production infrastructure. Another challenge was making WebMCP visible and understandable. We wanted judges and users to clearly see when the agent was inspecting, simulating, proposing, and changing the architecture rather than simply interacting with a generic chatbot. Finally, we designed the system so significant agent-driven changes require human approval, keeping the human architect in control while still allowing the agent to perform complex operations. Accomplishments that we're proud of We are proud that Synapse goes beyond simply adding an AI assistant to an existing application. The architecture canvas, simulation engine, WebMCP tools, agent activity timeline, visual highlighting, optimization workflow, and IaC generation are designed as one integrated experience. Most importantly, we created a workflow where the agent can work with the application's actual structured state rather than trying to guess its way through the UI. That makes the WebMCP integration central to the product instead of being an added feature. We are also proud of the human-in-the-loop approval model, which demonstrates a more practical way for people and agents to collaborate on high-impact engineering decisions. What we learned We learned that building for agents requires thinking differently about application design. A traditional interface is designed primarily for humans. With WebMCP, the application can also expose clear, structured capabilities for agents , creating a much stronger interaction model. We also learned that the best human-agent experiences are not necessarily about giving the agent complete control. The more interesting model is often shared control : the human defines the goal and constraints, while the agent handles inspection, experimentation, reasoning, and execution. Most importantly, we learned that making an application agent-native is not just an API integration. It requires designing the underlying state, tools, UI, and workflows so humans and agents can genuinely operate together. What's next for Synapse Studio We want to evolve Synapse from a simulation and design environment into a broader agent-native engineering workspace . Future directions include richer architecture simulations, more sophisticated optimization algorithms, deeper security and compliance analysis, collaborative architecture versioning, additional infrastructure providers, and stronger integrations with real development and deployment workflows. Our larger vision is for Synapse to become a place where engineers can design systems with agents, test them before deployment, understand the trade-offs, and turn approved decisions directly into production infrastructure . title: Cascade
pitch: A shared decision canvas where people and agents map hidden assumptions, stress-test plans against real world shocks, and turn uncertainty into resilient action.
about_excerpt: A shared decision canvas where people and agents map hidden assumptions, stress-test plans against real world shocks, and turn uncertainty into resilient action. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration When working on an app launch, we found ourselves sending planning docs back and forth between us and our agents. That was very problematic. We wanted to move beyond asking an AI, “What could go wrong?” and getting another list to read. What if the agent could work inside the plan itself, connecting assumptions, exploring consequences, and proposing alternatives that a person could inspect and challenge? That became Cascade: a shared decision canvas for people and their agents. What it does Cascade turns a consequential plan into a connected map of objectives, assumptions, dependencies, constraints, risks, and outcomes. Our demo starts with a product launch: six weeks, 500 teams, and a $12,000 budget. What happens if billing arrives three weeks late? An agent can create a separate what-if branch, apply the disruption, and trace modeled downstream effects. It can then stage possible responses, such as launching a free beta first. The human can inspect the map, drag cards with their connections following, compare scenarios, and accept or reject proposed factors and relationships. Applying a shock is allowed inside a what-if branch; proposed mitigations remain drafts awaiting review. Promoting a branch is a human action. Product launch is the starter. Cascade also includes a community tool-lending scenario and a blank workspace for other plans. Why WebMCP Cascade is built around a shared working surface, not a separate chat transcript. WebMCP lets the agent read and act on the structured model behind the page. Tool actions update the same interface the person is watching: branches appear, shocks enter the map, and proposals arrive for review. This makes an otherwise awkward workflow practical: the agent explores alternatives inside the live application while the person retains an inspectable record of the model and controls which proposals are accepted. There is no need to copy the plan into a chat and manually translate the answer back into a diagram. How we built it Cascade uses TypeScript and React, with a Next.js-style App Router implemented through vinext on Vite. React Flow provides the draggable node-and-edge canvas. Custom CSS and a Tailwind CSS build pipeline support the visual design. The app registers 11 imperative WebMCP tools through document.modelContext.registerTool(). They cover reading the workspace, staging factors and relationships, creating branches, applying shocks, proposing mitigations, running stress tests, and comparing or explaining results. Tools use structured schemas and bounded inputs. Version checks on scenario-editing tools help reject stale writes when a person and an agent are working on the same model. Draft revision is limited to unlocked draft factors. A local TypeScript engine propagates shocks through accepted relationships to produce deterministic sensitivity metrics and impact paths. Its outputs are modeling aids. Vitest tests cover stable metrics, shock propagation, draft exclusion from cost and schedule totals, and graph layout. The workspace is stored in browser localStorage and can be exported as JSON. The app does not need its own AI API key; a connected agent uses the page's tools. That agent still receives the workspace data exposed through those tools. Cascade is hosted on ChatGPT Sites with a Cloudflare Workers-compatible build, with source code on GitHub under the MIT license. Challenges we ran into One challenge was making the graph behave like a genuine working surface: cards needed to move freely while their connections stayed anchored. Another was separating exploration from commitment. An agent needs room to test a disruption without silently rewriting the baseline, and people need a clear distinction between proposed and accepted changes. Rehearsing the demo exposed a subtler problem: an agent created a scenario whose description mentioned a delay, but did not actually apply the delay to the model. That reinforced an important lesson: a success message is not proof of a state change. Reliable collaboration needs outcome verification, not just well-described tools. Accomplishments we're proud of We built a working shared canvas where agent actions become visible, reviewable changes rather than suggestions trapped in a conversation. The same decision model supports both the product-launch and community examples, and the app remains usable by a person when WebMCP is unavailable. Most importantly, human review is part of the interaction itself: proposals, locks, scenario branches, and promotion controls make the collaboration boundary visible. What we learned Agent-native design is as much about accountability as capability. Giving an agent tools is only the beginning; the application must make its actions understandable and checkable. We also learned to distinguish a useful model from a confident-looking number. Cascade's purpose is to expose assumptions and explore consequences, not claim certainty about the future. What's next Stronger end-to-end evaluations that verify actual model changes after agent actions. More explicit feedback when a scenario has been created but no disruption has been applied. Improved mitigation-effect modeling, uncertainty handling, and explanation of score contributions. Shared team workspaces with durable persistence. Evidence links and richer review history for the assumptions behind a decision. title: Personal Data Rights Workbench
pitch: Turn a vague “delete my data” request into a transparent plan that shows what can go, what must stay, and why.
about_excerpt: Turn a vague “delete my data” request into a transparent plan that shows what can go, what must stay, and why. Like Comment Story Updates Delete What You Can, Explain What You Must Keep 1. What we built The Personal Data Rights Workbench makes a synthetic account's data footprint legible before consequential actions commit. A person or browser agent can inspect a 14-category inventory, read four consent choices and two retention constraints, simulate a complete data-minimization partition, understand feature trade-offs, and stage consent, erasure, or portability actions. The responsive data map reorganizes into Delete , Retained by rule , and Kept by choice . The headline fixture shows exactly 9 / 2 / 3 categories and an honest 92.6% reduction of deterministic demo bytes. The review matrix shows the exact staged action IDs and values. Commitment through the normal visible page control updates inventory and consent, clears staging, and creates an immutable synthetic receipt. 2. How we used WebMCP The top-level page registers nine imperative JavaScript tools for inventory, consent, retention, simulation, plan-bound staging, cancellation, and receipt reading. It prefers document.modelContext and retains navigator.modelContext only for older Chrome preview builds. Registration is scoped with an AbortController and atomic: all nine calls are initiated in one synchronous task, then awaited as a group. If any call throws or rejects, every attempted name is removed, the lifecycle is aborted, and readiness rejects. Tool callbacks use execute(input, { signal }) , while tolerating older callers that omit options. Inputs are validated in code, every non-retained category must be explicitly classified, plans receive unique IDs, and all staging is bound to the exact current plan. No consequential commit tool is exposed through WebMCP. Final commitment uses the normal visible page control and remains subject to Codex/browser safety confirmation; ordinary browser actuation may still reach visible controls. The read-only receipt tool returns only after commitment. 3. Why it matters Privacy controls often split one intention across opaque settings, retention language, and destructive forms. This workbench explores a more inspectable model: structured agent assistance for inventory and planning, explicit user intent for every category, visible consequences, version-bound staging, and a clear commit point. The demo does not determine legal rights or establish compliance. It demonstrates how WebMCP can make a complex workflow composable, visible, and truthful before and after commitment. 4. What we learned Tool quality is inseparable from visible state. The same domain service powers the UI, WebMCP tools, and deterministic rehearsal. A mutating callback rejects if already cancelled, then commits state, synchronously flushes the React subscription update, and returns without awaiting post-mutation work. Confirmed receipts also close every staging path. We also learned that schemas are routing guidance, not authorization; omitted categories must not be interpreted as user intent; every staged action needs a plan version; partial tool registration is unsafe; and receipts should describe only actions that actually committed. For compatibility with the client used in the demo, tools are registered imperatively in the top-level page. How we used AI and Codex This is a new project created during the challenge period. I used Codex while working on the project. The recorded walkthrough uses Codex Site Tools to discover the nine page tools, inspect the synthetic account, simulate and stage the plan, and read the receipt after visible confirmation. Codex also helped prepare the project write-up and testing instructions and run the automated checks. The application itself uses deterministic client-side logic, not an embedded language-model backend. Testing instructions No account, credentials, payment, or real personal data is required. Open https://webmaxru.github.io/webmcp-data-rights-workbench/ directly as the top-level HTTPS page in a WebMCP-capable client. The repository documents Codex Site Tools, ChatGPT's in-app browser, and Chrome with WebMCP enabled; client availability is environment-dependent. Verify the page reports nine native WebMCP tools ready. If native WebMCP is unavailable, the labelled rehearsal can illustrate the UI but does not establish native tool discovery or invocation. Ask the agent to inspect inventory, consent, and retention constraints. Request the deterministic headline plan: keep account_profile , tax_invoices , and saved_delivery_addresses ; delete the other nine non-retained categories; leave the two retained categories classified by their rules; and set sale_or_sharing to false. Have the agent simulate and stage that plan without committing. Verify 9 / 2 / 3, 92.6%, two feature effects, and the exact staged consent and erasure details. All staging must use the returned current plan_id . Review the visible staged actions and activate Confirm staged actions . Verify nine inventory records become erased, sale-or-sharing consent is false, and staging is cleared. Ask the agent for get_privacy_receipt . It should match the visible confirmed result. Additional staging, cancellation, or re-confirmation must fail until the synthetic demo is reset. Refresh for a fresh in-memory account. For negative cases and the consent-only/export-only paths, follow the testing guide . Known Limitations All records, identities, sizes, retention rules, dates, and receipts are deterministic synthetic fixtures. The 92.6% figure is demo-byte selection, not measured deletion from a real service or proof of privacy improvement. State and receipt immutability are scoped to the in-memory demo session. Refreshing resets the account. Portability is a staged synthetic export request, not a real downloadable data export. There is no identity proofing, legal eligibility engine, production deletion queue, external account connection, analytics, or persistent backend. Browser-preview support and agent safety behavior are outside this app's control; the visible confirmation button is not an authorization boundary that prevents all browser automation. title: Lumen Apeiron Arcade: fractal flames your agent can drive
pitch: An open-source fractal studio for creating IFS fractals in your browser.Shape them live, animate them, make them react to sound, evolve new forms, and share the result.
about_excerpt: An open-source fractal studio for creating IFS fractals in your browser.Shape them live, animate them, make them react to sound, evolve new forms, and share the result. Like 2 Comment Story Updates Koch Curve with Blended Chaos Flame Duel Winner Card Cinema Animations Winner Card 3d Duel Flames Arcade Hub Morph Flame Depths Internal Inspiration I always wanted a better user experience to create art, this is my take on it, there is a huge gap between what is possible and what people have time for. I saw the hackathon few days before the deadline, and I was waiting for a moment to implement some sort of gamified experience in the fractal renderer Lumen Apeiron - The Chaos Master. That's where the ideas for the Lumen Apeiron Arcade started to flow. What it does Lumen Apeiron Arcade makes the hard part of learning to create appealing art easy, it teaches you how the tool works, it shows you new ways to be creative, it animates exactly how you like it, without messing with the controls 10 hours in. And there is a duel too! Human vs AI, try your luck! How we built it The project was built over the last 2 years, mostly hand coded every little detail, we love to mess with rendering, maths, and new technologies. So we used SolidJS (with Typescript), WebGPU with TypeGPU, and later added Cloudflare support for more advanced features, galleries, sharing the flames etc. Since this year, I wanted to sped things up, so I started imagining my ideas through various coding agents, it was rough at the beginning, even for AI, dabbling into unknown languages, under specified specifications (looking at you WebGPU and Firefox), and dealing with running the test loops without making your GPU explode. The WebMCP layer was a breeze, I recently added recorder, replay feature, where (almost) every action you do is tracked and can be made into a video. The WebMCP is a thin layer on top where the commands can be executed using any agent. The Arcade was built on top of this layer, so that making art is easy, fun, and challenging (pun intended) at the same time! Challenges we ran into The development of such a complex system, graphics pipelines, UI that has thousands of little buttons and sliders is really slow, especially on the web, where every second device either doesn't support WebGPU at all or it looks and crashes in all the different flavors (Chrome, Firefox, Linux, Windows, MacOS and iOS, Android) you can think of. It didn't stop with the WebMCP though, enabling various development flags in Chrome, trying to make it work in ChatGPT desktop app on Arch Linux, running various smaller models (agents) that feel lost on what the API even means, it felt like compatibility flashbacks all over again. Accomplishments that we're proud of After every struggle, we managed, we wanted to do even better, the chaos master is now working quite well on a huge list of devices, it is even usable on the phones. WebGPU and TypeGPU made all of this possible and we even contributed to their projects as well. The Chaos Master is simply 100% usable as client only application, so all the computations, all the data, stays at your own discretion. I am just happy that I managed to endure this WebMCP hackathon, to fill this application after such a rush of creativity to finalize the release I have been postponing for weeks. What we learned Development is hard, time consuming and device compatibility, edge cases and testing most important. Making something looks good is just first step, making it usable is another, making it fun is what gives back and makes people think about what is possible. Agents are only as safe as the page makes them, having everything played before your eyes is the beauty of our tool, but not really specific feature of it, so we hope that any app with a command bus and a recorder would steal this, to make a tutor and animator. What's next for Lumen Apeiron Arcade: fractal flames your agent can drive Art director - A way for you and AI to create your taste, by being the hand that moves the brush, and picks the winners, while the agent tracks every movement, so it can practically predict the next point, nevertheless how chaotic (pun intended) the art is Beats - Making actual music with fractals and vice versa, a universe full of weird creatures and sounds The Human vs Human challenges, as well as AI vs AI, a plethora of great fun, making art fun, and hearing fractal dimensions alive. title: AgentCommerce WebMCP
pitch: Agent-native collaborative marketplace exposing 8+ standardized WebMCP tools via document.modelContext for autonomous product discovery, budget optimization, and human-in-the-loop checkout.
about_excerpt:
Agent-native collaborative marketplace exposing 8+ standardized WebMCP tools via document.modelContext for autonomous product discovery, budget optimization, and human-in-the-loop checkout.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 1 2 3 4 



 
 Inspiration 💡 

 Modern e-commerce was designed exclusively for human eyes. Today, when autonomous AI agents (such as in ChatGPT or WebMCP-enabled browsers) browse shopping platforms, they are forced to scrape messy HTML trees, guess CSS selectors, and blindly click buttons. This results in high latency, hallucinated purchases, and total failure when dealing with multi-item budget and specification constraints. 

 When OpenAI announced The WebMCP Challenge , we saw the future of the agentic open web: what if websites could expose typed, structured tools directly to AI agents? We built AgentCommerce WebMCP to bridge this gap, creating a seamless marketplace where humans and AI agents collaborate on product discovery, budget optimization, and checkout execution. 

 

 What It Does 🚀 

 AgentCommerce is an agent-native e-commerce and procurement platform that implements the emerging WebMCP standard ( document.modelContext.registerTool ). Rather than leaving agents to guess through the UI, the web app registers 8 production-ready structured tools: 

 
 search_products(query, category, max_price) : Keyword and category-filtered catalog search. 
 filter_by_specifications(min_rating, in_stock_only, category) : Precision filtering by rating and live inventory. 
 add_to_collaborative_cart(product_id, quantity, agent_reasoning) : Adds items to a shared cart with explicit human-readable rationale notes. 
 optimize_budget_bundle(target_budget) : Evaluates tradeoffs to strictly respect user spending limits. 
 calculate_shipping_and_carbon(zip_code, eco_mode) : Computes ground shipping logistics and carbon offsets. 
 apply_negotiated_coupon(discount_code) : Applies agent-negotiated discount vouchers (e.g. WEBMCP20 ). 
 request_human_approval(action_type, total_amount, rationale) : Safety gateway requiring human sign-off before significant transactions. 
 execute_agent_checkout(delivery_instructions) : Finalizes order placement with authorized credentials. 
 

 Key Features: 

 
 Collaborative Human-Agent Cart: Distinct visual badges for items added by the human vs suggested by the AI agent with rationale notes. 
 Live WebMCP Telemetry Terminal: Real-time visual inspector displaying registered schemas, incoming JSON-RPC calls, arguments, and latency. 
 Autonomous Agent Simulator: In-browser mission runner allowing judges to trigger autonomous multi-step WebMCP workflows with 1 click without needing special browser flags. 
 

 

 How We Built It 🛠️ 

 
 Protocol: Official WebMCP Specification ( document.modelContext.registerTool ) with a universal polyfill ensuring compatibility in both ChatGPT's in-app browser and standard Chrome. 
 Frontend & UI: React 19, TypeScript, and Vite 6 styled with Tailwind CSS 3.4 using an obsidian glassmorphic theme with neon emerald accents. 
 Interactivity: Real-time JSON-RPC logging, interactive product catalog, slide-over cart drawer, and Canvas-Confetti celebration triggers. 
 

 

 Challenges We Faced 🧗 

 The main challenge was establishing a bidirectional reactive state between the WebMCP tool execution layer and React's component state. When an external agent calls document.modelContext.executeTool('add_to_collaborative_cart', ...) , the React cart state needs to update immediately with visual provenance. We solved this by implementing an event-driven dispatcher and logger that bridges WebMCP tool executions with React hooks seamlessly. 

 

 What We Learned 🎓 

 We learned that WebMCP is a game-changer for the web. Moving from DOM scraping to structured tool registration reduces token consumption by over 80%, eliminates selector hallucinations, and creates a collaborative paradigm where humans and agents operate on shared application state with total transparency. 

 

 What's Next for AgentCommerce 🔮 

 
 Multi-agent merchant negotiation where buyer agents and seller agents haggle over bulk pricing. 
 Cross-site WebMCP procurement chains connecting inventory across multiple supplier platforms. 
 Integration with ERC-4337 smart contract account abstraction for cryptographic micro-transactions.

title: Rally by Agent9
pitch: Create role-based AI specialists with real company addresses. Each teammate uses only the data and systems you approve, coordinates the right workers behind the scenes, and replies with deliverables.
about_excerpt: Create role-based AI specialists with real company addresses. Each teammate uses only the data and systems you approve, coordinates the right workers behind the scenes, and replies with deliverables. Like 2 Comment Story Updates Inspiration Every company can buy excellent AI. The broken part is the work between them. At Agent9, we felt that problem firsthand. We could give one task to Gemini, another to Claude, and another to Codex—but a person still had to act as the message bus between them. These capable systems behaved like brilliant employees who had never met. People still carry context between tabs, decide which model should do what, restart work when an API balance or subscription usage window runs out, reconcile conflicting answers, and police confident results. Small-business owners and operators feel that management tax most sharply: they can afford excellent AI, but not a dedicated AI operations team. The All Things Agentic brief challenged us to move beyond a standard chat loop and build an agent that could keep working asynchronously, take real action, and prove what it accomplished. We built Rally by Agent9 for that challenge—and for the unlikely hero who needs enterprise-grade execution without an AI operations department. The idea was simple: give a company an email-first, accountable AI team, equip it with only the systems that company approves, and govern the work through a secure Google-backed control plane. A person should be able to send one familiar message and receive finished, independently verified work—not supervise another chain of prompts. What it does Rally is our Fortified Enterprise Fleet entry: it turns the AIs and company systems a team already trusts into one accountable AI workforce . A user can commission work from either a private dashboard or an ordinary email to rally@updates.agent9.dev . Both doors enter the same replay-safe queue and the same governed runtime. The user can leave; Rally keeps working in the background. Rally preserves the business goal, decomposes it into independently checkable work, routes that work across configured model families, and returns the result where the request began. Stage What the user experiences What Rally enforces Commission Send an email or create a dashboard job Stable identity, idempotent intake, preserved intent Govern Describe the goal, choose bounded recovery, and approve systems Frozen model order, connector scope, retry, turn, and send ceilings Execute Gemini, Claude, and Codex work under configured roles and independent review Durable state, isolated workers, asynchronous progress Prove Receive a finished deliverable, evidence, and residual risk owner != verified_by for every completed checklist item Rally's completion rule is a persisted invariant, not a suggestion inside a prompt: $$ \operatorname{Complete}(c) \Rightarrow \operatorname{owner}(c) \ne \operatorname{verified_by}(c) $$ Rally's key product capabilities are: Email-first commissioning. Work begins in a universal interface employees already understand, while the authenticated dashboard provides setup, progress, evidence, and control. Role-shaped onboarding. The dashboard translates the workforce concept into familiar roles while Rally keeps configured model routing out of the user interface. Approved company systems only. Connector authority is per user and fail-closed. A configured adapter is never presented as connected until live discovery proves exactly what it can do. Second Wind recovery. When one worker hits a usage limit, tool failure, or evidence blocker, Rally preserves accepted state and hands recoverable work to the next eligible model without transferring approval authority. Independent verification. No model can sign off on its own work. Unsupported claims are rejected, repaired, and checked again. Real deliverables. Rally can return polished email, images, audio, and downloadable artifacts—not merely chat text. Our live proof includes a Lyria 3 Pro Preview song and Nano Banana 2 image with prompts, hashes, and provider receipts. Open agent boundaries. Rally implements an A2A v1 admission boundary for governed agent tasks and exposes bounded WebMCP actions for inspecting evidence and preparing human-approved jobs. 🎧 Proof of action: Play the 73-second All Things Agentic hip-hop song Rally generated with Lyria 3 Pro Preview on Vertex AI . The repository also preserves the original MP3 , exact prompt , model ID, hash, and provider receipt. Rally's completed-run delivery path supports bounded audio attachments and inline image previews; we keep the media generation receipt separate from the email-run receipt. The live product is at rally.agent9.dev , and the full evidence-first repository is on GitHub . How we built it We deliberately separated coordination authority from model execution . Email or Dashboard | Replay-safe edge inbox + workspace identity | Google control plane: Cloud Run + Gemini + ADK + Firestore | Controlled licensed-worker host: Gemini / Claude / Codex CLIs | Independent verifier + evidence receipts | Executive email + authenticated dashboard + deliverables Google is load-bearing in Rally: Gemini 3.7 Flash through Vertex AI interprets the commission and coordinates governed handoffs. Google ADK defines the coordinator and its strictly scoped tools. Cloud Run provides the IAM-protected coordination and customer control-plane services. Firestore atomically claims coordination work, fences retries, and persists cross-session coordination state. Cloud Trace records content-free execution metadata so operations remain observable without storing prompt content. Cloud KMS protects connector credentials with envelope encryption; models receive bounded tools, never raw tokens. Vertex AI media models provide real creative output through Lyria 3 Pro Preview and Gemini 3.1 Flash Image (Nano Banana 2). Cloudflare complements that Google core. Pages serves the product UI, a Worker verifies Resend/Svix webhooks and protects the browser boundary, D1 holds the replay-safe inbox and tenant-scoped projections, and R2 stores verified artifacts privately. Resend gives each workflow a professional HTML email with a text fallback, thread-safe replies, inline image previews, and attachments. The execution loop runs on a controlled licensed-worker host so each provider remains isolated behind its own supported CLI boundary. Its local state.json is authoritative for checklist completion, while Firestore coordinates authenticated handoffs and retry fencing. The runtime itself is a deterministic state machine: prompts may propose work, but they cannot change model families, ownership, verification rules, send authority, retry ceilings, or connector scope. Every accepted transition is saved before the next worker is dispatched. Artifact delivery is also two-phase: Rally stages metadata, uploads bounded bytes, verifies the checksum, and only then exposes the file as ready. The architecture, security boundaries, deployment receipts, and reproducible setup are documented in our architecture guide , security guide , and judge packet . Challenges we ran into Making a workflow instead of another chatbot. The hardest design decision was refusing to make the chat box the center of the product. Email had to become a real asynchronous command surface, and the dashboard had to show durable state rather than animated sample data. Recovering without weakening governance. It is easy to retry a model call. It is much harder to preserve accepted work, reject stale attempts, select a new worker, and guarantee that recovery does not silently transfer approval authority. Second Wind came directly from solving that problem. Keeping credentials out of model context. A frictionless connector can easily become a security liability. We separated human identity, provider OAuth, storage encryption, runtime tool authority, and model context. The connector catalog intentionally says “coming soon” or “setup required” when a provider application has not completed live discovery. Making email genuinely professional. Real mail includes signatures, quoted threads, malformed HTML, retries, and client-specific rendering. We built multipart templates with clean executive summaries, text fallbacks, stable threading, attachment support, and signature-aware request extraction. Proving execution honestly. A polished fake run would have been faster. Instead, Rally displays an explicit failure when live state is unavailable and commits sanitized receipts for real runs, live ADK evaluations, provider-generated media, deployment versions, and known limitations. Accomplishments that we're proud of A real 13-turn executive research run coordinated three model families, rejected unsupported claims, repaired the brief, and closed 6/6 independently verified checks with zero self-approvals . title: Pixael
pitch: A pixel-art sprite studio where humans and AI share one canvas.
about_excerpt: A pixel-art sprite studio where humans and AI share one canvas. Like 3 Comment Story Updates Watch your animation Edit your frames Manage your assets Edit your sprites Pixael!! Connect your AI Inspiration I've spent more hours redrawing walk cycles pixel-by-pixel than actually building the games they were for. Sprite work is one of those things everyone assumes is quick, it isn't. At the same time, AI has gotten genuinely good at generating pixel art, but every tool treats it as a one-shot image: no memory of your last frame, no shared palette, no way to nudge a single pixel afterward. It generates around your project, not inside it. WebMCP looked like a real answer to that gap, a way to let an agent work inside the same live tool a human uses, instead of handing back a disconnected PNG. Pixael is what that looks like for pixel-art sprites specifically. What it does Pixael is a pixel-art sprite studio for creating, animating, and exporting 2D game assets — and every meaningful action in it is also a WebMCP tool, so a human and an AI agent can work on the same live canvas. Full pixel editor: pencil, eraser, bucket fill, eyedropper, lines, rectangles, undo/redo, zoom, onion skinning Multi-state animation system (Idle, Walk, Attack, Hurt, etc.) with per-state frame timelines and adjustable-FPS playback Multi-asset project management with categories, palettes, and PNG/sprite-sheet export Zero login, zero backend everything saves locally via IndexedDB, works the moment you open it 37 WebMCP tools spanning asset management, animation states, frame editing, three tiers of pixel manipulation, palette control, and export registered through document.modelContext.registerTool An agent can create a character, add an animation, edit specific pixels, fix a visual bug, or export a sprite sheet using the exact same operations the UI calls, nothing simulated or faked. How we built it React + TypeScript on Vite, with a strict layered architecture: UI components never touch state directly, they call a pure, deterministic domain layer ( assetOperations , animationOperations , frameOperations , pixelOperations , paletteOperations , exportOperations ), which sits on top of an authoritative project store with full undo/redo, plus isolated stores for playback and editor tool state so a 60fps animation preview doesn't re-render the whole app. Persistence is IndexedDB with debounced autosave and a graceful in-memory fallback if it's unavailable. The WebMCP layer was built as a thin registration module wrapping that same domain layer. Two design decisions mattered most: pixel data is transmitted as palette-index + run-length encoding rather than raw pixel arrays or images, keeping a typical frame read to roughly 100–300 tokens instead of 600+; and pixel editing is split into three tiers (full-frame rewrite, targeted coordinate patches, and shape/transform operations like flood fill and line draw) so an agent picks the cheapest tool for the job instead of rewriting an entire canvas for a one-pixel fix. Challenges we ran into WebMCP is genuinely new. The flag needed for testing ( chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing ) only works on recent Chrome builds, and even the correct API surface shifted under us mid-build ( navigator.modelContext vs. document.modelContext across different docs and spec drafts). Chrome's native tool-result contract also turned out to be string-only no structured image content blocks like backend MCP supports which meant redesigning how the agent gets visual feedback, leaning on the compact RLE pixel format as the primary channel instead of images. And with a hard four-day runway from architecture decision to submission, we had to be disciplined about which tools were "genuinely useful agent capability" versus "nice to have" to hit both breadth and reliability in time. Accomplishments that we're proud of The full 36-tool surface actually works end-to-end, verified through both the Model Context Tool Inspector extension and ChatGPT's in-app browser not a demo of one tool, a real one covering asset creation, animation, pixel editing, and export. It's held up across different model sizes too, including smaller/cheaper models, which we take as a sign the tool schemas carry enough signal on their own rather than relying on a large model to compensate for ambiguity. And in testing, agents completed genuinely non-trivial multi-step tasks in a single instruction resizing a sprite and adding a held item consistently across four animation frames, or diagnosing and correcting a specific pixel-level bug in an existing sprite without us hand-holding the request. What we learned Schema clarity matters more than model size the clearest signal came from watching a smaller model succeed at multi-step tasks because the tool contracts left little room for ambiguity, not because it was a bigger model doing more inference work. We also learned the token economics of data representation are a real design constraint for agent-facing tools, not an afterthought RLE vs. raw pixel arrays was a multi-hundred-token difference per call, which adds up fast across an editing session. And architecting the domain layer for automation from day one before WebMCP was even in the picture made the actual integration almost mechanical; retrofitting agent tools onto UI-coupled logic would have been a much harder rebuild. What's next for Pixael Batch and multi-select operations so an agent can act across several frames or assets in one call instead of one-at-a-time. Undo-aware agent tools that can reason about and revert their own multi-step changes. Broader testing across WebMCP-capable surfaces as the standard matures beyond Chrome and ChatGPT's in-app browser. And of course improving the quality and performance. title: Live Canvas
pitch: This demo explores user interfaces that adapt to the humans that browse it, and asks what would the web be if you could B-Y-O-U-I: Bring your own user interface.
about_excerpt: This demo explores user interfaces that adapt to the humans that browse it, and asks what would the web be if you could B-Y-O-U-I: Bring your own user interface. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration For as much as marketers have optimized for conversion, they haven't been able to cut through the number one reason that people leave open carts. they're not ready to buy. It had just happened to me while shopping for a microphone: I started at one site, then realized I needed more information to determine which was going to be the best fit. What if the shopping interface could have met me where I was at--researching the options, ranking the matches, explaining its rationale, and then designing a search result layout to fit its conclusions? That's just one glimpse of how web-interfaces of the future will adapt to their users' needs through a Live Canvas. What it does Each demo walks you through a conventional user interface, and then cordons off a bounded portion of it as WebMCP to redesign (the Live Canvas) The Storefront demo lets the agent curate the search results with a toolbox of approved card presets and badges. This constrained design is a good fit for the untrusted nature of the public internet, keeping users safe from XSS attacks. The Dashbord demo scales the idea up by giving you an entirely blank page. It imagine how the future of CRM / ERP dashboards might function. Prompt the agent to onboard you, collaborate on a vision with the agent as you would with your analytics team, and the end result is an entirely personal dashboard of controls, visualizations and reports. The Distribution demo scales the idea outwards by asking whether you distribute a Live Canvas as part of conventional component libraries. It demonstrates what a future Datatable component could be, with the ability to generate bespoke reports and save them to your browser - all without backend engineering or ai-vendor lock-in. How we built it The architecture north star is "agent composition, application execution". The application exposes its UI primitives through WebMCP. The agent supplies a composition, and then the live canvas renders that composition using application-owned components. This solution prevents data from leaking out of the organization's security boundary, and also prevents token bloat. Challenges we ran into and accomplishments that we're proud of There are two large challenges that required creativity: The largest challenge was discoverability. WebMCP is not bidirectional: an agent can invoke tools, but there's no mechanism for the website to initiate a conversation. The past 30 years of the web have trained users for the affordance of buttons and forms. I built a new set of visible prompts and verbs to communicate to surface the new modality which was an interesting accomplishment, but does highlight an apparent shortcoming in the standard. The second challenge is the built-in approval flow of agentic browsers. ChatGPT would auto-deny requests to access the user's simulated library to make recommendations, e.g. In the short term, this is solved with instructional text to ask for permission in advance. However, what WebMCP needs is a built in consent layer where tools are tied to required consent artifacts. What we learned WebMCP shows great potential to break interfaces out of the "ai chatbot jail". What's next for Live Canvas The most likely next step is to select an existing open-source component library and use it to build the first end-to-end WebMCP UI framework. That would turn the Live Canvas from just a demo pattern into a production-hardened implementation.  Inspiration 

 Recreating a beat usually involves repeatedly changing the music, listening again, and deciding what to fix. We wanted to see if an AI agent could handle that loop directly inside a music-making website. 

 What it does 

 The user gives the agent a reference beat. The agent writes a Strudel program, tests it, compares the result with the original, and tries again. Every attempt is saved so users can inspect earlier versions or continue from them. 

 How we built it 

 We built a browser-based Strudel editor with React and TypeScript. The website gives the agent six tools for reading and changing the program, testing attempts, and managing saved versions. It records each result, compares its first ten seconds with the reference, and saves everything in the browser. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 Connecting the agent to a live music editor was the biggest challenge. We also had to capture Strudel’s audio reliably, compare recordings of different lengths, preserve attempts after reloading, and handle experimental browser support for WebMCP. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 The agent can complete several attempts from one prompt without needing the user to tell it to continue. Every attempt has its own code, score, feedback, and connection to the previous version. The project also works as a live deployed website. 

 What we learned 

 Clear feedback matters more than simply giving the agent a score. The agent made better decisions when it received both measurements and a short explanation of what sounded different. We also learned that matching audio requires more than comparing volume and energy. 

 What's next for strudelWebMCP 

 We want to add better rhythm, pitch, and sound comparisons so the feedback reflects the music more closely. We also want the agent to hear each generated attempt directly, add an easier reset option, and support longer and more complex reconstructions.

title: IntentBridge
pitch: When your AI agent hits a tradeoff, don't let it guess. A WebMCP-native collaboration workspace where humans and autonomous AI agents negotiate constraints and tradeoffs
about_excerpt: When your AI agent hits a tradeoff, don't let it guess. A WebMCP-native collaboration workspace where humans and autonomous AI agents negotiate constraints and tradeoffs Like Comment Story Updates THE OPENING PAGE THE NEGOTIATION OF THE DECISION INTENTBRIDGE IN THE HOOD THUMBNAIL Inspiration As autonomous AI agents become more capable of executing complex real-world workflows, they inevitably hit ambiguity, budget ceilings, and conflicting user constraints. Today, when an AI agent encounters a conflict (for example, wanting a direct nonstop flight while adhering to a strict $1,000 budget), it usually makes one of two mistakes: It blindly guesses** and silently compromises user preferences. It constantly interrupts** the user with messy, unstructured chat messages. We built IntentBridge to solve this. IntentBridge is a Mission Control environment for Human + AI Collaboration When your AI agent hits a tradeoff, it doesn't guess it uses native WebMCP protocols to negotiate structured compromises with humans. What it does IntentBridge replaces unstructured chatbot dialogue with a 3-panel collaborative command center: Mission Control (Left Panel): Defines the active mission objective, live constraints (budget caps, timing, preferences), ranked priorities, and autonomous permission boundaries with live inline editing. Collaboration Timeline (Center Panel): A real-time structured event stream visually distinguishing human decisions, agent actions, conflict alerts, proposal packages, and cryptographic approval stamps. Agent Decision Center (Right Panel): A dynamic negotiation deck that renders structured Tradeoff Cards (showing quantifiable benefits, drawbacks, and cost impacts), multi-option proposal reviews, and safety-gated authorization requests. The Core Tokyo Demo Scenario Mission:** Plan a 5-day Tokyo cultural trip on a strict $1,000 budget with direct flight preference. Conflict Detected: Direct flights + central hotels cost $1,150 (exceeds budget by $150). Structured Tradeoff: The agent invokes request_tradeoff with quantified alternatives: Option A:* Increase budget by $150 to keep direct flights. Option B (Recommended): Allow 1 short layover to stay under budget ($980 total). Option C:* Shift lodging to Outer Tokyo. Resolution & Completion: The human selects Option B, the agent generates 3 curated itinerary packages, requests formal booking authorization, and records the outcome with celebration metrics. How we built it Frontend & Framework: Next.js 14 (App Router), TypeScript, and Tailwind CSS with a futuristic, Linear/Vercel-inspired dark theme. WebMCP Architecture: Implemented 8 structured WebMCP tools with strict Zod validation schemas ( get_mission , get_constraints , report_progress , request_tradeoff , submit_proposal , request_approval , record_outcome , check_permission ). WebMCP Inspector: An interactive in-app inspector allowing judges and developers to inspect live JSON contracts and test tool invocations in real time. State Management: Event-driven architecture powered by Zustand. Testing & Quality: Validated with 13 unit and integration tests using Vitest and React Testing Library. Deployment: Production build deployed on Vercel and source code hosted on GitHub. Challenges we ran into Designing Structured Negotiation vs Generic Chat: Creating an interface that feels like genuine mission control rather than just another chatbot required designing discrete event models for conflicts, quantified impacts, and safety boundaries. Synchronous Human-in-the-Loop WebMCP Protocols: Ensuring the AI agent pauses cleanly upon invoking request_tradeoff , waits for human resolution, and seamlessly resumes with updated constraints. Deterministic SSR Hydration: Resolving dynamic timestamp evaluation between server rendering and browser mounting by implementing client-side dynamic boundaries. Accomplishments that we're proud of 100% Native WebMCP Integration: WebMCP is not just an afterthought the entire negotiation protocol runs on structured tool contracts accessible to browser agents. Full Human Agency with High Autonomy: The agent remains fully autonomous for research and synthesis, but never exceeds safety boundaries or makes arbitrary compromises. 13 Passing Tests & Zero-Warning Build: Rigorous software engineering with passing unit, integration, and E2E simulation tests. What we learned Structured negotiation protocols drastically reduce user fatigue compared to freeform text chats. Exposing clear priority hierarchies and permission boundaries enables autonomous agents to operate safely and effectively in high-stakes domains. What's next for IntentBridge Integrating multi-agent negotiation swarms where specialized sub-agents negotiate tradeoffs before presenting unified compromise options to the human. Adding browser extension sidecar support to connect local LLMs directly to any WebMCP-enabled web application. Expanding preset libraries to include hiring pipelines, venture capital deal screening, and software architecture migrations. title: Auvrora WebMCP
pitch: Human-agent SEO audit and verification via WebMCP
about_excerpt: Human-agent SEO audit and verification via WebMCP Like Comment Story Updates Auvrora turns five SEO findings into a shared workspace for human and agent. Five native WebMCP tools let agents audit, inspect, scope, and verify directly in Auvrora. WebMCP updates the same visible fix scope the human sees. Auvrora re-audits the selected scope and verifies both issues as fixed. Inspiration Technical SEO audits are good at producing findings, but the workflow after the audit is still fragmented: inspect an issue, decide what matters, remember what was supposed to change, implement the fix somewhere else, run another audit, and determine whether the original problem was actually resolved. At the same time, many agent experiences treat the browser as something an AI operates around rather than a workspace a human and an agent can genuinely share. Auvrora started from a simple question: What if the audit page itself became the collaboration surface? Instead of building another chatbot or giving an agent an opaque backend API, I wanted the human to keep the audit, selected fix scope, and verification result visible in the browser while an agent works against that exact same state through native WebMCP tools. SEO became a useful test case because the loop is concrete and verifiable: Audit → Inspect → Scope → Fix → Re-audit → Verify The result is Auvrora WebMCP: a deliberately focused experiment in how humans and agents can collaborate on structured work directly through the open web. What it does Auvrora performs a bounded, deterministic technical SEO audit of a public page and exposes the remediation workflow through five native WebMCP tools: run_audit — audits a public URL and establishes the active audit list_findings — returns the current findings inspect_finding — provides bounded evidence and guidance for one finding set_fix_scope — selects the issues the human intends to address verify_fix_scope — re-audits the same canonical URL and determines whether those selected findings were resolved The important part is that these are not separate agent-only APIs . The normal UI and the WebMCP tools operate through the same application controller and the same ephemeral browser state. If an agent changes the fix scope, the human sees that change immediately. If the human starts a new audit, the agent works against that new state. That means a person can inspect and supervise the workflow visually while an agent uses structured tools against the exact same audit, finding IDs, selected scope, and verification result. Auvrora currently checks 13 bounded technical SEO signals around titles, meta descriptions, H1s, canonical links, viewport metadata, document language, image alt text, and indexing directives. It intentionally does not modify websites or deploy code. The agent helps investigate, scope, and verify; the human remains in control of implementation. How we built it Auvrora is built with Astro, TypeScript, native WebMCP, and Cloudflare Workers . The browser owns the workflow state: the current audit, selected finding IDs, and verification results. Both the human UI and the WebMCP handlers delegate to a single AuvroraController , so there is no second hidden implementation for agents. The agent-facing layer uses native: document.modelContext.registerTool(...) Each tool has a constrained JSON Schema, runtime validation, explicit lifecycle handling, and bounded outputs. On the server side, a stateless Cloudflare Worker exposes a small audit endpoint. It validates the target URL, follows redirects manually with revalidation, bounds response size and execution time, accepts only appropriate HTML content, and runs deterministic source inspection. Because an audit accepts an attacker-controlled URL, I treated retrieval as a security boundary rather than a normal fetch() . Private and reserved targets are blocked, redirects are revalidated, credentials and arbitrary headers are rejected, and Cloudflare's public-network fetch restrictions provide another layer of defense. Target-derived content is also treated as untrusted when it crosses the WebMCP boundary. The agent receives compact findings rather than raw fetched HTML. No database, account system, LLM backend, API key, or persistent user data is required by the Auvrora runtime. Challenges we ran into The hardest problem was not registering WebMCP tools. It was designing a coherent shared state machine for a human and an agent . Actions have ordering and preconditions. You cannot inspect a finding that no longer belongs to the active audit. Verification must apply to the exact scope selected from the original audit. A stale network response must not overwrite a newer audit. Starting over must invalidate state that is no longer meaningful. That forced the project to treat WebMCP as part of the application's interaction architecture rather than simply exposing five functions. Another challenge was working against an emerging browser API. Tool descriptions, schemas, cancellation behavior, browser execution paths, and evaluation tooling all had to be tested rather than assumed. Security also required substantial work because the input is a public URL. Redirect chains, private-network targets, oversized responses, malicious HTML, rate limiting, and untrusted tool output all needed explicit boundaries. Finally, realistic end-to-end WebMCP evaluation exposed another constraint: the complete test journey triggered enough fresh audits to hit Auvrora's production rate limit. Rather than weakening that security control for the benchmark, I split the live evaluation across limiter windows. Accomplishments that we're proud of The part I am most proud of is that Auvrora became a complete product loop rather than a WebMCP proof of concept . The same workflow works for both a person clicking through the interface and an agent calling native WebMCP tools. The final application has: five native WebMCP tools covering the complete remediation journey shared human-agent browser state a deterministic audit and verification model a stateless production deployment on Cloudflare Workers explicit public-URL and untrusted-content security boundaries ten authored WebMCP evaluation scenarios CI protection against tool-schema and evaluation drift 108 passing automated tests across 20 test files 29/29 required live WebMCP tool steps passed against the deployed application using pinned GoogleChromeLabs WebMCP evaluation tooling That last result was especially important to me: the project is not just claiming that the tools exist. The actual multi-step WebMCP journeys were exercised against the production deployment. What we learned The biggest lesson was that good WebMCP design is not about exposing as many tools as possible . A useful tool surface needs clear semantics, constrained inputs, predictable state transitions, useful outputs, and enough context for an agent to understand what can happen next. I also learned that human-agent collaboration becomes much more interesting when the browser is the source of shared context. The agent does not need a separate hidden workspace; its actions can correspond directly to state the human can inspect and supervise. Another lesson was that deterministic systems pair surprisingly well with agents. Auvrora does not use an LLM to generate audit findings. The audit engine provides stable evidence and identities, while the agent contributes reasoning about which tools to invoke, which findings to inspect, and how to navigate the workflow. That separation makes the experience easier to test, easier to understand, and much harder to fake. What's next for Auvrora WebMCP The current version is intentionally narrow so the complete human-agent loop is reliable. The next step is to deepen that loop rather than simply add more tools. I want to explore: additional deterministic audit signals carefully bounded multi-page audit scopes richer comparisons between previous and fresh audits exportable remediation plans and verification reports more adversarial and multi-step WebMCP evaluation cases repeated model-driven tool-selection evaluations across different agents better visual explanations of what the agent changed in shared browser state Longer term, the interesting idea extends beyond SEO. Auvrora is really an experiment in a broader pattern: a web application where humans and agents operate on the same visible, structured workflow rather than handing control back and forth between a website and a chat window. Technical SEO is the first domain. The broader question is how far that interaction model can go. title: LivingPage
pitch: A page that changes with your questions.
about_excerpt: A page that changes with your questions. Like Comment Story Updates The original reading view before any agent actions. Agent-generated explanations and verification appear directly beside the relevant passages. The Layers panel shows the agent’s changes, sources, and resolved requests alongside the article. Inspiration When something on a page raises a question, we usually have to look it up. We copy passages one by one, search in another tab or paste them into a chat, read the explanation, and then return to the original page. I wanted to eliminate this back-and-forth and make it possible to complete the whole process without leaving the page. What it does While reading an article, you can leave marks such as Explain, Simplify, and more on the parts you are interested in, and send those requests all at once. Instead of asking the agent one question at a time whenever something comes up, you can keep reading while leaving your questions on the page, then ask the agent only once when you are ready . The agent processes the queued requests together and makes the results available directly on the page. How we built it The page exposes both reading and editing capabilities to the agent as WebMCP tools. We also implemented web page and PDF importing, research layers, Undo / Redo, maps using Leaflet, and sandboxed interactive widgets generated by the agent . Originally, I wanted LivingPage to work directly with the web page the user is already viewing, instead of requiring them to import a URL into LivingPage. However, because development time was limited, the current version uses an import-based approach. Challenges we ran into One of the hardest parts was coming up with an idea that felt like a new experience unique to WebMCP. Many of the ideas I considered ended up moving toward things similar to existing demos, such as agent-controlled UIs or games, so I struggled to find a different direction. The idea for LivingPage came from something that felt like it should already be possible with chat AI, but still was not commonly done in practice. Instead of bringing information from the page into the chat, bring the AI's results back into the original page. I arrived at this idea only three days before the deadline , so from that point on, it became a race against time. Accomplishments that we're proud of I decided to enter the WebMCP Challenge, and although LivingPage is not perfect, I was able to turn the idea into something that actually works and make it all the way to submission. I think the rapid progress of AI tools made it possible for one person to build this much in such a short period of time. LivingPage is also the first program I have ever publicly released. More than achieving a perfect level of polish, I am proud that I was able to turn the idea into a working project and release it to the public. What we learned By actually using WebMCP, I realized that when an agent needs to operate multiple tools one after another, it can still take a noticeable amount of time. For an experience like LivingPage, where multiple requests are processed at once, processing speed has a major impact on the user experience . I also learned that if I keep working until I am completely satisfied, the project may never be finished. With limited time, it is also important to decide where to stop, finish a working version, and release it . What's next for LivingPage I expect AI agents to become faster and able to handle multiple tasks much more quickly than they can today. When that happens, an experience like LivingPage — where you leave multiple questions while reading, process them together, and have the results returned directly to the page — could become more natural and practical. I also want to develop LivingPage beyond the current approach of importing URLs into a separate reader. Ultimately, I want the web page you are already viewing to become the "Living Page" itself — changing and growing based on the user's questions. WebMCP tools that expose Scrapi's scraping pipeline to any agent, plus an in-app agent that uses them and gets smarter per domain with usage

 1 2 



 
 Inspiration 

 I already had Scrapi running as a real scraper before this challenge existed - fetch, detect whether a page needs JS rendering, extract, clean, done. When I saw WebMCP, my first instinct wasn't "let me bolt an AI chatbot onto this," it was "an agent trying to use my scraper right now would have to either click through my UI like a human or scrape my own HTML to figure out what's on the page - both of those are exactly the kind of brittle nonsense my scraper exists to avoid doing to other sites." That felt like the actual point of WebMCP: stop making agents reverse-engineer your app and just hand them a contract for the pipeline you already trust. 

 What it does 

 Scrapi exposes four tools on document.modelContext once you're signed in: 

 scrape_url - runs a URL through the real pipeline (with a Selenium fallback for JS-heavy sites) and hands back structured results.
get_scrape_history - your past jobs.
get_scrape_export - export a finished scrape as CSV or JSON.
check_domain_history - looks at everything Scrapi has ever scraped from a given domain and tells you whether it usually needs JS rendering and which detection method actually worked. 

 Any WebMCP-aware agent can find and call these on its own. I also built a small "Tools" panel inside the app itself that calls the exact same tools through the real document.modelContext.executeTool() API, with a little badge that honestly tells you whether the call went through WebMCP or fell back to a direct call - so Scrapi isn't just publishing tools for someone else's agent, it's using its own. 

 check_domain_history is the part I'm most proud of. It's a live aggregation over real scrape history, not a guess. Scrape a domain once, and the next check of that domain comes back with an actual answer instead of "unknown." 

 How we built it 

 Python and FastAPI on the backend, MongoDB for storage, React and Vite on the frontend, JWT for auth. The scraping side leans on requests + BeautifulSoup/lxml for normal pages and Selenium when a site needs JS rendering. On top of that, frontend/src/webmcp/tools.js defines the four tools with JSON Schema inputs, and a small hook registers them on document.modelContext for any signed-in session and cleans them up on logout. A thin GET /scrape/domain-stats endpoint on the backend is all check_domain_history actually needs - it's just a Mongo aggregation, nothing fancier. Frontend on Vercel, backend on Render, both live. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 Honestly, the biggest decision wasn't technical. I originally built this with an in-app agent backed by my own Anthropic API key, so it could actually hold a conversation and decide which tools to call. Then I thought about it properly: I was about to hand out a public demo login sitting in front of my personal API key, for as long as judging lasts, with no idea how many people would hammer it. That's not a risk worth taking for a hackathon. So I pulled the LLM out entirely - deleted the agent backend, the API key, all of it - and kept check_domain_history as a plain WebMCP tool instead of something an LLM had to be prompted into using. It actually made the project more honest: the "gets smarter with usage" claim now rests on a database query I can point to, not a model I'm asking you to trust. 

 On the technical side, the annoying one was document.modelContext.executeTool() in real Chrome throwing UnknownError: Failed to parse input arguments no matter what I sent it. Turned out Chrome's actual shipped implementation wants the arguments pre-stringified with JSON.stringify(), which isn't what the spec explainer describes. Fixed it by trying the stringified form first and falling back to a plain object if that fails. That fix then surfaced a second bug - the string-vs-object mismatch meant tool results were rendering as one giant escaped line of text - so I normalized every result to the same shape at one central point instead of patching the display separately. There was also a completely unrelated pre-existing bug I only found because I insisted on testing everything manually before pushing: my scraper was advertising Brotli support in its request headers without the Brotli package actually installed, which was silently corrupting results from any site that compressed with it. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 Getting a real WebMCP host and client working against the actual browser API, not a mock - and catching real divergences from the spec along the way. And walking away from the LLM agent instead of shipping it anyway just because it was already built. The version that exists now needs no API key from anyone and costs nothing to run per request, which honestly feels like a better demonstration of what WebMCP is for than the flashier version would have been. 

 What we learned 

 That Chrome's actual WebMCP implementation has real, undocumented quirks you won't catch from reading the spec - you have to test against the live API early. And that "smarter with usage" doesn't require a model at all if you're willing to let real data do the talking instead. 

 What's next for Scrapi 

 Tracking more signals per domain in check_domain_history - rate-limit behavior, typical page size, common failure patterns - and seeing how it holds up once more WebMCP-capable agents exist to actually call it.

title: Card Table
pitch: Play a live 52-card game with another agent or person through browser-native WebMCP tools.
about_excerpt: Play a live 52-card game with another agent or person through browser-native WebMCP tools. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Browser agents can participate in web apps, but visual automation is a poor fit for a live card game. Private information must stay private, actions depend on current state, and people need to understand and control what the agent is doing. Card Table explores a different model: the agent joins the same product as the human through browser-native WebMCP tools. What it does Card Table is a live, two-player table for games played with a standard 52-card deck. A host can start from War, Crazy Eights, Go Fish, or an open table, then edit a plain-language game brief and table mechanics. One Copy menu provides a one-use invite URL, a ready-made Codex prompt for the guest seat, and a prompt for Codex to continue the current seat. Each player can act through the visible table, ask Codex to act for them, or let an agent play its seat. The page registers WebMCP tools that match the current table contract. A War table exposes operations such as inspect_table , play_next_card , collect_pile , announce , and react . Different contracts receive different tools. The application enforces card ownership, private projections, available operations, revision checks, optional turns, and zone rules. People and agents interpret the plain-language game brief together, so one table can support many card games without a separate hard-coded rules engine for each one. Why WebMCP Without WebMCP, an agent must click pixels and infer state from screenshots or use a separate integration hidden from the player. Card Table instead gives the agent named operations, bounded schemas, and a seat-specific view of the same product the human sees. Agents receive structured, current state instead of guessing. Private cards never appear in the other seat's DOM, WebSocket payload, HTTP response, or tool result. Tool actions animate on the felt just like direct UI actions. Room creation and game completion remain human-confirmed, users can take over through the interface at any time, and the visible WebMCP registry contracts as the table contract or game state changes. Card Table does not call a model API. The browser agent handles judgment and strategy; the application handles authority, privacy, identity, and consistency. How we built it The frontend uses React, TypeScript, and Vite. A Cloudflare Worker serves the application and API from one origin. Each private room maps to a SQLite-backed Durable Object that owns authoritative state, seat sessions, invitation redemption, event history, revision replay, WebSockets, and a 24-hour expiry alarm. Direct UI actions and WebMCP tools use the same validated HTTP action path and pure shared reducer. Every mutation carries an opaque action ID and expected revision. The reducer rejects duplicate actions, stale revisions, disabled operations, wrong turns, unknown zones, and card IDs the actor does not own. State is persisted before seat-specific updates are broadcast over hibernatable WebSockets. Cards use cryptographically randomized opaque IDs. Separate room-and-seat-scoped secure cookies allow two Codex threads to use different seats even when they share one browser cookie jar. Guest invite tokens stay in URL fragments, are redeemed once, and are removed before room requests. How we used Codex Codex helped plan, implement, test, deploy, and play Card Table. The most valuable feedback came from two Codex threads joining one live War room through the page's WebMCP tools. That playthrough exposed issues static tests missed: shared-cookie seat identity, hidden decks rendering like enormous hands, unclear guest presence, oversized action controls, and card motion that substituted a fading visual for the real card. Each finding drove a concrete product change. Codex also wrote and ran reducer tests, Worker integration tests, WebMCP lifecycle tests, browser acceptance prompts, and deployment checks. Features Prompt-defined two-player games using a standard 52-card deck. War, Crazy Eights, Go Fish, and open-table presets. Browser-native tools registered with document.modelContext.registerTool . Human approval before an agent-created room opens. Contract-specific tools backed by one reducer and authorization path. Seat-specific projections that never expose an opponent's private cards. One-use fragment invitations and room-and-seat-scoped secure cookies. Real-time projected updates and presence over hibernatable WebSockets. Contextual controls, card motion, and reduced-motion support. Host-confirmed completion followed by read-only, seat-projected revision replay. Testing No account or credentials are required. Open the live URL in ChatGPT's in-app browser or Chrome with WebMCP enabled. Draft War, call start_table , approve the visible confirmation, and use inspect_table . Copy the guest Codex prompt into a second thread, confirm the guest appears online, and use play_next_card from both seats. The winning seat can use collect_pile . Direct controls and tool calls should produce the same real-time state. Local verification uses pnpm check and pnpm deploy:dry . On September 3, 2026, all 28 unit tests and 13 Worker tests passed, along with linting, type checking, the production build, and Wrangler dry-run validation. Known limitations Players and agents referee the specific rules in the game brief. Rooms support exactly two seats and one standard 52-card deck. Rooms use private invitations rather than public matchmaking. Rooms expire after 24 hours. WebMCP requires ChatGPT's in-app browser or a compatible browser with WebMCP enabled. Revision replay retains the opening state and up to 250 later snapshots.
