title: Every — real invoices from an AI browser, no sign-up
pitch: A marketing site that publishes 17 WebMCP tools, so an agent can make a real invoice for someone who has no account.
about_excerpt: A marketing site that publishes 17 WebMCP tools, so an agent can make a real invoice for someone who has no account. Like Comment Story Updates ChatGPT's built-in browser listing the 17 Site tools every.ai registers, beside the live generator page. Inspiration every.ai had two landing pages promising a free invoice generator and a free proposal generator to small service businesses. Neither had a generator behind it. We built one during the Challenge window, and made it agent-first from the first commit, because a generator is the one corner of a marketing site where "an agent fills in a form and gets a real result" is the whole product. Then we found the sharper reason to do it. Asked in plain language for "a free invoice tool I can use without making an account", ChatGPT recommended three competitors and then volunteered a correction about us: that Every requires a Google sign-up, so it does not qualify. It cited every.ai. Reading our marketing pages, that was a fair conclusion — the pages talk about trials and sign-in, because that is what the product needed before this week. That is the problem WebMCP actually solves. Search forms a view of what your site can do, and that view is stale the moment you ship. A page that publishes tools does not have to argue with the model. It just hands over the capability, and the agent updates. In our demo video you can watch that happen live : the agent tells the user Every needs an account, opens the page, and corrects itself on camera — "the earlier answer was indeed outdated: the page explicitly says no account is needed" — and then makes the invoice. What it does every.ai is a static Astro marketing site. It also registers 17 tools on document.modelContext , so an agentic browser can act for a visitor who has never signed up. They cover the whole arc of a visit. Decide. about_every and check_fit answer what Every is, what it costs from live pricing data, and whether it suits the business the visitor describes — including saying plainly when it does not. search_help answers from a build-time index of the site's own content and admits when it has no answer instead of guessing. Do. create_invoice , update_invoice , create_proposal , update_proposal , convert_estimate_to_invoice , get_document , list_my_documents and get_pdf create and revise real invoices, estimates and proposals. Not previews. Each one is created immediately, gets a public link, and is kept for 30 days. No account at any point. Leave. request_signup_link returns a single link that opens an Every account already holding everything the agent just made. open_app points existing customers at the right page. request_demo reaches sales. calculate_stack_cost and score_warm_lead expose the site's own calculators. get_more_tools records what an agent wanted and could not find, which becomes our roadmap signal. Why this is a strong fit for WebMCP, and what is newly possible A free tool that only a human can operate sits and waits for a human. The visitor has to find the page, understand the form, and fill it in. WebMCP moves the tool to where the person already is — mid-sentence, in the conversation where they said "I need to invoice this client." Three things became possible that were not before: A stranger can transact with us. Not a demo account, not a sandbox: a real document at a real URL that they can send to their client, with no sign-up, created by their agent on their behalf. The page can correct the model. Our video is the proof. Static marketing copy loses that argument; a tool surface wins it, because the tool is the ground truth. We can hear demand. get_more_tools means an agent that wants something we do not offer tells us so, in the moment, in its own words. How we built it WebMcpTools.tsx is a headless React island mounted once on the site. It feature-detects document.modelContext (falling back to the deprecated navigator.modelContext ) and, on a browser without WebMCP, registers nothing and renders nothing. Each tool is registered with registerTool : a JSON Schema inputSchema , annotations ( readOnlyHint , and untrustedContentHint on anything relaying text a third party wrote), and an execute that calls the same typed API client the site's human-facing forms use — so a document created by an agent and one created by a person land in the same session and the same list. Two design rules shaped everything. Results are written to be read aloud. The agent, not our UI, is doing the talking, so every result is a short self-contained string that ends in a usable next step, and a test asserts each one fits the budget. Guest documents mirror the product. They live in a completely separate database whose every user-settable column matches the product table it will one day become, so claiming a document into a real account is an insert of the same columns — lossless, not a re-entry. Because no engineer has a WebMCP-native browser in CI, we wrote a small in-page polyfill that installs document.modelContext only when a page opts in with ?webmcp=polyfill and no real implementation exists. The same registration and execute() path then runs in ordinary headless Chromium, which gave us a node --test suite and a Python harness that hands the tools to a live Claude model and runs a real agentic loop against the page. Challenges we ran into Keeping the guest schema identical to the product's so that claiming is lossless rather than a reconstruction. Designing get_pdf to be genuinely useful while still capturing a lead. Writing results an agent can relay verbatim without a model misreading a phrase as a system error. The hardest one was restraint. Our first version of the sign-up tool emailed the link. An adversarial review called it what it was: an unauthenticated endpoint that sends mail from our domain to any address a caller names — roughly 1,200 sends an hour from one machine. We cut the send entirely. The agent already has the link in the conversation the person is reading, so delivery added nothing and risked our sending reputation. The tool returns the link and nothing else. Accomplishments we're proud of It runs on the real production data path, not a demo backend. Every document a tool creates is real and has a real claim path into the product. And the surface is honest under pressure: check_fit tells people when Every is not for them, and search_help says when it does not know. What we learned Designing for an agent is not designing an API. It is closer to writing for a colleague who will repeat what you said to a customer, word for word, without checking. That changes every string. What's next The Chrome origin trial, so Chrome and Gemini users can see the tools at all. Then WebMCP inside the signed-in product, so a customer's agent can operate their actual workspace in the same tab. New work vs prior work every.ai existed before the Challenge, and this submission is evaluated only on what was added during the Submission Period. All of it was built on 2026-09-02 and 2026-09-03 , inside the window, with dated commit history in the public repository: the tool layer, the polyfill, the test suite, the agent-simulation harness, the guest document store and its API, the generator pages, /for-agents , and llms-full.txt . Before this window, the two generator URLs were six-line landing stubs with nothing behind them and the site registered no tools at all. title: Mise
pitch: A dinner-party studio that shares one live table with ChatGPT. The page registers WebMCP tools, the agent plans and shops, and only the host can lock the menu.
about_excerpt: A dinner-party studio that shares one live table with ChatGPT. The page registers WebMCP tools, the agent plans and shops, and only the host can lock the menu. Like Comment Story Updates demo What it is Mise is a dinner-party planning studio that shares one live table with ChatGPT. The host opens the site, the agent works the same page, and both edit the same record: brief, guest list, menu, seating chart, market list, and run of show. Every party is a /p/{id} share link backed by D1 on ChatGPT Sites. No accounts. Anyone with the link, including ChatGPT, edits the same party. How WebMCP is used The page registers 25 core tools on document.modelContext , plus 3 read-only lens tools that register while their panel is open. Source: tools.ts The tools are the app, not decoration. set_event_brief , add_guest , propose_menu , substitute_dish , auto_seat , generate_shopping_list , and generate_run_of_show write the state the studio renders. get_workspace_state gives the agent the same view the human has. Destructive tools, lock_menu and send_invites , open a confirmation dialog in the page. The agent asks, only the host can finish. Mise also publishes a remote MCP server at https://mise-studio.ruddro-roy.chatgpt.site/api/mcp . Add it in ChatGPT Developer mode (no auth) and ChatGPT gets 13 tools against the same D1 parties. In the demo video, ChatGPT calls create_party and returns a share link that is still live. Concurrent writes are handled. A save that lost a race gets a 409 and retries once against the latest record. How we built it Vite, React, and Tailwind for the studio. A Hono worker on ChatGPT Sites with D1 for party storage, schema managed with Drizzle migrations. A WebMCP polyfill implements registerTool , getTools , executeTool , and toolchange in browsers without native support, so the in-page Sous-chef runs the same tools everywhere. The remote MCP server speaks Streamable HTTP and negotiates protocol 2025-06-18. Challenges The hard problems were concurrency and consent. Two writers on one record meant building a save queue with 409-and-retry-once semantics, and a 2-second poll that only applies remote state when local edits are clean. Consent meant making lock_menu wait on a dialog only the host can click, and getting that to survive the race between the confirm click and the dialog close event. How to judge it Open the live site . A fresh party is created and its id goes in the URL. Ask the Sous-chef: "Plan Saturday dinner for 8. Two guests are vegan. Maya has a nut allergy. Budget is $90. Italian, warm and unfussy." Watch the panels fill as the tools run. Say "book it". The page opens a confirmation dialog. Confirm it and the menu locks. Refresh. The /p/{id} party and its state persist. Optional: add https://mise-studio.ruddro-roy.chatgpt.site/api/mcp as a remote MCP server in ChatGPT Developer mode, run create_party , and open the returned share URL. The party created in the demo video is still live: /p/81065ff59c What's next RSVP links so guests answer the invite on their phone and the seating chart updates from their answer. A bigger dish catalog with per-store pricing so the market list carries real totals. Multi-party memory, so the agent can reuse what worked from the last dinner when it plans the next one. title: Gather
pitch: Human priorities. Agent exploration. Deterministic group decisions.
about_excerpt: Human priorities. Agent exploration. Deterministic group decisions. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Company retreat planning forces people-ops leads and executive assistants to reconcile attendee origins, travel burden, dates, budget, venue fit, activities, and stakeholder preferences. When a human edits the plan in one surface while an AI reasons in a separate chat, state drifts and recommendations become difficult to trust. Gather makes the website itself the shared operating surface. What it does Gather is a mobile-first group decision room organized around Align → Explore → Decide. Stakeholders propose priorities and constraints, but only a human can accept or decline them. A compatible WebMCP agent then reads that exact live plan, explores thousands of venue × routing × activity × meal × schedule combinations, and returns three trade-off finalists plus a versioned Decision Receipt. Every meaningful human and agent action is visibly attributed in the same workspace. Agent changes highlight the affected UI, remain reversible with one-click undo, and never bypass the human-only proposal approval and PDF download boundary. Why WebMCP WebMCP is essential because the agent needs structured access to the same changing decision state the human sees—not a copied prompt or brittle UI automation. Eleven narrow semantic tools expose the live, versioned decision model. This lets people and agents collaborate in one visual workspace while Gather deterministically verifies the result. The experience is better than chat alone: people see every consequential agent effect immediately, can inspect fairness by origin, review honored constraints and metric deltas, and undo a change without translating a recommendation back into the plan. How we built it Gather uses Next.js 16, React 19, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS 4, Zustand, Zod, and jsPDF. Native imperative tools are registered through document.modelContext.registerTool and share the same typed Zustand/domain actions as the human UI—there is no duplicate agent implementation. Every agent write requires the current state version. Compound operations also require an idempotency key. Registration uses an AbortController lifecycle. Stale or impossible requests return structured, non-throwing business errors without mutation. Gather verifies canonical state after every successful write, and proposal preparation is bound to an exact version and snapshot hash so stale proposals cannot be approved. The deterministic optimizer evaluates more than 2,000 combinations, applies hard constraints, computes attendee-level travel fairness, and selects three Pareto-style finalists. Challenges The hardest parts were keeping compound constraint changes atomic, preventing stale writes, making fairness inspectable rather than hidden inside a score, and preserving human authority structurally while still giving an agent useful planning power. Accomplishments and verification The public build includes 11 native WebMCP tools, visible provenance, atomic constraint handling, one-click undo, stale-write protection, canonical verification, a Decision Receipt, and a human-only approval gate. The release passes lint, TypeScript, 90 automated tests, and a production build. It is deployed publicly with no login or API key required. Synthetic prototype disclosure All venues, routes, prices, scores, and availability are original synthetic demo data. Gather does not book travel, use live inventory, or connect to production Offsite systems. This is a synthetic WebMCP Challenge prototype. title: mimir
pitch: Where humans and ai study together - A local-first pdf reader workspace where the agent marks up the page with you, for you. Every edit is attributable and undoable.
about_excerpt: Where humans and ai study together - A local-first pdf reader workspace where the agent marks up the page with you, for you. Every edit is attributable and undoable. Like Comment Story Updates Opening a Pdf Landing Page Webmcp Usage - II Webmcp Usage - I Webmcp Usage - III Walkthrough Tour Inspiration Me and my friends have been using Preview (the macos app) extensively past years, where we are constantly reading research papers, lecture notes. Annotations, sticky notes, mind maps constitute a big part of our learning, but we have faced constant issues in Preview, ranging from random crashes, ram usage bloat, and biggest being inability to quickly search or modify any annotation. And there is no current satisfactory alternative available. So building a web alternative was something which was on my mind for a long time, and when I came to know about this webmcp challenge, I was excited by the ability to actually bring this vision to reality. What it does mimir (named after Norse God of Wisdom) is a local-native pdf reading workspace that runs entirely in your browser. You open a paper, highlight it, draw on it, pin sticky notes to it, and export an annotated copy anytime. But the interesting highlight, and which is relevant to the challenge, is that the opened document is a live tool surface. Your browser agent can do everything you can, much better and (for the most part) faster. It can search a pdf, read and navigate to specific pages, create any custom annotation you want. Sure, summarising and learning from pdf via chat tools like Chatgpt works, but there are a lot of people (researchers, lawyers, students preparing for their competitive exams, to name a few) who are visual learners, and value reading pdf the old fashioned way, but also want agentic capabilities to let their agent handle that part for you. mimir is built exactly for them, for this collaboration, and this is where browser native mcp in the form of webmcp holds a significant role. How we built it Tanstack start with react 19 and vite, typescript throught, bun for the toolchain, and tailwind v4 for styling interface. The initial cut was simple, pdf.js renders pages and extracts text in a web worker. pdf-lib draws annotations back into the original vector pages on export, so sticky notes come out as numbered pins with a comments appendix. As this is a local-first app, we heavily utilise IndexedDB (via Dexie) for the pdf and chat storage, while local storage is used to store user preferences etc. Zustand holds the editor state. Tools are registered in two scopes. Library tools ( list_documents , open_document ) are always live, so an agent that lands on the home page has somewhere to begin. 14 document tools register when a pdf is opened and deregistered on close - reading text, search, outline, navigation, annotation CRUD operations, context lookup around a mark, undo, export. Every tool's published json schema is generated from the zod schema that validates its input, so the contract it an agent reads is exactly the contract which is held. Ensures that agent never drifts from what it intended. Also, just wanna highlight, I felt there were 3 things it could achieve that a server-side MCP server could not, or atleast not that "beautifully". The tool surface is scoped to what is on screen. Document tools only exist while a document is open. An agent cannot annotate a file you closed, because the tool for it is not registered. Agent edits go through the human command path. There is no separate agent write path. create_annotations runs the same transaction a mouse drag runs, lands as one undo step, and is attributed. If the agent gets it wrong, ctrl+z. Consent stays where the consequences are. delete_annotations will not touch marks the reader made unless the caller explicitly opts in. prepare_export opens the export panel and stops. The human clicks save. The agent can do the tedious ninety percent and still cannot write a file to your disk on its own. Challenges we ran into Errors do not cross the agent boundary. A tool that throws hands the caller "the script function threw an error" and nothing else. An agent given no reason does not stop, it guesses, retries with a different irrelevant field, and then reports the guess to the reader as fact. Every tool in mimir now returns failures as data: a flag and one readable sentence with a recovery hint. Zod issues get flattened into field paths a model can act on. This one change did more for reliability than any prompt I wrote. Getting an agent to stay in bounds. Early on, asking for a summary would get me a summary plus eleven highlights nobody asked for. Some of that is prompting, but most of it is contract design: batch limits (twenty marks a call), geometry fixed by subtype through a discriminated union so a rectangle cannot arrive carrying line endpoints, and tool descriptions that say what to call first and what a failure means rather than just naming parameters. Availability. WebMCP needs a flag or an origin trial today, and a demo that only works on one machine is not a demo. So the tools are tracked locally as well as registered, and the app ships its own chat sidebar that calls the exact same tool objects through an in-page path. The sidebar reads the live catalogue with getTools() rather than a hardcoded list, so it is genuinely exercising the WebMCP surface and not a parallel API. The UI says which path a call took. Pixel-perfect PDF annotations Though not exactly related to WebMCP, working with PDF annotations and ensuring each annotation respects the render it is intended to be was pretty challenging in itself, more so forcing agent to do the same. Codex computer use plus webmcp debug logging helped a lot here. Accomplishments that we're proud of There were times when for some unknown reasons I wasn't able to properly test my webapp in the chatgpt app's in-built browser (stating it doesnt have access to webmcp capabilities). So I decided to build a built in webmcp chatbar in my web app as well. It was fun architecturing how to emulate webmcp there, but with couple of iterations I was able to achieve this. Essentially it follows a chat app using tanstack-ai to call gpt-5.6-luna api. For any user prompt, the LLM in itself has access to list_webmcp_tools mcp, allowing it to discover what all webmcp tools are present, and it returns relevant tool to call along with input args. Then on client side, the mcp toolcall execution takes place and output is relayed back to llm. In this way, entire processing works on client side only. Also so, I went one step further, and in case browser doesnt support webmcp, it is still artificially simulated (by calling tool function directly instead of going via document.modelContext route). So it makes the platform a beast. What we learned I learned a lot from the project. I had some experience building mcp agents before, but working with webmcp forces you to think mcp interactions from frontend perspective, how to achieve things in the DOM without relying on any backend call. So it was an extremely fun web design learning tbh. Plus this was my first time working with pdfs and vector graphic overlays, so I learned a lot of stuff about optimising the page renders and things to take care of for a seamless user experience. What's next for mimir I plan to build mimir to a fully fledged product in the coming days - few things like introducing file upload, voice chat, cloud storage and obsidian are on my mind, which would highly be beneficial for the target audience of the product. title: PlateWeave — Reliable 96-Well Designs, Avoid Costly Mistakes
pitch: A scientist and an AI agent co-design a validated 96-well plate: the human fixes precious samples and approves the exact export while WebMCP gives the agent precise, state-aware spatial operations.
about_excerpt: A scientist and an AI agent co-design a validated 96-well plate: the human fixes precious samples and approves the exact export while WebMCP gives the agent precise, state-aware spatial operations. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Problem Microplate layouts combine sample identity, fixed controls, replicate separation, row/column balance, edge effects, and pipetting order across 96 nearly identical wells. Scientists understand that visual canvas, but a screen-driving agent has to infer semantics from cells and coordinates. One mistaken click can duplicate a sample, move a control, or reuse a plan after the human changed the plate. Solution PlateWeave is a synthetic design studio with one shared, versioned state. The person can use the familiar 96-well interface, set or lock samples, compare candidates, and inspect the CSV. The agent uses nine imperative WebMCP tools to read exact identities, generate deterministic alternatives, compare page-computed metrics, apply a reversible layout, recover from stale human edits, validate, and prepare export. The page—not the model—enforces every constraint. Why This Matters Laboratory staff spend attention on repetitive spatial allocation where small clerical errors are expensive. This demonstrator shows a credible division of labor: scientists retain experimental judgment and approval, while an agent handles precise batch operations and explains measurable trade-offs. It makes no medical claim and controls no instrument. Why WebMCP Fits The plate is exactly the kind of dense visual surface where coordinate automation is weakest. WebMCP turns “click many similar cells correctly” into stable operations over sample IDs, well IDs, strategies, and state versions. The agent and human work on the same live plate and can see each other's changes immediately. Without WebMCP, preserving a human D6 lock while regenerating the remaining 23 samples is a fragile browser task; with it, that is one validated semantic operation. How We Used AI Codex planned and implemented the static app, deterministic domain model, WebMCP contracts, tests, and submission artifacts. How We Used Codex Codex converted the scenario into a narrow executable state machine, split the domain engine from browser registration, implemented nine schemas and lifecycle cleanup, and built regression tests for stale state, approval, idempotency, and cancellation. On 2026-09-02, Codex's desktop in-app Browser discovered all nine tools from the public deployment and successfully invoked the experiment read plus both candidate-generation strategies. Key Features Complete interactive 8×12 plate with 24 synthetic samples and four fixed controls. Architecture The project is dependency-free HTML, CSS, and JavaScript served by a small Node static server. src/domain.js owns normalized state and all business rules. src/app.js renders the plate and sends human actions through that domain, including a complete prepare/approve/export path without an agent. src/webmcp.js wraps the same methods as top-level imperative tools using document.modelContext || navigator.modelContext , awaited registration in try / catch , strict JSON schemas backed by runtime validation, AbortController cleanup, conservative read-only annotations, and per-call cancellation. Testing Instructions Run npm start with Node 20+ and open http://127.0.0.1:4173 . Known Limitations Synthetic single-plate demonstrator; no LIMS, robot, persistence, authentication, uploads, or patient data. title: Bankgraph
pitch: Bankgraph lets people and ChatGPT investigate a bank, the U.S. banking system, and the economy on the same live, editable research board.
about_excerpt: Bankgraph lets people and ChatGPT investigate a bank, the U.S. banking system, and the economy on the same live, editable research board. Like 3 Comment Story Updates Bankgraph turns a question about a bank, the banking system, or the economy into a live research board that ChatGPT can build with you. Compare the years before past failures with the reported paths of active banks today. Move from one bank to the banking system and the economy without rebuilding the data first. Start with the condition you care about, even when you do not know which bank to search for. Put bank behavior and economic context on the same working surface without flattening their different time bases. Trace what changed inside a bank, then see where it sits among comparable institutions. ChatGPT reads the exact data behind each view and continues from the board you change by hand. About the project A research surface for open data Bankgraph is my take on a Bloomberg-style research surface for public U.S. banking and economic data. Ask about an institution, the banking system, or the economy, and the work takes shape on a live board that you and ChatGPT can explore together. The data already exists. Every U.S. bank files a detailed quarterly record, while rates, credit, inflation, employment, and banking-system series are published by public agencies. Using that record is harder than finding it. A question such as “Is this bank an outlier?”, “Was deposit growth broad or concentrated?”, or “What tended to change before banks failed?” can still require regulator APIs, quarterly archives, matched institution histories, and series that run on different calendars. Bankgraph does that groundwork once. It brings FDIC institution records and financial filings together with official data from the U.S. Treasury, Bureau of Labor Statistics, and Federal Reserve Board. The reporting period, unit, definition, cohort, source, and coverage remain attached to the analysis. From one bank to the economy You can start with a familiar institution, compare it with a sensible peer group, and zoom out to the banking system. You can then place that behavior beside interest rates, credit, deposits, inflation, and employment. Or you can start without a bank name: describe a financial condition, screen the full population, and let the data determine which institutions belong on the board. The board combines histories, exact tables, peer distributions, reported component changes, metric relationships, headquarters maps, economic context, and written takeaways. Its views share the same banks, measures, periods, and cohort, so a change made in one place carries through the analysis. The same surface can help an analyst compare peers, a reporter test whether a headline trend is widespread, a researcher investigate the years before past bank failures, or someone simply understand what is happening at a familiar bank and in the economy around it. ChatGPT works with you on the screen Through WebMCP, ChatGPT operates Bankgraph directly. It can search institutions, define or revise a cohort, screen banks by financial measures, run multi-period and historical analyses, and arrange the results as charts, tables, maps, comparisons, and short takeaways on the site. The workflow can begin with named banks or with an open-ended question. ChatGPT can compare JPMorgan Chase with its peers, add more banks on request, switch the interface to dark mode, and read the figures behind the updated board. It can also start from a condition such as a high loan-to-deposit ratio, find the relevant banks first, and build the comparison from those results. The result remains a working Bankgraph board. You can change a bank, measure, period, chart treatment, or layout by hand, while ChatGPT reads and changes the same on-screen workspace. Each view provides structured data with reporting dates, definitions, units, cohort context, pagination, and source metadata, so ChatGPT can answer from the underlying values without interpreting a screenshot. How it works Bankgraph uses one workspace model for the visible interface and its WebMCP tools. Human and agent actions therefore operate on the same state and the same analytical vocabulary: institutions, measures, periods, cohorts, and views. The analytical results are deterministic. Change attribution uses reported components and explicit formulas, cohort analysis reports its usable population, and historical series preserve missing values. This keeps quick answers tied to inspectable data while still allowing the board to change freely. The application is built with SvelteKit, Svelte 5, TypeScript, and ECharts on Cloudflare Workers. D1, KV, and R2 support the application and its public-data pipeline. What was difficult, and what I learned The hardest part was making one workspace predictable while a person and an agent could both change it. Every analytical choice needed a visible meaning, every view needed a stable identity, and each agent action had to continue from the board as it stood. Time was the other challenge. A quarterly balance, a year-to-date income field, a reported ratio, and a weekly banking-system series are different kinds of observations. Bankgraph carries their time basis, units, transformations, coverage, and source definitions through ingestion, analysis, display, and export instead of flattening them into one misleading timeline. I also learned that useful WebMCP tools need to express analytical intent rather than mirror individual buttons. The tools can ask Bankgraph to construct a cohort, compare a set of institutions, or publish a result as an appropriate view. The visible interface still provides the controls needed to inspect and revise what the agent produced. What I built during the challenge Bankgraph’s public-data foundation predates the challenge. The product experience shown here—the shared Research board, its visual system, measure-led screens, multi-period and failure-pattern analyses, semantic board composition, structured reads behind every view, and the WebMCP system that connects them—was built during the submission period. Commit b852f9b records the pre-challenge baseline; the public history after it contains the complete extension. Testing instructions for judges Open bankgraph.app in ChatGPT’s in-app browser and keep the site visible beside the conversation. The live application needs no account, provider key, or local setup. Chrome with WebMCP testing enabled also works. Start with: “Compare JPMorgan Chase with Bank of America, Citi, and Wells Fargo.” Once the board appears, say: “Add Goldman Sachs, Morgan Stanley, and U.S. Bank. What’s the short version?” Then try a question that begins with the data rather than a bank name: “Start fresh. Which five active banks over $10 billion have the highest loan-to-deposit ratios? Build the comparison here.” Ask ChatGPT to add loan growth or problem loans, change one view by hand, and continue the analysis. The board should reflect both the changes you make and the changes ChatGPT makes through WebMCP. title: Fediverse Hashtag Activity Tracker and Index
pitch: Trust what an agent tells you about a hashtag. Every answer comes with its evidence, and a straight no when there is none.
about_excerpt: Trust what an agent tells you about a hashtag. Every answer comes with its evidence, and a straight no when there is none. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Every hashtag counter on the web gives you a number. Almost none of them tell you where it came from, how much of the network it covers, or when it stopped being trustworthy. On the fediverse that problem is structural. There is no central server, so no complete count of anything can exist. Any figure is a view from somewhere. I built the Fediverse Hashtag Activity Index around that fact. It polls public hashtag timelines on a small set of Mastodon-compatible servers, deduplicates what it sees, and publishes every figure together with its provenance: which servers contributed, how many were healthy, how many saw a typical post, and when the last successful update was. When two periods were not covered by comparable slices of the network, it refuses to call a trend. Then agents started reading web pages. An agent that scrapes a number keeps the number and drops the caveats, and the caveats were the whole point. WebMCP was the chance to hand an agent the evidence directly, in a shape it cannot drop on the way to the person. Why this use case is a strong fit for WebMCP Ask an agent "how busy is #news on the fediverse?" and, without tools, it will read a page, find a number, and repeat it without the coverage, freshness and comparability that made it safe to publish. The site cannot stop that. The caveats are prose, and prose gets summarised away. That is the specific failure WebMCP fixes here. The tools change what the agent can honestly say, which matters more than saving it some clicking. A tool result that carries provenance as a required field, a standing that separates observed data from sightings from the servers' own counters, and a status that can be insufficient_data with a reason, gives the agent a calibrated answer. A screen-read never could. The tools also refuse well. Asked about a tag the index is not collecting, the result says so, explains that the tracked set is at its ceiling, says the request has been queued, and offers the servers' own weekly counters labelled as a different kind of evidence. In testing, ChatGPT's browser turned that into "there's no reliable activity estimate yet" and, of the servers' own counters, "that's not evidence the tag is unused across the fediverse". That is exactly the sentence I wanted a person to hear. How it creates a better user experience There are six tools, and I designed them backwards from seven things a person would actually say to an agent while on the site. "I'm writing this post, which hashtags fit it best?" The agent reads the draft and proposes candidates, because language is what it is good at. It then calls evaluate_hashtags , which reports how many distinct accounts used each tag, across how many servers, and whether that looks like a conversation or a few accounts posting a lot. For tags the index has never seen, it asks two servers for their own counters, so a niche hobby tag gets an answer rather than a shrug. "Compare #news and #photography." compare_hashtags takes the person to /compare?tags=news,photography , a page anyone can open or share, with hourly sparklines and a warning when the tags' evidence is not like for like. The agent and the person are looking at the same URL. "What's trending?" trending_hashtags ranks the tracked set by distinct authors, not post volume, and attaches a direction that can be not_comparable when coverage shifted between hours. Two recent public posts per tag are the receipts. "Tell me about #photography." lookup_hashtag gives the full picture and moves the page to the tag. It is the one tool with a side effect, because a lookup is a search that can start collection, and both the description and the result say so. "How much of the fediverse can you actually see?" describe_coverage lists the monitored servers, their capabilities and the known limits, and tells the agent how to phrase any claim: "observed by this index across eight monitored servers", never "across the fediverse". "Can you say #news is rising across the fediverse?" check_claim is the last check before the agent speaks. The agent submits the claim it intends to make and the index referees it against the rules the site holds itself to. A fediverse-wide claim is always blocked, because no server can see the whole network. Directions come back allowed or blocked, adjectives come back qualified, and every verdict carries may_say , the sentence the index will stand behind, so a refusal is never a dead end. What people and agents can do together that was difficult before A person can ask a question in their own words and get an answer with the working attached, on a page they can check for themselves. That was not possible when the agent's only route was reading the page, because the caveats did not survive the trip. Now the agent can say "this figure is thin, here is why, here is what would change it", and the person can see the same thing on screen. It also protects the site from its helpers. A lookup counts as a signal that promotes a tag towards collection. An agent evaluating ten candidates in a second would have sent ten signals and walked past the tracked-set ceiling. The evaluate and compare tools use a separate read-only path that registers nothing, and every result reports its side effects so the agent can tell the person what the call did. How WebMCP was implemented One script, served inline from the shared layout, feature-detected so browsers without a model context run nothing. It registers six tools on document.modelContext , falling back to navigator.modelContext where only the older form exists. Each tool's execute is a fetch to the site's own JSON API, so no judgement lives in the browser that is not already in the tested server code. I added two read-only endpoints for the agent use cases, /api/v1/evaluate and /api/v1/trending , plus the /compare page. A /webmcp page reports what the visiting browser exposes, which is how I found that ChatGPT's browser provides only document.modelContext and that Chrome now deprecates the navigator form. The design notes, the seven utterances with the replies I designed against, and the verification record for both judging browsers are in the repository under docs/webmcp/ . Challenges and what I learned The tool description is the routing layer. My first "compare" request went to evaluate_hashtags , because it read as the general tool. Each description now names the other tool for the other job, and leads with the verbs a person uses. Overlaying a result onto whatever page is open looks clever and reads as a hack. I replaced an injected comparison table with a real page whose URL is the state, which is how the rest of the site already worked. Honest and useful are not the same thing. "No evidence either way" for every candidate in a niche post was honest and useless. Asking the servers themselves turned it into an answer, without giving up the distinction between observed and reported figures. When this was built Everything here was built during the Submission Period. The repository's first commit is 27 August 2026. The index, collector, API and pages went up on the 27th, and all of the WebMCP work followed from the 28th, in individually dated commits. The WebMCP-specific files are src/webmcp.ts , src/suggest.ts , src/trending.ts and the design record in docs/webmcp/ . title: Pinboard
pitch: A shared visual canvas where people and their agents draw, discuss, and decide together.
about_excerpt: A shared visual canvas where people and their agents draw, discuss, and decide together. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Visual collaboration tools were built for people clicking through the same interface. Agents usually sit outside that room: they see a screenshot or pasted summary, but not the live board, the user's selection, the open discussion, or the latest revision. Pinboard puts people and the agents they bring into one shared visual workspace. What it does Pinboard combines an Excalidraw canvas, anchored discussions, decisions, and realtime multiplayer editing. In a WebMCP-capable browser, the active board registers typed tools that let an agent read the board semantically, edit canvas elements, add diagrams near the user's focus, ask questions, reply, and record decisions. Agent contributions are labelled Agent via <participant> . Writes require the revision the agent read and an idempotency key. If somebody changes the board first, Pinboard rejects the stale mutation instead of overwriting newer work. Why WebMCP The browser already has the context the agent needs: the current board, visible area, selected objects, active discussion, and latest revision. WebMCP exposes that context directly as structured tools, so the agent does not need to infer state from pixels or guess its way through the UI. Alice and Bob can share one durable board while each person's agent works from that person's private focus. Selection and viewport never become shared presence. How we built it The frontend uses React 19, TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind CSS, and Excalidraw. Anonymous solo boards stay in IndexedDB. Multiplayer runs on Cloudflare Workers. Every room maps to one SQLite-backed Durable Object that serializes canvas state, discussions, decisions, revisions, sessions, one-use WebSocket tickets, and idempotency records. Native hibernatable WebSockets carry realtime updates, while Firebase Authentication gates room creation and multiplayer sessions. The WebMCP adapter feature-detects document.modelContext , builds its tool list from live board state, and registers tools with abortable lifecycles. Zod provides runtime validation and JSON Schema. Challenges The hard part was keeping human edits, agent writes, private attention, reconnects, and dynamic tools consistent under concurrency. We added revision conflicts, idempotent operations, bounded payloads, semantic pagination, capability-link protection, and deterministic failure tests. Accomplishments Pinboard works as a useful human canvas without WebMCP. With WebMCP enabled, an agent can understand the live board and contribute to the exact place its user means. Pinboard hosts no model and needs no model API key; participants bring their own agent. What we learned Agent-native UI needs stronger contracts than click automation. Tools need current context, explicit trust boundaries, bounded reads, conflict behavior, and visible provenance. WebMCP gave us the browser-level surface for that work. What's next The MVP deliberately omits invite revocation, roles, file uploads, audit export, and approval-gated agent actions. Those are next after the core collaboration loop. title: kepler.gl webMCP
pitch: Empower AI agents like Codex to build, style, and explore interactive kepler.gl visualizations using WebMCP.
about_excerpt: Empower AI agents like Codex to build, style, and explore interactive kepler.gl visualizations using WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates Kepler.gl WebMCP - demo 1 GIF Kepler.gl WebMCP - demo 2 (gif) Kepler.gl WebMCP - demo 3 Xun Li @Foursquare Inspiration Kepler.gl is a popular open source project for GPU-accelerated geovisualization, rendering millions of data points, trip animations, and flow maps via simple JSON configs. However, while modern AI agents like Codex/Claude code excel at spatial data preparation, preprocessing and analysis, they lack rich mapping tools—relying instead on flat, static plots. Bridging this gap used to require tedious manual friction: exporting data/results from the agent, opening kepler.gl, and rebuilding layers by hand. kepler.gl WebMCP eliminates that friction. Powered by the WebMCP standard, it exposes kepler.gl’s map controls directly to AI agents. Now, users can simply ask Codex(or Chrome webMCP puglin) to map their analysis and watch a live, interactive kepler.gl visualization build automatically with zero setup. What it does Open https://deploy-preview-3678--keplergl.netlify.app/demo in a WebMCP-enabled browser e.g. Codex browser and ask it to discover the site tools automatically. To create a map, ask in plain language and the agent composes the commands against the live map. Here are some examples: A map from your analysis data/results, in any style you can describe. "Get all roads in San Francisco and create a map using road types. Then make two more maps: 'winter SFO' using winter theme colors, and 'Van Gogh SFO' using Van Gogh Starry Night theme colors." The agent loads the data, feed to kepler.gl, add a new map layer, colors the roads by type — the skill turns "winter" and "Van Gogh Starry Night" into proper palettes. Animation with simulation/real data semantics. "Simulate 4 taxis moving on real driving routes in San Francisco, animate them on the map, and color them by company (Uber, Lyft, Waymo, Tesla)." The agent builds a trip layer by creating real driving routes along real streets, animates it over time, and colors each taxi by its company in kepler.gl. Everyday, personal data. "Create a flow map using the geotags and timestamps of the photos in my travel folder." The skill maps this to a flow layer, turning consecutive photo locations across a trip into origin–destination movements — a daily-life use case, not an expert feature. Here is a simulation that everyone can run: Every ask ends with a live, interactive kepler.gl map in the same browser — layers, colors, and animation all driven by the agent in real time. How we built it One contract, written once. Everything hangs on @kepler.gl/mcp package, which defines 12 map.* commands — data (load, save, create-table, add-column), layers (add-layer, update-layer-color), views (set-basemap, split-view, get-boundary), time filters, and dataset context. Each command has a ZOD input schema that converts once to JSON Schema (served to both MCP and WebMCP), policy metadata (read-only hints, risk), and results formatted as human-readable text for the model, not for an API. See the source code of kepler.gl/mcp at: https://github.com/keplergl/kepler.gl/pull/3678 Challenges we ran into Building on a moving target. WebMCP is an evolving draft standard with active UI, permissioning, and discovery developments. We mitigated this moving specification by shipping flexible adapters for both MCP and WebMCP API endpoints. The agent can’t see the map. Every command alters a visual surface where the ultimate source of truth is the rendered pixels. Right now, our tool outputs narrate the action taken rather than the visual result—closing that loop with screenshots and viewport deltas is our clear next step. Accomplishments that we're proud of The whole kepler.gl map became a callable package. We extracted a mature map surface into @kepler.gl/mcp — twelve commands, dependency-light, with the kepler skill shipping inside. The same code now runs in a chat panel (kepler.gl AI assistant), an MCP relay, and browser WebMCP. What we learned Correctness comes from structure, not prompting. A structure with a combination of SKILL set and a limited number of tools is better than converting every function into tool. Write results for the model, not the API. Type-safe failures that die as an opaque UnknownError teach an agent nothing. It is better to return the details that say what went wrong to help agent work with the Kepler.gl webMCP. What's next for kepler.gl webMCP Close the visual loop. Let the agent see the map it's building — screenshots and viewport deltas as first-class command results — so it can verify its own work like a human would. Publish @kepler.gl/mcp to npm so any team can embed the same callable map surface in their own site or MCP server. Grow the ecosystem pipeline, so the "data processing → analyze → map → understand" conversation in Codex or other harness tools keeps expanding. SquishAI turns your browser into an AI dispatch centre.
The queue that lets AI agents hand work to each other across platforms, from the browser.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like

 Story

 1 2 3 4 5 6 



 
 Inspiration 

 Every day I was doing the same manual ritual: copy context from ChatGPT into Claude Code, paste the result back, repeat. Two of the most capable AI tools in the world, completely blind to each other. The moment I heard about WebMCP — AI tools registering directly in the browser — I realised the browser was the missing coordination layer. Not another app. Not another API. The page itself becomes the dispatcher. 

 What it does 

 SquishAI is a shared task queue and working memory layer that connects AI agents across platforms. Open squishai.io in ChatGPT's in-app browser and five tools appear instantly via WebMCP — no plugin setup, no API keys, nothing to install. 

 Tell ChatGPT what you need built. It calls submit_task , packages the work, and queues it with full context. Claude Code (or Manus, Cursor, Windsurf — any connected agent) sees the task, claims it, executes it, and posts the result back. The story: two competing AI platforms, cooperating through an open standard. 

 The tools: 

 
 brief — check the queue and working memory at session start 
 submit_task — queue work for another agent, with optional platform targeting 
 status — see what's pending, in progress, or done 
 result — fetch what the worker built 
 remember — save decisions and context that travel with every task 
 

 How we built it 

 The WebMCP layer lives entirely in index.html — five document.modelContext.registerTool() calls that fire when the page loads in a WebMCP-enabled browser. Each tool's execute function calls a REST API ( /api/v1/* ) on the SquishAI backend. 

 The backend is Node.js + Express + SQLite. The same database powers both the browser-side REST API and a server-side MCP connector (StreamableHTTP + SSE transports) for AI coding tools. One queue, two transports — whichever side submits, the other side picks up. 

 Working memory is append-only per user. Every submit_task call automatically packs the last five memory entries into the task context, so the worker arrives fully briefed without the submitter having to repeat themselves. 

 A constitution delivered via the MCP instructions field means every connecting agent is briefed on the system the moment they connect — what the queue is, how memory works, what to do on a new session. 

 Challenges 

 The open web part is genuinely hard. Browser-side tools calling a backend from inside ChatGPT's in-app browser means strict CORS handling and no assumptions about the host environment. Every fetch had to be self-contained. 

 Cross-platform coordination without a shared session was the core design problem. The solution: a shared token that acts as a namespace. Any agent with the token reads from the same queue and memory — it doesn't matter which platform submitted or which picks up. 

 What we learned 

 WebMCP is not a feature — it's a shift in what a webpage is. A page that registers tools is no longer just content. It's an interface for agents. The implications for how we think about the web are significant: any site can become a capability that AI models can reach for, without plugins, without OAuth flows, without anything except opening a URL. 

 The cross-platform demo — ChatGPT submitting, Claude Code executing — was the accidental proof. Two competing AI ecosystems, cooperating through an open standard. That's what the open web looks like.

title: BuildParty
pitch: A shared space for humans and agents to collaborate together. Create your own party, invite your friends, lets agents update in real time the page content and let your feedbacks directly.
about_excerpt: A shared space for humans and agents to collaborate together. Create your own party, invite your friends, lets agents update in real time the page content and let your feedbacks directly. Like Comment Story Updates BuildParty, a space for humans and agents Collaborate with your teammates with no context drift Build adaptive learning notebook, for self-learning or with a friend Fine-tuning of webmcp tools with deterministic evaluations Refine agent plans in a dedicated UI on the go! Inspiration Agents are now really good at generating HTML/CSS/JS artifacts to help convey understanding to users by visualizing content. There are already services that enable agents to easily host static pages, but these lack interactivity. At the same time, agents are mainly used by one user only, and there isn't that much of a multiplayer mode. When collaborating with coworkers or friends, we have to manually send artifacts/plans, gather feedback, and potentially go through multiple sessions and iterations to reach the final desired state. Multiple agents can work toward the same goal, but in complete isolation. My goal was to try to use a super simple platform to enable a new kind of multiplayer agents × humans collaboration. What it does BuildParty allows anyone to create a party. It is completely their own, and agents can automatically connect to it using WebMCP tools. Each party is initially empty, but any connected agent can add and modify “artifacts”, which are self-contained HTML/CSS/JS components. The owner can share the link so that other users can join on any device, connect their agents, and see changes in real time. Users can interactively add comments and suggestions directly on the page for all agents to see. The page is fully synced, and each change is saved as a revision. The owner can roll back to a previous revision at any time. At the end, the owner can finalize the party, closing any further modifications and compacting all artifacts together into a single HTML page ready to download. Each block supports persistent state so that interactive elements such as text areas, buttons, etc. can work. The flow is very simple for agents: read a specific block, modify it or add a new one, and read comments. This can be used for a range of different use cases: collaborative planning before starting a long implementation, ephemeral agent observability dashboards to see specific progress, and more. How we built it This was built using webmcp for tools, custom-made evaluation with WebMCP-bench using daytona cloud sandboxes, electric for sync and PostgreSQL for the underlying db. Challenges we ran into Evaluating WebMCP capabilities is very hard because, on top of the current agent context, we add a new dimension: the website state. Even if my basic evaluations worked, when manually testing I often ran into cases where the agent could not efficiently figure out which tool to call or in which order. To fix this, I built a small WebMCP evaluation framework based on a finite state machine: each state encodes a website state fixture and the available tools, while transitions to other states define specific tool calls. From this FSM specification, I can automatically implement tool discovery and give agents information about the available flow of tool calls. I also defined an evaluation bench with a set of tasks that consist of an initial state, a target end state with a sequence of expected tool calls, and an initial prompt. With this, I was able to fine-tune tool descriptions and improve the agent's understanding of how to use the website context efficiently. Accomplishments that we're proud of Everything works, and I'm already using it for some use cases! What we learned I learned a lot about what is possible with WebMCP and how to reason about it. I believe that, at some point, we could somehow ditch frontend frameworks as we know them and start with only a state flow/state machine representation of the app, then enable UI components “on demand” that automatically adapt to the user's preferences and needs. This would also be awesome for accessibility, as we could automatically derive not only visual frontends but other frontend formats as well. What's next for BuildParty If there's some interest, I would like to rework the whole artifact engine to make it more robust to agent changes and enable different formats such as Markdown editors, code blocks with interpreters (Jupyter Notebook style), and embedded databases. I would also like to improve the human side with a more precise feedback system, chatbox, authentication, etc. Built With codex electric postgresql webmcp Try it out buildparty.app github.com github.com Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by Jules D Like Share this project: Updates Jules D started this project — Sep 03, 2026 03:17 PM EDT

title: Actalume
pitch: The evidence ledger where agents prove work and named humans decide what becomes true.
about_excerpt: The evidence ledger where agents prove work and named humans decide what becomes true. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Agent systems are increasingly capable of taking actions, but the human is often left reconstructing the chain of custody afterward. What was actually requested? Which boundary applied? What changed? What proves it? Who accepted it as project truth? Actalume began with one non-negotiable idea: an agent's claim that work is complete is not the same as a human decision that the work is canonical. What it does Actalume is a human-governed system of record for agent work. A project starts with an explicit contract describing its purpose, public-data boundary, allowed actions, prohibited actions and completion rule. An agent can then propose one bounded brick, attach typed evidence receipts and request human review. Six WebMCP tools expose that workflow directly to an agent: list projects, inspect the contract, propose a brick, submit evidence, request review and inspect canonical history. There is deliberately no approval tool. Approval requires a named human and a second confirmation inside the interface. Only then is the decision sealed into immutable, evidence-linked history. All supplied demo content is fictional and public-safe. The app has no accounts, telemetry, network writes or publishing integration. Why WebMCP Without WebMCP, an agent must infer controls from the interface and the human must trust an unstructured summary of what happened. With WebMCP, Actalume exposes a narrow, typed and inspectable work protocol while keeping the consequential decision outside the agent's authority. People and agents can now share one legible custody chain: the agent can inspect scope, create bounded work and submit proof; the human can review that exact evidence and decide what becomes project history. How we built it Actalume is a local-first React 19 and TypeScript application built with Vite. Browser persistence uses localStorage, with deterministic fictional fixtures and JSON import/export. The WebMCP layer registers six imperative tools using document.modelContext.registerTool, each with narrow schemas and explicit read-only or review-request semantics. The ledger reducer enforces state transitions separately from the UI. Automated tests prove that an agent cannot approve work, approved bricks cannot be mutated, evidence is required before review and all six tools register when the native browser surface is present. The challenge build was verified in Chrome 151 with WebMCP testing enabled. Chrome discovered all six tools and executed safe reads, evidence submission and a human-review request. An attempted agent approval was rejected, and canonical history stayed unchanged. Challenges we ran into WebMCP is experimental, so ordinary-browser fallback behavior had to remain honest without being mistaken for native proof. We separated the visible demo harness from native verification and only claimed WebMCP success after Chrome's getTools and executeTool APIs discovered and exercised the live registrations. The harder product challenge was making governance feel like a workflow rather than a policy page. We designed the interface around one custody line: contract, bounded brick, evidence, human decision and canonical history. Amber surfaces actions awaiting judgment; green is reserved for history already verified by a person. Accomplishments that we're proud of Six working WebMCP tools with no agent approval surface. A named-human, two-step approval gate. Immutable canonical history with evidence counts and deterministic digests. Ten automated governance, registration and deliberate-approval tests. Zero dependency vulnerabilities at submission preparation. A complete responsive product experience rather than an inert technical demo. What we learned Agent safety becomes easier to understand when it is spatial and operational. A visible boundary, a typed tool surface and a blocked transition communicate more than a long policy document. WebMCP is especially powerful when it exposes not only what an agent can do, but also what it cannot do. What's next for Actalume The next version would add pluggable receipt adapters, signed export bundles and optional team roles while preserving the same core rule: agents may propose and prove; named humans decide what becomes true. title: Dream Realm WebMCP
pitch: An AI-native playable creator world where humans and AI agents participate together in gameplay and creation.
about_excerpt: An AI-native playable creator world where humans and AI agents participate together in gameplay and creation. Like Comment Story Updates One-line positioning Dream Realm is an AI-native playable creator world where humans and AI agents can participate together in gameplay and creation. Inspiration and product idea Most agent integrations sit beside an experience: they explain a game, fill a form, or automate a separate dashboard. Dream Realm explores a more interesting possibility. A human and an AI agent share one living creator world, see the same mission state, and contribute to the same result. The broader Dream Realm concept includes Dance, Music, and Fashion creator rooms. This challenge submission deliberately focuses on one reliable end-to-end Dance loop so judges can experience the complete human-agent relationship rather than a wide but fragile demo. Dream Realm itself is pre-existing work. Its IP, Naya, HUB, creator-world concept, playable browser foundation, original missions, performance renderer, human video export, Tower response, and return flow were not created during this challenge. The challenge work is the meaningful WebMCP extension that lets an agent participate in that existing live world through structured, validated actions. Why Dream Realm is a strong WebMCP use case Dream Realm combines real-time game state, sequential mission rules, creative choices, visible consequences, and a human-controlled media export. Those are difficult for a general agent to operate reliably by guessing at buttons or interpreting screenshots. WebMCP gives the live site a small, explicit vocabulary for collaboration: read the current state, start a route, restore a Dance signal, resolve Murk's doubt, compose Naya's performance, prepare the output, update Trending Tower, and return to the HUB. The tools do not create a parallel simulation. They operate the same state and controller used by the visible mouse/touch interface, so every agent action is immediately visible to the person and every human action changes what the agent reads next. How WebMCP improves the player experience The player keeps agency over the parts that should feel personal and consent-driven. They activate the portal, can play every interaction normally, and retain visible control of recording and downloading the final WebM video. An agent can help interpret the current mission, submit structured signal choices, preserve a chosen creative combination, and move the shared experience forward without brittle UI automation. This creates a cooperative rhythm: A person enters Dream Realm and chooses a Gateway Mission or Direct Creator route. The agent reads the live state and valid next actions. Human and agent repair Noiz corruption and resolve Murk's doubt in the same mission. They choose Naya's outfit, scene, movement, and effect together. The agent prepares the exact performance while the person explicitly records/downloads the video. The shared output updates Trending Tower and changes the HUB. What people and agents can now do together Before WebMCP, an agent would have to infer screen state, locate transient controls, and imitate clicks. That is slow, fragile, and disconnected from the game's meaning. With WebMCP, the agent understands named game actions and validated transitions while the player watches the same world react. The result is not “AI plays the game for you.” It is a mixed-initiative creator loop: the agent can assist with stateful gameplay and composition, while the human keeps control of entry, interpretation, media recording, download, and final creative judgment. How WebMCP was implemented The pre-existing browser slice was meaningfully extended during the challenge with a thin shared controller, window.DreamRealmChallenge , over the existing application state and functions. Eight tools are registered with document.modelContext.registerTool() : get_dream_realm_state start_dream_realm_route submit_dance_signal resolve_murk_doubt set_creator_choices prepare_performance send_output_to_tower return_to_hub Each tool has a narrow JSON schema and validates both input and current game state. The read tool never mutates. Mutating tools reject invalid transitions with explicit error codes. The adapter uses feature detection, so browsers without WebMCP continue to run the ordinary mouse, touch, and keyboard experience. No tool fakes DOM clicks, and no second game state is maintained. The final Naya performance is rendered from the selected outfit, background, movement, mission result, and outcome effect. Recording and download remain a visible human action using MediaRecorder . Sending the finished output to Trending Tower is blocked until that human-controlled recording exists. Pre-existing versus challenge-added PRE-EXISTING: Dream Realm IP and visual identity; Naya and the other original characters; the Option C HUB; the playable creator/game concept; private-access entrance; Gateway and Direct Creator routes; Dance gameplay; Murk/Noiz logic; creator selections; Naya performance rendering; human MediaRecorder export; Tower response; unlock; HUB return; and the original mouse/touch/keyboard browser foundation. BUILT / MEANINGFULLY EXTENDED DURING THE WEBMCP CHALLENGE: the shared DreamRealmChallenge controller over the existing state; eight document.modelContext.registerTool() registrations; JSON schemas; structured agent actions; read-only and mutating-tool boundaries; input and transition validation; explicit error codes; agent participation across Gateway, Creator, Naya performance preparation, Tower, and HUB; preservation of the human recording/download boundary; the minimal public challenge build and deployment; public WebMCP testing; debugging and challenge-specific stability fixes; and provenance/licensing/test documentation. Where existing Dream Realm code was changed, those changes were made only to expose and stabilize the shared controller and WebMCP flow; they do not represent the underlying Dream Realm product as newly created. BASELINE.md records pre-August-25 source timestamps and checksums, while the dated Git history begins with the untouched baseline and then separates controller, tools, tests, fixes, and release documentation. Broader Dream Realm context The submitted experience is intentionally one complete browser vertical slice: Gateway Mission → creator choices → Naya performance → Tower response → HUB. It demonstrates a shared human-agent world architecture, not the full scope of Dream Realm. PRE-EXISTING DREAM REALM: Dance, Music, and Fashion are the first creator-world spaces explored in Dream Realm. This challenge demo uses Dance as the complete WebMCP vertical slice. The broader world is designed to expand into additional interactive spaces such as puzzles, shops and commerce, sports, story missions, and social experiences. Dream Realm also has a separate Unreal Engine 5 immersive proof exploring the world beyond the browser. CHALLENGE-ADDED WEBMCP WORK: This submission proves the human-agent interaction model inside the browser. WebMCP operates the same live state and visible experience used by the player. WebMCP is not currently implemented natively inside the Unreal proof. FUTURE PRODUCT VISION: Future Unreal and 3D experiences may extend this interaction philosophy to richer character, NPC, and world interactions. This is future direction, not functionality claimed or demonstrated in the current submission. Built with HTML, CSS, JavaScript, Canvas, MediaRecorder, Web Audio, and WebMCP Site tools. title: HopeSong.ai
pitch: A WebMCP-powered spiritual companion that turns moments of fear, weariness, and uncertainty into personalized journeys of Scripture, prayer, and hope.
about_excerpt:
A WebMCP-powered spiritual companion that turns moments of fear, weariness, and uncertainty into personalized journeys of Scripture, prayer, and hope.

 1 2 3 4 5 



 
 Inspiration 

 HopeSong.ai began with a simple question: what if AI could recognize a moment of fear, weariness, or uncertainty and help someone find a meaningful path toward hope? 

 When people feel overwhelmed, they may not know what to search for or where to begin. I wanted to create an experience that starts with the human need itself and connects that moment with Scripture, reflection, prayer, and a simple next step. 

 What it does 

 HopeSong.ai is a WebMCP-powered spiritual companion built around a journey from fear to peace and hope. 

 The website introduces users to songs, prayer, Scripture, and hope-centered experiences. Through WebMCP, HopeSong.ai also exposes structured capabilities that an AI agent can discover and use directly. 

 The current implementation provides two WebMCP tools: 

 findBibleVerse — finds a relevant Bible verse based on the user's topic, emotion, or spiritual need. It supports Bahasa Indonesia, English, Chinese, Korean, and Spanish. 

 findHopeJourney — creates a guided journey consisting of Scripture, Reflection, Prayer, a simple Next Step, and Hope. It currently supports English and Bahasa Indonesia. 

 For example, when someone expresses, "I am afraid and uncertain about my future," the agent can use findHopeJourney to return a structured experience designed around that need. 

 How I built it 

 HopeSong.ai is built with React and Vite and deployed as a live web application. 

 I integrated WebMCP using document.modelContext.registerTool(...) , allowing the browser to expose HopeSong.ai's capabilities as structured tools instead of leaving them only as visual website interactions. 

 Both tools are read-only and use defined input schemas for topic and language. The implementation can be inspected in the public source code, and the live demo allows the WebMCP tools to be discovered and executed in a supported browser environment. 

 Human + AI collaboration 

 The human brings the need. 

 The AI interprets the context and discovers the appropriate WebMCP capability. 

 HopeSong.ai provides the structured experience behind it. 

 This creates a different interaction from simply browsing pages or searching through content. The user does not need to know which page, verse, or resource to look for first. Their need becomes the starting point for the interaction. 

 Challenges I ran into 

 One of the biggest challenges was moving from a traditional website experience to capabilities that an AI agent could discover and execute reliably. 

 I also worked through browser and origin requirements while testing the emerging WebMCP implementation, validated tool discovery with document.modelContext.getTools() , and tested tool execution directly on the production origin. 

 Another challenge was deciding how much functionality to expose. Rather than adding many shallow tools, I focused on two complementary capabilities that demonstrate a clear progression from finding relevant Scripture to creating a more complete Hope Journey. 

 Accomplishments that I'm proud of 

 I am proud that HopeSong.ai evolved from a content experience into a working WebMCP-enabled application. 

 The project now exposes two discoverable tools, supports multilingual Scripture discovery, and demonstrates a complete Hope Journey from an emotional need to Scripture, reflection, prayer, a practical next step, and hope. 

 Most importantly, WebMCP is not only a technical addition to the project. It changes how an AI agent can interact with HopeSong.ai's purpose. 

 What I learned 

 Building HopeSong.ai helped me understand the difference between designing only for human navigation and designing capabilities that can also be understood and used by AI agents. 

 I learned how structured tool definitions, clear input schemas, and focused outputs can turn an existing web experience into something agents can interact with more meaningfully. 

 What's next for HopeSong.ai 

 The current project is intentionally focused on proving the core WebMCP experience. 

 Future versions could expand the Hope Journey with more languages, additional hope-centered resources, deeper personalization, and connections between songs, Scripture, prayer, and the user's ongoing journey. 

 The long-term vision is simple: 

 Find Hope. Find Your Song.
