title: coSynth
pitch: A synthesizer you control by talking to AI. Describe a sound. The AI turns the knobs, plays it, shows every change, and guides you through the controls so you can tweak it and learn as you go.
about_excerpt: A synthesizer you control by talking to AI. Describe a sound. The AI turns the knobs, plays it, shows every change, and guides you through the controls so you can tweak it and learn as you go. Like Comment Story Updates Full Wavetable Synthesizer GIF Active AI state and tool visible in the UI coSynth – AI Web Synthesizer Sound design is hard to get into. A real synth has hundreds of knobs. coSynth lets you describe and get a sound. The AI turns the knobs, plays the result, listens to what it made, and shows all the changes in the UI. You keep it, undo it, tweak it, or ask the AI to show you how it got there. You can also ask AI to teach a complext topic and AI will guide you through step by step. Live: https://coSynth.vercel.app Code: https://github.com/brunnolou/coSynth (MIT) Why WebMCP fits A synth is a terrible thing to operate through text or screenshots. Too many parameters (in this case 224), knobs to drag, LFO curves to draw, etc. An agent can misclick, can miss an exact value, and can't hear the audio. The UI is too complex for someone to easily find things when they are not used to it. That makes a synthesizer one of the best interfaces for WebMCP. For the AI agent: It communicates to the synth directly. Every parameter has a name, a unit, and a range that can be edited directly in bulk. When the agent plays a note, it gets back attack time, decay, spectral centroid, and harmonics, then compares that with a reference clip. So it can "hear" with a tool call. For humans Instead of starting from scratch, you get very close to what you want. Then you can see the exact changes and tweak manually. If you don't know a concept or want to find something, AI can show you the exact location or teach you step by step. You can leverage AI's world knowledge to create any synth sound! What used to need trained ears you now can achieve by sending a reference sound and asking AI to replicate. How I Made the AI<>Human UX Better Each knob the AI touched gets a small animated marker. A status line shows which tool is running. You can reject a whole AI iteration and keep your own edits. Undo covers AI changes and yours. Old branches stay reachable in history. The AI can highlight controls step by step and explain them. Every AI performance is saved, so "play that again with my new adjustment" is one click. AI can save as a preset, and you can download it. How I implemented WebMCP Vanilla TypeScript and Vite. DSP in an AudioWorklet, UI in Canvas, WebGL2 and DOM. WebMCP sits on top of the same engine the UI uses, and the synth works without it. Tools register with document.modelContext.registerTool(tool, { signal }) . There are 24, each with a JSON Schema input and a readOnlyHint : Reading : get_synth_state , get_parameter_schema , get_ui_targets , list_presets , get_history Editing : update_parameters , set_modulation , set_fx_order , apply_patch , save_preset , load_preset , delete_preset , export_preset Sound : play_notes , render_audio , capture_audio , analyze_audio , analyze_reference_audio , compare_audio , suggest_patch , stop_performance Together : show_ui_guide , navigate_history , replay_history All 24 register at page load. play_notes needs the human to click Start first, because browsers won't play audio without a gesture. render_audio uses an OfflineAudioContext, so the agent can design and measure before anyone clicks anything. The page also documents itself. A clipped agent brief in the DOM, a JSON descriptor, ai-tools meta tags, llms.txt and robots.txt . An agent given only the URL can read the page and know what to do. How I tested the agent experience I want to ensure AI could call the tools easily. So I built a loop. A harness exposes only what a real WebMCP client sees, and logs every call. A fresh agent gets a fixed prompt and is never allowed to read the repo. Each round runs on Claude and Codex. When * both trip in the same place( , the tool is wrong . Fix the top blocker, run again. In self-improving loop. Four evals, each asking one question. Can the agent find out what to send ( docs/agent-ux-eval.md ). Can it steer toward a sound it cannot hear ( docs/agent-match-eval.md ). Given a "how do I" question, does it teach rather than edit ( docs/agent-teaching-eval.md ). Given only a URL, does it find the tools at all? Prompts, agent reports and raw logs are all in the repo. Learning all 224 parameters went from 45 calls to 1 . Failed calls went to zero on both models. The matching loop went from 87 calls to 36 . How to test Open https://cosynth.vercel.app in the ChatGPT in-app browser, or in Chrome 149+ with chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing . ChatGPT Desktop was the most reliable client for me. Click "CLICK TO START AUDIO" once. Try: "Make a bright plucked bass and play a short riff." "Show me where the amp envelope is and how to shorten the release." "Save that." Watch the markers, click the status dot for before and after values, and use Keep or Reject. No login. Presets and reference audio stay in the browser. What was already there, what is new I started from Soundgineer by noisyloop ( https://github.com/noisyloop/soundgineer , MIT). Its DSP engine and original UI date from July 6 to 11, 2026, and that version is still up at https://soundgineer.vercel.app . Everything WebMCP-related is from the submission period, August 26 to September 3, 2026, about 200 dated commits: the WebMCP layer and all 24 tools, offline rendering and audio analysis, change markers and Keep/Reject, shared undo history and replays, guided walkthroughs, the interface redesign, the four evals with their harness, and the in-page agent brief. title: REDLINE
pitch: A browser agent can propose shared changes, but only a human decides what becomes real. REDLINE makes that authority boundary visible with WebMCP.
about_excerpt: A browser agent can propose shared changes, but only a human decides what becomes real. REDLINE makes that authority boundary visible with WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates Shared plan — before the agent proposal Agent proposal — 5 changes, not committed Human review — 4 accepted, 1 rejected Committed result — only the accepted subset becomes shared state Architecture — page-held authority with exactly three WebMCP tools Inspiration AI agents can already read context and invoke tools. The harder question is what happens when an agent proposes a change that affects more than one person. Most interfaces collapse proposal and execution into the same moment. REDLINE explores a different boundary: an agent can prepare shared work, everyone affected can see it, but human review remains authoritative before anything becomes committed state. What it does REDLINE is a browser-local shared planning environment for two people: Alex, the reviewer, and Sam, a read-only observer. A visiting browser agent reads the live planning context through WebMCP and stages five typed changes as one proposal. Those changes immediately appear as visible, uncommitted proposal state in both browser views. Alex reviews each operation independently. In the canonical scenario, four changes are accepted and the proposed Browser QA compression is rejected. The projected outcome therefore changes from a Friday launch with compressed QA to a Monday launch with the full two-day QA window retained. Only the accepted subset becomes committed state. Sam sees the proposal, review decisions, and final result, but cannot stage, review, commit, or reset shared state. How we built it REDLINE is a deterministic TypeScript browser application built around three WebMCP tools: get_current_view reads the live browser-local planning context. propose_changes stages an atomic typed proposal against an expected plan revision. commit_proposal finalizes only the subset accepted through the page's human review state. The commit contract deliberately accepts only a proposal ID and expected proposal revision. It does not accept operation IDs or human acceptance decisions, so an agent cannot widen its own authority at commit time. The application also implements stale-revision refusals, deterministic impact calculation, idempotent commit receipts, synchronized same-origin views, and explicit observer-only enforcement. REDLINE uses native BroadcastChannel synchronization between the two open browser views. There is deliberately no server, backend, or database: the proposal exists only in the open page. How we used WebMCP WebMCP is the capability boundary between the visiting browser agent and REDLINE. Instead of exposing generic page automation, REDLINE exposes exactly three typed capabilities corresponding to the lifecycle of shared work: read context, stage a proposal, and commit an already-reviewed proposal. The page retains the authority the agent must not possess. WebMCP therefore does more than provide tool access here: its contracts define what authority crosses the browser-agent boundary and, just as importantly, what authority does not. Challenges The main challenge was preserving a strict distinction between proposed state, human-reviewed state, and committed state while keeping two browser views synchronized. The commit path also had to remain safe under retries and stale state. Repeating an already-applied commit returns the same receipt without duplicating mutation, while stale plan or proposal revisions return structured refusals without changing state. A second challenge was making these boundaries visible. Proposal geometry, human decisions, observer restrictions, projected impact, and final attribution all needed to remain understandable without hiding the underlying authority model. Accomplishments that we're proud of Exactly three typed WebMCP tools with deliberately bounded authority. Atomic proposal staging without immediate mutation of committed state. Human acceptance decisions that cannot be supplied through commit_proposal . Read-only synchronized observation for Sam. Deterministic projected impact before commit. Structured stale-revision refusal. Idempotent commit behavior. 31 passing behavioral, contract, and presentation invariant tests. A fully browser-local architecture with no backend or database. What we learned Agent tooling is only one part of the problem. Once agents operate inside collaborative applications, proposal visibility, authority ownership, concurrency, retries, and attribution become first-class interface and systems concerns. The most important boundary in REDLINE is therefore not whether the agent can call a tool. It is whether calling that tool can carry authority that belongs to a human. What's next REDLINE is intentionally narrow: one shared plan, two people, one proposal lifecycle. The next step would be to explore how the same explicit proposal-before-commit model generalizes to richer collaborative workflows while preserving typed authority boundaries and deterministic review semantics. title: Enactive Brand Portal
pitch: Brand Portals explain brands to humans working in marketing, who then prompt their AI systems. In this project we expose the brand rules directly via WebMCP to agents as tools they can directly call.
about_excerpt: Brand Portals explain brands to humans working in marketing, who then prompt their AI systems. In this project we expose the brand rules directly via WebMCP to agents as tools they can directly call. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Brand portals are built for human reading. When someone wants an AI assistant to apply their guidance, the usual workflow is surprisingly fragile: find the relevant page, interpret it, copy fragments into a prompt, and hope the important context survives. This especially leads to errors and failures when external suppliers, such as marketing agencies interpret the Brand Portal of their clients. Enactive Brand Portal explores a different model. The website remains a real, human-readable brand book, while WebMCP makes the active page available to a visiting assistant as structured capability. The goal is to remove the repeated manual retransmission of brand guidance without removing human intent, factual responsibility, or judgment. What it does The public site presents Enactive Wonderland, an original Carroll-inspired fictional creative house. Visitors can browse its brand foundation, core voice, six character communication modes, and pen-and-ink image world like an ordinary brand portal. On applicable pages, a compatible browser exposes Site Tools derived from that exact page. For the canonical language journey, the person opens the Cheshire Cat page and supplies a communication goal and source facts. The assistant: retrieves the active-page guidance; prepares a structured Language Studio brief; writes one complete draft; stages the result back in the portal. The Studio then displays the original source, proposed draft, material changes, applied rules, rationale, warnings, and ordinary human controls. The person can edit, keep, discard, copy, or reset the work. No tool approves or publishes anything. The same pattern is implemented for visual work. The assistant can prepare and stage a generator-neutral image prompt package containing positive guidance, negative constraints, composition, alt text, and applied rules. The portal does not pretend that it generated or approved an image. Why WebMCP WebMCP tools change the ontological status of the brand rules from static text to executable affordances by the agent. These can be offered context dependent, so that the right tool is available on the right page of the brand portal. Opening Cheshire Cat provides strategic reframing. Opening White Rabbit provides lucid urgency. Opening Image World provides linework, composition, colour, and provenance guidance. WebMCP lets the assistant use that structured active-page context without DOM scraping or requiring the person to reconstruct the brand rules in every prompt. Page and session state determine which tools are available. After a copy brief is prepared, the staging tool appears as the next session affordance. Without Site Tools, the website remains a useful brand book and manual briefing and review surface. With Site Tools, the assistant can perform the substantive transformation and return it to the same browser session for visible human review. How we built it Enactive Brand Portal is a static React and Vite application written in TypeScript. Its source of truth is a four-layer JSON-LD knowledge model: Brand meaning; portal-edition content; generic product and WebMCP contracts; traceability and acceptance evidence. The top-level page registers exactly nine browser Site Tools using: document.modelContext.registerTool(...) Five tools provide read-only brand and guidance access. Four prepare or stage session-local work. Local-effect tools update visible React state and sessionStorage only. There is no remote MCP server, backend, API route, database, CMS, authentication layer, embedded model, or runtime network dependency. Challenges I ran into The hardest product challenge was keeping the brand and the technology separate. An earlier version technically worked but made the public experience feel like a WebMCP demonstrator rather than a useful brand portal. I rebuilt the content architecture so that Enactive Wonderland remains the subject and WebMCP appears only as a restrained application capability. Other challenges included route-specific tool availability, dynamically adding the staging affordance after preparation, cancellation handling, output-size limits in a real host, preserving context across Studio navigation, and distinguishing native browser evidence from a local handler harness. I also had to keep every claim honest: deterministic copy checks are partial, staged image work is a prompt package rather than an image, and the assistant proposes while the person decides. Accomplishments A coherent human-facing brand portal that works without WebMCP. Nine page- and session-aware browser Site Tools. A real compatible-host copy journey covering discovery, guidance retrieval, brief preparation, dynamic staging, visible review, and reload persistence. A fully static architecture with immutable brand knowledge. Human-readable source, diff, rule, rationale, and warning inspection. Automated graph, schema, architecture, layer-separation, unit, accessibility, and browser checks. A public Vercel deployment with ten working direct routes. A public Apache-2.0 repository with recorded content and asset provenance. What I learned WebMCP is most valuable when the active page is not merely navigation but meaningful task context. The strongest interaction was not “an agent can click the website.” It was that the website could expose purpose-built, state-aware affordances while remaining understandable and useful to a person. We also learned that local tool execution is not equivalent to native browser proof, and that agent capability should stop before consequential human decisions such as approval or publication. What's next Next steps include reproducing the complete image-prompt journey in additional native hosts, testing compatibility across more WebMCP-enabled browsers, extracting the generic portal engine for other governed knowledge systems, and measuring the effect on task time, omitted rules, correction count, and reviewer confidence. The same pattern could be applied to design systems, policy portals, learning systems, editorial standards, and other websites whose knowledge currently stops at reading and downloading. Enactive Wonderland is an original fictional brand inspired by the public-domain works of Lewis Carroll. The project contains no brand assets, internal data, proprietary guidelines, or endorsement. Research, writing, design exploration, and implementation were AI-assisted under my direction and final conceptual, editorial, architectural, licensing, and release authority. title: Cdence AI
pitch: From intelligence to action—under human control
about_excerpt: From intelligence to action—under human control Like Comment Story Updates Here is the complete, submission-ready project writeup structured for your Devpost hackathon submission: Inspiration Every Tech Lead and engineering manager knows the dread of the "Wednesday 2 PM Crisis": standing 48 hours away from a critical launch with zero days of slack, discovering a key task is blocked, and realizing the entire downstream release chain is at risk. When teams turn to traditional AI chatbots for help, they get text advice like "Prioritize the critical path" or "Fast-track QA" . But advice is not action. Traditional chatbots cannot see the live project state, cannot validate hard organizational constraints, and cannot execute changes. Conversely, giving an autonomous agent direct, unchecked write access to modify a production workspace is reckless. We built Cadence AI to solve this exact dilemma: transforming AI from a passive advice-giver into a verified project operator that can safely understand, simulate, and stage changes directly inside the browser workspace under strict human control. What it does Cadence AI is a WebMCP-native project coordination workspace that connects directly with browser-based AI agents to diagnose critical bottlenecks and execute recovery plans. Live Workspace Inspection: Exposes structured read tools that allow the agent to inspect the reactive dependency graph, identify blocker cascades, and assess slack buffers in real time. Mathematical Schedule Simulation: Uses a dry-run simulation engine to test schedule permutations and verify whether a recovery plan is mathematically feasible before touching anything. Negative Constraint Reasoning: Honors human instructions (such as "Optimize schedule, but don't reassign Sarah" ) by locking assigned tasks and finding alternative parallelization paths without breaking team rules. Zero-Unchecked-Mutation Gate: Write operations never modify the project state silently. The agent creates a transparent, staged Proposal Card showing an exact before-and-after diff ( AT RISK ➔ ON TRACK ). One-Click Human Approval: The human in the loop reviews the proposed changes and clicks Approve to commit the updates atomically to the live Gantt timeline with instant visual pulse feedback. How we built it Cadence AI is engineered as a lightweight, zero-backend, client-side web application designed to run natively inside any agent-enabled browser session: Frontend & UI: Built with Next.js (App Router), TypeScript, and Tailwind CSS, featuring an interactive Gantt timeline, blocker dependency graph, and real-time telemetry log. Reactive State Layer: In-memory Zustand store acting as the single source of truth for all tasks, dependencies, active proposals, and agent telemetry (requiring zero external databases or API keys for 100% reproducible deployments). WebMCP Adapter Layer: Implemented a standard-compliant WebMCP integration supporting both navigator.modelContext and document.modelContext with double-registration guards to safely expose tools to AI agents. Deterministic Graph Engine: Built an in-browser topological sorting algorithm with cycle detection, transitive blocker traversal, slack calculation, and negative constraint parsing. Challenges we ran into Client-Side Tool Gating: Ensuring that write tools could not bypass the UI. We had to design an atomic staging system where write tool executions create pending proposal objects in the Zustand store and return a "pending_human_approval" status back to the agent without mutating the underlying task array. Negative Constraint Parsing in Natural Language: Interpreting nuanced user constraints (like "don't move Sarah" or "never touch security" ) and reliably translating those modifiers into hard boolean locks ( locked: true ) inside the topological scheduler. WebMCP Protocol Alignment: Handling client-side lifecycle timing so that WebMCP tools are properly registered and discoverable the instant an agent session attaches to the browser DOM. Accomplishments that we're proud of True Human-in-the-Loop Architecture: Proving that an AI agent can execute complex, multi-step project graph mutations safely without risking unverified state destruction. Deterministic Simulation Engine: Building a real-time scheduling engine in pure TypeScript that calculates critical paths and resolves parallel workflows instantly on the client side. Seamless Visual Telemetry: Creating an intuitive visual experience where every tool call, dry-run simulation, and approved proposal provides immediate visual feedback across the timeline and agent activity log. What we learned Advice vs. Execution: We learned that the true bottleneck in AI productivity is not the quality of the model's textual reasoning, but the absence of safe, standardized interfaces to turn reasoning into structured execution. Power of In-Browser MCP: WebMCP opens a massive frontier for web applications by turning DOM-level state into first-class tool interfaces for browser agents, eliminating the need for bulky server-side intermediary APIs. What's next for Cadence AI Two-Way Issue Tracker Sync: Adding WebMCP connectors for GitHub Issues, Jira, and Linear so approved proposals can synchronize directly back to enterprise tracking systems. Multi-Resource Workload Balancing: Extending the engine to calculate individual developer capacity curves, vacation constraints, and cross-team skill tags during topological recovery. Autonomous Telemetry Webhooks: Enabling ambient background monitoring where Cadence AI proactively flags newly introduced blocker cascades and prepares staged recovery proposals before a Tech Lead even asks. title: Out of Service
pitch: Two people, two agents, one page. The companion's agent cannot accept the reroute. Step-free NYC.
about_excerpt: Two people, two agents, one page. The companion's agent cannot accept the reroute. Step-free NYC. Like 1 Comment Story Updates The problem A wheelchair user at Court Sq is trying to reach Bleecker St. New York's subway has 160 accessible stations out of 472 , and almost every one depends on an elevator. Advocates counted at least 25 elevator outages a day, median about four hours ( Gothamist ). If the one you need is out, you find out standing in front of it. The person tracking that trip, a partner, an aide, an adult child, is somewhere else with a phone, reading the same feed the rider can and able to do nothing with it but text. Planning around it barely works. The MTA status page says what is broken this minute, never what breaks often. In July 2026 a class action about exactly this settled. CIDNY v. MTA now requires advance notice of outages, platform announcements every 15 minutes, and real-time alternate accessible routes ( Disability Rights Advocates ). The obligation exists now. The thing a rider holds does not. What Out of Service is Out of Service scores every step-free route between two accessible stations on the specific elevators it depends on, using eleven years of MTA outage history joined to the live feed, so a route arrives as a number and a named list of equipment instead of a hope. The rider and the companion open the same trip on the same page, each with their own agent, and the two agents get different tools. How it works Three keyless MTA sources, joined into one committed artifact ( docs/DATA.md ): 82,385 monthly availability rows over 695 equipment codes, 2015-01 to 2026-07, from NY State dataset rc78-7x78 ; the 704-row equipment master; and the live outage feed, 85 records at build time. The join is data/index.json : 695 records, 413 elevators and 282 escalators across 123 accessible complexes, each with 24 months of metrics, a percentile rank inside its own equipment type, a tier, and a tier_reason naming the thresholds behind it. All 77 live-outage ids join into the index ( data/index-meta.json ). Routing runs on a graph of those 123 elevator-dependent complexes: 558 ride edges over 23 lines, 472 of them asserted by the MTA's own next-accessible-station fields ( docs/ROUTING.md ). The score is a sum, not a verdict: 25 per dependent unreliable elevator, 10 watch, 8 unknown, 2 reliable, halved where a second elevator makes the same move, 15 per transfer, plus 60 and a broken flag if a required non-redundant elevator is out live. Broken is never "this station has an outage", always "this route needs this elevator, nothing else makes that move, and it is out". Every number on screen is dotted, and clicking it opens the dataset, the query and the row count. Two people, two agents, one page Creating a trip mints two unguessable keys. The rider gets /t/<id>?k=<riderKey> ; the companion link is the same trip with the other key. Tools register per session from those keys, so DevTools > Application > WebMCP lists 13 tools in the rider's window and 10 in the companion's, same origin, same page, before either agent says a word. Hiding a tool is not the boundary. POST /api/trip/:id/action derives the role from the key and ignores any role in the body, so a forged accept from the companion's session comes back 403: "Only the rider can accept route. You are the companion: propose a reroute instead." Every write parks inside execute behind a confirmation card and does not resolve until a person presses Confirm. Reject rejects it in the rider's own typed words, so the agent hears "that transfer is too long for me" and offers something else. The broken-equipment report is a declarative HTML form with no toolautosubmit : the agent fills it in, a person sends it. When the feed changes, the whole set re-registers and toolchange fires, and accept_reroute 's description goes from "0 pending proposals" to "1 pending proposal from your companion right now (p1)". Features Route scoring with tiers. Three routes, each with a risk number, a label and its elevators. Live station panel. Outages at both ends with the MTA's return estimates. Companion link. Its own capability key, its own tool set. Proposals and acceptance. The companion proposes with a reason, the rider accepts or rejects, both windows updating in about two seconds. Watch equipment. Subscribe to codes, see them in a watch list. Broken-equipment report. A declarative form the agent fills and a person sends. Source on hover. Every dotted number opens its dataset, query and row count. Simulated outage. Forces one elevator out for the session, labelled SIMULATED throughout. Origin trial. The Chrome WebMCP token is in the page head, so stock Chrome needs no flag. Why WebMCP is the right fit Why this use case is a strong fit for WebMCP. Two humans with different authority share one page. WebMCP registers tools per session from inside the page, so one origin and one path present 13 tools to the rider's agent and 10 to the companion's. A server-side MCP server can express two roles, but not without a second deployment, an auth handshake and an account for the companion. How it creates a better experience. Before: four equipment-code lookups across two MTA pages, two minutes of cross-referencing, an answer good only for this minute. After: one route_accessible call, under a second, three routes scored on their elevators' 24-month history. Court Sq (E M G 7) to Bleecker St returns the F at 26, G then F at 35 and F then M at 43 (2026-09-03 build). Take EL328 at Bleecker out and the F flips to 86, avoid, broken, and G then F is the recommendation. What people and agents can now do together that was difficult or impossible before. Two agents split one trip: the companion's watches the feed and proposes, the rider's surfaces it, a person confirms. The rider never has to trust the companion's agent, or ours, because the difference is enforced by the server and visible in DevTools. How we implemented WebMCP. document.modelContext.registerTool only, never navigator.modelContext , which moved to Document in the 27 May 2026 draft. Fifteen tools registered per session by role, each with a strict inputSchema and readOnlyHint , and untrustedContentHint on get_trip alone, the one tool returning text another human typed. Mutations build their own confirm gate inside execute , because WebMCP has no destructive-action annotation and requestUserInteraction() has not shipped; create_trip and report_broken_equipment are declarative forms without toolautosubmit . evals/ follows Chrome's guidance: 17 fixtures carrying role , page and state , one a companion asking to accept, where the right answer is no tool call. The runtime reads document.modelContext once before anything touches it and otherwise loads @mcp-b/webmcp-polyfill , with a badge printing native , polyfill or unavailable . What is real today, and what is next NYCT subway only: no PATH, no commuter rail, no buses. Tiers are percentiles of the equipment's own population, so "unreliable" means unreliable for New York, not against an absolute standard. Direction is the honest blind spot: 65 of 264 platform-touching elevators call themselves "Manhattan-bound", meaning south from the Bronx and north from Brooklyn, and the master's borough column is empty on all 704 rows. Those are reported as possible dependencies, inflating a route's risk rather than hiding one. Next: MTA alert subscriptions per watched elevator, so a watch list pushes instead of polls; more cities, because the same open-data shape exists elsewhere; and the two-agent pattern outside transit, a pharmacist and a caregiver on one prescription page, where one proposes a substitution and only the other accepts. video_transcript_excerpt: Hi everyone. My name is Kamal. Here's a problem I didn't know existed until I watched someone get stranded on a subway platform. New York has 160 accessible stations out of 472 and almost all of them depend on on an elevator. Advocates count at least 25 elevator outages a day, median 4 hours. If yours is out, you find out standing at the platform and whoever's tracking your trip can only text you. It got bad enough that a lawsuit over exactly this settled in July. The outage history is public data. Nobody had ever joined it to a route. So, here's what out of service does. It scores every accessible route by how often its elevators actually fail, live outages included, and gives the rider and their companion each their own agent on the same page. Under the hood, it's three sources. 82,000 monthly rows since 2015, the live outage feed, and the MTA's own equipment list with its next accessible station links. That feeds a reliability score per elevator, which feeds a route graph of the 123 stations that depend on elevators, and the page itself registers different tools for the rider and for the companion. That's route accessible. The first call firing when the agents ask for a trip from Court Square to Bleecker Street in a wheelchair. Three routes come back clean, F direct at 26. EL 445X is out at Court Square, but it's on the 7 platform, route aware, not station aware. The rider takes the F. A confirmation card pops up and a person clicks confirm, not the agent. Now the companion's window, same trip. It has proposed reroute, no accept reroute. The rider's is the opposite. We simulate a failure on camera labeled EL 328 at Bleecker goes out. The F flips to 86, broken tools re-register, accept reroute now says one pending proposal. The companion's agent proposes the G, then the F sitting at 35. The rider's agent picks it up, calls accept re-route, hits confirm, both windows update. Last, the rider opens the report broken equipment form. The agent fills it in, a human presses submit. You can't do this with a chatbot wrapper or by scraping the site. Nothing knows which tab is asking. Every number on screen links back to the query behind it, and it all runs on the open web MCP standard. The page configures its own tools, no scraping, no plug-in, and a person confirms every right. The settlement asks the MTA for advance notice and re-routing info. This is what that looks like when the rider's own agent does it. And what we own after today is the index.

title: Duet
pitch: Plan the room with your agent. You pin the judgment calls; your agent solves feuds, diets and table math through 25 WebMCP tools — live, on one shared floor plan.
about_excerpt: Plan the room with your agent. You pin the judgment calls; your agent solves feuds, diets and table math through 25 WebMCP tools — live, on one shared floor plan. Like Comment Story Updates Why this use case is a strong fit for WebMCP Seating a room is a two-brain problem. One brain holds context no form can capture: who is divorced, which sponsor is feuding with whom, which aunt needs to sit near the exit. The other has to satisfy a combinatorial pile of constraints: table capacities, conflicts, introductions, dietary needs, accessibility, company-mixing rules, and table balance. Humans are great at the first and bad at the second. Agents are the opposite. Before WebMCP, neither interface worked well. A drag-and-drop floor plan is a terrible surface for an agent to operate through pixels, while moving the task into chat throws away the human's spatial judgment. Duet lets both work on the same live state, in the same tab: the human drags, pins, and visually evaluates the room while the agent uses structured tools such as seat_guest , add_constraint , set_group_rule , and a real constraint solver. How it creates a better user experience Duet gives human-agent collaboration an explicit contract, enforced in code. Pins are law. Any guest placed manually is pinned 📌. The solver plans around those decisions, and agent tools are refused if they attempt to move or remove a pinned guest. Agents propose; humans decide. The preferred agent tool, propose_arrangement , does not mutate the room. It displays the reasoning and complete move list first. Only the human can Accept or Dismiss it. The tool surface follows human attention. Selecting a table dynamically exposes table-scoped tools such as seat_at_selected_table and clear_selected_table . Deselecting it removes them. The agent's available capabilities therefore reflect what the human is currently focused on. Everything is visible and reversible. Agent actions appear as a violet cursor on the board, every action enters a shared activity feed labeled ✳ agent or ● you, and undo/redo works across both human and agent actions. What becomes possible — together — that wasn't before Load a 120-guest fundraising gala. The human manually places two important guests, pinning them in place. The agent records "press away from the board", applies "maximum two people from the same company per table", and proposes a complete arrangement for the remaining 118 guests. The solver honors every constraint without touching the human's pins. The human reviews the proposal visually and accepts it in one click. Create a conflict deliberately and Duet pans to the affected table, identifies who conflicts and why, and lets the agent call explain_seating to justify individual placements. Then ask: "Give me the caterer's brief." The agent calls export_plan and returns dietary counts by table. That loop — human judgment steering an agent and a constraint solver through conversation, directly on a shared visual surface — is what WebMCP makes possible. The same engine includes five scenarios: wedding, fundraising gala, corporate networking dinner, office seating, and classroom seating. How we implemented WebMCP Duet exposes 21 base tools through document.modelContext.registerTool , covering: guest and table CRUD pair constraints with notes group spread and cluster rules solver execution arrangement proposals pins dietary reports Markdown export template loading undo explain_seating get_activity_log , allowing a returning agent to understand what the human changed while it was away It also exposes 4 dynamic selection-scoped tools registered and removed with AbortController as the user's selection changes. The WebMCP tool surface itself therefore mirrors the human's current focus. Tool results return structured JSON, including the conflicts an action would create, so agents can reason about consequences before modifying state. Guardrails are enforced at the tool layer: pinned guests cannot be moved by agents, and propose_arrangement is explicitly presented as the preferred workflow so agents default to human review rather than silent mutation. The constraint solver is dependency-free and combines greedy assignment, local search, targeted repair, and three-way relocation. A 120-guest room solves in roughly 75 ms while respecting pins, pair constraints, group rules, accessibility requirements, and table balance. Duet is built with React, Vite, and TypeScript and has no backend. The entire collaborative state lives in the browser tab — exactly where WebMCP operates. title: EvidenceBound WebMCP Authority Compiler
pitch: A human approves one release, the AI gains the WebMCP release tool, and correction or revocation makes it disappear.
about_excerpt: A human approves one release, the AI gains the WebMCP release tool, and correction or revocation makes it disappear. Like Comment Story Updates The problem A release manager wants an AI agent to help with one exact release. The failure mode is simple: the human approves it, then the evidence or the decision changes, but the agent still retains the consequential capability. EvidenceBound makes the capability follow the current human decision. The agent starts with three safe WebMCP tools. It can inspect the release and request approval, but it cannot approve, revoke, correct, or restore its own authority. When the release manager approves the exact current release snapshot, a fourth tool — execute_authorized_release — appears. If the human corrects the security evidence or revokes approval, that tool disappears. Execution also re-checks current authority, so stale discovery state cannot succeed after the decision changes. Judge moment: 3 tools → human approval → 4 tools → human correction/revocation → 3 tools . The controlled demo records externalSideEffect=false ; it does not claim to perform an actual external deployment or customer mutation. What the judge will see The agent starts with three safe tools and inspects the current release. The agent requests approval. The request becomes pending, but the AI still cannot approve itself. The human clicks Approve this exact release . execute_authorized_release appears as the fourth WebMCP tool. The agent invokes the controlled action; EvidenceBound revalidates current authority before recording a receipt. The human corrects the security evidence or revokes approval. The release tool disappears. A stale retained descriptor is rejected by execution-time revalidation. The public page separates Human and Agent actions and keeps the next step visible so this behavior can be understood without reading the architecture first. Why WebMCP is load-bearing This is not a generic MCP wrapper. EvidenceBound uses the real browser-native document.modelContext.registerTool(...) interface so current human authority changes which capability the agent can discover. Three baseline tools are available for safe inspection, approval requests, and receipts. execute_authorized_release is registered only while the exact current release snapshot is AUTHORIZED . Correction, revocation, stale evidence, or a hard evidence/policy failure removes or blocks that capability. That is different from exposing a consequential tool permanently and hiding a denial inside the handler. Here the human decision changes the model-visible browser capability surface itself. Execution-time revalidation is a second fail-closed boundary in case an agent retained stale discovery state. Human-only grant, revoke, correct, and restore controls are deliberately not WebMCP tools. The AI cannot mint or repair its own authority. Human + agent collaboration The useful division of labor is explicit: Agent: inspect the release, explain what is missing, request approval, and use the release capability while it is current. Human: approve one exact release, correct evidence, revoke approval, or restore fresh evidence. EvidenceBound: project the current human decision into the WebMCP tool surface and revalidate it at execution time. The result is easy to see: the human changes their mind, so the agent's consequential tool disappears. Who this is for The primary user is release engineering / DevOps / platform operations. Their recurring job is letting agents help with consequential operational actions without letting yesterday's approval become today's authority. A common alternative is to expose sensitive tools continuously and rely on prompts or a late authorization check during execution. EvidenceBound adds an authority-aware capability layer: the agent sees the consequential tool only while current evidence and explicit human approval justify it, and execution verifies again before success. A reusable version of this pattern could support release and administrative workflows that need revocable, evidence-bound agent capability. We are not claiming current customers, revenue, certifications, or production external deployments. Implementation The WebMCP surface lives under site/webmcp/ . A dedicated adapter feature-detects document.modelContext ; when the real WebMCP API is unavailable, the app does not emulate or label a fallback as genuine WebMCP. Internally, EvidenceBound distinguishes AUTHORIZED , HUMAN_REQUIRED , STALE , INVALIDATED , and BLOCKED . Tool registration follows that state. Execution revalidates authoritative state and includes race-condition hardening for authority correction during asynchronous verification and concurrent execution attempts. Automated tests cover state transitions, stale and invalidated authority, execution-time revalidation, concurrent execution behavior, and WebMCP registration/removal contracts. GitHub Actions runs both the WebMCP-specific suite and the broader EvidenceBound Core CI. The public site is deployed on Vercel and the repository is Apache-2.0 licensed. What was added during the challenge EvidenceBound Core existed before the WebMCP Challenge. It already contained evidence, provenance, policy, stale-state, invalidation, receipt, persistence, and fail-closed primitives. Challenge-period work added the WebMCP-specific authority projection and judge experience: browser-native WebMCP tool registration; dynamic 3 → 4 → 3 tool visibility driven by current human authority; agent request vs. human grant/revoke/correct separation; execution-time authority revalidation; correction/revocation propagation into the visible capability surface; adversarial stale, correction-race, and concurrent-execution tests; a public WebMCP judge surface and production acceptance evidence. The repository documents pre-existing work and challenge-period work separately so prior EvidenceBound primitives are not presented as new competition work. Try it Open https://evidencebound.org/webmcp/ in ChatGPT's in-app browser or Chrome with WebMCP enabled. The page contains the 60-second judge path and links to the public source and judge guide. title: Bridge Studio
pitch: A visible browser workspace that turns web workflows into typed, human-approved tools.
about_excerpt: A visible browser workspace that turns web workflows into typed, human-approved tools. Like Comment Story Updates Signal Lab: one approved configure_analysis call moves thirteen coupled controls, the chart, the KPIs and the provenance stamp atomically. The cross-origin boundary, shown rather than hidden: compatibility must not mean bypassing browser security. Civic Desk: a consequential-write tool whose result explicitly remains unsubmitted, with revocation visible in the trace. Inspiration The interesting question is not whether an agent can click a button. It is what happens to state that a person cannot see. We wanted a browser workspace where the capability an agent holds is a contract a person read and approved, and where every use of it is visible in the same interface the person is looking at. What it does Bridge Studio discovers meaningful workflows in the visible page and turns them into typed WebMCP tool proposals. Each proposal states its inputs and whether it reads or changes state. A person approves the contract before it is registered. When an agent uses an approved tool, the same interface updates, a live execution flow narrates what the protocol is doing, and the action is recorded in a durable trace. Signal Lab is the argument. Its configure_analysis tool collapses thirteen brittle UI interactions — coupled sliders, multi-select cohorts, linked date ranges, a chart brush — into one semantic call with a JSON Schema that enforces enums, array uniqueness, numeric bounds, date patterns, and cross-field invariants ( endDate > startDate , confidenceMax > confidenceMin ). A click-driven automation can get halfway through that sequence and leave the dashboard in a state no human asked for. A typed tool either applies the whole configuration or is rejected with a reason. Voyager Stays and Civic Desk keep the read-only and consequential-write cases visible, plus a guarded external-origin preview that demonstrates a boundary: compatibility must not mean bypassing browser security. How we built it The app uses the WebMCP Imperative API through document.modelContext.registerTool() . Three workspace tools register at startup. Page-specific tools are registered only after explicit human review and are revoked through AbortController signals when the user navigates away — with the reason shown in the trace. Every execute returns the spec-shaped { content: [{ type: "text", text }] } result. JSON Schema bounds every input, and a validator enforces types, enums, patterns, string and numeric bounds, array cardinality and uniqueness, and rejects unexpected fields. readOnlyHint communicates risk to the agent; untrustedContentHint is true on every tool, including the action trace, because the trace carries agent-supplied text and must never be laundered back as trusted context. The frontend is standards-based HTML, CSS, and JavaScript with no runtime framework and no build-time dependencies — the chart is hand-written SVG. Node's built-in test runner covers address handling, the full validator surface, the Signal Lab contract, and the annotation invariants. The deployment sends Content-Security-Policy with frame-ancestors 'none' , because an approval dialog that can be framed is not an approval. Challenges The hardest design problem was respecting the difference between native site tools and browser automation. Arbitrary pages cannot be safely inspected from another origin. Instead of hiding that constraint, Bridge Studio makes it visible and demonstrates a secure same-origin workflow while outlining the isolated-browser architecture an authorized external site would need. The second was resisting the temptation to overclaim. It would have been easy to show a tool as "registered" in browsers without WebMCP. We label it as an unregistered preview instead, because a project about honest contracts cannot lie in its own status bar. Accomplishments A complete human approval → tool registration → agent execution → visible audit loop One typed call that atomically synchronizes thirteen coupled controls, the chart, the KPIs, and a provenance stamp A live, reduced-motion-safe execution flow that shows what the protocol is doing as it happens Graceful, truthful operation both with and without a WebMCP-enabled browser Explicit protections against clickjacking, cross-origin overclaims, and trace-laundered prompt injection What we learned The most valuable WebMCP capability is not automation. It is a shared, inspectable contract between a website, a person, and their agent. Trust comes from narrow inputs, honest side-effect metadata, atomic application, visible execution, and revocation the user can see and reverse. What's next An isolated remote-browser worker for domains the user is authorized to automate, a tool-contract compiler that derives schemas from existing forms, saved organization policies, WebMCP evals, and cryptographically signed action receipts. title: Form Less
pitch: Turns a complex service into a personal interface built for the user's needs.
about_excerpt: Turns a complex service into a personal interface built for the user's needs. Like Comment Story Updates The initial form The simplified version based on the agent's contextual understanding of the user The final submitted version with MCP logs Inspiration I feel like most people who are technically oriented have at some point - and maybe with increased frequency - have found themselves frustrated with tech interfaces they encounter in their daily lives. Custom car interface software is a classic example, a needlessly long web form is another (as someone with ADHD I could go on for hours about other examples personal to me). But what if the interface adapted based on the personal facts about you, as well as your current intention? Most commercial consumer AIs have a memory feature these days, and most consumers are starting to get the reflexive habit of treating their AI not just as a chatbox, but as a companion that can be present when they need - so how can we get the agent to help in the example of a confusing interface that sits between a user and the problem they need solved/communicated? What it does Form Less shares the website's rules and structure with the user's agent, so that the agent can adapt its interface around what the user actually needs to do. To better demonstrate the functionality of Form Less, I built an example site/form: an application for repair support in the fictitious area of Alderwick. The default form - being a relic from days where the application was manual and has just been directly ported to a web version - can appear quite intimidating and confusing. But Form Less, via WebMCP, can take the user's specific situation into account and show them only what's necessary and what they need to understand and submit their application. The user would describe their situation to their agent, e.g. showing it a photo of the damage/what needs repairing, and the agent would The purpose isn't to complete the form for the user - not to 'remove thought' - but to present it and communicate it in a way that helps the user understand exactly what's being asked, and what they're submitting. So Form Less is the reusable WebMCP pattern behind that helps an agent to help its human navigate UIs How we built it It's a static React/Typescript application in 3 layers: The JSON schema defines the 34 questions and answer types The UI schema defines the complete form and the focused layouts that are permitted A rules document handles the expansions and checks with more complex conditional branches. Challenges we ran into The main challenge was product design, and thinking about the wider nature of the interaction between a human and their agent. It would be technically trivial to also expose submission tools to the agent, but I explicitly scoped it behind this. I didn't want it to be a 'form completer' kind of tool, but something to help the user better understand the issue I also wanted to make it technically easy for a site to implement - so the form and the agent's understanding is driven by the form's schema, so it learns the rules and requirements from the form's rules itself, so that a human 'deploying' it doesn't have to think and basically rewrite the rules of the form - no additional thinking/labour required here. Accomplishments that we're proud of I'm proud of the general idea and design of the execution. It's not just a one-time form-restyler, or 'get an agent to fill out a form for you', but a general approach that bridges the human-agent connection and the agent-browser connection, which I think is exactly what WebMCP enables. Providing the agent with structured JSON gives it the form's design and its rules, so that if a site wanted to adopt it, they wouldn't have to spend extra time explicitly rewriting the form's rules, and also passes the principle that if the form is correctly built, the agent will correctly understand it. What we learned I realised that the difficult/interesting part of webMCP is deciding what tools you want to expose, and how they relate to the visible interface and the authority they should share. My initial conception of WebMCP was that it was just a more reliable way for an agent to do browser tasks like fill in fields. But then I realised you can communicate a lot more in terms of structure and logic that unlocks a lot more possibility for the agent to enhance the experience for the user. What's next for Form Less Alderwick's one example of making it easier for people to fill out a complex form, but the whole point of Form Less is that the general approach can be applied to many other areas Built With react typescript vite webmcp Try it out fortydegrees.github.io github.com Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by David Pratt Like Share this project: Updates David Pratt started this project — Sep 04, 2026 03:59 AM EDT

title: MCP VisionQuote
pitch: MCP-based AI estimator that instantly calculates camera coverage, cable length, BOM, labor, and drafts commercial proposals for video surveillance & structured cabling projects.
about_excerpt:
MCP-based AI estimator that instantly calculates camera coverage, cable length, BOM, labor, and drafts commercial proposals for video surveillance & structured cabling projects.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 1 
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 


 



 
 Inspiration 

 After 22 years installing CCTV, access control, and structured cabling, I kept hitting the same wall: turning floor plans and site walkthroughs into reliable, itemized quotes still 
 took hours of manual counting and spreadsheet work. MCP VisionQuote was born from that friction — an AI estimator that combines Model Context Protocol (MCP/WebMCP) with domain 
 knowledge from real-world low-current projects. Every surveillance or cabling quote starts with the same questions: how many cameras, how much cable, which conduits, how many man-hours? Experienced integrators can estimate a site in
 minutes, but clients still wait days for a polished proposal. I wanted to capture that expertise in a tool that reads project context through MCP tools, reasons about layouts and 
 requirements, and returns a quote an installer can trust. 

 What it does 

 How we built it 

 MCP VisionQuote exposes domain-specific tools through MCP/WebMCP: estimate_project , get_bom , generate_proposal , and suggest_camera_placement . The backend is Python 3.12 + 
 FastAPI, with a lightweight SQLite store and a seed price catalog. A FastAPI web UI lets users enter site parameters and instantly see a BOM, labor estimate, and commercial proposal. I 
 used YOLOv8-nano for optional photo-based placement suggestions, and Render + Cloudflare Tunnel for the public deployment. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 The hardest part was not the code — it was encoding field reality. Camera counts change when a hallway has no ceiling access. Cable lengths explode when plenum routes are blocked. I 
 had to balance AI speed with installer-grade accuracy, so every recommendation includes assumptions that a human can review and override. Trust, not full automation, became the real 
 goal. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 What we learned 

 Domain experience is the differentiator. Generic LLMs can write a quote; only a system grounded in low-current installation practice knows why a quote is wrong. MCP proved to be the 
 right glue: it keeps project data separate from reasoning, making the estimator easier to audit, extend, and connect to other tools. 

 What's next for MCP VisionQuote 

 MCP VisionQuote is a practical step toward AI-assisted field estimating — built by someone who has pulled the cable, mounted the cameras, and argued about the labor hours. 

 

 
 Built With

 Created by
 

 
 
 
 
 I built MCP VisionQuote end-to-end as a solo developer, from the initial idea and architecture to the Python/FastAPI backend, WebMCP tools, user interface, testing, and deployment. I implemented project estimation, bill of materials generation, proposal creation, and camera placement suggestions.

title: WattKeep
pitch: Plan household outages with a WebMCP agent that compares energy strategies while people retain final control.
about_excerpt: Plan household outages with a WebMCP agent that compares energy strategies while people retain final control. Like Comment Story Updates Banner Household outage overview Plan Comparison Unsafe interval explained Visible proposal diff Human Review Boundary Stale proposal rejected Inspiration During an outage, a household with a battery has a simple but difficult question: what must stay on, and how long will the stored energy last? Most dashboards show readings, but the person still has to compare hourly demand, reserve limits and changing forecasts by hand. I built WattKeep to test a better working relationship. A browser agent handles the calculations and comparisons. The household sees the evidence, reviews the proposed change and keeps the final say. What it does WattKeep is a deterministic, local-first outage planner. The demonstration follows the Morgan household through a twelve-hour outage with 10.53 kWh stored in a 13.5 kWh battery and a protected reserve of 20 percent. A WebMCP agent can inspect the household and outage, simulate three plans, compare their reserve safety, explain an unsafe hourly interval, stage a feasible alternative and request human review. WattKeep exposes eight page-scoped tools: inspect_home inspect_outage simulate_plan compare_plans stage_plan explain_interval discard_plan request_review The agent cannot approve, commit or undo a policy change. Those actions stay in the visible human interface. If the forecast or workspace changes while a proposal is awaiting confirmation, WattKeep rejects the stale proposal and requires a fresh calculation. How I built it WattKeep is a React, TypeScript and Vite single-page application. A deterministic simulator and an observable local store power both the human interface and the WebMCP adapter. The adapter registers its tools through document.modelContext , with constrained JSON schemas and structured success or recoverable-error results. Every staged proposal records a proposal ID, base revision, scenario and simulation fingerprint. Commit-time validation checks those values against the current workspace before a person can apply the change. Human commits, undo, forecast refresh, discard and session reset are recorded in an append-only journal. The application remains fully usable when WebMCP is unavailable. It stores a versioned workspace locally and falls back to memory-only operation if browser persistence fails. Challenges I ran into The hardest design problem was giving the agent enough authority to be useful without letting it cross the household's decision boundary. Inspection and simulation are safe to automate. Applying a policy is not, so I separated proposal preparation from human confirmation and removed commit and undo from the tool surface. Stale evidence was the second problem. A proposal may be valid when it is created and wrong after a forecast refresh. Revision and fingerprint checks turn that race into a visible, recoverable error instead of silently applying outdated advice. I also kept the demonstration honest. WattKeep is a planning simulator. It does not connect to or control batteries, inverters or household circuits. Accomplishments that I am proud of The human interface and all eight WebMCP tools share one state model. The video shows tool calls changing the same state the person can see. Human-only commit and undo controls preserve the final decision. Stale-proposal rejection protects a decision after its evidence changes. The public build passed 62 unit tests, 15 WebMCP contract tests, 13 end-to-end tests and 7 accessibility and responsive checks. What I learned A page does not become agent-ready merely by exposing machine-callable actions. The useful part is the contract around those actions: clear descriptions, constrained inputs, inspectable results, versioned state and visible human boundaries. WebMCP removes much of the guesswork involved in operating a graphical interface. WattKeep showed me that reliable human-agent collaboration also needs transaction-style safety, especially when an agent prepares a decision that a person must approve later. What's next for WattKeep The next version could import read-only battery, load and forecast data from supported household systems, allow people to define their own appliances and compare saved scenarios across different outage windows. Any future connection to household equipment would retain explicit review and human-controlled policy changes. I designed the household outage scenario and human-agent approval model, implemented the deterministic energy simulator, React interface and eight WebMCP tools, added stale-proposal protection, human-only commit and undo controls, and completed the automated testing, accessibility checks, documentation, GitHub Pages deployment and demo production. title: Floortris
pitch: WebMCP agents turn dimensioned sketches into rule-checked 2D and 3D rooms, while people compare proposals and control every final change.
about_excerpt: WebMCP agents turn dimensioned sketches into rule-checked 2D and 3D rooms, while people compare proposals and control every final change. Like 1 Comment Story Updates 1 Inspiration I started Floortris late in the challenge with a practical question: why can an AI describe a room layout but struggle to work directly with the room planner already open in front of it? Before implementing WebMCP, I was surprised by how difficult it was for an AI agent to use the website reliably. It had to interpret controls visually, infer the state of the room and hope that each interaction had worked. Even when the result looked reasonable, the agent could miss important details such as door swings, walking routes, furniture orientation or the measurements of items someone already owned. I wanted to explore a better approach: a room planner designed from the beginning for a person and an agent to use together. The agent should understand the same measured room shown on screen, work under the same rules and produce a visible proposal—while the person retains control of every final change. What it does Floortris is a local-first room planner for people and agents. A person can enter a measured room, add doors and windows, record furniture they already own, lock its dimensions or position and edit the layout directly. An agent can use 16 native WebMCP tools to inspect the same document, construct a separate Proposal, arrange furniture, change finishes and check the resulting layout. The agent works in Proposal , while the accepted room remains in Yours . It does not switch the person’s view or apply its own work. Apply, room-input confirmation, discard, unlock and view switching remain human-only actions. Floortris checks more than whether two rectangles overlap. Its shared rule engine evaluates: door swings and open door leaves; hard and preferred walking clearances; routes between entrances and activity zones; TV positioning and seating relationships; coffee-table gaps; usable bed sides; storage and window access; linked desks and chair pull zones; radiators and wall-mounted objects; measured curtains, blinds and lighting fixtures. An agent can recreate rectilinear rooms with alcoves, recesses, nooks and L-shaped outlines from dimensioned information. The same measured outline is then used by the 2D board, 3D scene, collision rules, ceiling checks, walking routes and placement search. Agents can also create measured custom furniture inside a Proposal, including genuine connected L- and U-shaped sectionals. These use a closed, validated geometry format instead of arbitrary code or remote 3D assets. They remain subject to the same placement rules and human approval boundary as catalogue furniture. Why WebMCP The floor plan itself is the product. A hidden API response or a paragraph describing where furniture should go is not enough—the measurements, furniture, warnings and proposed changes need to remain visible and reviewable. Floortris registers 16 native tools through document.modelContext . These include generateRoom , getRoomState , createProposal , createCustomFurniture , placeFurniture , updateFurniture , findPlacements , setAppearance and checkLayout . These tools give the agent structured access to the same room state and rule engine used by the visible interface. Instead of guessing what a button does or interpreting the page from pixels, the agent can request exact measurements, submit a revision-bound change and receive structured feedback explaining whether the layout is healthy. WebMCP made the agent much more reliable, but I deliberately avoided giving it complete authority. It can perform substantial spatial work, but its result remains a Proposal until a person reviews and applies it. How I built it Floortris is built with TypeScript, React, Next.js on the vinext runtime, Three.js, Vite and Cloudflare Workers. At its centre is a shared rule engine operating on a measured 20 cm grid. Human controls and WebMCP commands pass through the same document store and validation logic. This prevents the visible room and the agent’s representation from developing different versions of spatial truth. Each WebMCP tool has a strict JSON Schema, explicit metadata, revision checks and abort-aware execution. Placement searches are bounded, and candidates are ranked by functional quality rather than simply returning the first coordinate without a collision. I also added seven difficult benchmark rooms, three checked planning strategies, static accommodation-provider packs, advisory accessibility planning packs, a local evaluation dashboard, furniture-schedule exports, printable move-in sheets and server-free share links carried in the URL fragment. Room, evaluation and share data is not sent to an application data backend. Share data only leaves the device when the person explicitly shares the generated URL. A Cloudflare Worker serves the client application; there is no application database or remote LLM service. Challenges I faced The hardest technical challenge was maintaining one spatial truth across every part of the application. A custom cut-out in an L-shaped room could not simply be hidden in the 2D view. It also had to be absent from collision cells, walking routes, ceiling placement, search candidates and the 3D shell. Custom sectional furniture created a similar problem: an L- or U-shaped sofa needed to behave as one connected object without treating its empty internal area as occupied floor space. Furniture rules were more relational than I initially expected. Whether a coffee table works depends on the sofa’s true facing edge and measured gap. Whether a desk works depends on its chair and pull zone. Whether shelving is correctly placed depends on which edge is actually its back—not merely whether some part of its bounding box touches a wall. I also encountered problems with door clearances, TVs appearing behind doors, shelving facing the wrong direction, disappearing 2D labels and stuttering 3D shadows. Fixing these required the rule engine and renderers to use explicit geometry rather than visual assumptions. Another challenge was protecting human work while an agent was operating. Proposal branches, revision-bound commands, immutable snapshots and exact-revision review checks prevent a delayed agent action from silently overwriting a newer human edit. What I learned I was most surprised by how difficult it was for an AI agent to use the website before I implemented the WebMCP tools. A page that feels obvious to a person can still be ambiguous to an agent when its capabilities and state are only communicated visually. That changed how I think about building websites. In future projects, I want to consider agent-native compatibility from the beginning rather than treating it as something added afterwards. As the world becomes increasingly reliant on AI, websites should expose clear, structured and constrained capabilities that allow agents to help without taking control away from people. I also learned that useful agentic interfaces need visible state, explicit authority and reversible proposals—not simply more tools. Geometry needs to be centralised as well. Once the 2D plan, 3D scene, placement search and validation engine all used the same measurements, complex room shapes and custom furniture became much easier to support correctly. I am proudest of how quickly I produced a working prototype despite starting late, while documenting the development publicly on TikTok at the same time. Building in public forced me to explain each problem clearly and showed how quickly an initial prototype could develop into a much more capable agent-native application. Floortris ultimately became more than a furniture visualiser. It became an experiment in how people and agents can share one visible, rule-checked document while the person retains ownership of the final decision. title: Thought Amplifier — Evidence Workspace for WebMCP
pitch: Turn a messy brain dump into a source-grounded, inspectable, human-approved decision with your existing browser AI.
about_excerpt: Turn a messy brain dump into a source-grounded, inspectable, human-approved decision with your existing browser AI. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration AI can clarify difficult decisions, but a chat answer is easy to detach from its source, blur facts with assumptions, or accept without a reviewable trail. We wanted a shared workspace where an agent can reason, the application enforces structure and freshness, and the human keeps the final word. What it does Thought Amplifier is a subject-independent WebMCP decision workspace for bounded plain-text brain dumps. A compatible browser agent invokes real page-defined tools to read the current source, revision, and fingerprint, then stages a structured amplification: objective, success criteria, facts grounded in exact source excerpts, assumptions, unknowns, options and trade-offs, a recommendation, reversal condition, and next actions. The result appears in the same visible page. The app validates the payload, binds it to the source revision, records the tool transition, rejects stale writes after the source changes, and exposes no agent approval tool. Only the human-facing UI can approve the exact displayed proposal. Our demo makes the product test itself: it analyzes the real decision between three challenge ideas—an MCP-readiness auditor, a residential concept coordinator, and Thought Amplifier. The workflow itself is general and supports clarify, decide, plan, diagnose, create, and learn modes. How we built it We built a React and TypeScript client with imperative WebMCP registration through document.modelContext.registerTool. Three typed tools share live application state: read_thought_source, stage_amplification, and read_thought_workspace. Closed schemas and runtime validation reject unexpected, malformed, duplicate, or out-of-bounds data. Every staged proposal must match the current source revision and fingerprint; changing the source invalidates the old result. Human approval remains outside the WebMCP tool surface. The public repository includes architecture and tool-contract documentation, a reproducible real-host verification receipt, a demo runbook, screenshots, tests, and an MIT license. Challenges The hardest part was making the integration genuinely useful without turning WebMCP into an unrestricted write channel. We also had to make the manual and agent paths converge on the same state, keep evidence and inference distinct, and ensure a plausible result based on an older source could never silently replace newer work. Accomplishments A compatible browser host discovered and invoked all three real page tools in a local end-to-end run. It read the exact live source, visibly staged a complete proposal, read it back, and received STALE_SOURCE when an old payload was replayed after an edit. The registered tool surface contains no approval, publication, submission, or arbitrary-action endpoint. What we learned Useful agentic browsing is not just more autonomy. It is precise semantic operations inside software that owns state, validates transitions, exposes provenance, and preserves a human authority boundary. Structured reasoning becomes more credible when the source, transformation, freshness check, and approval are visible together. What's next Next: source-span citations, multiple text sources, private document and image ingestion with visible extraction provenance, persistent branches and locks, exports, and permissioned collaboration. This submission deliberately remains a focused prototype: plain text only, session-local state, no embedded model, no autonomous approval, and no claim of production or universal browser certification.
