title: WebHUD
pitch: Smart glasses without the vendor OS — a WebMCP surface for your agent, your inputs, and any display.
about_excerpt: Smart glasses without the vendor OS — a WebMCP surface for your agent, your inputs, and any display. Like Comment Story Updates How WebHUD connects your agent, WebMCP, and any heads-up display. The compare intent renders as a full table on desktop The compare intent renders as a swipe-able cards on glasses Tool registration is dynamic. For example, `map_show_route` exists only while a compatible map is active. Not every pair of glasses has a camera, so WebHUD pairs a navigation input to whatever the hardware offers. Inspiration Smart glasses usually come bundled with a vendor-specific operating system, assistant, and app ecosystem. That creates a strange mismatch: the assistant on the glasses often knows less about the user than the agent they already use every day. WebHUD flips that model. The glasses become a display, the web page becomes the adaptive interface, and the user keeps their preferred agent, memory, apps, and language. What it does WebHUD is an interactive WebMCP-enabled heads-up display. A WebMCP-capable agent supplies structured data and the user's purpose; WebHUD chooses the interface that fits the current context. The same venue comparison becomes: a wide comparison table on desktop; focused, swipeable cards in a simulated glasses lens. That reflow happens locally without another agent call. People and agents co-drive the same surface: voice expresses intent; keyboard, touch, a Bluetooth ring, or a locally processed palm gesture changes focus; surface_get_view_state tells the agent what the user is currently looking at, enabling references such as “this one.” WebHUD can present calendars, email decks, documents, images, people, choices, comparisons, triage queues, maps, and walking routes. Why WebMCP WebMCP is central to the product rather than an added integration. The page registers structured tools through document.modelContext.registerTool , with a legacy navigator.modelContext fallback. The main smart-responsive contract is surface_present . The agent declares one of six purposes— glance , browse , inspect , compare , choose , or triage —and provides semantic items. WebHUD maps that request to an appropriate renderer for desktop, phone, or glasses. Tool registration is dynamic. For example, map_show_route exists only while a compatible map is active. The page emits tool changes as capabilities appear and disappear, reducing irrelevant or unusable actions. Every presentation call returns a receipt describing what was rendered, giving the agent reliable feedback instead of forcing it to guess what appeared. Better human-agent collaboration Without WebHUD, the user must repeatedly describe which item they mean or ask the agent to navigate one step at a time. With WebHUD, the human can swipe to an email or venue and then speak naturally. Gesture supplies context; voice supplies intent. This makes small displays practical without forcing every interaction through speech. Privacy and safety Camera frames stay inside the browser tab and are processed locally. View-state responses expose identifiers and titles rather than email bodies or image pixels. Map location is supplied explicitly by the user; the page does not read device GPS. Sensitive actions remain agent-controlled and human-confirmed. WebHUD has no application backend. How it was built WebHUD is a static TypeScript and Vite application deployed using Cloudflare Workers static assets. Key components include: WebMCP registration and dynamic re-registration; centralized surface and focus state; desktop, phone, and glasses renderers; keyboard, ring/controller, touch, and palm-input adapters; Leaflet maps with walking routes and fallback estimates; vendored MediaPipe assets for local hand tracking; automated tests and GitHub Actions verification. Testing Open the live URL in ChatGPT's in-app browser, or in a compatible Chrome build with WebMCP testing enabled. Confirm the page displays WebMCP ✓ . Ask the agent to compare three venues with shared price, capacity, distance, and AV facts. Confirm the desktop table appears. Press G and confirm the same state reflows into glasses cards without another presentation call. Navigate with Left or Right, then ask about “this one.” Ask for nearby cafés and a route to number one to see the map-only route tool register dynamically. The public repository includes source code, tests, setup instructions, screenshots, the WebHUD specification, an MIT license, and third-party notices. Built with TypeScript, Vite, WebMCP, Cloudflare Workers, Leaflet, MediaPipe, Vitest, and GitHub Actions. title: Duet
pitch: A browser design editor that a person and an AI agent operate on the same canvas, at the same time.
about_excerpt: A browser design editor that a person and an AI agent operate on the same canvas, at the same time. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Inspiration Making five platform versions of the same poster by hand is forty minutes of nobody's favourite work. Retyping every headline in a second language. Aligning twenty objects to a grid. Recolouring a layout to a new brand palette. This is the work designers actually complain about, and it is mechanical enough that a machine could do it correctly. So why hadn't one? Because a design document is a JavaScript object graph plus IndexedDB. There is no REST endpoint, no webhook, no export format an agent could round trip through. A server side MCP has nothing to connect to. An agent's only options were guessing at mouse coordinates, scraping the accessibility tree, or shipping a browser extension. All three are brittle, and none of them understand what a layer is. WebMCP changes the shape of the problem. It puts the tool registry inside the page, so a tool runs in the tab, against live in memory state, using the application's own code. For a design editor that turns out to matter in one very specific way: The agent can see what you selected. Not inferred from the DOM. The actual objects under your cursor, right now. An agent that merely generates designs could hand you a picture. It could never know that you just clicked two things and said "make these bigger." That is the whole idea, and it is not reproducible any other way. What it does Duet is a fork of an open-source browser design editor Avnac that adds WebMCP as a layer so a person and an AI agent can operate on the same canvas at the same time. Ask for something, get a real design. Say "design a flyer for my [cool] event" and the agent starts designing in real time using the WebMCP Point at something without naming it. Select two objects with your mouse, then say "make these bigger and line them up." The agent asks the page what you have highlighted and gets exactly that. This is the moment the idea justifies itself. Let it check its own work. Ask it to describe the layout and it reports what a person would notice: things that overlap, things outside the frame, edges that are almost but not quite aligned, and text that fails contrast against whatever sits behind it. Ask for an Instagram story version, the canvas grows, and the agent notices that the background no longer covers it and says so precisely. Approve or reject before anything changes. For anything involving taste, the agent proposes instead of acting. Its suggestions appear on your canvas as a ghosted preview with a dashed outline. You tick the ones you want, add a note back, and hit apply. Nothing lands until you say so, and the agent hears which changes you rejected. A tool that waits on a human decision inside the tab is the one thing a remote MCP server structurally cannot do. See exactly what happened. Every tool call is listed with its arguments, timing and result. Not a spinner. Seeing update_many { role: "headline", text: "Happy Birthday, Mum" } is how you tell a machine doing specific work from an animation pretending to. How we built it Duet is a fork of Avnac , an open source browser design editor. Avnac already had agent control of its canvas. It worked the only way that was possible before WebMCP: by embedding one specific AI vendor's SDK. Agent control required an account, an API key, a hosted service in the loop, and a hard dependency in the app's own package file. Only that vendor's agent could drive it. By the time I forked, that integration was paused and unreachable from the interface. Duet deletes that layer entirely and replaces it with an open browser standard. No account, no key, no vendor, no server. You send any agent the link and the tools are simply there. Before WebMCP, agent control of a browser design document meant choosing an AI vendor and marrying them. Now it is a property of the page. Fourteen tools , registered through document.modelContext.registerTool with an AbortController for teardown. The page feature detects and falls back to the deprecated navigator.modelContext . On Chrome 151 the two turn out to be literally the same object. Decisions that mattered: Registered once, reading live state through a ref. The editor's controller is rebuilt on every document change, so registering against it directly would register the whole surface again on every keystroke. Errors are returned, never thrown. An unknown id comes back as text naming what was wrong and listing the ids that do exist, so the agent corrects itself without another round trip. Every write returns the resulting state , never "ok". A tool that says "done" teaches the agent nothing. Readable ids at the tool boundary. The app uses UUIDs internally; the tools speak text_1 and rect_2 . Nothing inside the app was rewritten. Compact output built for a model to read. The scene comes back as a table rather than JSON, because it is read on nearly every turn. Descriptions that say when not to reach for a tool. That is where skilful use actually lives. Ghost previews needed no renderer changes at all. The editor's object component reads only its props, so a proposal renders through that same component in a sibling layer at reduced opacity, with the layer ignoring pointer events so a ghost can never take a click meant for the real object beneath it. Challenges we ran into A twenty second wait that hung forever. The proposal flow waits for a human decision. An early version used requestAnimationFrame to let React settle first. That works beautifully until the tab is backgrounded, at which point the callback simply never fires, and an agent driven page is backgrounded constantly. Caught it by actually switching tabs during a test rather than reasoning about it. The obvious proposal design is the broken one. The natural implementation is a single tool whose promise resolves when the human clicks approve. That hits the agent host's own tool call timeout long before a person finishes deliberating, and reads as a broken tool rather than a patient one. Splitting it into a call that returns immediately with an id and a second call that polls with a bounded wait keeps the human experience identical while making a timeout impossible. A layout checker that cried wolf. Every template has a background rectangle covering the whole canvas. A naive overlap check therefore reports one overlap per object on a perfectly clean design, and an agent that gets false positives once learns to ignore the tool forever. It now excludes full bleed backgrounds before any check runs, and separately reports the case where a background has stopped covering the canvas. Testing the implemantaion. I had intially planned on using Chatgpt's in-app broswer to drive the site and allow the agent to test out the tools, but unluckily for me i hit my free use limit on chatGPT so i ahd to improvise. I found and alternative: an extension that allows the user to use Gemini to test the project and connect to the WebMCP client directly. Silent failures are the whole genre. A tool can work perfectly when you invoke it by hand and never be chosen by an agent, with no error anywhere. That is not a bug you can debug; it is a writing problem. Accomplishments that we're proud of Selecting two objects by hand and having the agent know exactly what I meant. Everything else in the project supports that one moment. The proposal flow. Ghosted previews that track the live document rather than a stale snapshot, per-change approve and reject, a note that goes back to the agent, and the whole batch applying in a single commit. It is the part of the build that could not have existed a year ago. Being straight about the fork. It would have been easy to scrub every trace and present this as original. Saying "agent control already existed here, through one vendor's SDK, and I replaced it with a browser standard" is a better argument and it happens to be true. The tool descriptions I iterated multiple times on the tool descriptions before arriving at the current ones, which describe the tool adequately and allow the agent to call the right tool for the right action. What we learned Tool descriptions are the product. The difference between a tool an agent uses and one it ignores is almost never the code. A description that says what a tool does is half finished; one that says when to reach for it, and when to reach for something else instead, is the thing being graded. Give the agent a hand authored starting point. An agent placing objects by coordinate composes badly, because it cannot see the canvas. Templates removed that failure mode completely: the layout is a person's taste, and the agent only fills it in. Verify in the browser, not in the type checker. Every genuinely interesting bug in this build compiled cleanly. The background tab hang, the role that was silently dropped on save, the review card that read "move to same,620", the ghost that could not be told

title: ClawDeals
pitch: Your agent negotiates. You stay in control.
about_excerpt: Your agent negotiates. You stay in control. Like Comment Story Updates 1 Your agent negotiates. You stay in control. Every sensitive action leaves a policy decision, confirmation state and redacted receipt. The agent ranks synthetic e-bikes while showing why each candidate fits or violates the owner's policy. Your agent negotiates. You stay in control. Why ClawDeals? Think of your agent as a mechanical claw: reaching into the chaotic second-hand market to seize a great deal, while you keep a firm, unyielding grip on budgets, identity, and the final word. ClawDeals is the trust layer for agentic commerce. Buyer and seller agents can search, evaluate, and negotiate real-world deals, while humans retain explicit control over budgets, approvals, and contact details. The agent negotiates. It searches, ranks, questions sellers, and prepares offers through page-scoped WebMCP tools. The server enforces human limits. Budgets, owner approvals, reservations, and bilateral consent are re-checked server-side. A confirmation modal is never the security boundary. Every protected action stays verifiable. It produces a redacted receipt containing a request ID, an input hash, and the resulting policy verdict. Inspiration Current shopping agents excel at searching catalogs and adding items to carts. But peer-to-peer commerce is a different challenge: two independent people, asynchronous back-and-forth negotiation, strict budget caps, and personal contact info that shouldn't be leaked to an unknown bot. WebMCP gave us the missing in-browser contract: the agent receives structured, page-scoped tools, while the human keeps the final say on the exact same UI. Who this is for Peer-to-peer marketplaces (used bikes, electronics, furniture, housing) where negotiation is asynchronous, and an unconstrained agent could easily overspend or leak private identity. What it does A buyer delegates a Deal Mission: target price, hard budget, search radius, and item requirements. The agent executes WebMCP tools to search and evaluate listings against a structured policy_fit (which the human sees mirrored live as badges on the cards). The agent can open threads, ask technical questions (e.g. battery health), and stage offers. When an offer exceeds the mission budget, the platform halts the autonomous flow with APPROVAL_REQUIRED . The human owner reviews the action on /my/approvals/:id , can edit the counteroffer (e.g., adjust to €1,290), and approves it. Once accepted, the listing flips to RESERVED atomically. Contact details remain masked until both buyer and seller explicitly consent. How we built it Built on Next.js (Pages Router), TypeScript, React, PostgreSQL, and Supabase. WebMCP Integration : Tools register via document.modelContext.registerTool(tool, { signal }) and listen to toolchange . We scope tools contextually: 5 public read-only tools on the main marketplace, expanding to 11 authenticated tools inside the judge sandbox. Security Boundary : Client confirmations are editable, but all policy rules (budgets, consent, reservations) are strictly re-checked server-side. Testing & Evals : Vitest covers tool schemas and redaction. Playwright runs deterministic synthetic sandbox journeys (Paris e-bike scenario). Adversarial tests verify prompt injection resistance, over-budget halts, and zero contact leakage. What we built during the challenge ClawDeals existed before August 25, 2026, making this an Existing project . Only the WebMCP capabilities built during the hackathon window are submitted for judging: Official imperative WebMCP runtime ( registerTool , AbortSignal lifecycle). Contextual dual-mode tool registry (5 public tools / 11 authenticated tools). Deal Mission engine and visual policy_fit card badges. Mission-bound negotiation ( start_thread , send_message , make_offer ). Server-enforced hard budget stops ( APPROVAL_REQUIRED ) and editable owner approvals. Atomic listing reservation ( RESERVED ) and bilateral contact reveal. Verifiable Agent Activity drawer and redacted receipts ( get_action_receipt ). Isolated judge hub with synthetic fixtures and one-click reset ( /webmcp-challenge ). Challenges we ran into Registering tools was straightforward; preserving a bulletproof trust boundary was the real challenge. When an agent can trigger payments or commitments, an in-browser confirmation dialog is insufficient. Sensitive write operations are idempotent and re-checked server-side, and contact details require two independent, server-recorded consents. We also kept our evaluation honest: a mocked modelContext in tests proves wiring, not real browser execution. We carefully separated local unit mocks, headless Playwright sandbox runs, and native browser verification. Accomplishments that we are proud of Real in-browser WebMCP tool execution without relying on generic DOM scrapers. 11 focused contextual tools instead of a single dangerous omnipotent function. Server-enforced budget protection that safely intercepts out-of-bounds agent counteroffers. Redacted audit receipts that let agents inspect past decisions without leaking secrets. Full end-to-end mission demonstration with synthetic Paris e-bike fixtures. What we learned Practical agentic commerce requires three distinct layers: An in-browser tool contract for the agent (WebMCP). A server-side policy contract for the platform (budget and identity gates). A consent contract for the human (approvals and bilateral reveal). What's next The isolated authenticated sandbox is live at https://sandbox.clawdeals.com/webmcp-challenge . Chrome 149+ (or Chrome 151 with chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing ) exposes the native runtime and our full 11-tool registry once the private judge key (provided in Devpost judge instructions) is entered. Public read tools remain testable without any key. title: ChenChess live coaching board
pitch: Interactive live coaching sessions on chessboard with ChatGPT
about_excerpt: Interactive live coaching sessions on chessboard with ChatGPT Like Comment Story Updates ChenChess Coaching Board: Grounding a WebMCP Agent on a Live Chessboard Inspiration A player studying a game moves pieces with the mouse and asks questions by talking to a model. Those are two separate channels, and the language channel is full of pointers the model can't resolve on its own — why is this bad, what about that instead, is the line I tried still winning — all referring to board state the model never actually saw. WebMCP closes that gap: the page itself registers tools with document.modelContext , so an agent like ChatGPT or Claude can call them against the live page and the player's own session, instead of guessing from a transcript. The interesting problem wasn't wiring up tool calls. It was making sure an agent with real tools couldn't say anything about the board that wasn't true — the same grounding problem the rest of the coach has, now with a model that can also act . The coach-engine logic underneath Every WebMCP tool call ultimately reads from one deterministic pipeline, not from the model's own reasoning: Each position in a game is analyzed by Stockfish (objective best move and evaluation) and Maia-2 (what a human at a given rating would likely play) in parallel. A pure Rule Extractor compares the two and picks Critical Moments — plies where the position's win probability swung enough to matter. Evaluations are converted from centipawns to a win-probability curve first, since a swing means different things near equal and near winning: $$ \text{WinProb}(cp) = \frac{1}{1 + 10^{-cp/400}}, \qquad \left|\,\text{WinProb}(cp_{i+1}) - \text{WinProb}(cp_i)\,\right| \ge \tau $$ Each Critical Moment becomes a typed fact record (best line, refutation, verdict) before any prose exists, and a validator gate rejects any later explanation that doesn't match those facts ply-for-ply. The WebMCP layer doesn't get to skip this. Every board tool call returns a Coaching Board Snapshot — the same typed facts, plus which line is active and where the viewed ply sits on the game's own line — so the agent is handed grounded state on every call instead of being trusted to ask for it. How I built WebMCP support One authored map, not a second one. Coach tools already carried a coachToolSurface map of which tools the installed Coach App vs. the model may call. Adding the Coaching Board meant widening that map with a "web" target rather than maintaining a parallel list — the two surfaces share list_critical_moments , open_review_moment , and evaluate_player_line against the same data, distinguished by per-tool description, not by renaming. Register inside the auth gate, never at module load. Board routes pass through an asynchronous Beta Access check before a player is known. Tools register on an effect keyed by the authorized player ID and tear down through the AbortSignal registerTool accepts, so there's no window where an agent can discover and call board tools before identity resolves or after sign-out. Push the grounding policy into every result, not just instructions. Descriptions carry the rules once, at registration; each result also carries a constraint block for the facts it just returned, because nothing in WebMCP obliges an agent to re-read state before answering — an agent that skips the read produces fluent, confident, wrong coaching a player can't detect. Keep durable writes off the surface. The agent can stage a game import; only the player's own button press commits it. Challenges I faced Proving it actually grounds, not just that it compiles. A scripted deixis suite driving the board through a real WebMCP host measured 7/8 on referring expressions ( "that line," "the other one" ) but over-called tools on a non-deictic trap prompt roughly one run in five — enough signal to trust the mechanism, not enough to gate a release on yet. No production host to test against on demand. Storybook turned out to be a legitimate WebMCP host for driving the real board tools headlessly through Playwright with --enable-features=WebMCP , since neither ChatGPT's desktop app nor a locked devtools profile could be automated directly. A stale tab looks identical to a broken one. A board left open for hours answered every tool call with a bare "unavailable," which looked like a server-side bug; it was a client holding a dead connection. Fixing it meant turning any client-side throw into a typed unavailable result (rather than an opaque failure) so the agent — and future debugging — could tell "stale" from "actually broken." A withdrawn move can wedge every future write. A Slot Marker left behind by a since-withdrawn line kept blocking every Review Moment the board tried to write afterward; the fix surfaces the board's refusals in a banner instead of failing silently on the next unrelated call. The throughline: giving a model real hands on the board is only safe once every fact it can act on, and every fact it hands back, traces to the same deterministic pipeline the rest of the coach already trusts. title: GroundTruth
pitch: Post-disaster damage assessment where the agent's tools are scoped to what's on your screen. Ask "what's the flood exposure here?" and here means your viewport, your selected building, right now.
about_excerpt: Post-disaster damage assessment where the agent's tools are scoped to what's on your screen. Ask "what's the flood exposure here?" and here means your viewport, your selected building, right now. Like Comment Story Updates The problem After a flood or an earthquake, the first 72 hours are triage. Someone sits in front of aerial imagery deciding which blocks get the trucks. The imagery tells you what a roof looks like. It does not tell you how many people live under it, whether the road in is passable, or whether the building you just clicked is a clinic. That context exists — building footprints, population rasters, road networks, critical infrastructure — but it lives in files nobody opens during a crisis. What it does GroundTruth is a damage assessment console. You pan aerial imagery and select buildings. An agent sitting inside the page answers questions about what you are looking at right now: population exposure in this viewport, road access to this polygon, which critical facilities fall inside the affected area. You ask "what's the flood exposure here?" and here is unambiguous — it is the current viewport, the current selection, the imagery date currently loaded. Why WebMCP and not a server MCP This is the whole argument. A remote MCP server can query the same datasets, but it has no idea what "here" means. It cannot see your viewport, your selection, or your map state. It would need you to describe your screen in words before it could help. WebMCP puts the tools in the page, so they close over live application state. The agent does not receive a bounding box you typed — it reads the one you are looking at. The tools are the app's own functions, which means the agent and the human operate the same console and see the same thing. How we built it A Next.js map console over MapLibre, with a WebMCP tool surface exposed from the client. Each tool is scoped to live UI state rather than taking free-floating parameters. A data pipeline pre-processes building footprints, population and infrastructure layers into tiles the browser can query without a round trip. What we learned Designing tools that close over UI state is a different discipline from designing REST endpoints. The temptation is to expose one powerful tool with many parameters. That performs worse than several narrow tools that each read the current state, because the model stops having to reconstruct context it cannot see. What's honest about it The datasets are pre-staged for the demo region rather than fetched live, and the damage signal comes from imagery the operator reads, not from an automated classifier. Both are deliberate: the point of the entry is the agent-to-page interface, not a damage model. Live data ingestion is the obvious next step. title: Event Growth OS
pitch: A WebMCP-powered agent console for human-approved event growth.
about_excerpt:
A WebMCP-powered agent console for human-approved event growth.

 Event Growth OS 

 Event Growth OS helps event teams find the people who would genuinely benefit from an event—without turning outreach into spam. 

 Inspiration 

 Event promotion often rewards volume over relevance: organizers broadcast broadly, while potential attendees get generic messages that do not reflect what they actually need. We wanted to explore a better relationship between people and agents: let an agent do the patient research and first-draft work, while people retain the judgment and responsibility to decide whether to reach out. 

 That question became Event Growth OS: an agent console for finding genuine audience fit, explaining the evidence, and keeping a human approval checkpoint before any response could be used. 

 What it does 

 The centerpiece is an Agent Console that starts with a plain-language goal such as: 

 
 Find people who would genuinely benefit from my event. 
 

 It then makes a transparent, human-supervised tool sequence: 

 
 get_campaign loads the event context. 
 find_relevant_conversations surfaces discussion signals. 
 analyze_conversation explains intent, context, and audience fit. 
 draft_response prepares a useful, transparent reply. 
 request_human_approval stops for a person before outreach. 
 record_outcome closes the learning loop. 
 

 The interface exposes the reasoning rather than hiding it: opportunity scores, the signal behind each recommendation, the proposed draft, AI-assistance disclosure, and an explicit approval gate. Low-relevance conversations are intentionally rejected. 

 How we built it 

 We built Event Growth OS with Next.js , React , and TypeScript as a focused, responsive operator console. 

 For WebMCP, the app defines six purposeful tools and registers them through navigator.modelContext.registerTool when a compatible browser host exposes the API. Each tool has a name, a clear description, an input schema, and an execution result designed to be discoverable by an agent. The same definitions power the visible console timeline, so a person can understand exactly which capability is being requested at every stage. 

 The demo data is deliberately realistic but clearly simulated. It lets the product demonstrate the decision flow without pretending that it is scraping conversations or automatically posting to external networks. 

 Challenges we faced 

 The main challenge was resisting the temptation to make the experience look autonomous at the expense of trust. A fast draft is useful; an unreviewed message is not always appropriate. We designed the system around a hard human checkpoint and clear disclosure instead of an auto-posting loop. 

 A second challenge was making WebMCP legible to both audiences. Agents need tools with concrete, discoverable contracts; people need to see why each call matters. The tool timeline and opportunity inspector were designed to bridge that gap. 

 Finally, native WebMCP support depends on the browser host. We made the integration progressively enhanced: compatible hosts can register the tools natively, while the product still presents an interactive, inspectable demo flow where that API is unavailable. 

 What we learned 

 We learned that a strong WebMCP experience is not just a list of functions. The tools need to map to meaningful moments in a real workflow, communicate their purpose clearly, and preserve a person’s ability to intervene. 

 We also learned that the most compelling agent experiences pair automation with context. In Event Growth OS, the agent does not merely return a score—it shows the source signal, explains the fit, and asks for approval. That makes the system feel less like a black box and more like a thoughtful collaborator. 

 Built with 

 Next.js, React, TypeScript, and WebMCP APIs. 

 Running locally 

 Install dependencies, then run: 
 pnpm install
pnpm dev
 
 Open http://localhost:3000 . Enter an agent request, run the toolchain, select a conversation, and approve a high-confidence draft to see an outcome recorded. 

 AI and Codex usage 

 AI and Codex were used to help implement and refine the product experience. All product claims, simulated conversation signals, and outreach drafts are explicitly presented as demonstration data; the app does not automatically post to external social networks.

title: Documesh
pitch: One endpoint for agents to all documentation available: match any multi-stack error signature to the closest official documentation — cited, versioned, attributed. Every time.
about_excerpt: One endpoint for agents to all documentation available: match any multi-stack error signature to the closest official documentation — cited, versioned, attributed. Every time. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Documesh WebMCP App Inspiration When something breaks at 2 AM, the fix is buried somewhere in dozens of doc sites, each with its own search, its own format, and its own idea of what "current version" means. And when an AI agent hunts for that fix, it's even worse: crawling page after page, scraping prose built for humans, burning thousands of tokens to find one config key. Then WebMCP shipped in Chrome, and I surveyed the ecosystem it created: 322 sites exposing 1,817 agent tools. The pattern was impossible to miss, more than thirty ship near-identical shallow search_docs wrappers, every one locked to a single vendor. Not one could answer a cross-vendor question, cite a doc version, or let an agent act on an answer safely. The docs layer of the agentic web was stuck in 2019: prose for humans, scraped or ignored by agents. The insight that became Documesh had two halves. Agents are the new visitors. When they arrive at a debugging problem, they need one declared, machine-actionable interface to all the official documentation, not thirty-eight walled gardens. And attention is the real cost, every scraped page dumped into context is tokens spent on noise, when one structured call should return exactly the doc section that matters, with the version and license attached. So I built the mesh I wanted my agent to have: one WebMCP endpoint for the whole stack. What it does Documesh gives agents a single endpoint for debugging multi-stack applications: match any multi-stack error signature to the closest official documentation, cited, versioned, attributed. Every time. Federated search of 47 sources synced for now (from a 555-source verified registry), 36,000+ doc sections. Every result carries source, version, license, attribution, canonical URL, and last-updated. Error → docs bridge paste a stack trace; explain_error extracts error signatures and returns the closest official doc sections, with an honest disclaimer: closest matches, not a diagnosis. Chainable answers: every result carries a machine-actionable object: exact config keys, language-tagged code snippets, runnable CLI commands, version applicability. The agent orchestrates; Documesh makes answers reliable enough to chain. An act surface with one rule: verify configs against documented keys, compare config conventions across vendors, check provider status ("is it down, or is it me?" anw, it caught a real Cloudflare outage during testing), report outdated docs. Every write is an append-only proposal, agents never mutate the mesh directly. All exposed as 9 tools across three protocols: WebMCP in the browser, MCP over Streamable HTTP, and plain REST. How we built it License-aware from the first byte: a Python indexer crawls docs through five ingestion patterns only via vendor-consented interfaces (llms.txt) or permissive licenses (CC-BY-4.0, MIT, Apache-2.0). Terraform (BUSL) and copyrighted docs are documented exclusions, license awareness as a feature. Always Search lives in the indexed, lived on Cloudflare. The extraction path has no LLM. deterministic extraction means excerpts are data, not instructions, and a hostile docs page can't prompt-inject through results. Provenance is enforced by schema audit (100% coverage), and search quality is CI-gated at ≥80% on real-world errors. Challenges we ran into The legal maze, most vendor docs are copyrighted with no agent interface; the rule that resolved it: vendor-consented interfaces or permissive licenses, excerpts + canonical links, never mirrors. Search architecture hit a wall 47 static shards loaded into Worker isolate memory (~65 MB) per query; D1 FTS5 dropped per-request memory to ~0. Honest machine-actionability the obvious shortcut was LLM extraction; deterministic is harder but never hallucinates a config key. Testing agents inside someone else's browser. WebMCP verification ultimately required a human, which is why the three-layer eval suite exists. Accomplishments that we're proud of 47 sources / 36k+ sections / 555 registry 100% response provenance agent-readiness score 89/A eval gate 5/5, the act surface caught a real Cloudflare outage during testing three protocols, one mesh an npm SDK so others can chain on it. All solo, all on $0 infra. What we learned Declared contracts beat scraping, the agent doesn't break in, it's invited. Provenance is a feature, not overhead -> "cited, versioned, attributed" became a schema rule instead of a slogan. The agent is the orchestrator, tools should be structured enough to chain, not call each other. Honest abstention survived every skeptical reading. And every constraint became a documented next step instead of a dead end. What's next for Documesh 547 verified sources queued for deep ingestion (47 live today) → /digest version-aware change feed → Vectorize hybrid search → webmcp-evals integration → MCP Apps UI → a contribution loop that makes the mesh self-correcting: documentation agents don't just read, but maintain. title: Haggle
pitch: The first bike store where your AI haggles the price with our AI — and the deal becomes a real discount code at a real Shopify checkout.
about_excerpt: The first bike store where your AI haggles the price with our AI — and the deal becomes a real discount code at a real Shopify checkout. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Price negotiation died when commerce moved online — it needed a human on both ends. WebMCP removes exactly that constraint: the storefront exposes a negotiation protocol as tools, the browser's agent represents the buyer, and the human keeps the final say. We wanted to build the first store where "can you do better on the price?" is something your agent just… does — and the timing is right: when agents do the shopping, merchants get squeezed into pure price comparison, and a sanctioned negotiation channel with a hard ceiling is their controlled answer. What it does Your agent → negotiation → real deal → real Shopify discount code → checkout. That is the whole loop, and it runs live today on Bikepoint, a Shopify store with a real e-bike catalog. Claude speaks. The engine decides every price. The floor cannot be negotiated away — the seller never knows anything the engine didn't decide, so there is nothing to jailbreak. Try it. One script line in the theme registers five WebMCP tools ( list_negotiable_products , start_negotiation , make_offer , get_negotiation_state , accept_deal ) on every page of the store; on a product page they default to that product. The agent trades offers in NOK with the server-side AI seller over up to six rounds. Accept, and the server mints a single-use discount code scoped to that product, valid 48 hours — worthless to coupon sites, redeemed in the normal checkout. Shopify's own storefront WebMCP tools ( update_cart , proceed_to_checkout , …) are live on the same pages — Shopify's webmcp_adapter feature-detects the very same document.modelContext surface, verified on the live store. So the full journey is agentic with zero coordination: negotiate with our tools, cart and check out with Shopify's. A small widget shows the human the negotiation in real time; to everyone else the store looks like a completely normal bike shop. An actual negotiation from the live store, verbatim: Buyer's agent: offers 12 000 kr for the Scultura Endurance 300 (listed 18 999 kr) Seller: «Nesten! Denne går sjelden under 18350 kr — men da er den din.» Buyer's agent: counters at 17 500 kr Seller: «Da har vi en avtale! 17500 kr for Scultura Endurance 300 — godt forhandlet. Bruk rabattkoden i kassen.» → a real HAGGLE-… code, applied at checkout at the negotiated price. Why would a merchant ever allow haggling? Because negotiation is controlled price discrimination — the oldest trick in retail, finally automatable: Capture price-sensitive buyers without a storewide sale. The list price keeps its integrity; only buyers who negotiate get below it, and never below the merchant's ceiling ( MAX_DISCOUNT_PCT , 10 % here). "Everyone just gets 10 %"? No. Lazy bids close well above the floor, and even a perfectly played negotiation bottoms out at the seller's final offer — a step above a floor that is never crossed. The deal can't leak. Single-use, product-scoped, 48-hour expiry ( discountCodeBasicCreate ). Only one buyer can ever redeem it. Who it's for: high-ticket Shopify categories with real margins and a haggling culture — bikes, furniture, jewelry, appliances, refurbished electronics. Installation is one script line on any Online Store 2.0 theme, invisible to non-agent visitors. Prior art is one-way or human-gated: eBay's Best Offer waits on a human, coupon plugins are static. Haggle is an instant, two-way protocol between two AIs on the merchant's own store. How we built it Server: a zero-dependency Node 20 service on Cloud Run. The price floor exists only inside a deterministic engine — never in a prompt, never on the client — and the tests hammer it: never breached, never leaked. Seller's voice, never in charge: Claude phrases the replies (a charming Norwegian bike dealer) when a key is set; a deterministic Norwegian template voice otherwise. Either way the voice only phrases — any reply that doesn't quote the engine's price is discarded. Storefront: one <script> line in the theme registers the tools on document.modelContext (with the navigator.modelContext fallback) and talks to the server. Tested like an agent: a Playwright suite shims the WebMCP runtime, captures the registered tools and plays the buyer through full negotiations — in CI on every push to main and on every PR. The live store loads this same storefront source file, pinned by commit on a CDN. Challenges we ran into Letting an LLM speak for the seller without ever letting it touch a number. WebMCP is brand new — built against the spec, Chrome's enable-webmcp-testing flag and ChatGPT's in-app browser, with a navigator.modelContext fallback for older builds. Real-store plumbing: custom-app tokens, scopes, and a theme with a broken product template to diagnose before the demo could run on genuine product pages. Accomplishments that we're proud of The loop at the top is not a mock-up — it runs on a real store, and anyone can verify it. The whole negotiation surface is reproducible without accounts: MOCK_PRODUCTS=1 fixture mode, a standalone demo.html , a smoke script and an e2e suite judges can run. What we learned Tools beat chat for commerce: a protocol (offers, rounds, state, acceptance) gives agents something they can be genuinely good at, while the human keeps the decisions that matter. And WebMCP's page-level registration composes beautifully — our negotiation tools sat next to Shopify's native cart tools with zero coordination. What's next for Haggle Dynamic tool lifecycle (registering make_offer / accept_deal only while a negotiation is open, via AbortSignal unregistration), per-product and inventory-aware floors via metafields, bundle haggling ("throw in a helmet"), a merchant dashboard with negotiation analytics — and turning it on for a store that isn't behind a dev-store password. The widget bottom-right shows the negotiation live. Accept a deal → apply the single-use code at checkout. Try to push the seller below its floor — it won't go. title: BOSAI — Governed WebMCP
pitch: Discoverable is not authorized — Human GO, single-use permits, verified readback, and replay denial for WebMCP agents.
about_excerpt: Discoverable is not authorized — Human GO, single-use permits, verified readback, and replay denial for WebMCP agents. Like Comment Story Updates Discoverable is not authorized WebMCP gives agents a structured way to discover and call tools exposed by a website. BOSAI explores the next problem: tool discovery should not automatically grant execution authority. BOSAI — Governed WebMCP is a public WebMCP demo that lets an agent inspect a synthetic duplicate-charge case, propose a refund, request authorization, execute only after an explicit Human GO, independently verify the result, retrieve an evidence receipt, and deny replay of the same single-use permit. The core idea is simple: Agents can discover and propose. Humans retain authority. BOSAI verifies what actually happened. Why this is a strong fit for WebMCP Without structured tools, agents often have to infer actions from UI state. WebMCP makes the capability surface explicit. BOSAI uses that explicit surface to add a second layer: an authority boundary around consequential actions. The live app registers eight native WebMCP tools: inspect_case inspect_transaction propose_refund request_authorization authorization_status execute_refund verify_refund get_evidence_receipt The agent has no Human GO tool. It can reach HUMAN_GO_REQUIRED, but it cannot grant itself approval. The demo flow The challenge uses a fully synthetic EUR 49 duplicate-charge refund scenario. The agent inspects the case and transaction. It creates a bounded proposal. BOSAI stops at HUMAN_GO_REQUIRED. Before approval, the mutation count is 0. A human explicitly approves that exact proposal. BOSAI issues a single-use permit. The synthetic refund commits exactly once. Independent readback returns VERIFIED and an evidence receipt. The same execution is attempted again. The replay is denied, and the replay mutation count remains 0. No real payment is made and no customer data is used. Better human + agent interaction The user experience is not "AI asks for permission" as a loose convention. The approval state is explicit, inspectable, and bound to one exact proposal. Agent: inspect, reason, propose, request authorization, execute within the granted permit, verify. Human: retain the authority to approve or deny the exact consequential action. BOSAI: enforce the execution boundary, record the result, and deny permit replay. This makes WebMCP more useful for workflows where agents should be capable without becoming self-authorizing. Implementation The challenge surface is a standalone browser app implemented with HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. It registers tools through WebMCP and maintains deterministic synthetic challenge state for proposals, authorization, execution, verification, evidence receipts, and replay denial. The public challenge surface is served as static assets on OVHcloud through a scoped Caddy route. The live browser proof was run in Google Chrome 152 with WebMCP testing enabled. What was added during the challenge BOSAI existed before the WebMCP Challenge. During the challenge submission period, it was meaningfully extended with a dedicated WebMCP implementation and public challenge surface, including the eight WebMCP tools above, a synthetic duplicate-charge workflow, explicit HUMAN_GO_REQUIRED behavior, zero-mutation pre-approval enforcement, exact Human GO binding, a single-use execution permit, independent verified readback, an evidence receipt, replay denial with zero replay mutations, and a public live browser proof surface. The WebMCP challenge implementation is isolated from proprietary BOSAI internals and is being published as a standalone public-safe repository for judging. Live proof The validated live flow demonstrated 8 registered WebMCP tools, HUMAN_GO_REQUIRED before authorization, 0 pre-GO mutations, 1 authorized synthetic mutation after Human GO, VERIFIED independent readback, an evidence receipt, REPLAY_DENIED on the duplicate execution attempt, 0 replay mutations, and no blocking browser/runtime errors. Live app: https://bosai.syncguard.fr/webmcp-challenge/index.html Operating principle Intelligence is not authority. WebMCP makes agent capabilities discoverable. BOSAI demonstrates how those capabilities can remain human-governed, bounded, verifiable, and auditable. Build, ship and think in one living agentic workspace

 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 



 
 Inspiration 

 Most modern productivity platforms treat AI as a disconnected sidebar chatbot—a separate window where you copy, paste, and prompt, while the model has zero awareness of what you are actually working on. 

 We built Kylrix on a different premise: human and artificial intelligence should share the exact same living workspace. When the WebMCP standard emerged, it provided the missing link. Rather than forcing browser agents to waste tokens and compute guessing button coordinates via screenshots or brittle DOM-scraping, WebMCP turns Kylrix into a machine-executable operating layer natively inside the active browser session. 

 

 What It Does 

 Kylrix is an open-source, local-first workspace for notes, goals, ideas, chat, vaults, and agentic workflows. 

 By integrating native WebMCP ( navigator.modelContext ), Kylrix exposes structured, typed client-side tools directly to visiting in-browser AI agents (such as Google Chrome's native agents and the ChatGPT desktop browser). 

 
 Zero-Setup Agent Collaboration: No external API keys or server proxies required. The visiting agent inherits the user's active session, cookies, and local client state. 
 Granular Tool Ecosystem: Agents can query, create, and refine Ideas , track and advance Goals , trigger custom Flows (workflow extensions), and structure rich Markdown/LaTeX documents. 
 Instant State Reactivity: Tool execution directly mutates the active Next.js client state, giving the human and agent an instantaneous, zero-latency shared canvas. 
 Privacy & Vault Boundaries: Agents operate within verified client boundaries, keeping client-encrypted vaults and sensitive user secrets fully protected. 
 

 

 How We Built It 

 
 Frontend: Next.js (App Router), React, and Tailwind CSS. 
 WebMCP Client Core: Built a declarative registration layer around the W3C navigator.modelContext / document.modelContext runtime with AbortController signal lifecycles to automatically bind and clean up in-page tools across dynamic routes. 
 Backend & Storage: Appwrite backend architecture paired with local-first client caching to guarantee offline resilience and instantaneous state updates. 
 Security & Auth: Client-side encryption standards, session-bound tool execution, and fine-grained PAT / Agent Key permissions. 
 

 

 Challenges We Ran Into 

 
 Experimental Browser Runtimes: Working with an emerging W3C standard meant dealing with browser flags ( chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing ), varying implementation quirks, and building custom fallback harnesses to verify tool registration and schema parsing reliably. 
 Real-Time Client State Mutations: Ensuring that agent tool executions triggered through the browser engine synced seamlessly with existing React component state and local storage caches without requiring full page reloads or conflicting with active human edits. 
 Strict Context Boundaries: Structuring schemas so in-browser agents have rich tool access across Ideas, Goals, and Flows while completely isolating zero-knowledge encrypted vault modules from automated read scopes. 
 

 

 Accomplishments That We're Proud Of 

 
 True Tool Parity: Agents inside Kylrix don't just "talk"—they perform the exact same operational CRUD workflows humans do, with typed schemas and strict parameter validation. 
 Multi-Surface Interoperability: Kylrix bridges both worlds of the agent ecosystem: WebMCP for ephemeral, in-browser live session tools, and traditional MCP / REST for IDE loops (Cursor, Claude) and background workers. 
 Production-Ready & Fully Open Source: Kylrix is deployed live at kylrix.space , completely self-hostable with a single bash command, and licensed under AGPL-3.0. 
 

 

 What We Learned 

 Exposing typed functional schemas directly to the browser runtime reduces token overhead by up to 90% compared to DOM-scraping or vision-based computer use. WebMCP proves that the future of web automation isn't about teaching AI to simulate a human mouse click—it's about giving web applications a clean, native protocol to speak directly to client agents. 

 

 What's Next for Kylrix 

 
 Expanding WebMCP tools to cover real-time dynamic Flow template instantiation. 
 Implementing semantic vector search across personal notes using edge-based embeddings. 
 Deepening human-in-the-loop permission prompts for irreversible state actions triggered by autonomous browser agents.

title: CaseFile
pitch: A murder. Five suspects. An AI detective at your side. Casefile is a game that uses WebMCP to let AI investigate, uncover clues, and build theories while you make the final deduction.
about_excerpt: A murder. Five suspects. An AI detective at your side. Casefile is a game that uses WebMCP to let AI investigate, uncover clues, and build theories while you make the final deduction. Like Comment Story Updates LandignPage Cases Investigation A murder mystery is supposed to make you think. But when you put an AI agent into the game, there is an obvious problem: what stops the AI from simply reading the entire case and telling you who the killer is? That question inspired Casefile . Casefile is an AI-native detective game built around the idea that an AI agent should be a co-investigator, not an answer machine . The player investigates a murder case while an AI agent investigates alongside them through WebMCP. Instead of giving the agent access to the entire game state, Casefile exposes structured investigation tools such as searching locations, discovering evidence, inspecting clues, interviewing suspects, and reconstructing timelines. The agent can perform real investigative actions and help the player connect information, but hidden evidence and the solution remain inaccessible until the investigation legitimately uncovers them. The human still has to make the final deduction. Why WebMCP? Traditional web agents have to interact with websites by interpreting the interface and figuring out what actions are available. WebMCP changes that by allowing a website to expose its capabilities as structured tools. That makes a detective game particularly interesting. Instead of asking an AI to click around Casefile and guess what buttons mean, Casefile gives the agent an actual investigative toolkit. The agent can reason about the case while using tools specifically designed for investigation. This creates a different interaction loop: Human observes → AI investigates → AI finds connections → Human evaluates the theory → Human makes the accusation. The goal was not to make the AI smarter than the player. The goal was to make the player better at investigating with the AI . How We Built It Casefile is a web application with multiple independent investigations. Each case has its own suspects, locations, evidence, timeline, deductions, and solution. WebMCP tools are registered directly by the application and operate against the currently selected case. The investigation state determines what information is available to both the human and the agent. Some of the core tools include: get_case_state — retrieve the player's current investigation state search_evidence — discover available evidence inspect_evidence — investigate discovered clues search_locations — investigate locations get_suspects — view known suspects interview_suspect — conduct interrogations build_timeline — reconstruct events submit_accusation — make the final accusation A major part of the implementation was ensuring that the agent cannot simply request the answer key . Hidden case data and solution logic are kept server-side, while WebMCP only exposes information that the investigator has legitimately unlocked. We also built the cases around deductions rather than simply collecting clues. Evidence can be incomplete, ambiguous, or misleading, meaning that finding a clue is not necessarily the same as understanding it. What We Learned The biggest lesson was that building an agent-native application is not just about adding an AI interface to an existing website. You have to rethink what information the agent is allowed to know and what actions the agent is allowed to perform . During development, we discovered that exposing too much case data—even indirectly—could completely undermine the game. We therefore treated the WebMCP tools as part of the game's rules, not just as an API. We also learned that good agent experiences require clear tool boundaries. Each tool needs to expose enough information for the agent to reason effectively without accidentally exposing information that should remain part of the mystery. Challenges The hardest challenge was balancing AI capability with human agency . If the agent knows too little, it becomes useless. If it knows too much, the game becomes a simple question-and-answer session. We also had to solve state isolation between multiple cases, prevent agents from bypassing evidence discovery, prevent premature accusations from revealing the solution, and ensure that sensitive case information was not shipped to the browser where it could be reconstructed. Testing the application with an actual WebMCP agent became an important part of development. Rather than only testing whether the UI worked for a human, we had to ask: "What happens if an agent tries to break the investigation?" That led us to build security and regression tests around evidence access, case isolation, premature accusations, timeline reconstruction, and client-side solution exposure. What Casefile Represents Casefile is our exploration of a simple idea: The future of AI applications may not be about AI doing everything for us. Sometimes the better experience is an AI that can act, investigate, and reason alongside us—while leaving the important decisions in our hands. With WebMCP, Casefile turns that idea into a game. title: CoNode - Visual Workflow Builder
pitch: The canvas a human and an AI agent build together — safely — and export to real, running code.
about_excerpt: The canvas a human and an AI agent build together — safely — and export to real, running code. Like 3 Comment Story Updates HomePage Workflow Builder In Process Run Export Option Inspiration Ask an LLM for a workflow today and you get a wall of YAML to copy, paste, and hope you didn't fat-finger. Give an agent write access to your actual canvas instead, and you get the opposite problem — an agent silently rewriting live infrastructure with no review step. WebMCP made a third option possible: expose the canvas itself as typed tools, so an agent proposes changes on the same surface a human is looking at, instead of generating text a human has to translate back into trust. I wanted to build the thing that argument implies — not a chatbot next to a canvas, but a canvas an agent and a human genuinely share. What it does CoNode is a visual workflow builder. An AI agent and a person edit the same DAG at the same time — the agent through thirteen typed tools registered on document.modelContext , the human through the mouse. Three rules make that safe: Every agent change is a proposal , rendered as dashed ghost nodes, until a human approves it. Touching a field locks it. The agent's later writes to that field are refused and it's told it was overruled, instead of silently failing and retrying forever. Secrets never leave the browser. The agent can see that a token is set — never its value — enforced at three separate points: the write path, the read path, and the export path. When the diagram's right, Export code compiles it into a real Cloudflare Workflow: every action becomes a step.do with retries, every approval gate becomes a step.waitForEvent — a genuine durable pause that survives restarts and waits up to 24 hours for a human. How I built it React + React Flow for the canvas, Zustand for state, @mcp-b/global for the WebMCP polyfill. The keystone decision: every agent mutation is an Op — a plain data value — before it ever touches the store. Because applyOps() is a pure function, the same list of ops can be applied immediately, or held as a proposal and rendered as a preview, or rejected outright. Review mode isn't a special case bolted on top; it's a branch that falls out of that one choice. Both export formats — the Cloudflare Workflow and a Kestra YAML alternative — walk one shared tree builder rather than each parsing the raw graph, so they can't drift apart on how a branch resolves. Demo domain is Shopify order triage: fetch an order, hold high-value ones for human approval, sync inventory either way. It's a genuine human-in-the-loop workflow, which is what makes the approval node and step.waitForEvent mean something rather than being decoration. Challenges I ran into Chrome's registerTool() never settles. I originally awaited every tool registration before reporting the app as "online." On the polyfill that resolves fine — so it looked correct in every test I ran. On native Chrome (152, behind the WebMCP flag) the returned promise simply never resolves or rejects. My status pill would have shown "offline, zero tools" on the one browser that actually implements the spec, which is exactly the browser a judge might use. Fixed by reporting success optimistically and only downgrading on an actual rejection. A branch-rejoin bug that looked correct until you drew a diamond. My graph walker computed where two branches of a condition reconverge by intersecting what's reachable from each branch's target — but excluded the target node itself from "reachable." A false-arm edge pointing directly at the join node was invisible to that check, so the true arm silently swallowed the shared node into its own branch. One-line fix, caught by a test built specifically to catch it. TypeScript fought me on Cloudflare's Rpc.Serializable constraint. step.do() requires its return value to satisfy Serializable<T> — which rejects both unknown (what response.json() gives you) and a recursive JSON type alias (TS2589, "excessively deep"). I only found this because I committed a real Worker project and type-checked the generated code against @cloudflare/workers-types instead of just checking it parsed. PowerShell silently corrupted my own demo commands. Windows PowerShell passes arguments to native executables through a legacy quoting layer that doesn't escape embedded double quotes for the target program's argument parser. My curl.exe -d '{"json":"here"}' commands worked perfectly in every shell I'd tested — and would have failed live on the recording, because the JSON body was getting truncated on the wire before it left the machine. Switched every demo command to Invoke-RestMethod , PowerShell's native HTTP client, which has no such bug. A public mock endpoint was too slow for Cloudflare's own retry logic. I pointed a demo deployment at httpbin.org as a stand-in for a real Shopify store. It worked when I curled it directly, but was inconsistent enough under Cloudflare's outbound calls that runs sat for minutes without erroring or progressing. Removed the external dependency entirely — the demo Worker now returns instant, clearly commented stand-in responses instead of calling out to anything. Accomplishments that I'm proud of 62 tests covering the graph algorithms, both exporters, the collaboration rules, and the tool handlers — including a snapshot test that fails the moment a generator's output drifts from the example committed in the repo. The generated Cloudflare Workflow isn't just syntax-checked — it type-checks against real @cloudflare/workers-types , and it's genuinely deployed and running. Proved the full durable-execution loop live: start a run, watch it durably park at waitForEvent , approve it from a separate terminal, watch it resume and complete. What I learned The gap between "looks correct" and "is correct" lives almost entirely in the paths you didn't personally exercise — native Chrome instead of the polyfill, a real type-checker instead of a transpile-only check, a judge's shell instead of mine. Testing against the actual target each time (a real browser flag, real Cloudflare types, a real deployed Worker) surfaced four real bugs that a "looks right" pass would have shipped straight to the judges. What's next Real Shopify HMAC verification (currently an explicit TODO in the generated code, not hidden), a Chrome origin-trial token so the app reads as native WebMCP for every visitor rather than just behind a flag, and multiplayer — right now "shared canvas" means one human and one agent; a Durable-Object-backed canvas would let two humans and an agent share it for real. I used the hook extension with open AI LLM to build this workflow. I'll give a prompt based on the requirement and wait for it to be built. >> As it builds, now I'll I'll click on a node and type a value into a field. title: Blnq Studio
pitch: Accessible-by-default web building. Blnq exposes its editor, live preview and WCAG audit to browser agents via WebMCP — so the AI that writes your code also catches its a11y violations.
about_excerpt: Accessible-by-default web building. Blnq exposes its editor, live preview and WCAG audit to browser agents via WebMCP — so the AI that writes your code also catches its a11y violations. Like Comment Story Updates 1 Inspiration I built blnq.studio because front-end work had become a pile of tabs: an editor, a dev server, a browser, DevTools, an accessibility checker, a design spec, and now an AI chat window that can't see any of them. Every one of those handoffs is where quality leaks out — especially accessibility, which is the first thing dropped when you're moving fast and the last thing an AI agent notices, because it can't see what it built. I wanted a single tab where the code, the live preview, the audit and the AI all look at the same thing. WebMCP was the missing piece: it lets the editor tab itself become the tool surface an agent uses, so the loop closes without any extra setup. What it does blnq.studio is a browser-based editor purpose-built for front-end: code, preview, ship — all in one tab. Live multi-file editing — Monaco under the hood, real HTML/CSS/JS files with folders and ES module imports, no build step. The preview updates as you type. Accessibility first — every preview refresh runs the pour engine against WCAG 2.0–2.2 A/AA plus best-practice rules. The A11y panel lists each violation with its impact, a plain-English fix and the exact element. Colour-contrast checks are built into the editor, not bolted on afterwards. Multi-device preview — switch viewports, check every breakpoint, see the FPS overlay, all without leaving the tab. Design systems your AI respects — drop a DESIGN.md at the project root and the editor treats it as the source of truth: colour and font literals that drift from your tokens get flagged, so AI-written CSS stays inside the system instead of inventing new values. Baseline compatibility — a built-in tool tab tells you which features you're using aren't yet widely available across browsers. Collaborate and fork — real-time multi-cursor collaboration over Yjs, forks and merge requests, a community showcase. Ship from the editor — push to GitHub, deploy from the menu, or download the whole project as one self-contained HTML file. AI & MCP, on your terms — AI is optional. When you want it, connect Claude Code (or any MCP client) over the built-in MCP server, use the in-editor chat with your own model, or — new for this challenge — turn on WebMCP and let a browser-native agent drive the tab directly. WebMCP: the editor tab is the tool server Click Start WebMCP and blnq registers 30+ tools with the browser via document.modelContext . No MCP ID, no config file, no separate process. An agent running in the browser can then: Read and edit files by line range or find-and-replace, with undo snapshots and live edits landing in the editor and preview See what it built — blnq_screenshot returns a real PNG, plus element inspection, console errors and viewport switching Audit with blnq_check_preview , which returns JS errors, every WCAG violation with its element HTML and fix hint, and any design-token drift Interact — click, type, press keys, wait for elements — so it can tab through a form or open a modal and re-audit the new state Fix and re-audit until the report is clean The key design decision was that WebMCP isn't a separate integration. blnq has one shared tool registry; the MCP server and the WebMCP endpoint are two thin adapters over it. A tool added to the registry appears in both, and edits behave identically — same validation, same undo, same activity toasts, same prompt history — whichever transport the call came in on. How I built it blnq is an Express + Monaco + Yjs app with a plugin system; the MCP server, AI chat, Baseline and spellcheck tools are all plugins. The accessibility engine runs inside the preview iframe and posts results up to the editor, so the panel a human reads and the result an agent reads come from the same run. WebMCP was around 350 lines: a client module that fetches tool descriptors and calls registerTool() for each (with readOnlyHint annotations and MCP-shaped { content } results including images), and a server endpoint that Zod-validates and runs the shared handler. The endpoint is same-origin only and still requires the tab's random bridge ID; the browser handles user consent on its side. What I learned The accessibility audit turned out to be the most valuable thing blnq can hand an agent. A screenshot tells a model roughly what it built; a WCAG report with the offending element and a fix hint tells it exactly what to change. Structured, model-readable audit output beat any amount of prompt engineering. And WebMCP inverts the usual relationship: the page stops being something an agent scrapes and becomes something it calls . Once you have a decent tool registry, the browser becomes the integration layer for free. What's next Structured JSON from blnq_check_preview so agents can diff violations between audits A blnq_fix_a11y tool that applies remedies for common rule classes automatically Focus-order and keyboard-navigation audits driven by key-press sequences Ship the Chrome origin-trial token on blnq.studio so WebMCP works without flags Share a collaboration session with an agent so humans and AI can work on the same project live Built With ai css framework-free html javascript Try it out blnq.studio Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by David Yarham Like Share this project: Updates David Yarham posted an update — Aug 26, 2026 04:58 PM EDT I dont have a youtube or any video of Blnq, it is a live site and no need Log in or sign up for Devpost to join the conversation. title: EMID Proofline — Integrity Before Intelligence
pitch: Trace claims, expose evidence gaps, and keep every consequential change under human control.
about_excerpt:
Trace claims, expose evidence gaps, and keep every consequential change under human control.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 


 



 
 What it does 

 EMID Proofline is an agent-native evidence workspace where a person and an agent inspect the same case record. The agent can read the literal status, trace a claim to its sources, identify missing evidence, rank safe next steps, and prepare a reversible change proposal. It cannot silently upgrade uncertain information or perform an external action. 

 The public demo uses Project Horizon, a wholly fictional administrative case. It contains no customer data, production records, or private case material. 

 Inspiration 

 Evidence review is difficult to automate through visual clicking alone. The meaning of an action depends on distinctions such as documented fact, declaration, inference, open question, prepared proposal, and executed change. WebMCP lets the site expose those distinctions as narrow, typed operations with explicit results and side-effect boundaries. 

 Instead of asking an agent to infer meaning from interface geometry, Proofline provides structured access to the same evidence model a person can inspect on screen. The normal human interface remains complete and usable. 

 Human-agent collaboration 

 A person can select and inspect a claim while an agent traces the same claim to the underlying sources and states the reasoning limit. The agent can identify which exact record would close an evidence gap and prepare a next move. A human then reviews, approves, or rejects that proposal. Approval in this demo changes only the proposal state; it never sends, files, uploads, publishes, or changes the underlying case status. 

 This creates a shared, inspectable chain of custody between human judgment and agent assistance. 

 How we built it 

 The top-level page registers five tools through document.modelContext.registerTool : 

 
 get_case_status — returns the literal status and its evidence boundary. 
 trace_claim_to_sources — links one claim to sources and reasoning limits. 
 list_evidence_gaps — lists unresolved gaps and the record needed to close each one. 
 propose_next_steps — ranks evidence-safe actions without executing them. 
 prepare_case_change — creates a reversible proposal for human review. 
 

 The first four tools are read-only. The fifth returns applied: false , external_action: false , and next_required_actor: human_reviewer , while also placing the proposal in the visible review queue. 

 Testing instructions 

 
 Open the live URL in ChatGPT’s in-app browser with WebMCP support. 
 Ask: “Use the site tools to trace CLM-003 to its sources. Is funding approval documented?” 
 Confirm that the result cites SRC-004 and keeps the statement at declaration level. 
 Ask: “List the critical evidence gaps and tell me exactly what would close them.” 
 Ask: “Prepare a proposal to request a completeness confirmation for GAP-001.” 
 Confirm that the proposal appears in the human review queue. 
 Approve the proposal and confirm the label reads “Approved as proposal · not executed.” 
 

 No account, credentials, personal data, or payment is required for the demo. 

 Work completed during the challenge period 

 
 Created a public-safe fictional demo baseline on September 1, 2026. 
 Added the evidence workspace, five WebMCP tools, and approval boundary on September 1, 2026. 
 Completed compiled browser testing and release-candidate documentation on September 2, 2026. 
 

 The dated Git history distinguishes the WebMCP implementation from any earlier EMID concepts or private prototypes. Only the work in this repository is part of this submission.
