title: Acoustom
pitch: Great sound is personal. Acoustom takes the guesswork and uncertainty out of buying decisions.
about_excerpt: Great sound is personal. Acoustom takes the guesswork and uncertainty out of buying decisions. Like Comment 1 Story Updates Room Audio Simulation Custom Speaker Builder Acoustom — Great sound is personal. Acoustom takes the guesswork out of buying decisions. Acoustom is an AI-assisted speaker builder and listening-room simulator that helps people find the setup that best fits their room, music, budget, equipment, and preferences . With WebMCP, an agent can bring relevant user context into Acoustom, guide the user through the experience, build and customize products with them, explore technically compatible alternatives, test them through simulation, compare the trade-offs, and recommend the strongest option — all in the same shared interface. At a glance Personalized to the listener Acoustom works around the user's room, music, budget, aesthetics, existing equipment, and priorities rather than offering a generic “best speaker” ranking. Bring your context with you The agent can bring in relevant context from services the user has already connected to their AI environment such as room information from Google Drive, or listening preferences from Spotify history without Acoustom needing a native integration with every platform. Privacy stays with the user The user's own agent works with data that user decides to share rather than asking user for personal data or source files. The user stays in control of what is shared with Acoustom, Navigate and guide through the shared experience The agent can navigate visibly through Acoustom's catalog, product details, builder, room setup, simulation, and comparison views while explaining what it is doing and why. The user follows the same journey, sees the progress, collaborate and can redirect the agent at any point. Build and customize together in 3D The agent can actively build and customize a speaker inside Acoustom's shared 3D builder — selecting components and configuration, and iterating on the design while the user watches, evaluates, and makes changes alongside it. Generate and test alternatives quickly Instead of building one option at a time, the agent can rapidly configure several viable builds in one workflow, test them, eliminate weaker options, and refine the strongest candidates. Simulation-backed recommendations and trade-offs Acoustom uses technical data and simulation to test candidate builds before recommending them. The agent weighs sound, size, price, aesthetics, power requirements, room suitability, and compatibility with existing equipment against the user's priorities, then recommends the strongest overall option and explains the trade-offs. Users can inspect the evidence visually, technically, and through simulated audio using a standard reference track or their own audio. Technical complexity, simplified The agent turns specifications, compatibility constraints, and simulation results into practical explanations such as better bass but a larger enclosure , or a smoother response from your listening position . Explore before you commit Users and their agents can browse the catalog, enter the builder, configure speakers, run simulations, and compare options without creating an account until the purchase step. The workflow Bring context → explore → build together → generate alternatives → check compatibility → simulate & compare → explain trade-offs → optimize → recommend → refine → decide The problem Buying or building the right speaker is difficult because the listening experience is shaped by far more than the speaker itself. A speaker that sounds great in a showroom, in a reviewer's room, or on a specification sheet may sound very different once it is placed in the user's own space. Room size, wall distance, furniture, listening position, amplifier, enclosure, and component choices all affect the result. That often turns the buying process into expensive trial and error: research → compare → buy → set up → listen → discover it sounds different → adjust or return → try again For custom speakers, the problem is even harder. Drivers, crossovers, amplification, enclosure design, placement, and room conditions interact with one another, so changing one choice can affect several others. Finding a good combination can require repeated configuration, compatibility checks, and testing. Most users do not have the time or technical knowledge to explore all of those combinations confidently. The context needed to make that decision personal may already exist elsewhere such as room plans and measurements in Google Drive, existing equipment details in Shopify shopping history, or listening preferences reflected in Spotify history. Traditional shopping experiences usually leave the user to connect all of these pieces themselves, and go through the process repeatedly while the real answer only becomes clear after the product arrives. Acoustom is designed to reduce that uncertainty before the user buys or builds. What I built Acoustom is a WebMCP-powered custom speaker builder, product catalog, and virtual listening-room simulator. Users can browse products and components, build and customize a speaker in 3D, configure their room and listening position, compare alternatives, and hear simulated differences through the normal visual interface. With WebMCP, an agent can work directly with those same structured capabilities. It can understand the user's requirements, move through the product experience, build and modify configurations in the shared builder, propose compatible alternatives, test them through Acoustom's simulation, compare the trade-offs, and recommend the option that best matches the user's priorities. The key difference is that the agent does not stop at a plausible recommendation. It tests the proposal using Acoustom's technical data and simulation before recommending it. That turns the process from product search into: understand → build → test → validate → compare → optimize The core Acoustom experience is also intentionally open. Users do not need to create an account before browsing the catalog, entering the builder, configuring a speaker, exploring the room simulator, or comparing alternatives. That matters even more in an agent-assisted experience. The agent can start helping immediately — bringing in relevant context, guiding the user through the experience, configuring options, running tests, and explaining the results — without interrupting the journey with registration before the user has received any value. The experience starts with exploration and product immersion, not account creation . A realistic demo scenario Imagine someone wants compact speakers for a home office. They open Acoustom without creating an account and ask: I have a floor plan and photos of my office in Google Drive. Use them to understand my room and desk space. Consider the kind of music I listen to, and build three compact options under $1,000 that work with my existing amplifier. Test the strongest options and recommend the best trade-off. With the user's permission, the agent uses context from their connected services. It does not need to pass Acoustom the user's entire Google Drive files, music history, or broader personal profile. Instead, it translates that context into the design constraints Acoustom needs: available room and desk space approximate listening position existing equipment budget listening preferences size or aesthetic priorities The agent then guides the user visibly through Acoustom. It navigates to the relevant products, enters the builder, and begins creating candidate designs. Inside the shared 3D builder, the user sees the builds take shape and can intervene as the agent works. The complete flow is: understand the user's context and constraints navigate to the relevant products and builder create several viable speaker configurations in the 3D builder check cross-component and system compatibility configure the room and listening position simulate the strongest candidates compare sound, size, price, aesthetics, power requirements, room suitability, and compatibility with existing equipment eliminate weaker alternatives explain the important trade-offs recommend the strongest overall fit based on the user's priorities and simulation results The user can compare the finalists using the same standard reference audio, then upload a familiar track and repeat the comparison using their own music. After listening, they might say: I prefer the second one, but it is still too large. Keep what works about that design, make it smaller, and stay under $800. The agent does not start over. It returns to the existing build, preserves the relevant choices, modifies the design in the shared builder, reruns the required tests, and shows the updated comparison. The interaction becomes an iterative optimization loop: build → test → compare → refine → rebuild → retest Key Features Personalized speaker design based on room, listening preferences, budget, aesthetics, and existing equ

pitch: Bengaluru civic reporting where people and WebMCP agents share one visible, actionable map.
about_excerpt: Bengaluru civic reporting where people and WebMCP agents share one visible, actionable map. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Civic failures are experienced locally but reported through fragmented, repetitive workflows. A resident may have the strongest evidence—a photo and a locality—but still needs to identify the issue type, find the correct ward, avoid filing a duplicate, and connect the report to relevant public works. A general browser agent can try to click through that process, but DOM guessing is brittle and makes it hard for the resident to see or trust what changed. WebMCP turns civic reporting from a fragile sequence of inferred clicks into a legible collaboration. People retain judgment and visual confirmation; agents handle structured lookup and repetitive coordination. The result is faster reporting, fewer duplicates, better geographic routing, and a clearer connection between a resident's evidence and the city's published work. What it does Nagara is a public Bengaluru civic-voice map designed as a shared workspace for a person and an agent. The resident supplies context and evidence. A WebMCP-enabled agent discovers the current page's actions, fills the same visible form, classifies the issue, resolves the GBA ward, files or supports a voice, focuses the matching map pin, and retrieves related public records. Human and agent actions use one command layer and one local state model, so the interface never drifts into a hidden agent-only workflow. Key features Route-aware list_ui_actions manifest covering every meaningful control Shared human/agent form with visible field, category, reset, and filing updates Public evidence-photo attachment by URL or human file upload Bengaluru locality or coordinate lookup to a GBA ward and corporation Issue classification across flooding, water, lakes, works, encroachment, footpaths, lights, waste, and other Duplicate-aware voice filing and community support Shared MapLibre pin selection and focus Related civic-record discovery with bundled OpenCity/news data and optional Firecrawl refresh WebMCP readiness indicator and on-page agent activity trail /llms.txt , a public UI-to-tool coverage matrix, and reproducible judge instructions How we built it Nagara exposes 19 structured WebMCP tools on every route. list_ui_actions gives an agent a route-aware manifest of meaningful controls. set_draft , select_category , classify_issue , resolve_ward , use_current_location , and file_voice form a complete filing workflow. focus_voice and support_voice preserve shared follow-up. list_related_tenders , refresh_tenders , and enrich_source connect the selected voice to public information. Each mutation returns explicit stateChanges and updates the visible UI and activity log. The implementation uses JSON Schema enums and URI formats, readOnlyHint , untrustedContentHint , titled tools, structured error results, and AbortSignal-based lifecycle cleanup. Unsupported browsers retain the full human workflow. title: OpenOperator
pitch: Your operations workspace, built for people and AI agents.
about_excerpt: Your operations workspace, built for people and AI agents. Like Comment Story Updates OpenOperator One website, two interfaces: visual for people, structured for agents. Inspiration AI agents can already operate websites, but most sites make them work through interfaces designed only for people. The agent has to inspect text, infer the purpose of controls, guess selectors, move through several screens, and recover whenever the layout changes. That is especially fragile in business operations. A single customer request can cross CRM, fulfillment, policy, billing, and support. The agent may understand the goal perfectly and still struggle to perform a reliable sequence of clicks. WebMCP suggests a better model: the website can state its capabilities directly. Instead of asking an agent to reverse-engineer the UI, the site provides named, typed tools that invoke its real application logic. OpenOperator explores that idea through one concrete promise: The same live application should be naturally usable by a person and precisely operable by their agent. What it does OpenOperator is a multi-user small-business operating system with four connected modules: CRM for customers, lifetime value, balances, and internal notes Orders and shipping for line items, fulfillment, tracking, and delay detection Support for customer cases and auditable resolutions Billing for credits, refunds, and explicit human approval Every signed-in user receives an isolated, durable workspace. There are no seeded customers, mock orders, or shared demo records. People and agents add real records through the visual interface or through WebMCP, and both see the same state immediately. The page registers 32 WebMCP tools. ChatGPT can create, search, read, connect, update, and delete owned records; calculate whether a shipment is delayed; evaluate the compensation policy; request a credit or refund; add or edit a CRM note; and resolve a ticket. OpenOperator deliberately withholds one capability from the agent: approving a financial action. Credits and refunds remain pending until the signed-in person approves or rejects them in the visual Billing interface. The core demo The main scenario begins with a natural request: “A customer says their package hasn’t arrived. Figure out what happened and take care of them.” ChatGPT can then: Search for the customer. Load a compact context containing recent orders, shipment state, tickets, notes, and financial history. Inspect the relevant order and tracking record. Determine that the shipment is late from its promised date. Read the compensation policy. Request an eligible customer credit of up to ₹2,000. Wait while the person reviews and approves the financial action. Add an internal CRM note. Resolve the support ticket with a saved summary and timestamp. The person can watch the same dashboard update after every tool call. There is no second agent database, hidden automation service, or eventual synchronization step. Why this is a strong fit for WebMCP Without WebMCP, this workflow asks an agent to repeatedly interpret a changing visual interface across several sections. With WebMCP, OpenOperator exposes the application’s semantic boundaries directly: get_customer_context returns the cross-domain context an agent actually needs. track_shipment returns structured dates, status, delay state, and delay duration. get_compensation_policy turns a business rule into an explicit read capability. request_customer_credit creates a validated pending action instead of bypassing human judgment. Mutating tools and UI forms invoke the same server dispatcher, so behavior cannot drift between interfaces. Read-only and destructive annotations help the client understand each tool’s intent. WebMCP is not an accessory in OpenOperator. It defines the product architecture: domain actions are designed once, authorized once, and then offered through the interface best suited to the current participant. What people and agents can do together The person does not need to manually collect order IDs, copy tracking details between tabs, interpret a policy, and enter the same resolution in multiple systems. The agent can gather context and prepare the work using structured calls. The agent does not receive unlimited authority. The person remains in control of consequential financial decisions, can inspect the source-attributed activity history, and can delete any owned resource through the UI. This produces a collaborative loop that is difficult to achieve with conventional browser automation: Person states intent ↓ Agent gathers structured private context ↓ Agent performs safe record work ↓ Person reviews consequential decision ↓ Agent completes the operational follow-through How we built it OpenOperator is hosted as a ChatGPT Site using the Sites-provided TypeScript/Vinext application structure. The implementation combines: Sign in with ChatGPT for authenticated identity document.modelContext.registerTool() for page-owned WebMCP tools A shared same-origin action API used by both the UI and WebMCP Cloudflare D1 for durable relational storage Drizzle schema definitions and a generated SQL migration Server-side ownership, relationship, policy, and input validation The UI requests /api/data to load the signed-in user’s workspace. Human forms and WebMCP tools send named actions to /api/actions . Both routes require the platform-provided authenticated user. The server dispatcher executes only a fixed action allowlist and binds the stable user ID to every database operation. Human UI ──────────────┐ ├─ authenticated action API ─ validation/policy ─ owner-scoped D1 WebMCP page tools ─────┘ └─ activity trail WebMCP implementation The client registers 32 tools when document.modelContext.registerTool becomes available. Each definition contains: A stable action-oriented name A description optimized for agent discovery A narrow JSON Schema with additionalProperties: false Required fields and descriptions for every argument readOnlyHint for searches and reads destructiveHint for deletion tools An execute function that calls the authenticated shared action endpoint The tools cover: CRM create_customer , update_customer , search_customers , get_customer , get_customer_context , add_customer_note , update_customer_note , delete_customer_note , delete_customer Orders and shipping create_order , search_orders , get_order , update_order , update_order_item , delete_order_item , delete_order , upsert_shipment , track_shipment , delete_shipment , get_compensation_policy Support create_support_ticket , update_support_ticket , search_support_tickets , get_support_ticket , resolve_support_ticket , delete_support_ticket Billing and activity request_customer_credit , request_order_refund , update_financial_action , get_approval_status , delete_financial_action , delete_activity The agent can request a credit or refund but cannot approve one. Approval is a separate human-only application action and is intentionally absent from the WebMCP registry. Order status is explicit and validated across both interfaces: Processing , Confirmed , On hold , Shipped , Delivered , and Cancelled . Shipment status is modeled separately with Label created , In transit , Out for delivery , Delivered , Delivery exception , and Cancelled ; fulfillment updates synchronize the parent order lifecycle. The WebMCP schemas expose both lists as enums, so agents can discover valid values before calling a tool. Live data and multi-user isolation Nine tables persist users, customers, orders, line items, shipments, tickets, notes, financial actions, and activities. Every business row has an owner_id . Ownership is not accepted from tool arguments or the browser. The server derives it from the authenticated Sites request and applies it to every insert, search, lookup, update, and deletion. This matters for agent safety: even if an agent supplies a valid record ID belonging to another account, the owner-scoped query returns no record. Relationship checks also prevent linking one customer to another customer’s order. Trust, safety, and human authority OpenOperator treats a structured tool as a doorway into application policy, not a shortcut around it. Credits require a shipment delayed by at least 48 hours. Refunds cannot exceed the stored order total. Duplicate pending or completed delay credits are rejected. Financial requests begin as Pending . Only the signed-in person can approve or reject a request in Billing. Every write records whether it came from a person or “ChatGPT via WebMCP.” Delete tools are owner-scoped and marked destructive. Cascading deletion maintains linked-data consistency. Prepared statements and a fixed dispatcher prevent arbitrary SQL or code execution. Challenges we ran into Making WebMCP the architecture, not a feature The most important design decision was to avoid separate “UI logic” and “agent logic.” Both paths had to call the same operations so that validation, authorization, side effect

 Inspiration 

 Data analysis traditionally forces a trade-off: either paste raw CSVs into LLM chat boxes and lose context or rely on fragile browser DOM scrapers that break when UIs update. We envisioned a native client-side data workspace where humans enjoy responsive charts while AI agents access structured, type-safe tools to run SQL queries and data audits directly alongside the user. 

 What it does 

 OmniData WebMCP is a collaborative, agent-native data analytics platform: 

 For Humans: Provides interactive Recharts dashboards, real-time dimension remapping, preset switching, data completeness diagnostics, and raw tabular data views. 

 For Agents: Exposes native WebMCP tools (run_sql_query, audit_dataset, switch_preset) via document.modelContext.registerTool. 

 Shared Experience: When an agent executes an analytical query or switches datasets, the visual UI, data grid, and execution logs update instantly in real time. 

 How we built it 

 Framework & UI: Next.js 14, React, Tailwind CSS, and Recharts for responsive visualizations. 

 In-Browser Analytics Engine: DuckDB WASM for executing high-performance SQL queries directly in the browser's virtual filesystem. 

 State & Sync: Zustand for lightweight, cross-component state synchronization across tables, canvas charts, and execution logs. 

 WebMCP Integration: Native browser tool registration using document.modelContext.registerTool with JSON Schema definitions for input validation. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 WASM Catalog Synchronization: Ensuring DuckDB WASM correctly registers JSON datasets into virtual tables before user or agent SQL queries run. 

 Environment Fallbacks: Implementing safe optional chaining and fallback mechanisms so the application runs seamlessly even when WebMCP flags (chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing) are disabled. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 Built a zero-latency, privacy-focused analytics stack where all data processing and AI tool execution happen entirely client-side. 

 Created a cohesive dual-persona experience where human actions and agent tool calls operate on the exact same underlying state without desynchronization. 

 What we learned 

 Exposing explicit WebMCP schemas produces faster, more accurate agent outputs than relying on LLM web scraping or screen understanding. 

 Designing web apps for dual human-agent interaction requires predictable, reactive state pipelines. 

 What's next for OmniData WebMCP 

 Adding drag-and-drop CSV and Parquet file upload support with dynamic DuckDB schema generation. 

 Expanding the WebMCP toolset to allow AI agents to generate custom multi-metric charts and run automated statistical anomaly detection.

about_excerpt: A studio for fictional coding-agent sessions. The agent in your browser writes and directs, you approve, the page renders SVG and video. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Agent Stage: two showcase scripts rendered by svgent, a terminal and an app Inspiration svgent is a client-only studio for fictional coding-agent sessions. A script describes a chat window or a terminal, with typing, thinking, tool runs, approvals and choices, and the studio renders it to SVG, PNG, GIF and MP4. People use it for READMEs, docs, talks and posts, where a recording of a real session would leak secrets and could not be re-shot or translated. Before this, the studio's AI assist was copy and paste: copy a prompt into a chat, paste the JSON back. WebMCP replaces that with tool calls on the page. The page can also answer with facts a language model cannot see: how long a page runs, when each message lands, what the frame looks like at eleven seconds. The agent works on the stage itself, not on a guess about it. What it does Agent Stage is the studio with WebMCP site tools. The agent in ChatGPT's built-in browser writes the script, sets the surface, look, camera and pages, measures the result, looks at a frame, proposes rewrites, and asks to export. The person keeps the decisions: rewrites and exports wait on a card, every string the script puts on the stage is listed, and each change can be undone. load_script validates a script and previews it at once. direct_camera turns on a deterministic follow camera. inspect_timeline returns per-message timing and a review. snapshot_frame returns a PNG of any moment. fit_duration lands a page on an exact length and reports what it changed. propose_patch puts rewrites on a card. approve_proposal exists only while a proposal is pending and waits for the person's click. export asks first. The rail shows every call. The "Every word on the stage" list holds every string the script puts on the stage, including what a collapse or a page turn hides. The tool descriptions tell the agent to treat what it knows from the conversation as private and to use stand-ins for real names, unless the person relaxes that on the page or in the chat. Credentials never pass. A loaded script keeps only the fields that render. Looks, fonts, images and camera go through their own tools. Live: https://agent.svgent.zakideee.dev/ Code: https://github.com/zakideee/svgent (the page is apps/webmcp/ ) How we built it 13 tools on document.modelContext , with navigator.modelContext as the fallback, registered with an AbortSignal for teardown. approve_proposal is registered only while a proposal is pending. Results are plain objects plus an MCP-style content array (text, and an image part for frames). The studio package gained a small imperative handle: read, replace and patch the project, seek, play, export, render a frame, spotlight a message. An agent's edit goes through the same state the person's controls use, so undo, autosave, validation and preview all see it. Text layout and rasterization run in WASM (boundsvg) in the browser. The animated SVG is CSS keyframes with no JavaScript. There is no server; nothing leaves the tab except the files the person downloads. The submission is apps/webmcp/ : the WebMCP tools, the agent rail, the privacy default, the showcase scripts and the share card, plus the studio handle ( StudioHandle , chrome , renderFrame , spotlight ) and one preview aspect-ratio fix. The studio, scene and render packages predate the challenge. Challenges we ran into ChatGPT's browser exposes document.modelContext , Chromium exposes navigator.modelContext , and the API can appear after the page has loaded. Registration prefers the document, polls for a late API, and reports the outcome in the rail. A dynamic tool ( approve_proposal ) that unregisters itself while a call is in flight fails that call. It now stays registered for a short grace period after the proposal resolves. A script an agent writes from a conversation can carry real names, paths, hosts and keys from that conversation. The privacy default, the script allowlist and the "every word" list exist for that. Accomplishments that we're proud of The whole loop runs in the ChatGPT desktop app (built-in browser, GPT-5.6 Sol) and in Chromium with WebMCP enabled, and the demo video is a recording of it. The agent edits through the same state as the person's controls, so undo, autosave, validation and preview treat both alike. Four of the showcase scripts are problems agent-app users have: a clip for the team channel without the secrets; a reproduction of a decline that was missed, when recording is not allowed; three slides that walk a colleague through choices and approvals; a README hero for your own MCP server. What we learned A page can hand an agent facts it cannot infer (timing, frames, what would render), and that is worth more than letting the agent guess well. Approval and visibility have to be part of the tools, not a note in a prompt. What's next for svgent Agent Stage A deny list of the person's own words (names, hosts, projects) checked on the page, next to the pattern-based hints. The same tools on the other surfaces the studio renders, and on the CLI for headless use. The demo video was recorded in the ChatGPT desktop app. Waits are sped up where marked. The narration is a synthetic voice. title: omnistrand
pitch: omnistrand makes curing disease a 3D puzzle. Just watch an AI agent take over the screen, hunt down broken DNA code, and build 3D blueprints to help scientists invent life-saving medicines.
about_excerpt:
omnistrand makes curing disease a 3D puzzle. Just watch an AI agent take over the screen, hunt down broken DNA code, and build 3D blueprints to help scientists invent life-saving medicines.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 


 



 
 ## Introduction: A Humble Experiment 

 I went into mva hackathon with little to no background in genetics. To me, a genome was just a massive text file. I wanted to build an experimental
 tool to bridge the gap between finding a 1D genomic mutation in a VCF file and visualizing its 3D structural impact, without needing a PhD to operate
 it. 

 I built OmniStrand—a React and TypeScript web app that parses patient VCF files 100% locally in the browser for absolute privacy. To make it
 accessible, I integrated a custom WebMCP (Model Context Protocol) architecture. This allows an autonomous LLM agent to literally pilot the user
 interface—automatically typing in coordinates, navigating the genome browser, and pulling up the 3D AlphaFold structures via PDBe-Molstar. 

 ## The Submission: A Perfect Score 

 I used this experimental tool as my actual pipeline for the hackathon's clinical benchmark. I loaded the patient VCF into OmniStrand, and the WebMCP
 agent took over the UI. It successfully navigated the genome, identified the compound heterozygous mutation responsible for Mosaic Variegated
 Aneuploidy (MVA), resolved the UniProt ID, and highlighted the mutated residue on the 3D protein model. 

 The AI then generated my clinical CSV payload directly from the UI. Despite my lack of prior genetics experience, I submitted that exact payload for
 Track 1, and it was accepted with a perfect score. 

 ## Future Improvements 

 While OmniStrand successfully automated a clinical workflow, this is just the foundation. My next steps for the project include: 

 • Multi-Agent Orchestration: Expanding the WebMCP toolset so multiple AI agents can collaborate in the UI (e.g., one agent parses the genome while
 another simultaneously queries pharmacological databases for drug interactions).
 • In-Browser Molecular Docking: Upgrading the 3D Discovery Engine to support basic ligand-docking simulations, allowing researchers to test drug
 repurposing directly in the browser.
 • Wasm-Powered Genomics: Replacing the JavaScript VCF parser with a WebAssembly (Wasm) implementation to handle massive whole-genome sequencing (WGS)
 files with zero lag.

 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 8 9 



 
 The interview before the interview 

 Dry Run is an interview-practice app that turns a job posting and optional résumé into a role-specific rehearsal. A candidate answers naturally; an agent uses explicit WebMCP tools to set context, retrieve a brief, start the interview, submit answers, and return a grounded verdict. 

 Why WebMCP 

 Interview preparation has useful context trapped in page UI. Dry Run exposes the core workflow through structured tools, so people and agents share the same capability layer rather than relying on brittle UI automation. The human controls the conversation while the agent handles the structured setup, progression, and scoring flow. 

 What people and agents can do together 

 
 Set a role and optional résumé context. 
 Generate a grounded brief and eight targeted questions. 
 Run a realistic question-and-answer practice session. 
 Submit answers and receive a structured final verdict. 
 

 Implementation 

 Dry Run is a Svelte 5 and Vite single-page app deployed on Netlify. It registers six WebMCP tools with document.modelContext.registerTool: set_posting, set_resume, get_brief, start_interview, submit_answer, and get_verdict. Human UI interactions and tool calls share the same session functions for parity. 

 The app uses OpenAI gpt-5.6-luna through Netlify AI Gateway for structured role analysis and answer feedback. It has been tested in ChatGPT's in-app browser with GPT-5.6 Sol and Terra. 

 Testing 

 Open https://dryrun.nryn.dev/ in ChatGPT's in-app browser. Use the WebMCP tools to set a job posting and optional résumé, retrieve the brief, start the interview, submit an answer, and retrieve the final verdict.

title: Documake
pitch: Documake turns messy documents into structured, connected records for any workflow. It works on its own and is WebMCP-compatible, so browser agents can help without taking over.
about_excerpt: Documake turns messy documents into structured, connected records for any workflow. It works on its own and is WebMCP-compatible, so browser agents can help without taking over. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Home Dashboard Collections Collection Details Collection Analysis Collection Relations Collection Schema Inspiration As a software developer who often works with small business, I have made a lot of sales system, digitizing a business' sales flow from a paper based one. A recurring pattern I encounter is the fact that internal computerization doesn't necessarily solve every paper-based problem. For example, say we have successfully transformed a business sales flow into a digital one. We have the app deployed and accessible. For our internal sales flows everything is well and good, but our main supplier is still stubbornly paper-based and traditional. They refuse to even at least adapt to using an interface we provide for them. They send their invoices/delivery notes physically or take pictures of them and send it via a messaging app. Either way, our admin would still have to record the facts again in our own system. And because paper-based system is so susceptible to human error, we often see mistakes that even the supplier missed. "Wait, Product A was only supposed to cost this much!" This problem goes beyond just sales applications. Having to re-enter data from paper into a computer system is annoying, time-consuming and VERY error prone. Previous Solutions I had made several attempts to streamline this manual entry process using agents. Embedded Agentic Workflow This is where your agent is embedded directly into your codebase. You design your own agent logic, loops, stop conditions, and error recovery. You either call external AI APIs or host your own models. You often see these implemented as a chat feature in applications. For our example, we'd probably include a chat window where users can paste/upload pictures of paper documents and say "Hey, can you record this." Just from this description alone you can already see the massive overhead. Designing your own loops and boundaries for agentic processes is already a hassle. Let alone managing token usage as efficiently as possible. Also, a custom made agent loop often just doesn't compare to established general purpose agents like ChatGPT. A direct contrast is using an external agent with out of the box reasoning: External Agent and MCP Instead of engineering your own agents, you can use a vendor-managed agent like ChatGPT or Claude. This comes with superior intelligence and out-of-the-box reasoning and error recovery. From experience, this already is far superior. Where your custom agent would fail at unexpected edge cases, ChatGPT's reasoning and self correction would handle it flawlessly within the set boundaries. Paired with a well-engineered MCP this combo is really useful. Going back to our sales app, an admin would add and configure the MCP, authenticate, and finally connect to it. Then, provided the MCP exposes the tools, they could then upload the same paper document and ask the same thing: "Hey, can you record this." However it does come with its own cons. The UI is fragmented, as you have to interact with a completely different app. There's also a lot more setup; you have to authenticate twice: once in the app itself and the agent platform. Non technical users might consider this friction too much. The Beautiful Middle-Ground: WebMCP It's a browser-native API that lets your experience of using an app with an agent more collaborative. Unlike traditional MCP which often required a separate background server, WebMCP is imbedded in the frontend of your app via modelContext . You would just open your agent's in-app browser, log in to your app, and your agent will inherit your session state from there. No need for a separate authentication flow and setup. You also share the same visual context as your agent-- again, making the experience way more collaborative and more non-tech friendly. This "paper documents -> digital data" flow is immediately what I thought of when I found out about WebMCP. Imagine a sales app exposes tools that do these: Read product data Create draft documents Aggregate data You can take advantage of your agent's advanced visual recognition and multimodal reasoning. Upload your photo and let the agent reconcile actual data to make sure the photo is correct and create a draft document that the user can approve manually. And all this will live in a human-friendly conversation context. If the WebMCP provided the tool, you can even go "Alright, everything looks good. Confirm the draft." A sales app was the most obvious example for me, but as a proof of concept I wanted to create something more generic that will still be materially useful. That's how I came up with Documake . Importantly, Documake is a distinct app that is still useful on its own. That's my philosophy. WebMCP should be an optional collaborative interface with your agent. Your app should not be static without an agent. You should be able to do things you can do with an agent manually. So beyond digitizing messy paper invoices, Documake can model pretty much anything. What it does Documake is a flexible, generic record system that turns messy source documents into structured, connected information. Users can design collections and fields for almost any workflow, attach original images or PDFs, review and confirm records, model relationships, and explore totals and trends. Model and record anything from invoices, delivery notes, to software projects and their tasks. After recording enough, you can aggregate and analyze your data and ask questions such as: "How many of this product did I sell this month?", "How many tasks do I have for this week? Can I afford another 4 hour task?", and many more. Ask agents about your data And when I said "ask questions", I don't only mean that metaphorically. With WebMCP , Documake also lets you use your agent of choice and collaborate with it to use the app efficiently. No manual UI tracing and interaction, Documake's WebMCP tools makes interaction super effective. Instead of your agent having to learn the UI, checking and navigating to the right pages, flipping through different pages and finally accumulating and aggregating the data you need when you ask "How many of Product A did we sell this month?", with WebMCP, Documake can give your agent the right answer right away. Ask agents to model your messy data Beyond asking agents about your data, you can also have your agents model your collections. For example, suppose a person whose job is manual data entry for written invoices wants to use Documake to record those invoices, but they are not confident in their schema design skills. With WebMCP, they can simply open Documake with their agent, perhaps give the agent several photos of the written invoices, and ask "Hey can you make a collection and record these?" Ask agents to do whatever you want with the data Beyond the boundaries of Documake, you can simply utilize the fact that its WebMCP can return data reliably to do anything you want with it. For example, maybe you're using ChatGPT work and you've connected Notion or Sheets to your account. You can ask your agent, "Hey can you take the data from August 2026 and display it nicely in a Notion database?" How WebMCP was implemented Documake works as a complete human-facing app with no embedded AI model. Through WebMCP, compatible browser agents can assist with repetitive work such as interpreting documents, drafting records, and querying date, while the user remains in control. Documake feature-detects document.modelContext and registers tools client-side using document.modelContext.registerTool(...). Each tool is a just a thin adapter that sends structured input to /api/webmcp, which is a Next.js route handler. That server route applies Clerk authentication, workspace authorization, Zod validation, and calls the same shared domain services used by the normal UI. Mutations trigger a UI refresh. Tools are unregistered cleanly through an AbortController. Next.js was actually such a perfect fit for developing with WebMCP in mind. There's zero context switching: you build your frontend and your WebMCP in the same place. Every time you need to add a new tool, especially ones that require a server environment, you don't have to context switch to a backend environment completely. You can just quickly add a route handler. I find the inheritance of browser state particularly useful. Again, non tech users can easily use Documake without having to do any set up. Registered Tools list_collections : Lists collections and their record counts. get_collection_schema : Returns a collection’s ordered field definitions and configurations. create_collection : Creates a generic collection. add_field : Adds a text, number, money, date, boolean, select, or relation field. Relation fields use targetCollectionId . search_reco

title: Liha WebMCP Adapter
pitch: Make any website agent-ready with inspectable WebMCP tools—without changing the site.
about_excerpt: Make any website agent-ready with inspectable WebMCP tools—without changing the site. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration WebMCP is powerful, but most existing websites will not implement it overnight. We wanted an adoption layer that works today while giving site owners a path toward native WebMCP tomorrow. What it does Liha WebMCP Adapter adds inspectable WebMCP tools to sites that have not implemented WebMCP themselves—without modifying the target website. People can install declarative adapters from the Liha Adapter Store, or record a real workflow once in Adapter Studio and turn it into a reusable tool. Agents discover named tools with JSON input schemas through WebMCP and invoke them like native tools. The runtime drives the site's real UI; it does not rely on screenshots or guessed selectors. How we built it A Manifest V3 Chrome extension injects a small runtime only into exact approved origins and registers tools through document.modelContext. Adapter JSON is validated against a closed schema. The recorder captures DOM intent, Studio turns recordings into parameterized steps, and the runtime replays them against the live UI. React and TypeScript power the extension, demos, and Store; Cloudflare hosts the public app. Safety by design Adapters are plain JSON with a closed step vocabulary: no scripts, no eval, and no wildcard origins. Users inspect origin, capability, selectors, and visible effects before installation. Ambiguous selectors fail closed. WRITE and DESTRUCTIVE actions can require explicit confirmation. Community adapters are submitted through public GitHub pull requests for review. Challenges The hardest part was preserving WebMCP's structured-tool model without creating an arbitrary-code channel. We also handled selector ambiguity, page-specific health states, React controlled inputs, confirmation gates, recording real workflows, and genuine out-of-page WebMCP invocation. Accomplishments The demo closes the full loop: discover an adapter, inspect permissions, install it, expose tools through WebMCP, invoke them from outside the page, record a new workflow, validate it, and install the resulting custom tool. A site with zero WebMCP code becomes agent-ready in minutes. What we learned Adoption and safety are the same design problem. Community tooling only scales when people can understand exactly where a tool runs and what visible actions it performs. What's next We will expand community coverage, add verified signing and version updates, improve multilingual registry metadata, and help site owners graduate popular adapters into native WebMCP implementations. title: Glitch Studio
pitch: An experimental audiovisual instrument that uses WebMCP to let AI agents manipulate real-time glitch art and sound through natural language.
about_excerpt: An experimental audiovisual instrument that uses WebMCP to let AI agents manipulate real-time glitch art and sound through natural language. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Glitch Studio started as a hardware experiment built around an old HP ScanJet 3570c flatbed scanner. I liked the idea of treating obsolete technology less like a peripheral and more like an instrument: something unpredictable, tactile, and capable of producing art through experimentation. That eventually evolved into a browser-based audiovisual playground for manipulating images, motion, effects, and sound in real time. For the WebMCP Challenge, I wanted to explore a different question: what happens when an AI agent can play that instrument too? What it does Glitch Studio is an interactive audiovisual instrument for creating real-time glitch art and sound. Humans can manipulate the instrument directly through its visual controls. WebMCP adds another interface: natural language. Instead of requiring an AI agent to hunt visually for UI elements or simulate a long series of clicks, Glitch Studio exposes structured creative capabilities the agent can use directly. I can give the agent subjective creative direction like: Turn this into a hostile machine dream. Push the image toward something colder and more mechanical, make the motion unstable, and give the audio a darker, more degraded character. Surprise me. The agent translates that intent into changes across the instrument's controls. I can then react to the result and continue directing it conversationally. The result is a collaborative workflow where the human and AI are playing the same creative instrument through different interfaces. How we built it Glitch Studio is a web application whose creative controls are exposed to compatible agents through WebMCP. Rather than making an AI model infer how the application works from pixels and click coordinates, WebMCP provides structured tools with defined capabilities and parameters. Importantly, the existing interface remains intact. I didn't want to build a chat box that happened to generate glitch art. I wanted to build an actual creative instrument that remains fun for a human to operate while also becoming legible and controllable to an AI agent. Challenges we ran into One of the most interesting challenges was deciding how much control to expose and at what level of abstraction. Software works in parameters. Humans rarely give creative direction that way. We say things like darker , more chaotic , subtle , mechanical , or hypnotic . The challenge wasn't simply making an agent capable of changing a setting. It was exposing enough structured control that the agent could translate higher-level creative intent into combinations of actions. There's also an inherent tension between control and experimentation. Glitch Studio is supposed to produce unexpected results. Giving an agent meaningful control without eliminating that sense of discovery became part of the design. Accomplishments that we're proud of I'm especially proud that the WebMCP integration feels like part of the instrument rather than an AI feature bolted onto it. The same application can now be played in two very different ways: directly by a human through its visual interface, or by an agent through structured tools. More importantly, those modes can work together. A human can give subjective creative direction, let the agent interpret it across multiple controls, react to the result, and continue iterating. The result isn't simply an agent pressing a button on command. It can interpret an idea like "hostile machine dream" and translate that creative intent into actions within the instrument. And, importantly, Glitch Studio is still weird and fun to play manually. What we learned WebMCP changed how I thought about the interface itself. Web applications have traditionally been designed around humans clicking, typing, dragging, and tapping. Agents can imitate those behaviors, but that doesn't necessarily mean they should have to. WebMCP lets the visual interface remain optimized for humans while a structured interface exists alongside it for agents. For creative software, I think that's especially interesting. Natural language doesn't have to replace the instrument. It can become another way of playing it. What's next for Glitch Studio I'd like to expand the creative vocabulary available to agents, expose more of Glitch Studio's audiovisual capabilities, and experiment with agents responding to the evolving state of a creative session rather than simply executing individual requests. More broadly, I'm interested in the idea behind the project: software that humans and agents can operate together, each through the interface that makes the most sense for them. Glitch Studio is a deliberately strange example of that idea. But that's kind of the point. title: JiuTuanZhuo 揪團桌
pitch: Group ordering, agent-native
about_excerpt: Group ordering, agent-native Like Comment Story Updates JiuTuanZhuo home — open a table in one tap. Share link generated after opening a table. Only people with the link can join. Ask Claude in Chrome to order combo vermicelli and sausage for Joe. The agent starts reading the page's WebMCP tools. The agent calls submit_order on the page. Joe's order appears instantly, tagged "Agent order," with no clicks on the UI. Host Elsa orders manually through the UI. The table now shows 2 people, 4 items, NT$220. Human and agent orders sit side by side. Host Elsa orders manually through the UI. The table now shows 2 people, 4 items, NT$220. Human and agent orders sit side by side. The host closes the table. Status flips to Closed and sent to the store; each share is locked. Inspiration Office group orders in Taiwan are rarely voluntary. Someone gets picked to ask everyone what they want, and that person has often never run a group order before. After a wall of "+1" messages in the LINE group, figuring out who ordered what, who changed their mind, and who hasn't paid lands entirely on them. JiuTuanZhuo was built for that person: open a table, drop the link, let the system handle the rest. What it does The official website of 油庫口蚵仔麵線 (Youkukou Oyster Vermicelli) now has a built-in "open a table" feature. The host gets a private link; only people with the link can order. Everyone orders from their own phone, every view syncs in realtime, and the host always sees the current combined order. Tables are fully isolated: three companies can each open a table at the same time without their orders mixing. Humans order through the UI; agents order through WebMCP tools declared on the same page. How we built it Lovable (React) + Supabase (anonymous auth, RLS, RPCs, realtime). The frontend is an interface, not a boundary: pricing, item validation, and permissions are all enforced in Postgres RPCs under RLS, so agents and humans go through the same rules. The page declares three WebMCP tools: get_table_status : marked readOnlyHint , returns structured JSON, with user-entered fields wrapped as user_content so they are treated as data, not instructions add_order : writes require an on-page human confirmation before execution close_table : registered only in the host's session; other participants' agents never see this tool All tools unregister when the table closes. Challenges we ran into The hardest part came first: breaking "+1 in a LINE group" into three actions (open, order, close) and deciding which rules belong in the database layer rather than the frontend. The second was environment setup: getting Chrome to actually call the WebMCP tools on the page took a fair amount of configuration and debugging. The third was pinning down where the latency actually lives. Measured on the page, tool execution is in the millisecond range: read tools return frontend state directly in 0.1–0.3 ms; write tools take 498 ms on the first call and settle at 66–72 ms after that. End to end, one order still takes about a minute. The gap sits entirely in the browser-side agent's tool discovery and reasoning; the page implementation itself is not the bottleneck. Accomplishments that we're proud of This is a 40-year-old street-food institution, and the second-generation owner built the system herself with AI vibe coding, so that customers' agents can place orders directly. Planning, architecture, and deployment were all done in-house, with no outside software vendor and no engineering team. The shop is the test bed: what gets built one day is in front of real customers the next. What we learned When the goal is clear enough, AI can build it. Writing code is not the barrier; knowing whose problem you are solving is. What's next for JiuTuanZhuo 揪團桌 First, reshape the flow around how people in Taiwan actually buy: separate pickup and delivery after an order comes in, and print tickets straight to an IoT kitchen printer. Then, service by service, connect Google Maps scooter-distance calculation, payment, the Lalamove delivery fleet, and e-invoicing, until every step from order to handoff is linked. JiuTuanZhuo is the entry point. From here we build inward, one piece at a time, into a full internal operating system for the shop that agents can run directly, ending with the POS itself. Ordering, ticketing, payment, fulfillment, and invoicing on one shared data layer is what a real closed loop looks like. title: Grand Adventure Engine
pitch: Grand Adventure Engine brings tabletop worlds to life. With WebMCP, ChatGPT becomes a safe Co-DM—reading campaign lore, messaging players, and proposing consequences that stay under human control.
about_excerpt: Grand Adventure Engine brings tabletop worlds to life. With WebMCP, ChatGPT becomes a safe Co-DM—reading campaign lore, messaging players, and proposing consequences that stay under human control. Like 1 Comment Story Updates AI Co-DM cockpit Co-DM cockpit, showcasing an approval Player view Inspiration I’ve been thinking a lot about how we’re naturally wandering back toward old-school terminal interfaces. Games like Zork amazed me as a kid because it felt like I could do almost anything, even though everything still operated within certain boundaries. I’m a huge fan of old-school MUDs, D&D adventures, and good storytelling. When I was ten, I connected through Telnet and played games that way. Grand Adventure Engine draws from all of that: it’s a retelling of an old idea, now guided by an LLM so the world can react when I decide to do something clever, unexpected, or just plain dumb. What it does Grand Adventure Engine turns a text-adventure campaign into a shared workspace for players, human Dungeon Masters, and browser agents. Players explore and act through natural language while the AI narrator maintains the story and game state. Meanwhile, a WebMCP-enabled Co-DM can inspect live scenes, search campaign lore, examine characters and quests, message players, and propose mechanical interventions. High-impact changes—such as applying conditions, adjusting health, or correcting suspicious actions—remain queued for human approval, combining the speed of an agent with visible, accountable DM control. How we built it We extended an ASP.NET Core and PostgreSQL RPG engine with five browser-native WebMCP tools registered through document.modelContext.registerTool: scene inspection, world search, entity inspection, player messaging, and governed mechanical-change proposals. The vanilla JavaScript dashboard provides a real-time DM console and player view through SignalR, while server-side authorization, ownership checks, typed schemas, bounded searches, audit receipts, and human approval gates protect the game state. The application is containerized, deployed over HTTPS through Azure Container Apps, and backed by automated unit, integration, security, and browser tests. The original project was build a few months ago, mostly over the course of a week. I sat on it, doing occasional work, and popping in to update it, play with it, or test it on a newly released model. Originally the plan was to set it up for local LLM use only, but it naturally progressed into using Codex OAuth (on a local node) and it worked really impressively and quickly. When I decided to join the hackathon, I added the admin console, and updated the site to handle the incoming changes. I opened it up to (hopefully) allow the admin to do basically anything they wanted to from Codex. Challenges we ran into The biggest challenge was flexibility—specifically, finding the right balance between hands-on and hands-off control. We needed a way for the DM—or God, depending on how dramatic they’re feeling—to step into a scene, rebalance an encounter, influence an outcome, or simply monitor the game to make sure everyone is having a good time. It’s frustrating when you give an LLM a basic command and it simply says “no.” At the same time, even with strict guidance, players will inevitably find ways to break things. I can’t justifiably blame them for that. If a character wanders off the edge of the map, that’s the developer’s problem—not the player’s. Accomplishments that we're proud of I’m especially happy that I originally architected this project in a way that could be meaningfully extended for this hackathon. I’m proud that I found a balance between giving players free rein and preserving human control when intervention is necessary. The project is also bootstrapped: I designed it to be inexpensive to operate and straightforward to manage. Finally, I’m proud of how quickly I was able to iterate, incorporating the latest WebMCP guidance into an existing project under an extremely short deadline. What we learned The biggest lesson was the difference between having a cool idea, merely bolting WebMCP onto it, and creating something where WebMCP is genuinely useful. This competition forced me to assess ideas honestly and pivot quickly when something wasn’t coming together. ChatGPT provided valuable feedback throughout the process, helping me turn the project into something fun and functional while still aiming for a creative and novel use of the technology. What's next for Great Adventure Engine Honestly: playtesting and gathering interest. This is an iterative project, and so far it has only been playtested by me—which means someone else will almost certainly discover an imaginative new way to break it. The plan is simple: playtest, study the logs, fix the problems, and keep going. I’m particularly interested in bringing it into Discord communities, where I can host the engine from my own machine and let the AI respond directly in Discord. That would make it an inexpensive, accessible way for groups to run persistent adventures together. title: FinalPick
pitch: FinalPick turns human choices between AI generated text and image option into reusable decision memory, while 6 WebMCP tools help agents prepare reviews without taking final authority away from people
about_excerpt: FinalPick turns human choices between AI generated text and image option into reusable decision memory, while 6 WebMCP tools help agents prepare reviews without taking final authority away from people Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration AI gives creative teams more options than ever, but the reasoning behind a final choice often disappears in chat, spreadsheets, or handoff notes. The next teammate or model sees the result without knowing the brief, rejected alternatives, or why the decision made sense at that moment. We built FinalPick around a question raised by agentic browsing: how can an agent reduce review work without quietly taking over human judgment? What it does FinalPick is a browser-based decision workspace for reviewing actual text and image candidates. Each round contains one medium, a brief, constraints, and evidence, so options are compared on equal terms. A person selects a candidate, records reasons and an optional note, and saves that context as decision memory. In later rounds, FinalPick requires a current assessment before revealing compatible past decisions as useful, non-binding precedent. Six WebMCP tools let an agent inspect the review and candidates, retrieve precedent, and stage a comparison or follow-up question in the same visible interface. The agent can commit only after a person creates a short-lived, one-time approval in the page. How we built it We built FinalPick as a static top-level web app using HTML, CSS, and JavaScript ES modules, with localStorage for versioned rounds, staged work, and decisions. When a browser exposes document.modelContext.registerTool , the page registers six narrow WebMCP tools; without it, the complete human workflow still works. Tool schemas reject extra fields, read tools are annotated as read-only, and UI actions and tool handlers share the same validated state layer. We used Codex in a recursive improvement loop: define a small slice, implement it, run unit and Playwright browser checks, inspect responsive captures and UX feedback, then use those findings to shape the next slice. This loop expanded the prototype from built-in image examples to user-created text and HTTPS-image rounds while preserving the authority boundary. Challenges we ran into The hardest challenge was making WebMCP essential rather than decorative. A chat recommendation alone would not improve the product, so agent work had to appear visibly in the review and reduce copying between systems. We also had to make chained tool calls reliable by returning the candidate, analysis, decision, and approval identifiers needed by later calls. Human approval introduced edge cases around changed selections, expiration, cancellation, and token reuse. Finally, early screens felt like dense metadata dashboards, so we progressively disclosed evidence, agent staging, and history while keeping the creative artifact and decision controls prominent. Accomplishments that we're proud of The prototype supports complete create, select, save, and reload flows for real text and image candidates. It registers exactly six WebMCP tools in the local integration harness, keeps staged agent work visibly separate from committed decisions, and rejects missing, revoked, expired, or reused approvals. Decision memory preserves the brief, chosen artifact, reasons, note, and later superseded revisions. The current verification suite reports 27 passing unit tests, a successful static build, six registered tools in the browser roundtrip, responsive desktop and mobile captures, and no browser console errors. What we learned Structured tools are most useful when they act on the same state people can see, not when they create a second agent-only workflow. Human control is stronger when enforced by application state—here, an approval that no WebMCP tool can create—rather than by prompt wording. We also learned that memory should provide context, not automatic preference: showing what changed between then and now makes precedent useful without turning it into a hidden scoring model. What's next for FinalPick Next, we want to harden hosted-browser interoperability across supported ChatGPT configurations and test the workflow with more first-time users. Beyond the prototype, we would add collaborative persistence, accounts, richer asset versioning and uploads, and explicit review or dispute states only after designing the necessary permission, privacy, retention, and conflict-resolution rules.
