title: SAW-Bridge — Self-Assembling WebMCP Bridge
pitch: Don't wait for the web to write tools for agents. Let agents write them, and make that safe to allow.
about_excerpt: Don't wait for the web to write tools for agents. Let agents write them, and make that safe to allow. Like Comment Story Updates SAW Bridge Inspiration I kept reading the same sentence in every WebMCP write-up: give agents tools, not DOM. I agreed with it completely. Then I opened a handful of sites I use every day with WebMCP enabled in Chrome, and every single one of them handed the agent an empty document.modelContext . That's the whole problem, right there. The standard is good. The tools don't exist yet, because somebody has to sit down and write them for every site, one at a time. So agents are back to guessing from screenshots on 99% of the web while we wait. I got stuck on a question: why does registerTool exist as a runtime API at all? If tools were meant to be a fixed list, you'd declare them once at load. But WebMCP lets you register at any moment, and it ships a toolchange event so listeners find out when the surface changes. Most people use that for SPA routing. I wanted to see what happens if you take it literally. What if the agent registers the tools? What it does SAW-Bridge gives a page three meta-tools instead of a catalogue: saw_inspect_page_scope — look at the page and report what it actually exposes saw_suggest_and_register_tool — design a schema and register a real, lasting WebMCP tool saw_execute_code_mode — write code and run it once, for one-off work The demo is a dashboard of world happiness and AI readiness data. It has a filter chip for happiness above 7.5. It deliberately has no chip for 7.4, and no tool for it either. So I asked ChatGPT's in-app browser for 7.4. It listed the page's tools, called saw_inspect_page_scope , found the site's own filterByMinHappiness function, and then it stopped and asked me before touching anything. I said yes. The table dropped from twelve rows to four — Finland 7.82, Denmark 7.64, Iceland 7.56, Netherlands 7.42. All above 7.4, and the chart re-rendered through the app's own code path, not a simulated click on something that looked clickable. The part I didn't expect is that the agent chose between the two strategies. For a one-off threshold it wrote code and ran it once, which is the cheaper call. Ask for something reusable and it takes the other path and registers a lasting tool — and then Chrome's own DevTools WebMCP panel lists that tool and will invoke it with your parameters, because by that point it's an ordinary WebMCP tool. It isn't picking between one blessed tool and scraping the screen. It's deciding how permanent its new capability should be. Every mutating call goes through an approval dialog first, showing the exact tool and the exact arguments. There's a live audit drawer so you can watch what was discovered, assembled, approved and refused, and why. There are two delivery surfaces sharing one engine: a single-file SDK a site drops in, and a Chrome extension that injects the same thing into sites that ship nothing. How we built it The core is plain WebMCP. Tools register through document.modelContext.registerTool() . Consumers discover with getTools() and invoke with executeTool() . Registration takes an AbortSignal , so aborting genuinely unregisters. Assembled tools get untrustedContentHint: true ; read-only ones get readOnlyHint: true . Two pieces took actual thinking. Finding what a page exposes. The interesting stuff on a page is buried among roughly a thousand standard browser globals, and a hand-written denylist rots the moment Chrome ships a new API. What worked: create a hidden iframe, read Object.getOwnPropertyNames off its contentWindow to get a reference set of standard globals from the browser itself , then diff the real window against it. Whatever's left is the page's own surface, and it stays correct as browsers change. Then rank candidates before truncating — an object with callable methods outranks a bare object, which outranks a loose function. I learned that one the hard way, see below. Compiling what the agent writes. This lands on the same insight as Cloudflare's Code Mode : models handle capability better when they can write code against an API than when they pick from a long list of tool definitions. I want to be precise about the relationship — I did not use @cloudflare/codemode . Cloudflare runs model-written code in a server-side Worker isolate. This runs it in the page's own realm, and that difference is the reason the project exists. The currently applied filter, the selected row, the chart instance holding the data — none of that exists outside the page. A sandbox elsewhere can't touch what the user is actually looking at without replicating the whole session. The token math lands in the same place by a different road. Code Mode collapses N tool definitions into one code tool. Here there's no catalogue to collapse: three meta-tools, and concrete tools show up only when a task calls for one. That's progressive disclosure, which MCP's own client guidance recommends when definitions start eating context — except the tools being disclosed don't have to exist yet. Challenges we ran into The demo was completely dead and looked fine. The SDK called init() at the end of its bootstrap. There was no function called init anywhere in the file. The whole thing threw on the last line, so the three meta-tools never registered — but the polyfill and the global had already been assigned, so the page looked healthy and every button failed silently. I only caught it by building a jsdom harness that clicked the actual buttons on the actual HTML. My REPL couldn't run its own demo. The code path wrapped snippets in return (...) , which only accepts a single expression. My own demo passed a statement body. It threw a SyntaxError every time. Now it tries the expression form, falls back to a statement body, and compiles async so snippets can await . executeTool doesn't take a tool name. The spec says it takes a RegisteredTool object from getTools() and resolves with the stringified result. I'd written it to accept a string and return a plain object. Against my own polyfill it worked perfectly. In a browser with native WebMCP it would have rejected on the first call — the exact environment judges test in. That was a genuinely unnerving thing to find. It worked from file:// and broke as soon as I deployed. WebMCP needs an origin-keyed agent cluster, which means an Origin-Agent-Cluster: ?1 response header. file:// is exempt, and localhost is a secure context but is not origin-keyed, so this fails only after hosting, with a SecurityError and no hint. Both runtimes now check at startup and name what's missing instead of letting you guess. The security dialog could be hijacked by the thing it was guarding against. This one bothered me most. When an agent authors tools, tool metadata becomes untrusted input, and I'd built the approval dialog with innerHTML . A payload like x renders live markup inside the security gate and can click its own Approve button. I wrote the test first, watched it fail, then fixed it: closed shadow root, DOM references captured at document_start , every agent-supplied string inserted as text. Turns out this is a named attack class — tool surface poisoning — and the spec's own boundary section is still marked TODO. I also found window.SAWBridge.setSettings sitting there in public, which meant one line of page script could switch the approval gate off before an agent did anything. I spent an evening debugging the wrong browser. I asked ChatGPT's browser plugin which WebMCP tools it could see and got a confident, detailed, completely wrong answer — it listed my UI button labels as if they were tools, and reported the tool counter as "0", which is the value in the static HTML before JavaScript runs. It had fetched my page, not executed it. That plugin surface isn't the WebMCP-enabled in-app browser. Once I tested in the right place, everything worked on the first try. And the ecosystem was further along than I thought. Somewhere in the middle of this I found @mcp-b/webmcp-polyfill , the desktop relays, the React hooks — all shipped, all solid. I sat there for a while genuinely wondering whether I'd built something nobody needed. What snapped me out of it was noticing what those projects have in common: they all treat the tool surface as trusted freight to be transported. None of them ask what happens when the freight writes itself. Accomplishments that we're proud of The 7.4 moment. Not because it's technically dramatic, but because the page genuinely could not do it before and nobody wrote code for that specific request. It came out of inspection at runtime. Fixing the injection bug properly instead of quietly. The test with that payload is in the repo and it fails against the old build, which means it measures something real rather than decorating the README. Being honest in the polyfill. It rejects duplicate names, enforces the spec's 1–128 character name rules, hides execute from getTools() , and ret

title: Knoww
pitch: Knoww is the prediction market layer for the internet. It turns research and live market odds into a shared human-agent workspace for taking trades and preparing decisions with people in final control
about_excerpt: Knoww is the prediction market layer for the internet. It turns research and live market odds into a shared human-agent workspace for taking trades and preparing decisions with people in final control Like Comment Story Updates What Knoww does Knoww turns live prediction markets into a shared research workspace where people and agents can explore market information together. A person can ask an agent to find relevant events, narrow the visible market list, open a valid result, compare related markets, inspect the selected order book, change the chart range, and prepare the trade interface for review. Every step happens on the same page the person is viewing. The result remains visible, understandable, and easy to correct. Knoww gives the agent structured access to market discovery and analysis without giving it control of a wallet, a signature, or trade submission. The problem Prediction market research involves more than opening a result page. A single event may contain several related markets, outcomes, probabilities, charts, and order books. The useful context also depends on the filters, selected market, and chart range currently visible on the page. A browser agent can attempt to reconstruct this workflow through page inspection and clicks, but it must infer the meaning of interface elements and continuously track changing page state. That process can be fragile. WebMCP lets Knoww expose the meaning behind the interface directly. Instead of guessing which card, control, or outcome represents the user's intent, the agent receives narrow and typed operations connected to the current page. Why WebMCP is the right fit A separate market data integration could return probabilities and market information, but it would not naturally share the interface state the person is currently inspecting. WebMCP allows the person and the agent to work with the same filters, selected market, order book, and chart range. When the agent changes something, the person sees the result immediately through the normal Knoww interface. This creates one continuous research workflow. The agent can discover relevant events, narrow the market list, open a valid result, compare related markets, inspect the selected order book, adjust the chart range, and prepare the trade interface for review. Every action remains visible on the page. The person can verify the result, correct the agent, or stop the workflow at any point. What I built I added 12 WebMCP tools across the market discovery page and individual event pages. On /markets , get_markets_page_context reads the current page state. search_events searches public events. set_market_filters changes only supported visible filters. load_more_markets advances the visible results. open_event can open only an event already returned by Knoww. On an event page, get_current_event_context reads the active event and current selection. find_markets_on_page finds relevant markets within the event. compare_markets returns a focused comparison. get_selected_order_book reads the currently selected order book. select_market_view changes the visible market. set_chart_range changes the visible chart period. prepare_trade prepares the trade interface for the person to review. The available tools change with the page context. The market discovery page exposes discovery and navigation capabilities. An event page exposes comparison, order book, chart, and trade preparation capabilities. This keeps the tool set focused while supporting a complete workflow from market discovery to decision preparation. Example experience A person can ask: "Find Bitcoin related prediction markets, narrow the list, open the most relevant event, compare its markets, inspect the selected order book, and prepare the trade view for my review." The agent can complete this workflow through structured WebMCP tools while the person watches the same page change and remains free to correct any step. This is more reliable than asking the agent to infer the entire workflow from buttons, cards, and page layout. Human control and safety The WebMCP tools cannot connect a wallet, sign a transaction, or submit a trade. prepare_trade only prepares the visible trade interface. The person must inspect the values and complete any action with financial consequences. Every tool uses a typed and bounded input schema. Search limits, filter values, pagination, and navigation targets are constrained. open_event accepts only events already returned by Knoww. Tool results are marked as untrusted public content. These boundaries give the agent enough capability to provide meaningful assistance while preserving human control. Technical implementation Knoww uses Next.js, React, and TypeScript, and is deployed with Cloudflare Workers. It reads public Polymarket market data. I connected the WebMCP handlers to Knoww's existing React state and page actions instead of recreating the market logic in a separate integration. This means the person and the agent work with the same filters, selected market, order book, and chart range. When a tool changes the page state, the normal Knoww interface reflects that change. Tool registration runs through top level page JavaScript so the tools can be discovered by ChatGPT's in app browser. I also added registration cleanup so a normal React unmount does not incorrectly report a registration failure. Testing I tested the production /markets page in ChatGPT's in app browser. ChatGPT discovered all five tools registered on that page. I successfully executed get_markets_page_context and used search_events to find Bitcoin related events on the live production site. The remaining seven tools are registered only on event pages, where their event specific context is available. Challenges and lessons The difficult part was not exposing more control. It was deciding exactly which control the agent should receive. The WebMCP tools had to stay synchronized with React state while maintaining clear boundaries. Search limits, filter values, pagination, navigation targets, and available page actions all needed to be constrained. The page lifecycle also required careful handling so route changes and normal React cleanup did not appear as tool registration failures. The most important lesson was that WebMCP is strongest when it reveals the semantics of an existing interface without bypassing that interface or its permission model. Knoww now gives an agent enough structure to help someone reason about live prediction markets, while stopping exactly where financial authority should remain with the person. title: Zingposts
pitch: Interesting things, organized together: a WebMCP-native marketplace where people work with the outside agents they already trust.
about_excerpt: Interesting things, organized together: a WebMCP-native marketplace where people work with the outside agents they already trust. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Browsing old cars, boats, campers, motorcycles, and machinery is fun. Managing the hunt is not. Good finds get lost across tabs, marketplace search misses obvious matches, alerts are rigid, research lives in scattered notes, and negotiations have no shared memory. A three-way trade is almost impossible to reason about cleanly. Zingposts starts from a different premise: the marketplace should be equally legible to people and their agents without embedding a model in the product. The site owns its native listings and structured deal workflow, while outside listings can be tracked as clearly labeled snapshots. What it does Zingposts is a complete peer-to-peer marketplace and durable workspace for interesting things. People can browse realistic native inventory, create and publish listings, upload photos, save finds, build boards, set alerts, keep research notebooks, message sellers, prepare offers, and create structured multi-party trade rooms. Outside finds can be tracked without confusing them with Zingposts-owned inventory. A connected outside agent receives a compact persistent core plus one focused pack drawn from 121 structured WebMCP tools. It can search with compound criteria, compare candidates, organize boards, tag and rank finds, record cited research and inspection risks, monitor price changes, draft communications and offers, calculate acquisition cost, propose trade scenarios, and coordinate the shared gallery, focus, or thumbnail canvas. The human uses the same structure through a canvas-first interface. Zingposts itself contains no LLM. The centerpiece is the shared canvas: an outside agent opens a durable session, places a shortlist, recommendation, or focused question beside the marketplace objects, and pauses only when human judgment matters. The person can inspect the exact listings and rationale, choose an option or add context, and return structured guidance. The agent reads that durable response on its next tool call and continues. This is turn-taking over shared marketplace objects, not a chatbot transcript. The loop now extends across visits. get_workspace_resume returns the last acknowledged checkpoint, everything that changed since, structured blockers, human responses, proposal status, and safe next actions. An agent can acknowledge the checkpoint only after processing it, so “come back later” is an explicit protocol rather than a hope that conversation context survived. For broad edits, the agent can prepare a sourced, versioned change set instead of making a trail of one-off mutations. Zingposts previews each proposed change in plain language, checks the expected object versions, and lets the person selectively accept only the changes they want. Agents cannot approve their own change sets. Completed deals can be recorded as private outcomes, and transparent aggregate patterns report counts, prices, and reasons without inventing a model-generated score. Either side can arrive first. A person can explore immediately in a prototype workspace, then replace a test email and verify the real address through Supabase only when work reaches the marketplace boundary. One Bring my agent click copies the canonical guide URL. Or an unauthenticated agent can inspect five setup-only tools and open a prototype handoff for the person. Once the person signs in, safe private tools appear automatically to an outside agent operating that browser document. Independent 12-hour revocable sessions remain available through one-use invites or codes for separate-browser or unattended work. The human remains in control. Publishing, enabling notifications, sending a message, submitting or responding to an offer, and inviting a trade participant stop at a visible confirmation gate. Every human and agent action is attributed, and reversible work can be undone. Why WebMCP is essential Without WebMCP, an agent has to infer intent from buttons and screen position. That is brittle for a marketplace with dozens of interdependent objects: listings, boards, research, alerts, conversations, offers, people, assets, and constraints. WebMCP gives Zingposts a stable collaboration language. “Find pre-1980 boats under $15,000, put the best four on a board, record the title risks, and draft a message to the strongest seller” becomes a sequence of typed, attributable actions. The human can watch the same state change, refine it directly, and approve the parts that cross a consequential boundary. That makes the product meaningfully better with an agent—not merely automatable. How we built it Zingposts uses React 19 and Next.js on Netlify. Supabase Auth provides verified human sessions, Supabase Postgres holds marketplace, identity, agent-session, and workflow state, and Supabase Storage holds listing photos. Versioned SQL migrations keep direct browser access locked behind row-level security. The browser client exposes 121 declarative tools through the WebMCP modelContext surface, but only five setup tools while signed out. After the person signs in, AbortSignal-managed registration keeps a compact persistent core plus one replaceable focused capability pack, so navigation never accumulates an oversized registry or silently unlocks business actions. get_agent_bootstrap returns setup guidance while signed out, then canonical browser-delegated identity, workspace, attention, active collaboration, capability index, and guide version after sign-in. activate_capability switches the focused pack without moving the person; open_for_human_review is optional. The action layer derives canonical human and agent identity on the server, prevents duplicate profiles, enforces ownership and state-transition enums, creates reviewable drafts, writes attributed activity, stores inverse operations for undo, supports idempotency keys and optimistic versions, returns stable deep links and WebMCP-native structured errors, and converts consequential operations into pending confirmations. Isolated QA runs register only their own artifacts, provide an exact cleanup preview, and require human approval before deletion. The marketplace is seeded with original project-owned imagery and realistic records so the full human-agent workflow is understandable immediately. WebMCP registration is document-scoped, while Zingposts durably stores connection profiles, scopes, alerts, boards, research, drafts, versions, and audit history. The public /for-agents guide and /api/agent-guide contract show agents how to reconnect safely without storing an invite, code, or stale catalog. Challenges The main design challenge was not adding more agent power; it was deciding where that power should stop. We separated preparation from commitment. Research, organization, comparison, and drafting can proceed quickly. Communication, publication, notifications, invitations, and financial commitments pause for the human. We also designed external-listing tracking so provenance stays honest. Zingposts can organize an outside find, but it never claims that its cached price, availability, or seller statements are authoritative. Accomplishments A coherent marketplace, not a WebMCP proof of concept 121 tools spanning authentication, onboarding, resumable work sessions, versioned proposals, outcomes, canvas views, discovery, organization, negotiation, and multi-party trade Agent-first and person-first onboarding with a five-tool setup surface before human sign-in Durable agent-to-human-to-agent turn-taking with a unified attention queue Explicit resume checkpoints and structured blockers for work that continues across agent runs Sourced, versioned change sets with semantic previews and selective human acceptance Private outcome recording with transparent, non-AI aggregate patterns Live agent activity, exact-payload approval, idempotency, dry runs, structured errors, and stable deep links No built-in AI or model dependency Supabase human authentication plus opaque invite URLs, code fallback, and single-use, expiring, revocable agent sessions—without password or session sharing Persistent bootstrap plus navigation-independent focused capability activation Structured errors, strict workflow transitions, optimistic concurrency, and namespaced QA cleanup Durable attribution, confirmations, and undo Native seller photo upload and publishing workflow Clear separation between owned listings and outside tracked snapshots Production build, automated API smoke tests, desktop browser testing, and mobile verification What we learned Human-agent collaboration works best when both sides operate on the same durable objects. A board is better than a chat-only list. A research notebook is better than an ephemeral summary. A pending confirmation is better than asking the model to remember which action is sensitive. We also learned to separate document-scoped WebMCP
video_title: Zingposts — Human + Agent Commerce on One WebMCP Canvas
video_transcript_excerpt: What if a marketplace did not contain its own AI? What if it simply gave people and any outside agent a beautiful shared place to work? This is Zing Posts, peer-to-peer commerce designed for Web MCP. The first visit is deliberately small. While signed out, the browser exposes only five setup tools. An agent can inspect the bootstrap guide, prepare a handoff for the person, or accept a one-use credential. After sign-in, it re-discovers the real workspace. Now, human and agent share the same durable canvas. The person can browse visually, flip through finds, drag items onto colored boards, and set preferences. The agent can search the same listings, compare candidates, rank a board, tag discoveries, and leave its reasoning beside the work. Web MCP is not hidden behind one giant prompt. Zing Posts keeps a persistent core, then activates the focus capability for the page. Here, the marketplace pack includes search, view control, comparison, board organization, and the option to open exactly the item a person should review. On a listing, the collaboration gets deeper. An outside agent can build a cited research notebook, record comparable sales, calculate a price range, and draft an offer plan with repair, transport, tax, contingency, and budget assumptions. The evidence stays visible. The private target stays private. The workbench is the shared memory: agent findings, human notes, decisions, undo history, alerts, conversations, offers, and even multi-party trade rooms persist as structured marketplace state. The agent does not own the experience. It helps move evidence toward a decision, while the person stays in control. That control becomes explicit at the verification boundary. Browsing, organizing, research, and drafting stay fluid. Publishing a listing, enabling an alert, contacting a seller, sending an offer, or advancing a trade creates a pending approval. Only the human can cross that line, and every outcome is recorded. The result is a web MCP native marketplace with no built-in model and no agent lock-in. Five tools for setup, 34 focused tools on this marketplace canvas, and 121 across the complete signed-in catalog. zingpost.com Bring your agent and find something worth saving.

title: CliDeck MCP — Network Evidence Workbench
pitch: Turn real network evidence into version-aware, source-backed answers that people and WebMCP agents can inspect together.
about_excerpt: Turn real network evidence into version-aware, source-backed answers that people and WebMCP agents can inspect together. Like Comment Story Updates CliDeck MCP — Network Evidence Workbench One-line Summary Turn real network evidence into version-aware, source-backed answers that a person and a WebMCP agent can inspect together without giving the agent hidden access to the complete file. Problem Network engineers regularly work from device output, configurations, logs, and vendor manuals. A general-purpose agent can reason about that material, but it may rely on stale command knowledge, mix guidance from the wrong platform, or lose the exact device and software context as the investigation changes. Copying an entire configuration or manual into a chat is also a poor control boundary. The engineer needs to decide which evidence is shared, see what was redacted, and distinguish verified product results from the agent's own interpretation. Solution CliDeck's Network Evidence Workbench gives the engineer and browser agent one revision-safe case workspace. The engineer supplies a question and real device evidence, chooses the exact line or PDF-page window, and reviews local redaction before anything leaves the browser. CliDeck detects the device context and searches its active, version-aware network knowledge and operational workflows. The browser agent discovers six narrowly scoped WebMCP tools for the same live case. It can analyze the selected evidence, search CliDeck, explain only the current sourced results, and track a real research task when the answer is unknown. Agent interpretation is visibly separated from official CliDeck results, and stale responses cannot overwrite a newer case. The page never connects to a network device and never executes commands. Why This Matters This is a concrete example of a web application becoming better when people and agents use it together. The engineer keeps the controls that require judgment: which evidence to share, which context is correct, and whether a result is applicable. The agent gets a typed, current capability surface instead of guessing from pixels or asking the user to copy data back and forth. For network operations, the difference is material. An answer for Cisco IOS XE 16.10 must not silently become an answer for NX-OS or for a newer release. The workbench carries model, operating-system, version, result revision, provenance, and case version through the interaction so that the collaboration remains inspectable. How We Used AI The browser agent uses WebMCP to reason over the current case and place a bounded interpretation beside CliDeck's deterministic results. The agent does not become the source of truth and does not receive the selected evidence until the person enables one explicit sharing control. CliDeck's production knowledge-growth pipeline also uses isolated GPT-5.6 Luna runs for work that requires semantic judgment: discovering official material, analyzing ambiguous fragments, independent verification, and deep review. The deterministic core—not the model—enforces schemas, applicability, provenance, risk rules, conflict handling, quality thresholds, and immutable publication. Once published, a known answer is returned without a model call. How We Used Codex Codex was the primary engineering environment and collaborator throughout the project. During the challenge it helped replace an early artificial simulator with the real Network Evidence Workbench, design the WebMCP lifecycle, implement the React and TypeScript surface, add local text/PDF processing and redaction, connect the workbench to production MCP services, and build the evaluation and deployment workflow. Codex also helped find and correct material boundary defects before release, including over-wide evidence exposure, incomplete structured-secret redaction, stale async updates, missing production grants, and cross-platform retrieval mixing. The final release was exercised against unit, integration, privacy, security, WebMCP lifecycle, product-evaluation, production smoke, and browser tests. Key Features Six stable WebMCP tools: read_network_case , analyze_network_case , search_network_case , present_network_case_analysis , start_case_research , and get_case_research_status . A complete manual experience through ordinary controls when WebMCP is not available. TXT, LOG, MD, CSV, JSON, JSONL, HTML, and text-layer PDF input with explicit file, page, line-window, and byte limits. Local secret redaction before network requests, with a visible disclosure of the operational identifiers intentionally retained as diagnostic context. A monotonically increasing case_version , request cancellation, and stale-result rejection across parsing, analysis, search, presentation, and research polling. Version-aware knowledge and workflow retrieval with active-revision source metadata and honest nearest-version or cross-platform warnings. A separate agent-analysis block whose citations are limited to the current result set. Real tracked expert research for genuinely unknown questions, with idempotency and no task credential exposed to the browser agent. Architecture The public React/Vite application is served at /webmcp . Complete files and raw extracted text stay in browser memory. Only the explicit, locally redacted evidence window is sent through a byte-bounded same-origin JSON-RPC client to CliDeck's public MCP endpoint. The six WebMCP tools are registered with document.modelContext.registerTool . Their React lifecycle carries WebMCP's AbortSignal into the same-origin MCP request and aborts registrations on unmount. The backend is TypeScript/Hono with PostgreSQL for immutable knowledge revisions, applicability, provenance, workflow retrieval, research tasks, audit, and publication state. Testing Instructions Open https://mcp.clideck.com/webmcp in ChatGPT's in-app browser, or in a WebMCP-enabled Google Chrome browser. Click Load Cisco 16.10 sample , then Analyze evidence . Confirm that the detected context is Catalyst 9300 / IOS XE / 16.10 and the case version increases. Click Search knowledge . The closest EFSU guidance should be labelled as nearest guidance rather than an exact version match. Enable Share redacted evidence with browser agent and ask the agent to read the case and explain the current result. Its text should appear in the separate Browser agent analysis section. Click Load Cisco 17.8.1 sample , analyze, and search again. Confirm that the case version changes and the EFSU result now shows an applicable version range. Optionally upload a safe text-layer PDF or LOG, select a page/line window, and repeat the flow. Complete files remain local to the browser session. Ask a genuinely unanswered question and use Research this gap to see the real tracked research lifecycle. Click Reset and confirm that evidence, results, analysis, polling, and local file references are cleared. No credentials are required for the public demo. Public Demo Link https://mcp.clideck.com/webmcp Public Repository Link https://github.com/SmartRoot7/clideck-mcp The repository is public and includes a visible Apache-2.0 license, all source code, test suites, deployment scripts, and judge walkthrough instructions. Production knowledge and third-party manuals are intentionally not bundled. title: Barge In
pitch: A human and an AI drawing on the same canvas — and the page can say no.
about_excerpt: A human and an AI drawing on the same canvas — and the page can say no. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Most WebMCP demos hand an agent tools that read the page. I wanted to hand it tools that touch something a person is touching at the same time, and see what breaks. Everything broke immediately, and in an interesting way. In the first experiment a human drew seven strokes across the agent's work-in-progress. The agent never noticed. Not a bug — WebMCP is pull-only. A page cannot speak to its agent. It has no notify , no event, no way up the pipe. It can only answer when it is called. So the question became: with only that one channel, how much control can a page take back? What it does The page gives an agent nine drawing tools. Ask it for a lion; it draws one. Then pick up the mouse and draw two wheels underneath it while it works. 19:18:40 You Drew a line (9 points) ← you barge in mid-batch … You × 7 more 19:18:48 AI ⛔ Blocked canvas_batch — canvas changed by human 19:18:48 AI Inspected the updated canvas 19:19:02 AI Updated the plan — A cute smiling male lion car, using the completed red user-drawn wheels and connecting them to the mane-body with a simple axle. 19:19:12 AI Drew 39 shapes in one batch Its half-finished mane stops where it stopped, because the rest of that batch was dropped . It cannot draw again until it has looked, and then said what your wheels changed about the plan — and what it is giving up because of them. In this run it said, unprompted: "Both red wheels now have hubs, inner rims, and tread marks. I'll keep those wheel details untouched and add only the axle connection." Then it drew the axle. Not a lion that happens to still have wheels beside it — a lion joined to your wheels by a bar it decided to add. About sixty seconds, start to finish, with nothing scripted anywhere. Every one of those decisions came out of the agent reading tool output. The drawing is deliberately crude. An image model would draw a better lion. The log is the deliverable. How I built it First, a word on what this is not . WebMCP already has a human-in-the-loop hook — requestUserInteraction , which lets a tool pause and ask the person to confirm. That is agent-initiated : the agent decides to ask, the person waits in front of a dialog, and says yes or no to something already drafted. It is consent. This is the opposite shape. It is human-initiated : the person acts whenever they like, without asking, and the agent finds out afterwards that it has been overruled. It is pre-emption. Both belong in a page people and agents share, and the spec currently offers only the first. Someone who is making something does not want to approve the agent's plan — they want to reach in and change it, and have the agent catch up. Then four rules, each one arrived at by watching the previous version fail. 1 — Refuse, don't stop. A page cannot interrupt an agent. But an agent calls a tool every few seconds, so refusing the next call feels, to the person watching, like an instant stop. Every writing tool calls guard() first. 2 — If you cannot push, answer when you are pulled. Everything the page needs to say rides back on the tool the agent already calls. canvas_describe always appends what the human did since the last check. It is the only channel WebMCP offers, so the page uses it as one. 3 — Seeing is not accepting. The first version asked , in prose, for the agent to re-plan around the interruption. It obliged — narrated the change beautifully, then carried on drawing its original picture. So looking stopped being enough: canvas_describe now hands over to a second gate, and only canvas_replan(observed, new_plan, abandoning) opens it. All three fields are required. abandoning is the load-bearing one — a plan you have given nothing up for is the old plan wearing a new sentence. 4 — The human's marks are never painted over. Told to incorporate the wheels, the agent laid its mane straight over them. Nothing was deleted and the counts were honest, but half the wheels vanished from the picture, and the picture is what people read. Paint order is now fixed: whatever the agent draws goes underneath. Challenges I ran into Requests land; prohibitions do not. "Check the canvas before you draw" was ignored, however it was worded. Refusing the call was not. Every rule here is enforced by a code path, not by asking nicely. Batching fixed the speed and broke the premise. A realistic lion took six minutes — the agent called canvas_stroke with three points every four seconds. Adding canvas_batch cut it to one call . The next tester's report was one sentence: "It drew everything at once, so I had no time to barge in." Painting the batch slowly to look interruptible would have been a lie — the picture was already decided. So a batch is now accepted and laid down one shape at a time over a few seconds, and if the human draws during that, the rest is dropped and never happens. Batching gained an honest price: bigger is faster, and bigger loses more. The agent answers in the conversation's language. Asked in Japanese, it wrote its new plan in Japanese, onto an English canvas. Fixed by asking for English in three places — the tool description, each parameter's description, and the return value read immediately before the call. One place was not enough. Accomplishments I'm proud of The measured finding that surprised me most has nothing to do with drawing: A tool's description changes how an agent batches its work. With a neutral description, the agent drew a spiral as 2 points per call, ~40 calls, over a minute. After adding "Pass every point in one call. Each call costs a few seconds, so the number of calls is the wait the user sees" — 121 points in a single call, in 4 seconds. Same tool, same model, 15× fewer round trips, from one paragraph of prose. What I learned That a page under WebMCP is not a passive surface. It is the only party in the room that knows what the person just did, and the return value of a tool is a real communication channel — one the agent reads carefully and acts on. Almost all the design work turned out to be writing. What's next The mechanism is now a standalone file, barge-in.js , that knows nothing about drawing. It knows only who touched the page last, and it is four lines to add to a page: const bi = BargeIn.create({ describeTool: 'doc_read', replanTool: 'doc_replan' }); editor.addEventListener('input', () => { bi.note('you', 'edited a paragraph'); // look() reports this bi.humanActed(); // this refuses the agent }); function doc_insert(p) { bi.guard(); /* … */ } // guard every write function doc_read() { return Object.assign({ text: editor.value }, bi.look()); } The first application already runs, as a second page in the same repo: examples/doc.html , a document a person and an agent write at the same time — six tools, the same barge-in.js behind them, about 250 lines of page on top. Rule 4 changes shape there, and that is the interesting part. On the canvas it means the agent's paint goes underneath. In a document it means a paragraph you have typed in is yours : ⛔ That paragraph belongs to the user — they typed in it. It can never be rewritten or deleted. Write around it: use doc_insert to add a paragraph before or after, and leave theirs exactly as it is. The agent has to compose around you — and on the first live attempt it went further than the rule required: "You replaced paragraph 2 during the edit, so it now belongs to you and must remain unchanged. I'll adapt the surrounding paragraphs to present your sentence as the central instruction and keep the document concise." It did not just leave the sentence alone. It restructured the document around it : the one paragraph it was forbidden to touch became the thing the other two were rewritten to support. That is the difference between a lock and a collaboration, and it came out of the same barge-in.js , with none of the canvas's code. Next in line is a form: an agent fills fifteen fields, you correct the third while it works, and rule 4 becomes a field the human has touched is never written again . A canvas is simply the smallest place where you can see this conflict happen. The rest — a spreadsheet, a slide deck, a whiteboard, a CAD model — is the same four rules with different nouns. Two pages to try Live (canvas): https://mcp.kitemir.jp/canvas/ Live (shared document): https://mcp.kitemir.jp/canvas/examples/doc.html Repo (MIT): https://github.com/zz08matsujp-max/barge-in Video: https://youtu.be/B3qbrK8W5Kw Requires the ChatGPT desktop app's built-in browser with Settings > Browser > Permissions > Enable site tools on, and GPT-5.6 Sol or Terra. The badge at the top right says whether WebMCP is live; if it is not, click it and the page prints a diagnostic table instead of failing silently. title: Storyforge
pitch: Have you ever wanted to play a collaborative video game but your friends aren't available? Meet Storyforge — a fantasy rpg game where humans and AI agent (using WebMCP) collaborate on fantasy quests.
about_excerpt: Have you ever wanted to play a collaborative video game but your friends aren't available? Meet Storyforge — a fantasy rpg game where humans and AI agent (using WebMCP) collaborate on fantasy quests. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Most game companions feel like scripted followers, while AI assistants usually live in a separate chat window. We wanted to explore what happens when an agent becomes a genuine party member—one that understands the battlefield, remembers the journey, offers useful advice, and acts through the same rules as the player. Storyforge grew from the idea that AI should not replace the player or secretly rewrite the game. It should make the adventure feel more social, strategic, and alive. What it does Storyforge is a fantasy action RPG in which the player becomes the Last Heir and travels across five corrupted realms to recover the Eclipse Seals. The player fights enemies, completes realm-specific objectives, collects weapons, recruits companions, and confronts multi-phase bosses. Each companion has a distinct personality, ability, tactical role, trust level, and independent motivation. Through WebMCP, an external agent can: Inspect the live battlefield and fellowship state Understand health, enemies, inventory, objectives, pressure mechanics, and boss phases Explain the next valid quest action Recommend companion abilities and battle strategies Issue reversible tactical commands Propose coordinated party plans for the player to approve Agent actions appear in a visible activity feed, keeping the collaboration understandable and accountable. How we built it We built Storyforge with React, TypeScript, Vite, Zustand, and a deterministic TypeScript game engine. The WorldEngine is the canonical source of truth for combat, quests, inventory, companions, relationships, and campaign progression. Both the React interface and WebMCP tools operate on this same state. The game registers typed, JSON-schema-based WebMCP tools through document.modelContext or navigator.modelContext . Read tools expose purpose-built views of the battlefield and fellowship. Action tools pass validated commands into the engine rather than manipulating the interface or inventing results. Consequential agent actions create visible proposals that the player can accept or reject. Activity is persisted locally, and the project includes automated tests for combat, quest progression, companion behavior, and WebMCP integration. Challenges we ran into The hardest challenge was making agents useful without allowing them to bypass the game. Early versions made companions feel cosmetic because the player could complete most objectives alone. We redesigned the campaign around companion-specific abilities, recruitment trials, trust, pressure mechanics, coordinated attacks, and independent initiatives. We also had to keep agent reasoning grounded. Instead of asking an agent to interpret pixels, we exposed structured battlefield state and enforced every action through the game engine. Another challenge was browser compatibility. WebMCP, browser speech synthesis, microphone access, and deployment environments expose different capabilities. We added feature detection, captions, typed-command fallbacks, visible status indicators, and a Chrome Origin Trial token. Finally, presenting a large game world alongside combat information, party controls, dialogue, recommendations, and agent activity required several UI redesigns to prevent overlapping panels. Accomplishments that we're proud of We are proud that WebMCP is part of the actual gameplay rather than a decorative chatbot. The agent sees the same canonical state that drives combat and can affect the encounter through real, constrained tools. At the same time, the player retains authority over movement, major plans, and consequential changes. We are also proud of the fellowship system. Companions persist across realms, fight alongside the player, develop trust, unlock combinations, offer contextual advice, and sometimes leave to pursue opportunities based on their own priorities. The result is a complete five-stage campaign with distinct environments, collectible equipment, recruitment challenges, escalating realm mechanics, multi-phase bosses, persistent progression, remappable controls, and a visible human-agent collaboration history. What we learned We learned that believable agentic gameplay depends more on constraints and consequences than unlimited freedom. Agents feel intelligent when they receive accurate context, understand what is currently possible, and make decisions that visibly affect the world. Giving an agent unrestricted control would have made the game less coherent and less enjoyable. We also learned that transparency improves trust. Showing tool calls, recommendations, proposals, and outcomes makes the agent feel like a teammate whose reasoning can be understood—not an invisible system changing the game behind the scenes. Most importantly, AI companions become compelling when they have specialized capabilities, incomplete information, relationships, and motivations of their own. What's next for Storyforge Next, we want to deepen the social and strategic side of the fellowship: Dynamic voice generation with a distinct voice for every companion and boss Longer companion memory and relationships shaped by player decisions Procedurally generated quests grounded in persistent world rules More companion disagreements, personal missions, and conflicting priorities Drop-in cooperative play between human and agent-controlled party members Additional realms, weapons, enemies, and branching endings Improved tactical planning with environmental interactions and party formations Shareable campaign histories that preserve every important human-agent decision Our long-term goal is for every Storyforge adventure to feel like playing with a group of friends who understand the world, surprise you, and help create a story none of you could have produced alone. title: Cursus
pitch: A course planner whose tools refuse, say what a choice closes off two years before it bites, and hold a limit you set against the agent — including when you are the one asking.
about_excerpt: A course planner whose tools refuse, say what a choice closes off two years before it bites, and hold a limit you set against the agent — including when you are the one asking. Like Comment Story Updates Fourteen courses, put there by hand. Term 3 has six credits left, and the page has registered its thirteen tools with the browser. The student asks in their own words, naming no tool: what are my options, and what does each one cost? Both futures in one call. Either choice closes a specialisation — the slot is what costs, not the course. The student draws a line. Anything that would close Graphics is refused from now on, including if they ask for it themselves. A lock beside the track, and a line naming who it binds. Every other rule here belongs to the university. This one belongs to the student. The agent asks for NUM-201. The page refuses, citing the student's own instruction, and names both ways out. The refusal comes back as prose, so the agent reports it rather than retrying. Nothing instructed it to. Every call is an event and the plan is their reduction, so undo is replaying fewer of them. The protection unwinds with the rest. Each description says when to reach for it. That string is the only thing a model has to choose on, so the strings are the product. registerAll, on document.modelContext. No build step, no dependencies, no server: what is in the repository is what is served. The page counts calls by origin and states plainly that it cannot verify the second number. WebMCP gives the handler no caller identity. Apache-2.0, thirteen tools on document.modelContext, and no server behind any of it. Eleven files, no build step and no dependencies. Every import points downward, which is the whole reason the layering is worth drawing. Every tool call is an event, and the plan is their reduction. Refusing, undoing and auditing all fall out of that. Both environments named in the challenge rules, and both make real tool calls. The problem, and who has it A student picks four courses for their third term because those are the ones that fit. Two years later a specialisation they wanted is out of reach — not because anything refused them, but because the one course it needed runs in a single term, and that term filled up. No warning appeared. The cost landed twenty-one months after the decision, and by then it was not a decision any more. An adviser can work this out with the handbook open and twenty minutes. Most students never think to ask, and most advisers have more students than twenty-minute slots. So the calculation that decides which doors stay open is the one nobody performs — not because it is hard to explain, but because it has to be redone from scratch whenever anything changes. A timetable shows what you picked. That is all any timetable shows. What Cursus does Thirteen tools, registered with document.modelContext.registerTool , that do six things a rendered timetable cannot. They refuse. Ask an agent to enrol you in Advanced Calculus and the page says no — naming the missing prerequisites and, crucially, what would unblock them. That last clause changes the agent's behaviour: it stops reporting a failure and starts proposing a fix. In our first end-to-end test it went further and asked permission before applying it. Nothing instructed it to. They answer what the screen cannot. what_this_closes is forward reachability over the prerequisite graph under a credit budget. With terms 1–2 full and six credits left in term 3: Taking NUM-201 closes Graphics and Animation — GEOM-201 only ever runs in term 3, and the term is now full Taking GEOM-201 closes Data and Machine Learning — NUM-201 is required for ML-202 and everything after One slot, two futures, and either choice forecloses the other. They price the way out. Asked whether a specialisation is still possible, the page does not answer "no". It names the blocking course, the rule that stops it, and every way to make room — with what each one costs. In that fixture there are five ways, and every one of them closes another specialisation. They can be undone. Every tool call is an event and the plan is the reduction of those events, so rewinding is the same reducer with a smaller number rather than per-tool inverse logic. The timeline on the page is the log with a cursor. And they hold the student's own limits against the agent. This is the one that runs the other way. Every rule above belongs to the university — a prerequisite, a clash, a credit cap, the same for everyone. protect_track belongs to the person: say "whatever else happens, do not close Graphics" and from then on any course that would close it is refused, including when you ask for it yourself an hour later , and the refusal cites your own instruction rather than the handbook. The planner will not even propose a route through it. A tool surface that only exposes capability lets an agent do whatever the UI could do, faster. One that also carries the user's policy lets them say what they will not have done to their plan , and have it hold while they are not watching. It cost almost nothing to build, because a protection is an event like any other — so undo_to unwinds it with everything else, and no code was written to make that true. And this part is not really about courses. Anyone handing work to an agent has the same question: how do I let it act for me without it doing the one thing I would have vetoed? The usual answer is a prompt, and a prompt is a request. A page that carries the user's policy and enforces it structurally is a different answer — the limit lives with the state it protects, survives the conversation that set it, and applies to whoever asks next, including the same person in a hurry. Course planning is where we could demonstrate it. It is not where it stops. And they can be handed to someone else. share_plan returns a link, and there is no server behind it: the link carries the actions. What makes that more than a persistence trick is what happens when it is opened — every action is replayed through the same tools , so a link edited by hand cannot produce a plan the page would have refused to build, and anything the rules reject is named rather than quietly dropped. The rules are the gate on the way in as well as the way through, because there is no second path into the state. Why this fits WebMCP rather than an API Three reasons, and they are properties of the standard rather than of this domain. The tools act in the user's own session, on the page they are looking at , with no key to provision and no account to link. The plan is theirs, in their tab, and they watch it change. The tools are things the DOM cannot do . If an agent could get the same answer by reading the page and clicking, the tool surface adds nothing. Reachability under a budget is not on the screen. And the interface is prose . execute returns a string the model reads, so the strings are the product. That is why every mutation returns the resulting plan instead of ok — otherwise the agent's picture of the state silently drifts from the page's — and why every refusal carries a remedy. What people and agents can do together here that was hard before A student could always ask an adviser "what am I giving up if I take this?" and an adviser could always work it out, slowly, with the handbook open. What was not possible was asking the page , in the middle of choosing, and having it answer with a number instead of a shrug. And the direction that matters is the other one: the page can say no to the agent, in a way the agent can act on. A tool that refuses with a remedy turns an agent from something that either succeeds or fails into something that negotiates — it repairs the situation and, in our tests, asks before committing. That behaviour was not prompted. It came from the shape of the refusal. Where it was tested Both of the environments named in the challenge rules were tested, and both make real tool calls. Chrome 149+ with the WebMCP flag and the Inspector extension: an agent chose the tool on its own, was refused, and proposed the fix. That is the gate in docs/GATE.md , and it has no plan, mode or workspace conditions. ChatGPT's in-app browser : the page registers its tools and a model calls them — in Work mode . Outside it, four different phrasings produced no call at all, and confident answers read off our own README instead. Finding that out took an afternoon and is written up in docs/CHATGPT-WORK-MODE.md , including the part a judge most needs: site tools are not available in Enterprise or Edu workspaces , no setting changes it, and nothing on screen says so. On those, use Chrome. The video is recorded in ChatGPT's in-app browser , because that is the environment the rules name first and the one most judges will reach for. How it is built No build step, no dependencies, no server. Plain ES modules on GitHub Pages: what is in the repository is what is served. The rules allow any provider, and with nothing to compile

title: OpenPath Studio
pitch: People set the learning goal. Agents weave the open web into a transparent, editable path.
about_excerpt: People set the learning goal. Agents weave the open web into a transparent, editable path. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Project The problem The open web contains excellent learning resources, but turning them into a realistic learning path is fragmented work. A learner or teacher must search across sites, compare formats and levels, inspect reuse terms, calculate a time budget, choose an order, and keep the plan current. A conventional browser agent can click through that workflow, but it has to infer meaning from visual controls and repeatedly reconstruct the page's state. Why WebMCP is the right fit OpenPath Studio makes the website's learning-planning capabilities explicit. Its WebMCP tools let an agent read the current goal, search a structured catalog, compare resources using stable IDs, build a time-bounded draft, add or remove items, reorder the path, mark progress, and export the result. The agent operates on the same client-side state and interface the person sees, so it never bypasses the product experience. WebMCP is not an API wrapper added for the challenge. It is the interaction model that makes the collaboration reliable. Schemas remove ambiguity, tool outputs keep context compact, read-only annotations distinguish discovery from action, and the activity ledger makes every state change visible. A better human experience The person still leads. They define the topic, level, schedule, and preferences. The agent handles catalog search, comparison, sequencing, and repetitive edits. Every recommendation includes its source, provider, duration, level, format, URL, and license metadata. The draft remains fully editable with human controls, and it works without an agent as a progressive enhancement. Publishing demonstrates a deliberate trust boundary. The agent can activate and prepare an annotated HTML form, but the form does not use toolautosubmit . A person must visibly review the title and learner, then click Publish. No data leaves the browser in this prototype. What people and agents can now do together Before WebMCP, an agent had to scrape filters, guess at card actions, and infer an ordered plan from the DOM. OpenPath lets the human state a goal in natural language while the agent composes multiple reliable domain actions against live browser state. The result appears immediately in the same interface for inspection and correction. The human contributes judgment and consent; the agent contributes speed, consistency, and structured comparison. Example collaboration: “Build me a 5-day beginner path on web accessibility with 30 minutes per day.” The agent calls build_learning_path with explicit constraints. The person reviews the visible draft and asks for a practical checklist. The agent searches, adds the resource by stable ID, and moves it to position two. The person marks progress or changes the sequence manually. The agent prepares publication and waits for human confirmation. How WebMCP was implemented OpenPath registers 11 imperative tools through document.modelContext.registerTool() and exposes one declarative publish_learning_path form. The prepare_publish_review imperative tool provides a cross-client bridge that opens and optionally prefills the same visible checkpoint but can never submit it. JSON Schemas validate inputs. Read-only and untrusted-content annotations communicate tool safety. Tool output stays concise. An AbortController manages registration lifecycle, and the site sends origin-isolation and tools permission headers. Both agent and human actions reuse the same state layer and are recorded in a visible activity ledger. The app is built with Next.js and React, has no external runtime dependencies beyond the framework, needs no account or API key, and stores its workspace locally. It is responsive, keyboard accessible, reduced-motion aware, and fully functional in manual mode. title: Agentic Sandbox
pitch: A deterministic factory decision lab where a human and a WebMCP browser agent safely replan the same live system together.
about_excerpt: A deterministic factory decision lab where a human and a WebMCP browser agent safely replan the same live system together. Like Comment Story Updates Current post-lock recovery with human Packaging lock, stale-write rejection, and receipt-backed evidence. Six narrow WebMCP Site Tools discovered in the live host. Scenario comparison: same output, cheaper standard-supplier plan passes the cost cap. Deterministic lock-bound proof: 9,252 < 10,937 under the human Packaging lock. The problem Factory planning decisions rarely happen in one place. They move through dashboards, spreadsheets, a simulation specialist, and an approval meeting, and each handoff loses context and authority. A generic assistant can make that worse by recommending a control that an operator has just taken off the table. What it does Agentic Sandbox makes the website itself the shared, inspectable decision surface. It is a deterministic factory decision lab where a human and a browser agent plan against the same versioned state. The demo mission is concrete: increase good output by at least 20%, keep total cost within 8% of baseline, add no machine, and do not increase defects. The agent reads the line, creates two bounded hypotheses, simulates a 16-hour shift, and compares immutable receipts. Scenario A reaches 11,114 good units but costs €47,670.51 and fails the cost cap. Scenario B reaches the same 11,114 units for €45,170.51 and passes all four constraints. Then comes the important moment: while the agent is working, the human locks Packaging. That click advances the factory revision and makes earlier evidence historical. The agent’s next write still carries the old revision, so it fails atomically with STALE_FACTORY ; nothing is applied or silently rebased. The agent re-reads the authority state, replans with only controls that remain available, and receives an auditable answer: under the Packaging lock, at most 9,252 good units are possible while the mission requires 10,937. The target is proven infeasible by deterministic evidence, not by model prose. That safe disagreement is the product. The human can change the admissible action space without restarting the conversation, and the agent can recover without overriding the new rule. Why WebMCP is essential Without WebMCP, the agent would have to infer state from pixels and click by coordinates, or the product would need a separate chatbot and backend with a second source of truth. Instead, the page exposes exactly six narrow Site Tools through document.modelContext.registerTool : get_factory_snapshot get_scenario_snapshot create_scenario apply_scenario_changes run_factory_simulation compare_simulation_runs The human interface and these tools share one application-owned command bus. Schemas are closed, handlers validate independently, and every mutation carries a request ID plus expected factory, scenario, and lock revisions. There is deliberately no agent-accessible lock, unlock, force, arbitrary patch, optimizer, ERP, PLC, SCADA, or machine-control tool. Human authority stays human. How it was built Agentic Sandbox is a self-contained React 19 + TypeScript + Vite app deployed on Vercel. The deterministic engine models 64 fixed ticks, uses integer/fixed-point arithmetic, and computes production, defects, energy, cost, constraints, invariants, and bottleneck evidence in the page. Each simulation creates an immutable, content-addressed SHA-256 receipt with exact operands, accepted/rejected operations, tick-level state, and an optional lock-bound proof. No displayed KPI comes from the language model. The hardest implementation problem was making a mid-plan disagreement trustworthy rather than dramatic: old authority must fail closed without erasing evidence that was valid when created. That required explicit revision precedence, atomic stale-write rejection, immutable receipts, and visible current-versus-historical states. The submitted flow was replayed against the public deployment in a supported WebMCP host, including discovery, comparison, the human lock, stale rejection, re-read, replan, and proof. What I learned WebMCP is most useful when a website already owns meaningful state, rules, and actions. Exposing those capabilities directly is more reliable than asking an agent to reconstruct them from pixels. A refusal can be more valuable than another recommendation: STALE_FACTORY proves that human authority survived concurrency, and 9252 < 10937 proves why the target cannot be met under the active lock. Potential impact and what’s next The first users I have in mind are plant planners, industrial engineers, and continuous-improvement teams working on line balancing, shift planning, and supplier what-if analysis. A production version could connect this exact capability, revision, lock, and receipt pattern to a validated digital twin, while ERP, PLC, SCADA, purchase, and physical-machine changes remain behind existing approvals. The broader pattern applies to any high-consequence planning interface: expose narrow capabilities, bind actions to explicit versions, preserve the human veto, and return evidence a machine can check. video_transcript_excerpt: Factory planning moves across dashboards, spreadsheets, specialists, and approval meetings. A Gent Sandbox brings it into one shared versioned decision space for a plant planner and a browser agent. The mission is concrete. Increase good output by 20%, keep extra cost below 8%, add no machine, and do not increase defects. The page exposes exactly six narrow WebMCP tools over the same command path as the interface. They read state, create planning branches, apply bounded settings, run the deterministic simulator, and compare stored receipts. No DOM guessing, separate chatbot state, or agent-only shadow model. The agent reads the factory, creates two one-shift hypotheses, applies explicit settings, simulates both, and compares their evidence. Both scenarios reach 11,114 good units. Scenario A uses an expedited supplier, but the premium adds no output and breaks the cost cap. Scenario B uses the standard supplier and passes all four constraints. It is the best evaluated option under this policy, not a claim of global optimality. Every number comes from a simulator receipt, never from Model Pros. Then the human changes the rules. I lock packaging directly in the product. The factory and a factory revisions advance. Earlier evidence remains visible as auditable history, but it is no longer current. The agent intentionally retries its old scenario B right with the revisions it held before my intervention. A Gent Sandbox rejects the batch atomically with stale factory. No operational or scenario state is changed. After a fresh read, the capability map is explicit. Mixer, quality gate, and warehouse are available. Packaging is human locked. Supplier is phase closed. The agent creates a clean post lock branch and changes only available controls. The new receipt shows 9,114 good units, below the required 10,937. More importantly, the deterministic engine proves a conservative upper bound. 9,252 is less than 10,937. The target is proven infeasible under the current human constraint. The decision packet preserves the mission, human authority, revisions, receipt hashes, constraints, comparison claim, and proof. This is the agent native web. The human can change authority at any moment. The agent uses explicit browser native capabilities. Deterministic software owns the evidence, and both inspect the same state. Same page, clear authority, shared proof.

title: Quorum
pitch: Scheduling, negotiated by your agent — approved by you. Humans and AI agents vote, counter-propose, and converge on a meeting time together via WebMCP, with every agent action visibly logged.
about_excerpt: Scheduling, negotiated by your agent — approved by you. Humans and AI agents vote, counter-propose, and converge on a meeting time together via WebMCP, with every agent action visibly logged. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Group scheduling is a negotiation over everyone's constraints - and it's still done by making humans click checkboxes in polls. When WebMCP launched, we realized the missing piece was never a smarter poll: it was letting each person's AI agent join the negotiation itself . Quorum is our answer: scheduling, negotiated by your agent - approved by you. What it does Quorum is a meeting scheduler where humans and agents are equal participants in the same live session. Humans get a normal UI: candidate times, yes/maybe/no voting, counter-proposals. Agents get seven WebMCP tools registered by the page itself - they can read the event state, join on their human's behalf, vote with reasons, counter-propose new times, and rank the slots. Every action lands in a shared negotiation log tagged HUMAN or AGENT , and only the human organizer can accept proposals or lock in the final time. Agent proposes; human approves. Why this is a strong fit for WebMCP Scheduling is a multi-step, stateful interaction - exactly where screen-scraping agents fail. With WebMCP, the page tells agents what's possible via typed, self-describing tools. In testing, an agent that had never seen the app correctly chained four tools on the first try (read state -> join -> vote with a conflict note -> report the winner) purely from the tool descriptions. What people and agents can do together that wasn't possible before A mixed negotiation - some parties human, some agents - on the same page, in real time, with full mutual visibility. Before WebMCP, agents couldn't reliably operate voting UIs built for humans, and sites had no way to declare what actions they support. Quorum shows the new shape of the open web: agents handle the tedium, the audit trail keeps trust, and humans keep the final word. How we built it Vanilla JS frontend + Express backend, live-synced over server-sent events. Every WebMCP tool executes the same functions the human UI uses , tagged via: "agent" - one code path, one audit trail: document.modelContext.registerTool({ name: "submit_availability", description: "Submit availability for candidate slots on behalf of your user…", inputSchema: { type: "object", properties: { responses: { type: "array" } }, required: ["responses"] }, execute: async ({ responses }) => submitAvailability(responses, "agent"), }); Deployed on Vercel; Upstash Redis keeps event state consistent across serverless instances, with a per-stream Redis poll so every open tab stays live. The visual design was created in Claude Design and implemented as a hand-written design system. Challenges we ran into - Serverless broke our state. Events lived in memory; on Vercel, an SSE stream landed on a different instance and couldn't find the event. We added a storage layer (Upstash Redis in production, in-memory locally) and cross-instance live updates via polling. - The WebMCP API surface is still moving (document.modelContext vs the earlier navigator.modelContext), so we wrote a small adapter that registers against whichever exists. - Tool descriptions are prompts. Agents chained our tools correctly only after we rewrote descriptions to say when to call each tool and what to fetch first. Accomplishments that we're proud of - **A never-before-seen agent used our app correctly on the first try.** In our final test, a Gemini-backed agent autonomously chained four tools - read the event state, joined as a new participant, voted with a conflict note attached to the right slot, and reported the winning time - guided by nothing but our tool descriptions. That's the whole WebMCP promise, working. - **One code path for humans and agents.** Every WebMCP tool executes the exact same functions the human UI calls - so the audit log, validation, and permissions are identical no matter who acts. No parallel "agent API" to drift out of sync. - **Trust as a first-class feature.** The negotiation log tags every action HUMAN or AGENT in real time, organizer-only tools are genuinely scoped, and an agent can never finalize a meeting on its own. - **A one-click seeded demo event**, so any judge can see a mid-negotiation session - votes, an agent counter-proposal, a live log - in under ten seconds, then take over as the organizer. - **Shipping the full journey in days**: idea -> working local app -> designed UI -> deployed on Vercel with Redis-backed state that survives serverless cold starts. What we learned - **Tool descriptions are prompts.** Agents started chaining our tools correctly only after we rewrote descriptions to say *when* to call each tool and what to fetch first ("Call this first to understand the current state"). Designing for a model reader is a real skill, and WebMCP makes it part of frontend work. - **The trust problem matters more than the automation problem.** The feature people react to isn't that agents can vote — it's seeing exactly what an agent did on your behalf, and knowing the final decision always needs a human. - **Serverless changes your assumptions.** Our in-memory state worked perfectly until the first live SSE request landed on a different instance. Moving to Redis-backed storage with cross-instance live updates taught us to design for "any request, any instance" from the start. - **Build for a moving standard defensively.** WebMCP's surface has shifted between Chrome previews (`document.modelContext` vs `navigator.modelContext`), so a small adapter layer saved us from breaking on every browser update. What's next for Quorum - **Calendar integration**, so your agent votes from your real availability instead of being told your constraints. - **Agent-to-agent negotiation rounds** - agents exchange counter-proposals automatically until they converge on a shortlist, and humans only see the final choice to ratify. - **Invites addressed to agents**: send an event link straight to someone's assistant, which handles everything and pings its human only for approval. - **Richer constraints in tools** - recurring meetings, time-zone fairness scoring, and "must attend / optional" roles that agents can reason about.
